q: What is the FCA’s operational objective relating to consumer protection under FSMA?

Principle 3, which requires responsible organisation and control of affairs

Principle 6, which requires responsible organisation and control of affairs

Principle 4
Principle 10
Principle 9

o: The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA)
The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)
The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA)
The Bank of England's financial policy arm
The Pensions Ombudsman service (PO)
w: The Competition and Markets Authority became responsible for enforcing unfair contract terms after the OFT was abolished.

n.2: The PRA is a prudential regulator, not the OFT's successor.
n.3: The Bank of England did not take over the OFT's consumer role.

q: What remedy does the CRA provide if digital content supplied is faulty?

An automatic increase in the consumer's pension
An exemption from the operation of competition law
A referral of the dispute to compulsory arbitration
A right to repair, replacement or a price reduction
w: Consumers have the right to repair, replacement, or a price reduction if digital content provided under contract is faulty.

n.3: The CRA does not force disputes into compulsory arbitration.
n.0: No tax rebate arises from faulty digital content.
n.2: Competition law exemptions are not a consumer remedy.

q: Which principle guides transparency under the CRA 2015?
o: Only orally agreed contracts are treated as valid
All contracts must first be approved by HM Treasury
Every term must be individually negotiated with the consumer
Terms must be plain, intelligible and prominent to the consumer
Contracts must be registered with Companies House
w: The CRA requires contract terms to be transparent—plain, intelligible, and prominent—so consumers can understand their effect.

n.2: The CRA does not require every term to be individually negotiated.
n.1: HM Treasury does not approve consumer contracts.
n.0: Written contracts are valid; the CRA does not require oral ones.
n.4: No Companies House registration is required for consumer contracts.

q: What happens if a term is deemed unfair under the CRA 2015?
o: It voids the entire contract automatically
It requires referral to the Supreme Court
It mandates repayment of all previous contracts
It is not binding on the consumer
It triggers criminal liability for the trader
w: An unfair term is not binding on the consumer, although the remainder of the contract can still be enforced if workable.

n.0: The whole contract is not automatically voided.
n.1: Cases do not go straight to the Supreme Court.
n.4: Unfair terms are not criminal offences under CRA.
n.2: The CRA applies per contract, not retroactively to all agreements.

q: Which phrase best summarises the impact of the CRA 2015?
o: It created the UK's regime for merger control
It set the country's official interest rate policy
It introduced new occupational pension funding rules
It overhauled the prudential supervision of banks
It modernised and consolidated UK consumer protection law
w: The CRA 2015 modernised consumer protection by consolidating previous law, addressing digital content, and clarifying unfair terms provisions.

n.2: The CRA did not create pension funding rules.
n.3: Bank supervision is a PRA matter, not the CRA's effect.
n.0: Merger control is competition law, not the CRA's.

q: What is the main role of The Pensions Regulator in relation to occupational pension schemes?

To protect members' benefits and promote good scheme administration
To collect income tax from pension scheme members
To issue government bonds and manage public borrowing
To enforce UK competition law against merging firms

n.0: Consumer complaints are the FOS's function, not TPR's.

q: Which schemes fall under The Pensions Regulator’s remit?
o: Retail bank deposit and current accounts
Workplace occupational pension schemes, both DB and DC
Consumer credit and personal loan agreements
Individuals' personal ISAs and share dealing accounts
General insurance policies sold to consumers
w: TPR oversees occupational pension schemes, including defined benefit and defined contribution workplace pensions.

n.0: Bank deposits fall under the PRA and FCA, not TPR.
n.4: Insurance policies are regulated by the FCA/PRA, not TPR.
n.2: Consumer credit is an FCA matter, not within TPR's remit.

q: Which power does The Pensions Regulator hold over scheme trustees?

n.3: Tax penalties are imposed by HMRC, not TPR.
n.0: Merger approval is a CMA function, not TPR's.
n.1: Insurer solvency rules are set by the PRA, not TPR.

q: What funding-related rules does TPR oversee?

Defined benefit scheme funding and deficit recovery plans
The caps imposed on companies' dividend payments
The maximum limits placed on consumer lending
The capital adequacy requirements applied to banks
w: TPR ensures defined benefit schemes are properly funded, requiring recovery plans where deficits exist, to safeguard member benefits.

n.4: Bank capital adequacy is set by the PRA, not TPR.
n.3: Consumer lending limits are an FCA matter, not TPR's.
n.2: TPR does not cap company dividend payments.

q: What is the objective of TPR’s governance requirements?
o: To regulate and approve corporate merger activity
To handle and resolve individual consumer complaints
To ensure trustees act in the best interests of members
To supervise the pricing of consumer insurance policies
To set the rates of corporation tax that firms pay
w: TPR sets governance standards requiring trustees to act prudently, honestly, and in the best interests of pension scheme members.

n.0: Merger control is the CMA's role, not TPR's.
n.3: Insurance supervision is an FCA/PRA matter, not TPR's.
n.1: Consumer complaints are resolved by the FOS, not TPR.

Reporting the amount of corporation tax the scheme has paid
Filing periodic reports on the conduct of monetary policy
Disclosing the outcomes of competition law investigations

q: How does TPR reduce risks to the Pension Protection Fund?

By regulating how insurers underwrite their policies
By setting the minimum capital ratios that banks hold
By supervising the conduct of consumer credit lenders
By collecting additional tax contributions from employers
w: TPR enforces funding and governance rules for occupational schemes, reducing the risk of schemes collapsing and passing liabilities to the PPF.

n.3: Consumer credit supervision is an FCA role, not TPR's.
n.2: Bank capital ratios are set by the PRA, not TPR.
n.1: Insurance underwriting is regulated by the FCA/PRA, not TPR.

q: What criminal powers were given to TPR under the Pension Schemes Act 2021?

Power to set the Bank of England's base interest rate
Power to authorise and supervise retail banks
Power to regulate the fairness of consumer contracts
Power to prosecute reckless or wilful conduct harming a scheme
w: The 2021 Act strengthened TPR’s powers, allowing it to bring criminal prosecutions against those who recklessly or wilfully endanger pension schemes.

n.3: Consumer contract fairness is a CMA/FCA matter, not TPR's.
n.0: Tax enforcement is HMRC's role, not TPR's.

Tax compliance
Client focus
Corporate governance
Monetary policy

q: What remedy may a court provide regarding an unenforceable FSMA agreement?
o: A requirement for shareholders to approve the deal
Automatic validation of the unenforceable agreement

q: When might an unauthorised firm still benefit from an unenforceable agreement?
o: If both parties agree to continue
If an auditor confirms fair value
If the FCA issues a temporary waiver
If the court allows restitution
If the firm registers with Companies House

n.2: The FCA cannot waive statutory unenforceability provisions.
n.0: Consent does not cure statutory unenforceability.
n.4: Companies House registration does not affect FSMA enforceability rules.
n.1: Auditor confirmation cannot override statutory provisions of FSMA.

q: How does unenforceability affect consumers contracting with unauthorised businesses?
o: It cancels any FSCS protection the consumer would have

It lets the unauthorised firm enforce the contract in court
It requires the consumer to repay any money already received
It protects the consumer from being sued on the agreement
w: Consumers cannot be sued on unenforceable agreements, giving them statutory protection against unauthorised firms.

n.3: The consumer can recover money and compensation, not repay it, under FSMA.
n.1: Unenforceability does not affect Ombudsman eligibility.
n.0: Unenforceability does not remove FSCS protection.

q: Which contracts are most at risk of being unenforceable under FSMA?

Contracts of carriage covering the transport of goods

n.2: Employment contracts are outside the FSMA regulated-activity regime.
n.0: Directors' service contracts are governed by company law, not FSMA enforceability.
n.4: Carriage of goods contracts are unconnected to regulated activities.

By checking the firm's authorisation on the FCA register

o: The court imposes only a civil fine

n.4: It does not aim to reduce retail investor numbers.

q: Which defence is available to a person accused of unauthorised regulated activity under FSMA?

n.3: Holding a bank account is irrelevant to a FSMA defence.
n.0: Filing tax returns has no bearing on regulated-activity offences.

When the accused genuinely believed no authorisation was required

n.0: Market position does not establish a defence.

q: What must firms appoint under SYSC 18.4.4?

q: What is the current legal status of the UK Market Abuse Regulation (MAR) following the UK’s exit from the EU?
o: A regime fully replaced by the Criminal Justice Act 1993 in 2020

A regime applying only to instruments traded on EU venues
An EU regulation still administered by ESMA for UK trading venues
An onshored UK regime, amended for EU exit and supervised by the FCA
w: Post-Brexit, the UK retained MAR by onshoring it into domestic law and amending it via The Market Abuse (Amendment) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019. The FCA is responsible for supervision and enforcement in the UK. This ensures continuity of the substantive framework while allowing UK-specific amendments over time.

n.3: MAR was onshored into UK law; ESMA no longer administers it for the UK
n.1: UK MAR is directly enforceable by the FCA, not mere guidance
n.0: MAR was retained, not replaced by the CJA 1993, which is a criminal statute
n.2: UK MAR applies to UK venues and instruments, not only EU venues

q: Which behaviours are within the scope of UK MAR’s market abuse framework?
o: Mis-selling, unfair contract terms, and pension liberation

Fraud, money laundering, and the financing of terrorism
Insider dealing, unlawful disclosure, and market manipulation
w: UK MAR targets three core behaviours: dealing on the basis of inside information, unlawfully disclosing such information, and manipulating markets (e.g., spoofing, disseminating false signals). These behaviours undermine market integrity and investor confidence.

n.3: These are financial-crime offences under POCA and terrorism law, not MAR
n.1: Bribery and tax evasion fall under other statutes, not the MAR framework
n.0: These are conduct and consumer matters governed by COBS, not MAR
n.2: Competition matters fall to the CMA; MAR covers abuse of markets

q: For information to qualify as ‘inside information’ under UK MAR, which combination of attributes is required?
o: Contained in an issuer's audited financial statements before they are signed off

Concerning scheduled macroeconomic data due to be released by a government body
Precise, publicly disclosed, and prepared by a firm's authorised investment analyst
Precise, non-public, related to an issuer or instruments, and likely to move the price significantly

n.3: Inside information must be non-public; once publicly disclosed it is no longer inside information.
n.1: Inside information must be precise; imprecise or speculative material does not qualify.
n.0: Being in draft accounts does not by itself make information inside information under the MAR test.
n.2: Routine scheduled macroeconomic releases are not, of themselves, inside information about an issuer.

n.2: Issuers need not file a STOR for ordinary price movements
n.0: Journalists have no STOR duty; it rests with market intermediaries

n.1: Delisting involves the trading venue and listing authority processes, not an automatic FCA sanction for market abuse.
n.2: The FCA regularly imposes financial penalties where appropriate; it is not limited to private warnings.
n.0: Citizenship is outside the FCA’s sanctioning powers.

n.3: The Companies Act focuses on company law and reporting, not the insider dealing offence.
n.1: POCA deals with money laundering and confiscation, not the creation of insider dealing offences.

n.4: Post-announcement information is public, so sharing it is not disclosure

n.1: Due diligence before a placing is legitimate, not manipulative
n.4: Seeking best execution via a smart router is a lawful practice

n.0: Properly caveated forward-looking guidance is lawful.
n.4: Correctly holding client money is compliant, not an offence.

n.4: Self-reporting alone is not an adequate surveillance control.
n.0: A client newsletter is not a market-abuse detection control.
n.3: Cross-venue activity must be monitored; excluding it creates blind spots.

q: Which statement best distinguishes the civil market abuse regime from the criminal insider dealing regime in the UK?
o: The criminal regime applies the balance of probabilities standard and results only in prohibition notices.
Both regimes require proof beyond reasonable doubt and can result only in fines.
The civil regime applies the balance of probabilities standard and can result in unlimited fines and public censure.
The criminal regime is limited to behaviour on regulated markets while the civil regime covers only unregulated venues.
The civil regime requires proof beyond reasonable doubt and can result in imprisonment.
w: The civil market abuse regime (FCA MAR/FSMA s.123) is pursued by the FCA using the civil standard of proof (balance of probabilities). Sanctions include unlimited financial penalties, public censure, and prohibitions. The criminal regime (CJA 1993 Part V and Financial Services Act 2012 ss.89–91) requires the criminal standard (beyond reasonable doubt) and can lead to imprisonment and/or fines.

n.1: Criminal cases require proof beyond reasonable doubt; the civil regime does not. Civil penalties are not limited to fines alone.
n.4: The civil regime does not use the criminal standard and cannot impose imprisonment; imprisonment arises only in criminal proceedings.
n.0: The criminal regime uses the criminal standard of proof and can include imprisonment; prohibition notices can also arise from civil/regulatory action.
n.3: Venue distinctions are not that narrow. Both regimes can capture behaviour across a range of venues depending on the instrument and conduct.

q: Under the FCA’s Decision Procedure and Penalties manual (DEPP 6), which of the following is one of the core steps in calculating a financial penalty for market abuse?

Offset the penalty fully against future remediation spend.
Apply a fixed statutory percentage of firm revenue.
Multiply the daily value at risk (VaR) by a fixed factor.
Cap the penalty at the higher of £1 million or 10% of turnover.
w: DEPP 6 sets out a structured, step-based approach. One of the initial steps is disgorgement of any financial benefit gained from the misconduct, followed by assessing seriousness, factoring aggravating/mitigating elements, adjusting for deterrence, and applying any settlement discount.

n.2: DEPP 6 does not rely on a single fixed statutory percentage of revenue; it uses a multi-step framework keyed to seriousness and benefit.
n.3: VaR is not a prescribed input in DEPP 6’s penalty steps.
n.4: There is no universal statutory cap in DEPP 6 of this form; penalties can be unlimited in serious cases.
n.1: Remediation spend does not provide a full offset; it may mitigate but does not eliminate penalties.

q: Which behaviour falls within the criminal offences introduced by the Financial Services Act 2012 (Sections 89–91)?

Failing to keep an insider list of all employees with access to confidential firm information
Making a false or misleading statement intending to induce another person to deal

n.3: An incomplete insider list is a systems failing, not one of the s.89-91 criminal offences.
n.1: Late internal notification of a PA deal is a conduct breach, not a s.89-91 offence.
n.0: Stabilisation within the permitted period is expressly lawful, not an offence.
n.2: Early publication of a report is not among the s.89-91 misleading-statement offences.

q: Which of the following accurately describes offences under Part V of the Criminal Justice Act 1993 (insider dealing)?

n.4: Encouraging another to deal is specifically captured under the CJA 1993.
n.2: Territorial application is nuanced; conduct with a UK nexus can still be within scope.
n.0: Mere possession without dealing, disclosure, or encouragement does not in itself complete the criminal offence.
n.3: These are criminal offences; enforcement can involve prosecution and imprisonment, not only civil penalties.

q: A case involving suspected insider dealing and offences under the Financial Services Act 2012 is being escalated for prosecution. Under FSMA s.402, which body is empowered to institute criminal proceedings?

n.1: The CMA focuses on competition matters, not prosecutions for insider dealing or FS Act 2012 offences.
n.4: The exchange is not the criminal prosecuting body for these offences.

q: The FCA decides to pursue a market abuse matter through the civil regime rather than criminal prosecution. Which outcome is available under the civil regime but is not a criminal sentence?

n.1: A criminal record results from conviction, not from a civil market abuse finding.
n.4: Confiscation orders are tied to criminal convictions and proceeds of crime frameworks.
n.2: Community sentences are criminal penalties, not civil outcomes.

q: A compliance officer explains the scope of the FCA's civil market abuse regime under MAR 1.1.3. Which categories of behaviour fall within that civil regime?

n.3: The civil regime applies to any person, including individuals, not just firms

q: A trainee is learning which sanctions attach to which market abuse regime. Which pairing correctly matches a regime with a sanction available under it?

Civil market abuse — criminal record

w: Civil market abuse outcomes include public censure, financial penalties, and prohibitions. Imprisonment and criminal records are consequences of criminal proceedings, not civil action.

n.4: A supervisory visit is a supervisory tool, not a criminal sanction for insider dealing.
n.3: Criminal offences under FS Act 2012 can lead to imprisonment and fines; a private warning alone is not the typical outcome.
n.2: A criminal record arises from conviction, not from a civil market abuse finding.

q: The FCA is weighing whether to pursue criminal prosecution rather than civil action in a market abuse case. Consistent with the Enforcement Guide (EG 12.3), which factor most supports criminal prosecution?
o: The misconduct is especially serious or dishonest, needing deterrence
The case shows minor systems lapses with no personal culpability
Investors have already filed a parallel private civil claim
The behaviour occurred over six years ago with no market impact
The firm has already paid full redress to the affected clients
w: EG 12.3 indicates that, among other factors, seriousness, dishonesty, and the need for general deterrence may justify criminal prosecution rather than civil action.

n.1: Minor lapses without culpability point away from criminal prosecution
n.4: Paying redress does not by itself justify criminal rather than civil action
n.3: Age and lack of impact weigh against pursuing a criminal prosecution
n.2: A private civil claim is not an EG 12.3 factor for choosing criminal action

q: A trader is convicted of insider dealing in the Crown Court under the Criminal Justice Act 1993. What is the maximum custodial sentence typically available for that offence?
o: Five years
Two years
Ten years
Fourteen years
Seven years
w: The CJA 1993 provides for a maximum custodial sentence of up to seven years for insider dealing, alongside the possibility of an unlimited fine.

n.1: The statutory maximum is higher than two years.
n.0: The statutory maximum exceeds five years.
n.2: Ten years is above the typical statutory maximum historically associated with CJA 1993 insider dealing.
n.3: Fourteen years is not the stated maximum for this offence.

q: Which statement best reflects how the civil and criminal regimes interact for market abuse conduct?
o: Civil action becomes available only after a jury has acquitted the defendant in a criminal trial
Only one of the civil or criminal regimes can ever apply to any given set of facts
Once the FCA opens civil action, criminal prosecution of the same conduct is legally barred in every case
The same conduct can engage both regimes, but authorities avoid duplicative punishment
A criminal prosecution must always be concluded before any civil enforcement action can begin
w: Conduct may be addressed under the civil market abuse framework or prosecuted criminally where appropriate. The FCA and prosecuting authorities coordinate to avoid double punishment for the same conduct while choosing the route that best protects market integrity and deters misconduct.

n.2: Civil action does not automatically bar criminal prosecution of the same conduct.
n.4: There is no rule that criminal proceedings must precede civil enforcement.
n.1: The same facts can engage both the civil and criminal regimes.
n.0: Civil action does not depend on a prior criminal acquittal.

q: What criminal legislation specifically governs insider dealing in the UK?
o: Enterprise Act 2002
Fraud Act 2006
Companies Act 2006
Financial Services Act 2012
Criminal Justice Act 1993
w: The Criminal Justice Act 1993 Part V sets out the specific criminal offences for insider dealing in the UK.

n.3: The Financial Services Act 2012 addresses misleading statements and impressions, not the core insider dealing offence.
n.2: The Companies Act 2006 governs corporate governance, not insider dealing offences.
n.1: The Fraud Act 2006 addresses general fraud, not insider trading.
n.0: The Enterprise Act 2002 concerns competition law, not market abuse.

q: A compliance trainee is asked where the civil regime for market abuse is set out in the FCA Handbook. Which provision should she point to?
o: FCA SYSC 6
FCA PRIN 11
FCA DISP 1
FCA COBS 4
FCA MAR 1.1.3

n.3: COBS 4 governs financial promotions, not market abuse
n.2: DISP 1 sets complaint-handling rules, unrelated to market abuse
n.1: PRIN 11 is the principle on regulator dealings, not market abuse

q: Following an investigation, the FCA decides to act against an individual for market abuse using its civil powers rather than pursuing a criminal prosecution. Which sanction is available to it in that route?
o: Maximum five years imprisonment
Disqualification from being a company director
Community service order
Unlimited financial penalty
Revocation of UK citizenship

n.2: Community service orders are criminal penalties, not FCA civil remedies.
n.1: Director disqualification arises under the Companies Act, not FCA civil enforcement.
n.4: Citizenship revocation is unrelated to financial regulation.

q: Under the Financial Services Act 2012, which section deals with misleading impressions of supply or demand?

Section 90
Section 62
Section 92
Section 404

n.4: Section 404 deals with consumer redress schemes, not market abuse.
n.0: Section 118 was repealed when MAR replaced it, so it is not relevant under current law.
n.2: Section 62 does not address misleading market impressions.

q: What is the maximum custodial sentence for insider dealing under the Criminal Justice Act 1993?
o: Ten years
Life imprisonment
Five years
Seven years
Two years
w: The Criminal Justice Act 1993 prescribes a maximum custodial sentence of seven years for insider dealing offences.

n.4: Two years is below the statutory maximum for insider dealing.
n.0: Ten years exceeds the maximum penalty under the Criminal Justice Act 1993.
n.2: Five years is less than the prescribed maximum sentence.
n.1: Life imprisonment is not applicable to insider dealing offences.

q: A compliance trainee researching how the FCA sets fines for market abuse needs the correct manual reference. Which FCA manual section outlines the penalties policy for market abuse?
o: ICOBS 7
DEPP 6
COBS 12
SYSC 3
MCOB 4
w: DEPP 6 sets out the FCA’s policy on imposing penalties for market abuse under FSMA.

n.2: COBS 12 relates to investment research and financial promotions, not penalties.
n.3: SYSC 3 covers systems and controls, not enforcement penalties.
n.4: MCOB 4 concerns mortgage sales, not market abuse sanctions.
n.0: ICOBS 7 deals with insurance communications, not enforcement policy.

q: Which FCA guidance describes how it uses criminal prosecution powers for market abuse?
o: SYSC 4
DISP 3
CASS 7
COCON 2
w: EG 12.3 in the Enforcement Guide sets out the FCA’s use of criminal prosecution for insider dealing and market abuse.

n.0: SYSC 4 covers organisational requirements, not prosecution policy
n.3: COCON 2 sets individual conduct rules, not prosecution guidance
n.1: DISP 3 concerns Ombudsman procedures, not FCA prosecutions
n.2: CASS 7 governs client money, unrelated to prosecution powers

q: The FCA has concluded an investigation and intends to impose a financial penalty on a firm for market abuse. Which FSMA provision empowers it to do so?
o: Section 137A
Section 402
Section 348
Section 166
Section 1B
w: Section 402 FSMA allows the FCA to impose financial penalties for breaches relating to market abuse.

n.0: Section 137A relates to rule-making powers, not penalty imposition.
n.2: Section 348 restricts disclosure of information, not market abuse penalties.
n.3: Section 166 allows skilled person reviews, not the imposition of penalties.
n.4: Section 1B defines the FCA’s objectives, not enforcement powers.

q: Which of the following is a civil, not criminal, outcome of market abuse?
o: A conviction on indictment at Crown Court
Imprisonment imposed in place of a fine
A community order imposed by a court
A financial penalty imposed by the FCA
A custodial sentence of up to seven years
w: Civil outcomes include FCA-imposed financial penalties, unlike criminal outcomes such as imprisonment or conviction.

n.4: A custodial sentence is a criminal, not a civil, outcome
n.2: A community order is a criminal sentence handed down by a court
n.0: A conviction on indictment is a criminal outcome, not civil
n.1: Imprisonment is a criminal penalty, not a civil sanction

q: Who prosecutes criminal market abuse cases in the UK?
o: Financial Conduct Authority
Financial Ombudsman Service
Serious Fraud Office
Bank of England
Crown Prosecution Service
w: The FCA itself prosecutes criminal cases of insider dealing and market abuse under FSMA and related statutes.

n.4: The CPS handles general crime; the FCA prosecutes insider dealing
n.2: The SFO handles serious or complex fraud, not FCA market abuse cases
n.3: The Bank of England is a prudential regulator; it does not prosecute
n.1: The Ombudsman resolves complaints and brings no criminal prosecutions

q: A surveillance analyst spots trading that looks like possible market abuse and prepares a STOR. What is the primary purpose of a Suspicious Transaction and Order Report?
o: To request guidance from the regulator on disclosure
To confirm compliance with anti-money laundering obligations
To notify the FCA of suspected market abuse
To disclose conflicts of interest in research
To inform clients of unusual price movements
w: A STOR is submitted to the FCA to alert them of suspected market abuse or insider dealing activity.

n.4: Client communications about price movements are separate from STOR obligations.
n.0: A STOR is a notification, not a request for guidance.
n.1: AML reports go to the NCA, not through a STOR.
n.3: Research conflicts must be disclosed, but not via a STOR.

q: Which trading venues must establish systems to detect suspicious transactions?
o: Insurance brokers
Regulated markets and MTFs
Firms operating crowdfunding platforms
Credit reference agencies
Retail banks offering mortgages
w: Regulated markets and multilateral trading facilities must monitor and detect suspicious transactions and report them through STORs.

n.2: Crowdfunding platforms are not specifically mandated under MAR to detect and report STORs.
n.4: Retail banks monitor AML issues, not specifically MAR suspicious orders.
n.0: Insurance brokers have regulatory duties but not STOR reporting obligations.
n.3: Credit reference agencies do not operate trading venues under MAR.

q: When must a firm submit a STOR once suspicious activity is identified?
o: At the next quarterly compliance review
Only if FCA requests information
Within seven business days
After internal audit sign-off
Without delay
w: STORs must be submitted to the FCA without delay once suspicion of market abuse arises.

n.2: Seven business days would be too late for regulatory expectations.
n.0: Quarterly reviews are not an acceptable timeline for reporting suspicions.
n.3: Internal audit approval is not required before filing a STOR.
n.1: STORs are proactive obligations, not dependent on FCA requests.

q: Which staff members require training to detect market abuse?
o: Only members of the firm's senior management team
Only the firm's designated compliance officers
Only staff who deal directly with retail clients
All relevant employees involved in trading or handling orders
Only employees who draft the firm's financial promotions
w: All relevant employees handling orders or transactions must be trained to recognise and escalate suspicious behaviour.

n.0: Training extends to all relevant staff, not just senior management
n.1: Compliance staff are not the only ones needing this training
n.2: Order-handling staff need training regardless of client contact
n.4: Promotions drafters are not the only staff requiring training

q: Which regulator is the recipient of STORs in the UK?
o: Prudential Regulation Authority
Financial Conduct Authority
Bank of England
Serious Fraud Office
Competition and Markets Authority
w: STORs must be submitted to the Financial Conduct Authority as the UK’s competent authority under MAR.

n.0: The PRA regulates prudential risk, not STOR reporting.
n.2: The Bank of England supervises monetary policy and stability, not STORs.
n.3: The SFO investigates fraud but does not administer STORs.
n.4: The CMA focuses on competition issues, not market abuse detection.

q: What is the role of surveillance systems in preventing market abuse?
o: They record staff absence and annual leave for HR
They calculate the firm's regulatory capital adequacy
They submit the firm's periodic tax returns to HMRC
They detect unusual trading patterns that may indicate abuse
They compile shareholder communication and voting packs
w: Surveillance systems are designed to identify unusual trading activity that may indicate insider dealing or manipulation.

n.2: Tax reporting is a finance function, not the purpose of surveillance
n.1: Capital adequacy is a prudential calculation, unrelated to surveillance
n.4: Shareholder communications are unrelated to abuse-detection systems
n.0: Absence tracking is an HR matter, not a surveillance function

q: What obligation does a firm have when it becomes aware of suspicious client orders?
o: Submit a STOR to the FCA
Cancel the order without explanation
Request client clarification only
Delay reporting until settlement
File a SAR to the PRA
w: Firms must file a STOR with the FCA when suspicious transactions or orders are detected.

n.2: Asking the client for clarification does not replace the duty to report.
n.3: Delaying until settlement would breach the 'without delay' obligation.
n.1: Cancelling the order is not a substitute for reporting.
n.4: SARs relate to money laundering, not MAR market abuse.

q: Why must firms retain records of submitted STORs?
o: To calculate year-end bonuses for the trading staff
To prepare forecasts of shareholder dividend payments
To evidence compliance with the firm's regulatory obligations
To support the planning of staff annual leave
To satisfy workplace health and safety requirements
w: Retention of STOR records evidences regulatory compliance and allows inspection by the FCA if required.

n.3: Leave planning is unrelated to STOR record retention
n.0: Bonus calculation has no bearing on STOR record retention
n.1: Dividend forecasting is unrelated to STOR record-keeping
n.4: Health and safety rules do not drive STOR record retention

q: A surveillance analyst is scanning trading activity for signs of manipulation. Which of the following is a key indicator they must monitor for?
o: Staff compliance training attendance
Wash trades creating false volume
Correct completion of client forms
Timely settlement of trades
Quarterly publication of results
w: Wash trades, where no genuine risk transfer occurs, are a red flag for market manipulation and must be monitored.

n.3: Timely settlement is standard practice, not indicative of abuse.
n.2: Form completion relates to administration, not abuse.
n.4: Publishing results is disclosure, not manipulation.
n.0: Training attendance demonstrates compliance but is not an abuse indicator.

q: What is the minimum expectation for firms regarding internal escalation of suspicious trading?
o: Wait until the year-end compliance review
Discuss with colleagues informally
Only escalate if client confirms misconduct
Escalate to auditors during annual audit
Prompt escalation to compliance or MLRO
w: Suspicious trades must be escalated promptly to compliance or the MLRO to ensure timely reporting obligations are met.

n.0: Year-end reviews are too late for timely escalation.
n.1: Informal discussions do not satisfy escalation requirements.
n.2: Client admissions are not required before escalation obligations apply.
n.3: Auditors review after the fact, not during live suspicious activity.

q: Which activity is expressly prohibited under UK MAR Article 14?
o: Reporting suspicious activity to the FCA as required
Dealing in financial instruments while holding inside information
Delivering compliance training to newly hired staff
Paying an approved final dividend to the shareholders
Publishing a company's duly authorised full annual report and accounts
w: UK MAR Article 14 prohibits dealing in financial instruments while in possession of inside information.

n.4: Publishing authorised accounts is a normal disclosure, not a breach
n.0: Reporting suspicions to the FCA is required conduct, not prohibited
n.2: Staff training is legitimate and not prohibited by Article 14
n.3: Paying dividends is ordinary corporate activity, not insider dealing

q: What does Article 14 of UK MAR prohibit beyond insider dealing itself?
o: Improper disclosure and recommending dealing on inside information
Misclassifying a client's category under the COBS rules
Failure to keep the statutory company registers up to date
Late filing of the company's annual confirmation statement
Poor record-keeping of client complaints under DISP
w: Article 14 prohibits insider dealing, improper disclosure of inside information, and recommending or inducing others to deal on it.

n.3: Late filings are company-law breaches, not Article 14 market abuse
n.2: Statutory register failures fall under company law, not MAR
n.4: Complaint record failures are DISP breaches, not Article 14
n.1: Client classification errors are COBS matters, unrelated to Article 14

q: An analyst passes price-sensitive information to a friend outside the ordinary course of their job. Under Article 14 UK MAR, what does this constitute?
o: Explaining the financial promotion rules during training
Circulating published research notes to the firm's clients
Telling clients about publicly quoted current stock prices
Revealing inside information outside the normal course of duties
Giving analysts the results after their official release
w: Improper disclosure occurs when inside information is revealed outside the normal course of employment, profession, or duties.

n.1: Published research is public, so sharing it is not improper disclosure
n.2: Public price data is not inside information
n.4: Post-release results are public and lawful to discuss
n.0: Explaining rules in training involves no inside information

q: Which type of recommendation is prohibited under Article 14 UK MAR?
o: Advising a client on their annual ISA eligibility
Suggesting another person deal on the basis of inside information
Proposing a risk assessment under the SYSC rules
Encouraging a client to diversify into pooled investment funds
Recommending an investment based on public research reports
w: Article 14 prohibits recommending or inducing another person to engage in dealing while in possession of inside information.

n.3: Diversification advice involves no inside information and is permitted
n.4: Recommendations from public research are lawful, not prohibited
n.0: ISA eligibility advice is ordinary and uses public information
n.2: A SYSC risk assessment is a control, not a prohibited recommendation

q: Which of the following best describes 'inside information' under UK MAR?
o: Acquisition plans that have already been publicly announced
Any opinion publicly voiced by a market analyst
Precise, non-public information likely to affect a price
General market rumours circulating without any evidence
Past information that has already been published in reports
w: Inside information is precise, non-public information that would likely have a significant effect on the price of financial instruments.

n.3: Rumours are not precise information and are not inside information
n.1: An analyst's public opinion is public, not inside information
n.4: Already-published information is public, not inside information
n.0: Publicly announced plans are, by definition, not non-public

q: What is the key element that makes disclosure of inside information improper under Article 14?
o: It is filed as a statutory return at Companies House
It appears within a formally published company prospectus
It happens during routine periodic financial reporting
It is not made in the normal course of the person's duties
It is issued to the market through a regulatory news service
w: Improper disclosure arises when inside information is revealed outside the proper course of employment, profession, or duties.

n.2: Routine reporting is a normal disclosure, not improper
n.4: RNS releases make information public and are proper disclosure
n.1: A published prospectus is public disclosure, not improper
n.0: Companies House filings are lawful public disclosures

q: Which of the following is an example of insider dealing prohibited by Article 14?
o: Buying shares before a takeover using confidential knowledge
Selling shares just after a public trading update is issued
Recommending a stock using widely available public research
Advising clients on the basis of an FCA press release
Buying an ETF that tracks a published market index
w: Dealing on confidential, price-sensitive information such as a takeover announcement before it is public is insider dealing under Article 14.

n.1: Trading on already-public updates is not insider dealing
n.4: Buying an index ETF uses public data, not inside information
n.2: Using publicly available research is lawful, not insider dealing
n.3: Acting on public FCA releases involves no inside information

q: Which category of persons does Article 14 apply to?
o: Only professional investment analysts
Only employees of a regulated market operator
Any person who possesses inside information
Only firms that are authorised by the FCA
Only the directors of a listed company
w: Article 14 applies broadly to any person who possesses inside information, not just regulated firms or professionals.

n.3: Article 14 binds any person, not only FCA-authorised firms
n.4: It is not limited to directors; anyone holding inside information is caught
n.1: Market-operator employees are not the only persons covered
n.0: Analysts are not the only persons subject to Article 14

q: What is the consequence of breaching Article 14 under the civil regime?
o: Loss of the person's shareholder voting rights
Automatic imprisonment imposed by the FCA directly
Unlimited financial penalties and public censure by the FCA
Revocation of the person's British citizenship
A requirement to restate the firm's annual accounts
w: Civil breaches of Article 14 can result in unlimited fines, public censure, and prohibitions from the FCA.

n.1: The FCA imposes civil penalties; imprisonment is a criminal court outcome
n.0: Voting rights are unaffected by a civil market abuse penalty
n.3: Citizenship cannot be revoked as a market abuse sanction
n.4: Restating accounts is not a civil sanction for insider dealing

q: Which form of inducement is prohibited under Article 14?
o: Publishing regulated announcements through an RNS
Recommending diversification using publicly available data
Encouraging another person to trade while holding inside information
Offering colleagues training on the firm's compliance policies
Promoting a listed company's already public research reports

n.3: Compliance training is legitimate and involves no inside information
n.4: Promoting public research is lawful, not a prohibited inducement
n.0: RNS announcements are proper public disclosure
n.1: Advice from public data is not a prohibited inducement

q: A trader receives a tip and asks compliance whether it counts as inside information under UK MAR Article 7. Which feature would confirm that it does?
o: It is derived solely from rumours

It is contained in press releases
It is precise and not public
It is based on speculation

n.2: Press releases are public and cannot constitute inside information.
n.1: Financial research is analysis, not non-public precise information.
n.0: Rumours are not precise and therefore fall outside Article 7.

q: A compliance officer is assessing whether some unpublished data amounts to inside information under Article 7 of UK MAR. Which element must the information have?
o: A likelihood of a significant effect on the price
A direct connection to the issuer's credit rating
Origination solely from a company's board minutes
Publication within the company's next annual report
Automatic notification to the FCA upon its receipt

n.4: Inside information need not be notified to the FCA automatically
n.2: It can arise from many sources, not only board minutes
n.3: Published information is public, not inside information
n.1: A credit-rating link is not a required element of inside information

q: Under Article 8 UK MAR, what constitutes insider dealing?
o: Discussing quoted prices during a media interview
Using inside information to acquire or dispose of instruments
Buying shares after a public RNS announcement is made
Relying on analyst forecasts that are already published widely
Selling a holding on the strength of general market rumours

n.2: Trading after a public RNS uses public information
n.4: Rumours are not inside information under Article 8
n.0: Discussing public prices is not insider dealing

q: Which activity is prohibited under Article 10 UK MAR?
o: Unlawful disclosure of inside information to another person
Delivering training sessions on the FCA's rules to staff
Filing the required statutory documents at Companies House
Distributing the FCA's published consultation papers
Publishing a company's audited financial statements

n.4: Publishing audited statements is proper public disclosure
n.2: Statutory filings are lawful public disclosures
n.3: Circulating public consultation papers is not unlawful disclosure

q: Which of the following best illustrates inside information under Article 7?
o: Minutes from an already-published company AGM
A share price movement shown live on Bloomberg
An analyst's forecast that is already published widely
An unverified rumour spreading across social media
Knowledge of an as-yet unannounced company merger

n.2: A published forecast is public, not inside information
n.3: A rumour lacks the precision required for inside information
n.1: A visible price movement is public market data
n.0: Published AGM minutes are public information

q: Under Article 8, which of the following is considered insider dealing?

Selling bonds while knowing of unpublished default risk
Trading on the basis of consensus analyst reports
Rebalancing a portfolio after year-end results are public
Investing regular sums into an index tracker fund

n.4: Index-tracker investing relies on public data, not inside information
n.2: Consensus analyst reports are public, so trading on them is lawful
n.3: Rebalancing on published results involves public information

q: Improper disclosure under Article 10 occurs when:
o: A firm issues a prospectus approved by the regulator
Aggregate trading volume reports are published
An FCA consultation paper is circulated among the firm's staff members
Inside information is shared outside the person's normal duties
Publicly available market data is discussed openly
w: Improper disclosure occurs when inside information is shared outside the normal course of employment, profession, or duties.

n.4: Discussing public data involves no inside information
n.2: Circulating a public consultation is not improper disclosure
n.0: Issuing an approved prospectus is proper public disclosure
n.1: Published volume reports are public, not inside information

q: Which of the following is NOT inside information under Article 7?
o: General opinions about overall market sentiment
A pending, unannounced change of key management
A company's unpublished quarterly financial results
Confidential and ongoing acquisition talks
Non-public details of a currently pending takeover
w: General market opinions are not precise information and therefore do not meet the MAR definition of inside information.

n.1: An unannounced management change can be inside information

q: Which scenario breaches Article 8 insider dealing prohibition?
o: Buying shares before earnings known only to insiders
Selling shares after the audited results are published
Trading ETFs based purely on public index data
Hedging with derivatives after an FCA announcement
Following analyst recommendations printed in newspapers

n.2: ETF trades on public index data are not insider dealing

q: Which of the following is an unlawful disclosure under Article 10?

A firm publishes quarterly earnings through an RNS
A bank issues its legally required risk disclosures
A listed company files its ordinary statutory returns
w: Leaking takeover details to an unauthorised person constitutes unlawful disclosure under Article 10 UK MAR.

n.0: Citing public Bloomberg data is not unlawful disclosure
n.3: Required risk disclosures are lawful public statements
n.4: Filing statutory returns is lawful public disclosure

q: An analyst is unsure whether information about a possible corporate event counts as inside information. Under Article 7, when is information considered 'precise'?

When it relates only to a company's past performance
When it rests solely on unverified market gossip
When it indicates circumstances that may reasonably occur
When it is vague and entirely speculative in nature

q: A fund manager becomes aware of a not-yet-announced acquisition and considers how to act. Which of the following is an example of insider dealing under Article 8?

n.0: Widely reported forecasts are public, not inside information

n.1: Tracker-fund investment uses public index data

q: Which type of disclosure is considered lawful under Article 10?

Texting market-sensitive data to a financial journalist
Whispering a profit warning to a few selected investors
Sharing takeover details with friends over lunch
Disclosure made in the normal course of a person's employment

q: Which of the following best describes the link between Articles 7 and 8?

Article 7 sets the criminal penalties for dealing offences

q: An analyst becomes aware of several pieces of information about a listed firm. Under Article 7 of MAR, which of these would most likely amount to inside information?

A consultation paper already published by the FCA

n.0: An RNS takeover announcement is proper public disclosure
n.1: Annual-report updates are public disclosures
n.4: Post-release TV discussion involves public information
n.3: Publishing a prospectus is lawful public disclosure

q: A trainee is studying the market abuse regime and asks what Article 8 of MAR actually forbids. What is its central prohibition?
o: Publishing a company's audited accounts after the deadline
Withholding client complaint data from the FCA
Failing to report a suspicious order to the FCA
Failing to keep proper staff training records
Dealing, or attempting to deal, using inside information
w: Article 8 prohibits dealing or attempting to deal while in possession of inside information.

n.2: STOR reporting failures fall under the STOR rules, not Article 8
n.3: Training-record failures are systems breaches, not Article 8
n.1: Complaint-data failures are DISP matters, not Article 8
n.0: Late accounts are a company-law breach, not insider dealing

q: A compliance trainer lists several items and asks which would NOT count as inside information under Article 7. Which is it?
o: Draft annual financial figures
Published dividend announcements
Confidential negotiations for a merger
Unpublished product launch dates
Unannounced changes to board leadership
w: Published dividend announcements are already public and therefore not inside information under Article 7.

n.4: Board leadership changes can be precise and price-sensitive, fitting Article 7.
n.2: Merger negotiations are classic inside information.
n.3: Unpublished launch dates are precise and non-public.
n.0: Draft financial figures are confidential and price-sensitive.

q: Which of these illustrates the offence of unlawful disclosure under Article 10?
o: An analyst references public Bloomberg data
A company issues official financial results via RNS
A regulator publishes enforcement outcomes
An employee emails takeover details to a relative
A listed company files accounts at Companies House
w: Emailing takeover details to a relative constitutes unlawful disclosure of inside information under Article 10.

n.1: Official RNS disclosures are lawful and required, not improper.
n.0: Bloomberg data is public information and not unlawful disclosure.
n.2: Enforcement outcomes are published by regulators and not inside leaks.
n.4: Statutory filings are public and not unlawful disclosure.

q: A trainee compliance analyst is studying the market abuse regime and asks how Articles 7, 8 and 10 of MAR fit together. What is the correct description of the relationship between them?
o: Article 7 defines inside information; Articles 8 and 10 prohibit its misuse
Articles 7 and 8 define training rules; Article 10 defines disclosure forms
Article 7 sets fines, Article 8 defines disclosure, Article 10 sets training duties
All three articles require firms to submit STORs
Article 7 creates offences, Articles 8 and 10 define public announcements
w: Article 7 defines inside information, while Articles 8 and 10 prohibit dealing or disclosing it unlawfully.

n.2: Article 7 does not set fines; it defines inside information.
n.4: Offences arise from Articles 8 and 10, not Article 7.
n.3: STOR obligations arise separately under MAR, not directly from Articles 7–10.
n.1: These Articles regulate misuse of inside information, not training or disclosure templates.

q: What is the purpose of a market sounding under Article 11 UK MAR?
o: To publish the issuer's annual financial statements
To gauge investor interest ahead of a possible transaction
To provide the statutory audit disclosures required by law
To report a suspicious transaction to the FCA
To announce a confirmed corporate action to the market
w: A market sounding is the communication of information to assess investor interest before transactions such as placements or debt issues.

n.4: Soundings gauge interest before a deal, not public announcements
n.0: Publishing statements is a separate disclosure obligation
n.3: Suspicious-transaction reporting is the STOR process, not a sounding
n.2: Audit disclosures are unrelated to the purpose of a sounding

q: Before disclosing inside information in a market sounding, what must the disclosing party obtain?
o: The recipient's consent to receive the information
A confirmation letter from the issuer's external auditor
A signed copy of the issuer's latest annual report
Prior written approval obtained from the FCA
A formal board resolution passed by the issuer
w: The disclosing party must obtain the recipient’s consent to receive potentially inside information during a market sounding.

n.2: A sounding requires consent to receive information, not an annual report
n.3: No prior FCA approval is required to conduct a market sounding
n.1: Auditor confirmation is not a precondition for a sounding
n.4: A board resolution is not required before making a sounding

q: What record-keeping requirement applies to firms conducting market soundings?
o: They must keep records for at least five years
They must store records only until settlement
They must rely on the counterparty’s records only
They must submit all records to Companies House
They must destroy notes after one month
w: Firms conducting market soundings must maintain detailed records of disclosures and consents for at least five years.

n.4: Records cannot be destroyed after one month under MAR obligations.
n.1: Retention is not limited to settlement periods.
n.3: Companies House does not administer market sounding records.
n.2: Each firm must maintain its own records, not rely solely on counterparties.

q: An analyst is contacted as part of a market sounding and told the disclosed information is inside information. Under Article 11, what duty does the recipient have?
o: To share the information freely with other analysts and colleagues
To ignore the information until its official release
To treat the information as inside information if so identified
To file the information promptly with the PRA
To disclose the information to the market immediately
w: Recipients must treat disclosed information as inside information if so identified, until it becomes public or ceases to be inside information.

n.4: The recipient must keep it confidential, not disclose it publicly
n.3: There is no duty to file sounding information with the PRA
n.1: The recipient must safeguard the information, not simply ignore it
n.0: Sharing it with analysts would be unlawful disclosure

q: A corporate finance team conducts a market sounding following the Article 11 conditions. What protection does compliance with Article 11 provide to the disclosing parties?
o: Right to delay disclosure indefinitely
Exemption from capital adequacy requirements
Immunity from all FCA enforcement
Safe harbour against unlawful disclosure allegations
Automatic exemption from insider dealing prohibitions
w: Article 11 provides a safe harbour for disclosing parties that follow the market sounding requirements, protecting them from unlawful disclosure allegations.

n.2: It does not grant immunity from all FCA enforcement actions.
n.4: It does not exempt insiders from Article 8 prohibitions.
n.0: Disclosure cannot be delayed indefinitely under MAR rules.
n.1: Capital adequacy is a prudential matter, not MAR Article 11.

q: A compliance officer is designing surveillance controls and reviews which practice Article 12 of UK MAR prohibits. Which practice is caught?
o: Publishing audited financial reports
Providing annual training
Market manipulation
Submitting a STOR
Maintaining insider lists
w: Article 12 prohibits engaging in or attempting market manipulation, including creating false or misleading signals about financial instruments.

n.4: Maintaining insider lists is required under MAR, not prohibited.
n.3: STORs are regulatory obligations, not prohibited actions.
n.0: Audited reports are lawful disclosures, not manipulation.
n.1: Training is a compliance requirement, not a manipulation offence.

q: Which is an example of market manipulation under Article 12?
o: Circulating research reports that are already public
Entering wash trades to create artificial trading volume
Providing tax planning advice to the firm's clients
Publishing a prospectus that is approved by the FCA
Trading shares after an official public announcement
w: Wash trades designed to mislead by creating false volume are a classic form of market manipulation under Article 12.

n.3: Publishing an approved prospectus is legitimate disclosure
n.4: Trading after a public announcement uses public information
n.2: Tax advice is unrelated to market manipulation
n.0: Sharing public research is lawful, not manipulation

q: Which behaviour could amount to market manipulation?
o: Training new staff on conduct rules
Filing statutory accounts on time
Spreading false rumours to move prices
Holding client money in trust
Submitting annual returns to Companies House
w: Spreading false rumours to influence market prices is market manipulation under Article 12.

n.1: Filing accounts is a legal duty, not manipulation.
n.3: Client money obligations are CASS rules, not MAR manipulation.
n.4: Annual returns are company law obligations, not MAR prohibitions.
n.0: Training staff is compliance, not manipulation.

q: What type of signal is prohibited under Article 12?
o: Risk warnings issued directly to firms by the FCA
Verified results set out in the company's annual report
False or misleading signals as to supply, demand or price
Accurate disclosures released to the market through an RNS
Announcements made within a published company prospectus
w: Article 12 prohibits creating false or misleading signals regarding supply, demand or price of financial instruments.

n.3: Accurate RNS disclosures are legitimate, not prohibited signals
n.1: Verified published results are lawful disclosures
n.0: FCA risk warnings are not misleading market signals
n.4: Prospectus announcements are proper public disclosures

q: A surveillance team spots a trader repeatedly entering large buy orders and cancelling them before they can execute. Which conduct could this be investigated as?
o: Preparing the firm's annual FCA regulatory fee return
Running a training session on MAR compliance for staff
Submitting an insider list to the FCA on its request
Placing large orders with no intention of executing them
Recording client complaints within the firm's DISP logs
w: Placing large orders without intent to execute, known as spoofing, is a form of attempted market manipulation.

n.2: Submitting an insider list is a compliance duty, not manipulation
n.4: Logging complaints is routine record-keeping, not manipulation
n.1: MAR training is legitimate and not manipulation
n.0: Preparing a fee return is administrative, not manipulation

q: What is the general obligation under UK MAR Article 17?
o: Issuers must publicly disclose inside information as soon as possible
Issuers must notify only their largest shareholders of inside information
Issuers must file annual accounts within six months
Issuers must disclose all employee salaries
Issuers must report quarterly tax payments to HMRC
w: Article 17 requires issuers to disclose inside information to the public as soon as possible to ensure market transparency.

n.1: Disclosure must be to the entire market, not just shareholders.
n.2: Annual accounts are required by company law, not Article 17.
n.3: Employee salaries are not disclosure obligations under MAR.
n.4: Tax filings are not part of MAR disclosure rules.

q: Which mechanism is typically used to disclose inside information under Article 17?
o: Verbal announcement at a shareholder dinner
Internal staff bulletin
Private email to clients
Annual general meeting minutes
Regulatory News Service announcement
w: Issuers use Regulatory News Service (RNS) or equivalent channels to ensure simultaneous public disclosure of inside information.

n.1: Staff bulletins are internal only and not public disclosure.
n.2: Private emails breach equal access rules under MAR.
n.0: Dinner announcements are selective disclosure, not compliant.
n.3: AGM minutes are retrospective and not immediate disclosure.

q: A listed issuer's advisers want to hold back an announcement of price-sensitive information for a short period. Under Article 17, on what condition may disclosure of inside information be delayed?
o: The information is expected to leak into the market anyway
The issuer has not yet notified its own members of staff
The shareholders have voted in favour of delaying disclosure
The market is currently experiencing a period of high volatility
Immediate disclosure would prejudice the issuer's legitimate interests
w: Disclosure may be delayed if it would prejudice legitimate interests, provided confidentiality is maintained and the market is not misled.

n.1: Not yet notifying staff is not a valid ground to delay disclosure
n.0: An expected leak undermines, rather than justifies, a delay
n.3: Market volatility is not a permitted ground for delay
n.2: A shareholder vote is not a condition for delaying disclosure

q: What must an issuer do after delaying disclosure of inside information?
o: Seek shareholder approval for the delay
File a report with HM Treasury
Provide confidential notice to competitors
Inform the FCA once disclosure occurs
Disclose only to its largest creditors
w: Issuers must inform the FCA when disclosure has been delayed, explaining how conditions for delay were satisfied.

n.0: Shareholders do not authorise delays; MAR governs this.
n.2: Competitors must not receive confidential inside information.
n.4: Creditors are not the disclosure audience under MAR.
n.1: HM Treasury is not the relevant regulator under MAR.

q: Which key principle underpins Article 17 disclosure obligations?
o: Limiting disclosures to annual results
Equal access to information for all investors
Disclosure only to market makers
Confidentiality of information at all times
Priority access for institutional shareholders
w: Article 17 aims to ensure equal access to inside information, preventing selective disclosure that advantages certain investors.

n.4: Institutional shareholders must not receive preferential access.
n.3: Confidentiality is important but disclosure must still occur publicly.
n.2: Market makers cannot be privileged with information.
n.0: Disclosure applies continuously, not only annually.

q: An issuer working on an unannounced deal must maintain an insider list under Article 18 of MAR. What is the purpose of that list?
o: To disclose the salaries paid to the company's directors
To record board members' attendance at meetings
To track the company's historic dividend payments
To publish the names of the company's shareholders
To identify the individuals who have access to inside information
w: Article 18 requires issuers and advisors to maintain insider lists to identify those with access to inside information.

n.3: Insider lists are not a public record of shareholders
n.1: They record access to inside information, not meeting attendance
n.0: Directors' pay disclosure is a separate reporting requirement
n.2: Dividend history is unrelated to the purpose of insider lists

q: A company preparing an announcement must maintain an insider list under Article 18 of MAR. What information must each entry on that list include?
o: The identity, the reason for inclusion, and the date of access
The aggregate salary data for all the listed staff
The trading volumes attributed to each listed employee
The pension contribution history of each listed person
Only the personal tax code of each person on the list
w: Insider lists must record the identity of individuals, reason for inclusion, and the date/time they gained access to inside information.

n.4: Tax codes are not part of the required insider-list content
n.1: Salary data is not required on an insider list
n.2: Trading volumes are not recorded on the insider list
n.3: Pension details are not part of an insider list

q: A corporate broker advising a listed company on a deal wonders whether it must keep an insider list under Article 18. Who is required to maintain such lists?
o: Issuers and the persons acting on their behalf
Only the market makers active in the instrument
Only individual retail investors in the shares
Only the issuer's institutional shareholders
Only the Financial Conduct Authority itself
w: Both issuers and anyone acting on their behalf (such as advisers) must maintain insider lists.

n.4: Issuers and their advisers keep the lists, not the FCA
n.2: Retail investors have no duty to maintain insider lists
n.1: Market makers are not the parties required to keep them
n.3: Institutional shareholders do not maintain insider lists

q: For how long must insider lists be retained under Article 18?
o: At least five years
Ten business days
Three months
Until the insider leaves employment
One year
w: Insider lists must be retained for at least five years after they are created or updated.

n.4: One year is below the minimum requirement.
n.2: Three months is far too short for retention under MAR.
n.3: Retention is required beyond employment termination.
n.1: Ten business days is not the statutory requirement.

q: A listed company maintains an insider list of everyone with access to a pending acquisition announcement. From the FCA's perspective, what is one purpose of requiring such lists?
o: To help the FCA investigate potential market abuse
To calculate the company's dividend distributions
To monitor the firm's ongoing tax compliance
To calculate each firm's regulatory capital ratio
To help set the Bank of England's interest rate policy
w: Insider lists assist the FCA in identifying who had access to inside information during investigations into possible market abuse.

n.3: Capital ratios are a prudential matter, unrelated to insider lists
n.2: Tax compliance is not the purpose of insider lists
n.4: Interest-rate policy has nothing to do with insider lists
n.1: Dividend calculations are unrelated to insider lists

q: A listed company's advisers are considering how to release price-sensitive news to the market under Article 17 of UK MAR. What is the overriding aim of that disclosure requirement?
o: To ensure transparency and prevent selective disclosure
To coordinate disclosures with the issuer's tax filings
To give the company's directors advance notice
To let shareholders vote on each announcement
To minimise the administrative costs for the issuers
w: Article 17 is designed to ensure transparency and equal access to inside information, preventing selective disclosure.

n.2: The aim is equal market access, not advance notice for directors
n.4: Article 17 is not designed to reduce issuers' costs
n.3: Shareholders do not vote on inside-information announcements
n.1: Disclosure timing is not tied to tax filings

q: When delaying disclosure under Article 17, what condition must always be met?
o: The board must notify all shareholders
The firm must publish the information on its website first
The FCA must pre-approve every delay
The auditor must sign off on the decision
Confidentiality of the information must be preserved
w: Delays are only valid if confidentiality is maintained and investors are not misled.

n.0: Shareholder notifications are not a requirement under Article 17.
n.2: The FCA does not pre-approve delays, though it must be informed after.
n.3: Auditor approval is not required for disclosure delays.
n.1: Website publication alone does not satisfy disclosure obligations.

q: What must be provided to the FCA after disclosing inside information that was previously delayed?
o: An explanation of how the conditions for delay were met
A summary of the relevant shareholder meeting minutes
A copy of the company's most recent annual report
A confirmation of the dividend payments that were made
A list of all the directors present at the decision
w: Issuers must explain to the FCA how conditions for delaying disclosure were met once information is released.

n.4: The FCA requires the reasoning for delay, not an attendance list
n.2: The annual report is not what must be provided after a delay
n.1: Meeting minutes are not the required post-delay explanation
n.3: Dividend confirmations are unrelated to a delayed disclosure

q: A listed company is drawing up its insider list ahead of an unannounced acquisition. Under Article 18 of MAR, which individuals must appear on the list?
o: Only the firm's designated compliance officers
Only the company's external shareholders
Only the company's statutory external auditors
Anyone who has access to the inside information
Only the members of the company's board
w: Insider lists must include all individuals with access to inside information, regardless of role or seniority.

n.4: The list covers all with access, not only board members
n.1: External shareholders are not automatically insiders
n.0: Compliance officers are not the only people listed
n.2: Auditors are not the only individuals recorded

q: A listed company adds and removes staff who have access to a confidential deal. Why must its insider lists be updated promptly under Article 18?
o: To comply with the company's corporation tax rules
To keep track of the staff holiday schedules
To monitor the outcome of staff performance reviews
To reflect changes in who can access inside information
To ensure the dividend calculations remain accurate
w: Insider lists must be kept accurate and updated whenever new individuals gain or lose access to inside information.

n.4: Dividend accuracy has nothing to do with insider lists
n.1: Holiday tracking is an HR matter, not an insider-list purpose
n.0: Tax compliance is unrelated to updating insider lists
n.2: Performance reviews are not the reason for updating the list

q: What legal risk does maintaining insider lists help mitigate?
o: Market abuse investigations
Breach of health and safety law
Breach of data protection
Employment law disputes
Unpaid corporation tax
w: Insider lists help regulators identify who had access to inside information, supporting market abuse investigations.

n.2: Data protection issues are not the purpose of insider lists.
n.4: Tax is unrelated to MAR insider lists.
n.3: Employment disputes are outside MAR obligations.
n.1: Health and safety is unrelated to insider list compliance.

q: How long must issuers retain evidence of delayed disclosure decisions under Article 17?
o: One year
At least five years
Until the next shareholder meeting
Three months
Ten business days
w: Issuers must retain records of delayed disclosure decisions for at least five years to demonstrate compliance.

n.0: One year is shorter than MAR requires.
n.2: Shareholder meetings do not govern retention periods.
n.3: Three months is insufficient under Article 17.
n.4: Ten business days is far too short for MAR retention rules.

q: A listed company's company secretary is compiling its insider list ahead of a results announcement. For each person with access to the inside information, what detail must the list record?
o: Their voting record at the company's AGMs
Their current trading account cash balance
Their full personal pension contribution history
Their identity, their function, and their contact details
The length of their current employment contract
w: Insider lists must include identity, role or function, and contact details of individuals with access to inside information.

n.1: Account balances are not part of an insider list
n.4: Contract length is not required on an insider list
n.2: Pension history is not recorded on the list
n.0: AGM voting records are not insider-list content

q: A listed issuer is preparing an insider list ahead of a confidential deal. Under Article 18, which regulator must be able to request that list on demand?
o: Competition and Markets Authority
Prudential Regulation Authority
Financial Conduct Authority
Bank of England
Serious Fraud Office
w: The FCA, as the UK’s competent authority for MAR, must be able to request insider lists on demand.

n.0: The CMA handles competition law, not MAR insider lists.
n.4: The SFO investigates fraud, not insider list compliance.
n.1: The PRA supervises prudential issues, not insider lists.
n.3: The Bank of England handles monetary policy, not MAR lists.

q: Why must individuals on insider lists acknowledge their inclusion?
o: To agree to disclose their personal tax history
To confirm they understand their duties over inside information
To accept a permanent reduction in their statutory employment rights
To consent to the publication of their salary
To confirm their personal trading account balances
w: Individuals must acknowledge their inclusion to confirm they understand their duties not to misuse inside information.

n.2: Acknowledgement confirms duties; it does not cut employment rights
n.4: It is about legal duties, not confirming account balances
n.0: Tax history disclosure is not part of the acknowledgement
n.3: Salary publication is unrelated to the acknowledgement

q: Under CJA 1993 Section 52, what is the principal offence?
o: Breach of directors’ duties
False accounting
Market manipulation
Insider dealing
Money laundering
w: Section 52 of the Criminal Justice Act 1993 makes insider dealing a criminal offence.

n.4: Money laundering is dealt with under POCA, not Section 52 CJA 1993.
n.2: Market manipulation is addressed separately under MAR, not CJA Section 52.
n.0: Directors’ duties are under the Companies Act, not CJA 1993.
n.1: False accounting falls under the Theft Act, not insider dealing legislation.

q: Which section of the CJA 1993 defines the term 'inside information'?
o: Section 56
Section 52
Section 58
Schedule 2
Section 61
w: Section 56 of the Criminal Justice Act 1993 provides the definition of 'inside information'.

n.2: Section 58 addresses when information is treated as made public, not its definition
n.1: Section 52 creates the offence of insider dealing, not the definition
n.3: Schedule 2 lists the securities covered, not the definition
n.4: Section 61 deals with penalties and prosecution, not the definition

q: How is an 'insider' defined under CJA 1993?
o: A person who has information through a position or access
Any person who simply buys shares in a listed company
A journalist who reports on the financial markets
An employee who completes mandatory annual training
A shareholder who attends a company's AGM
w: An insider is someone who possesses inside information by virtue of their position, office, or access to information.

n.1: Merely buying shares does not make someone an insider
n.4: Attending an AGM does not confer insider status
n.2: A journalist reporting on markets is not, by that fact, an insider
n.3: Completing training does not make an employee an insider

q: Which section of the CJA 1993 covers defences to insider dealing?
o: Schedule 2
Section 61
Section 57
Section 56
Section 52
w: Section 57 sets out the statutory defences available to insider dealing charges.

n.4: Section 52 creates the insider dealing offence, not the defences
n.3: Section 56 defines inside information, not the defences
n.1: Section 61 covers penalties and prosecution, not the defences
n.0: Schedule 2 lists the covered securities, not the defences

q: A trader is convicted of insider dealing under the Criminal Justice Act 1993. Which section of the Act sets out the penalties for the offence?
o: Section 60
Section 56
Section 58
Section 52
Schedule 2
w: Section 58 of the Criminal Justice Act 1993 specifies the penalties for insider dealing offences.

n.3: Section 52 sets out the offence, not the penalties
n.1: Section 56 defines inside information, not the penalties
n.4: Schedule 2 lists the covered securities, not the penalties
n.0: Section 60 contains supplementary provisions, not the penalties

q: A prosecutor is confirming which instruments fall within the insider dealing regime under the CJA 1993. What types of financial instruments are listed in Schedule 2?
o: Residential mortgages and personal bank loans
Real estate holdings and property title deeds
Gold bullion and other physical commodities
Insurance contracts and personal pensions only
Securities such as shares, bonds, and derivatives
w: Schedule 2 lists securities such as shares, bonds, and derivatives covered by the insider dealing provisions.

n.3: Insurance and pensions are not the securities listed in Schedule 2
n.0: Mortgages and loans are not covered by Schedule 2
n.1: Property deeds are not securities under Schedule 2
n.2: Physical commodities are not Schedule 2 securities

q: Which of the following is an offence under Section 52 CJA 1993?
o: Failing to disclose a personal conflict of interest to the firm's clients
Breaching the listing rules on timely disclosure
Filing the company's annual accounts after the deadline
Issuing a misleading financial promotion to clients
Dealing in price-affected securities while holding inside information
w: Section 52 makes it an offence to deal in securities that are price-affected by inside information possessed by the individual.

n.0: Conflict-of-interest failures are SYSC or COBS matters, not a s.52 offence
n.3: Misleading promotions breach COBS, not the s.52 dealing offence
n.1: Listing-rule breaches are separate from the s.52 offence
n.2: Late accounts are a company-law matter, not s.52 insider dealing

q: In an insider dealing case, the prosecution must establish that certain material amounted to 'inside information'. Under Section 56, what quality must such information possess?
o: It must be precise and price-sensitive
It must be speculative and vague
It must relate only to government securities
It must be based solely on market gossip
It must always come from annual reports
w: Inside information under Section 56 must be precise, non-public, and likely to affect security prices.

n.1: Speculative information does not qualify as inside information.
n.4: Annual reports are public, not inside information.
n.3: Market gossip is not precise or reliable under CJA definitions.
n.2: Inside information can relate to a wide range of securities, not just government ones.

q: What is the maximum custodial penalty for insider dealing under Section 58 CJA 1993?
o: Three years' imprisonment
Five years' imprisonment
Seven years' imprisonment
Ten years' imprisonment
Life imprisonment
w: Section 58 provides for a maximum penalty of seven years’ imprisonment for insider dealing offences.

n.0: The maximum custodial term is seven years, not three
n.1: The maximum is seven years, not five
n.3: Ten years exceeds the seven-year statutory maximum
n.4: Life imprisonment is not available for insider dealing

q: An individual is charged with insider dealing after trading in a listed company's shares. Which of the following would provide a defence under Section 57 of the CJA 1993?
o: The insider disclosed the information only to close friends
The insider acted on the basis of general market rumours
The individual was not a registered FCA-approved person
The information was already generally available to the public
The transaction ultimately turned out to be profitable
w: A key defence is that the information was already generally available to the public at the time of the transaction.

n.2: FCA registration status is irrelevant to an insider dealing defence
n.4: Making a profit is not a defence; it is closer to the harm targeted
n.0: Disclosing to friends is itself improper, not a defence
n.1: Acting on rumours is not a recognised statutory defence
