q: Which of the following best describes 'price-affected securities' under Section 52 CJA 1993?
o: Only bonds and other debt instruments issued by a national government
Any security that is admitted to trading on a recognised regulated market
Any position taken in the foreign exchange or spot commodity markets
Securities whose price would be significantly moved by the inside information
Shares that are held directly by the directors of the issuing company
w: Price-affected securities are those whose price would likely change significantly if the inside information were made public.

n.1: Being traded on a market does not make a security price-affected in the statutory sense.
n.0: The concept is not limited to government bonds.
n.4: Directors' holdings are not the definition of price-affected securities.
n.2: FX and spot commodities are outside this definition.

q: According to Section 56, what must inside information relate to?
o: Rumours about overall market confidence levels
General macroeconomic conditions and trends
Speculative commentary appearing in the media
Long-term historic trading volume data only
Particular securities or a particular issuer
w: Inside information must be specific to particular securities or issuers and not general or speculative data.

n.1: Inside information is issuer or security specific, not general economic data
n.0: General confidence rumours are not specific inside information
n.2: Speculative media commentary is not precise inside information
n.3: Historic volume data is public, not issuer-specific inside information

q: What is a key statutory defence under Section 57 CJA 1993?
o: The person was an FCA-authorised insider at the time
The person had consulted their own financial adviser
The person had first obtained approval from the shareholders
The person would have acted the same way without the information
The person did not directly profit from the trade
w: It is a defence if the person would have acted in the same way even without the inside information.

n.2: Shareholder approval is not a statutory insider dealing defence
n.0: Being FCA-authorised is not a defence to insider dealing
n.1: Consulting an adviser does not provide a defence
n.4: Absence of direct profit is not by itself a statutory defence

q: What is the maximum fine under Section 58 for insider dealing?
o: A fine capped at 500,000 pounds
A fine of up to 1 million pounds
An unlimited fine
A fine of up to 50,000 pounds
A fine capped at 100,000 pounds
w: Section 58 allows for an unlimited fine to be imposed alongside custodial penalties.

n.3: The fine is unlimited on indictment, not capped at 50,000 pounds
n.4: There is no 100,000-pound cap on the fine
n.0: The fine is not capped at 500,000 pounds
n.1: The fine is unlimited, not limited to 1 million pounds

q: Which type of instruments are included in Schedule 2 CJA 1993?
o: Personal pension scheme entitlements
General insurance policies and annuities
Property deeds and land registrations
Consumer credit and personal loan agreements
Shares, bonds, options, and futures
w: Schedule 2 specifies securities such as shares, bonds, and derivatives including options and futures as covered instruments.

n.2: Property deeds are not Schedule 2 securities
n.0: Pension entitlements are not covered by Schedule 2
n.3: Consumer credit agreements are not Schedule 2 securities
n.1: Insurance policies are not covered by Schedule 2

q: A friend passes an analyst a tip and mentions it came from someone inside a listed company. Under the CJA 1993, who qualifies as a 'secondary insider'?
o: A person who receives inside information indirectly and knows that it is inside information
An auditor carrying out the statutory audit of the company's accounts
Any person authorised and regulated by the FCA to conduct investment business
A director or other primary insider of the company whose securities are affected
Any retail investor who happens to hold shares in the relevant company
w: A secondary insider is someone who receives inside information indirectly and knows, or ought to know, it is inside information.

n.3: That describes a primary insider, not a secondary one.
n.2: Being FCA-authorised does not make someone a secondary insider.
n.4: Merely holding shares does not make a retail investor a secondary insider.
n.1: An auditor is not a secondary insider by virtue of the audit.

q: A dealer receives inside information and is unsure which behaviours could expose him to prosecution. Which of the following actions is covered by the Section 52 insider dealing offence?
o: Failing to attend a scheduled company board meeting
Publishing the company's annual accounts after the deadline
Failing to record and investigate the firm's client complaints properly
Dealing, encouraging another to deal, or disclosing inside information
Not completing the required FCA-related staff training
w: Section 52 covers dealing, encouraging another to deal, and disclosing inside information unlawfully.

n.0: Missing a board meeting is not an insider dealing offence
n.1: Late accounts are a company-law breach, not s.52 conduct
n.4: Incomplete training is not an insider dealing offence
n.2: Poor complaint records are a DISP matter, not s.52

q: The FCA is building a case against an individual for insider dealing under Section 52 of the Criminal Justice Act 1993. What must prosecutors prove for the offence to be made out?
o: That the person actually made a financial profit on the deal
That the person was a director of the relevant company
That the person was a shareholder of the issuer
That the person disclosed the annual results late
That the person dealt while in possession of inside information
w: Prosecutors must show that the accused dealt in securities while in possession of inside information.

n.0: Profit need not be proved to establish the s.52 offence
n.1: Director status is not a required element of the offence
n.3: Late results disclosure is not an element of insider dealing
n.2: Being a shareholder is not what prosecutors must prove

q: Which statement about Section 58 penalties is correct?
o: They apply only to companies, not to individuals
They require mandatory community service orders
They include imprisonment and unlimited fines
They allow imprisonment of up to fifteen years
They are capped at a maximum of 50,000 pounds
w: Section 58 provides for custodial penalties up to seven years and unlimited fines for insider dealing offences.

n.0: The penalties apply to individuals, not only companies
n.4: The fine is unlimited, not capped at 50,000 pounds
n.3: The maximum custodial term is seven years, not fifteen
n.1: Community service is not a mandatory penalty for the offence

q: A trader is unsure whether a particular instrument falls within the insider dealing regime. Which best describes the scope of instruments covered by the CJA 1993 rules?
o: Securities listed in Schedule 2, including shares and derivatives
All pension schemes and life insurance policies
All everyday consumer banking and savings products offered by banks
All tangible physical commodities and raw materials
All foreign currency spot exchange transactions
w: CJA 1993 insider dealing applies to securities in Schedule 2, such as shares, bonds, and derivatives.

n.2: Consumer banking products are not Schedule 2 securities
n.4: Foreign-currency spot trades are not covered by Schedule 2
n.3: Physical commodities fall outside Schedule 2
n.1: Pensions and insurance policies are not Schedule 2 securities

q: An accused trader argues he would have made exactly the same trade even without the inside information he held. Which general defence under Section 53 CJA 1993 does this represent?
o: The person was not a director of the company
The person would have acted the same way without the information
The person disclosed the information only to family
The person had been trading in these particular shares quite regularly
The person made no profit at all from the trade
w: Section 53 provides a defence if the accused can show they would have acted the same way without the inside information.

n.4: Absence of profit is not the s.53 same-decision defence
n.0: Not being a director is not a statutory defence
n.2: Disclosing to family is improper, not a defence
n.3: A history of regular trading is not a statutory defence

q: What must a defendant prove to rely on the 'same decision defence' under Section 53?
o: That they would have traded regardless of the inside information
That the FCA had not prohibited the transaction
That the information came from public news outlets
That the trade produced no financial gain at all
That the information involved was merely speculative and unverified in nature
w: The same decision defence applies if the defendant can show they would have made the trade even without the inside information.

n.3: No-gain is not what the same-decision defence requires
n.4: Speculative-information claims are not this defence
n.2: Public-source claims relate to a different point, not this defence
n.1: Lack of an FCA prohibition is irrelevant to the defence

q: Which factor supports the defence of prior intent under Section 53?
o: Evidence the trade was ordered before the information was received
Evidence the person held a well-diversified portfolio
Evidence the person was completely unaware of any circulating market rumours
Evidence the person consulted a financial adviser first
Evidence the person traded through a nominee account
w: Prior intent is a defence if there is evidence that instructions to trade were given before the inside information was obtained.

n.4: Using a nominee account does not establish prior intent
n.3: Consulting an adviser does not evidence prior intent
n.1: Portfolio diversification is irrelevant to prior intent
n.2: Ignorance of rumours does not prove a pre-existing order

q: A trader accused of insider dealing is trying to establish a Section 53 defence with his solicitor. Which of the following is NOT a valid statutory defence?
o: That the trade was required under a prior agreement
That the person would have traded anyway without the information
That the person already had binding obligations to trade
That the decision to trade was made before receiving inside information
That the person gained no profit from the trade
w: Absence of profit is not a statutory defence; liability depends on dealing while in possession of inside information.

n.3: Prior decisions before receipt of inside information can be a defence.
n.1: Trading regardless of the information is a valid statutory defence.
n.2: Pre-existing binding obligations may provide a defence under Section 53.
n.0: Trading under a prior agreement is a recognised statutory defence.

q: How does Section 53 treat trades made under pre-existing contractual obligations?
o: They are always prohibited whatever the circumstances
They are valid only if executed by an external broker
They may be defended if entered before the information was received
They are permitted only with the shareholders' approval
They are excused only if the FCA specifically authorises them
w: Trades under binding obligations entered into before receipt of inside information can be defended under Section 53.

n.0: Such trades are not always prohibited; a defence can apply
n.4: No FCA authorisation is needed for this defence
n.3: Shareholder approval is not the relevant condition
n.1: Using an external broker is not what validates the trade

q: An individual with inside information completes a share sale, but the trade fulfilled a contract entered into before he received that information. Which statutory defence may apply?
o: The director independence defence
The nominee account trading defence
The shareholder vote approval defence
The prior contractual obligation defence
The transaction profitability defence
w: Section 53 provides a defence if the trade occurred under a binding legal obligation existing before receipt of inside information.

n.4: There is no profitability defence to insider dealing
n.2: A shareholder vote does not create a statutory defence
n.0: Director independence is not a recognised defence
n.1: Using a nominee account is not a statutory defence

q: A defendant in an insider dealing case relies on the 'same decision regardless' defence. What must they demonstrate to succeed?
o: That the decision to trade was not influenced by the information
That the trade had been recommended by an analyst
That the FCA had been notified of the trade in advance
That the transaction ultimately produced no net profit
That the securities were very widely held in the market
w: The defendant must show that the decision was not influenced by inside information and would have been taken in any case.

n.3: No-profit is not what this defence requires
n.2: Advance FCA notification is not part of the defence
n.1: An analyst recommendation does not establish the defence
n.4: Wide ownership of the securities is irrelevant to the defence

q: Which burden of proof applies to statutory defences under Section 53?
o: The defendant must prove the defence on the balance of probabilities
The burden rests automatically on the regulator alone
The FCA must prove beyond reasonable doubt that no such defence exists
The firm's auditor must certify that the defence applies
The court must simply assume the defendant's honesty
w: Defendants must prove statutory defences on the balance of probabilities, unlike the prosecution’s burden of proof for offences.

n.2: The defendant bears the defence burden; the FCA need not disprove it
n.4: The court does not presume the defendant's honesty
n.1: The burden for the defence rests on the defendant, not the regulator
n.3: No auditor certification is involved in proving a defence

q: Which example best illustrates the defence of prior intent?
o: A spontaneous share trade placed after overhearing confidential boardroom news
Buying shares after a public company results announcement
Trading based on analyst speculation printed in a newspaper
Selling bonds following the release of an FCA press statement
A dividend reinvestment instruction set before the information was received
w: Automatic reinvestment instructions set prior to receiving inside information are an example of the prior intent defence.

n.0: A spontaneous trade after learning inside news shows no prior intent
n.2: Acting on newspaper speculation is not the prior-intent defence
n.1: Buying after a public announcement involves public information
n.3: Selling after an FCA release involves public information

q: Why is Section 53 important in insider dealing prosecutions?
o: It prevents the FCA from prosecuting company directors
It exempts institutional investors from their MAR duties
It removes all penalties for insider dealing offences
It allows the regulators to bring only civil enforcement actions, never criminal
It provides statutory defences balancing the offence's strict liability
w: Section 53 is important as it provides statutory defences, ensuring individuals are not convicted where trades were independent of inside information.

n.2: Section 53 provides defences; it does not remove penalties
n.3: It does not restrict enforcement to civil actions only
n.0: It does not shield directors from prosecution
n.1: It does not exempt institutions from MAR obligations

q: Which special defence under CJA 1993 applies to market makers?
o: They may ignore their reporting obligations to the FCA
They may trade in good faith in their legitimate market-making role
They may delay disclosure until after a profit has been made
They may trade using information shared with their family members
They may pass inside information on to research analysts
w: Schedule 1 provides a defence for market makers who act in good faith while carrying out their legitimate market-making role.

n.3: Trading on family-shared inside information is not a defence
n.2: Delaying disclosure to secure profit is not a market-maker defence
n.4: Passing inside information to analysts is unlawful disclosure
n.0: Market makers are not exempt from FCA reporting obligations

q: What is the purpose of the special defence for market makers?
o: To remove their record-keeping requirements altogether
To permit the disclosure of confidential inside information
To exempt them from the market abuse laws altogether
To exempt market makers entirely from all FCA oversight
To let market makers provide liquidity without fear of prosecution
w: The market-maker defence exists to protect legitimate liquidity provision activities from being classed as insider dealing.

n.3: The defence is narrow; it does not remove all FCA oversight
n.1: It does not permit disclosing confidential inside information
n.0: Record-keeping duties are not removed by the defence
n.2: Market makers remain subject to the market abuse laws

q: Which special defence under Schedule 1 applies to trading on market information?
o: Where the trade uses information legitimately available in the market
Where the trade uses unpublished company earnings figures
Where the trade relies on private family knowledge
Where the trade rests solely on unverified and speculative market rumours
Where the trade is based on leaked company board minutes
w: Schedule 1 provides a defence when trades are based on information that is legitimately part of the market itself.

n.3: Trading on rumours is not the market-information defence
n.4: Using leaked board minutes is insider dealing, not a defence
n.2: Private family knowledge is not legitimate market information
n.1: Unpublished earnings are inside information, not a defence

q: Why is the 'market information' defence important?
o: It permits dealing on data that has been stolen from another market participant
It exempts company directors from any liability for their own trading decisions
It allows an insider to deal on inside information for their own personal gain
It excuses trading that is based on information obtained through a deliberate leak
It protects traders acting on legitimate knowledge of supply, demand or price
w: This defence ensures that genuine market activity based on legitimate knowledge of supply, demand, or pricing is not treated as insider dealing.

n.0: The defence does not cover stolen data.
n.3: It does not excuse trading on deliberate leaks.
n.2: It does not permit insider dealing for personal gain.
n.1: It does not give directors blanket immunity.

q: What is the price stabilisation defence under Schedule 1?
o: A defence for journalists who publish inside information
A defence letting market makers withhold required disclosures
A defence for shareholders who delay required disclosures
A defence for permitted stabilisation after a new securities issue
A defence for trading on the basis of insider leaks
w: The price stabilisation defence permits stabilisation activity following new issues of securities when carried out under proper rules.

n.4: Trading on insider leaks is never a defence
n.1: There is no defence for market makers withholding disclosures
n.0: Publishing inside information is not a stabilisation defence
n.2: Delaying required disclosures is not the stabilisation defence

q: An underwriter supporting a new share issue engages in price stabilisation during the offer. Why does the law provide a defence for this activity?
o: To allow controlled activity that keeps markets orderly during issues
To let insiders profit without any regulatory oversight at all
To place underwriters beyond the FCA's enforcement powers
To exempt underwriters from all of their disclosure rules
To override the market abuse prohibitions entirely
w: Price stabilisation helps maintain orderly markets during securities issuance and is recognised as a legitimate activity under CJA defences.

n.1: The defence supports orderly markets, not unchecked insider profit
n.3: It does not exempt underwriters from disclosure rules
n.2: Underwriters remain within the FCA's enforcement reach
n.4: It does not override the market abuse prohibitions generally

q: Which party often relies on the price stabilisation defence?
o: Financial journalists reporting on the issue
Ordinary retail shareholders in the company
Government financial regulators and agencies
Underwriters of a new securities issue
The external auditors of the listed company
w: Underwriters conducting stabilisation after a new issue may rely on the statutory defence if rules are followed.

n.1: Retail shareholders do not rely on the stabilisation defence
n.0: Journalists are not the party conducting stabilisation
n.4: Auditors do not carry out stabilisation activity
n.2: Regulators supervise; they do not rely on the defence

q: A compliance officer is briefing traders on the special defences to insider dealing set out in Schedule 1 of the Criminal Justice Act. Which of the following would NOT count as a recognised defence?
o: Price stabilisation following a new issue
Trading for personal enrichment using inside leaks
Trading based on legitimate market information
Trading to provide liquidity in a regulated market
Trading in good faith as a market maker
w: Trading for personal enrichment using inside leaks is never a defence; it constitutes insider dealing.

n.4: Good-faith market making is a recognised Schedule 1 defence
n.0: Price stabilisation after a new issue is a recognised defence
n.2: Trading on legitimate market information is a recognised defence
n.3: Providing liquidity is part of the market-making defence

q: Which statutory document sets out the special defences to insider dealing?
o: FCA Handbook rule MAR 1.1.3
Schedule 2 to the CJA 1993
Schedule 1 to the CJA 1993
Part VIII of the FSMA 2000
Section 52 of the CJA 1993
w: Special defences such as market making, market information, and price stabilisation are set out in Schedule 1 of the CJA 1993.

n.1: Schedule 2 lists the covered securities, not the special defences
n.4: Section 52 creates the offence, not the special defences
n.3: FSMA Part VIII concerns the civil market abuse regime, not CJA defences
n.0: MAR 1.1.3 is FCA guidance, not the CJA special defences

q: How must a market maker demonstrate good faith to rely on the defence?
o: By showing the trades produced no gain for the firm
By showing the trades were part of its normal market-making activity
By showing the trades were pre-cleared by the market operator
By showing it held no inside information when it dealt
By showing it acted only on instructions from its clients
w: The market maker must show that trades were carried out in good faith and as part of their normal role of providing liquidity.

n.3: The defence exists precisely for dealing while holding inside information; absence of it is not the test.
n.2: There is no pre-clearance-by-operator requirement for the market-maker defence.
n.4: Acting on client instructions is not the basis of the market-maker defence.
n.0: Whether a profit was made is irrelevant to establishing the defence.

q: What does the 'good faith' requirement mean for market makers under Schedule 1?
o: Trades must be matched against a client order each time
Trades must avoid any instrument the firm has researched
Trades must be reported to the FCA before they are executed
Trades must be part of a genuine market-making liquidity function
Trades must be limited to the firm's own proprietary book
w: Good faith means market makers must trade genuinely to provide liquidity rather than exploit inside information.

n.2: There is no pre-trade FCA reporting condition for the defence.
n.4: The defence is not confined to proprietary-book trades.
n.0: No requirement to match each trade against a client order.
n.1: Good faith is about liquidity provision, not avoiding researched instruments.

q: Which activity is covered by the 'market information' defence?
o: Using legitimate knowledge of market supply, demand or price movements
Dealing on a tip received in confidence from a family member who is an insider
Acting on the contents of a private boardroom discussion one was told about
Trading ahead of confidential earnings figures obtained from within the issuer
Dealing on the basis of a merger announcement that has been leaked before release
w: The market information defence protects trades made using legitimate knowledge of supply, demand, or price available within the market system.

n.4: Trading on leaked merger information is not the market-information defence.
n.3: Confidential earnings figures are inside information, not market information.
n.2: Private boardroom discussions are inside information.
n.1: A confidential insider tip is not legitimate market information.

q: Which instrument issues typically involve price stabilisation activities?
o: Routine foreign exchange dealing
Exchange-traded fund redemptions
Money-market repo transactions
New issues of shares or bonds
Secondary trading in listed gilts
w: Price stabilisation activities are associated with new issues of securities such as shares or bonds to ensure orderly markets.

n.4: Stabilisation attaches to new issues, not ordinary secondary gilt trading.
n.0: FX dealing is not the context for price stabilisation.
n.1: ETF redemptions are not price-stabilisation activity.
n.2: Repo transactions are not stabilisation of a new issue.

q: A market maker must continue quoting and dealing in a stock despite holding confidential client order-flow information. Why is the market-maker defence necessary under the CJA?
o: Because they must often deal while holding confidential order-flow information
Because they must publish every quote they receive from clients
Because they are supervised directly by the Bank of England
Because they are barred from ever holding any inside information
Because they trade solely as agents for the issuing company
w: Market makers may hold confidential order flow and still need to trade; the defence ensures legitimate activity is protected from prosecution.

n.3: Market makers are not barred from holding inside information; the defence assumes they may.
n.1: There is no rule requiring publication of every client quote.
n.4: Market makers act as principals providing liquidity, not solely as issuer agents.
n.2: Market makers are supervised by the FCA, not directly by the Bank of England.

q: An investment bank running a book-build wants to rely on price stabilisation as a defence to a market abuse allegation. What condition must be satisfied for that defence to be valid?
o: It must be disclosed to the issuer's shareholders after each trade
It must follow the relevant rules and stay within permitted time periods
It must be carried out only on a recognised regulated exchange
It must be confined to trades below the daily average traded volume
It must be approved in advance by the issuer's external auditors
w: Price stabilisation is only a defence when carried out under proper rules and within specific permitted time periods.

n.4: Auditor approval is not a condition of the stabilisation defence.
n.3: There is no daily-average-volume cap governing the defence.
n.2: Stabilisation is not restricted to regulated-exchange trades only.
n.0: Per-trade shareholder disclosure is not required for the defence.

q: What role do underwriters play in the price stabilisation defence?
o: They may buy unlimited stock at any price after listing
They may delay publishing the issue's results for a period
They may make stabilising trades to support orderly markets in new issues
They may allocate shares only to their own client accounts
They may set the final offer price without the issuer's agreement
w: Underwriters may rely on the defence when stabilising transactions are necessary to support orderly markets in new issues.

n.4: Underwriters do not set the offer price without issuer agreement under the defence.
n.1: The defence does not allow delaying publication of results.
n.0: Stabilisation is capped, not unlimited buying at any price.
n.3: The defence is about orderly markets, not self-favouring allocation.

q: A dealer intends to rely on the market information defence after a trade. What is a key limitation of that defence he needs to understand?
o: It covers only transactions made by authorised persons
It requires the trades to be approved by the market operator
It applies only to trades executed on a regulated market
It protects only trades below a set monetary threshold
It does not apply where the information is in fact inside information
w: The market information defence does not apply if the information used is inside information rather than legitimate market data.

n.2: The defence is not limited to regulated-market execution.
n.1: No market-operator approval is required for the defence.
n.0: The defence is not confined to authorised persons.
n.3: There is no monetary threshold limiting the market-information defence.

q: Which example would qualify under the market information defence?
o: Trading on advance notice of a rights issue
Trading on confidential merger negotiations
Trading on observed order-book supply and demand
Trading on an unannounced change of chief executive
Trading on a leaked draft of the annual results
w: Using legitimate order book data relating to supply and demand is covered under the market information defence.

n.4: Leaked unpublished results are inside information, outside the market-information defence.
n.3: An unannounced CEO change is inside information, not legitimate market data.
n.0: Advance notice of a rights issue is inside information.
n.1: Confidential merger talks are inside information, not order-book data.

q: During a new share issue, an underwriter engages in activity aimed at supporting an orderly market. What is the purpose of recognising price stabilisation as a statutory defence?
o: To support orderly securities markets during new issues
To exempt the issue from prospectus disclosure rules
To let underwriters recover their full fees quickly
To guarantee the issue is fully subscribed at launch
To fix the secondary market price for twelve months
w: Price stabilisation is recognised to ensure new issues of securities are not destabilised by short-term volatility.

n.2: The defence is about market order, not helping underwriters recover fees.
n.3: Stabilisation does not guarantee full subscription.
n.4: It does not fix a price for a year; it operates only briefly.
n.1: It has no bearing on prospectus disclosure obligations.

q: Which statute contains the specific special defences to insider dealing?
o: CJA 1993 Schedule 1
Companies Act 2006
FCA Handbook MAR 1
CJA 1993 Schedule 2
FSMA 2000 Part VIII
w: Schedule 1 of the CJA 1993 sets out the special defences including market making, market information, and price stabilisation.

n.3: Schedule 2 lists regulated markets and securities, not the special defences.
n.4: FSMA Part VIII deals with market abuse penalties, not CJA insider-dealing defences.
n.2: MAR 1 is FCA guidance on market abuse, not the statutory special defences.
n.1: The Companies Act 2006 does not contain the insider-dealing special defences.

q: A compliance officer is briefing staff on the operative prohibition under UK MAR. What is the effect of Article 15 in relation to market manipulation?
o: It requires proof of intent for any enforcement action to proceed
It prohibits engaging in or attempting to engage in market manipulation
It permits manipulation below a de minimis threshold if promptly disclosed
It applies only to behaviour on regulated markets, not MTFs or OTFs
It defines the four categories of market manipulation
w: Article 15 is the operative prohibition: a person must not engage in, or attempt to engage in, market manipulation. The definitional detail of what constitutes manipulation sits primarily in Article 12, but Article 15 is the rule that outlaws both completed and attempted conduct. The prohibition is technology- and venue-neutral within the scope of UK MAR, reflecting an outcomes-based approach focused on market integrity.

n.4: Article 12, not Article 15, sets out examples and forms of market manipulation. Article 15 contains the ban itself.
n.2: There is no de minimis safe harbour for manipulation under Article 15; conduct within scope is prohibited regardless of size.
n.0: The civil prohibition does not hinge on proving subjective intent where behaviour is of a kind that misleads or is likely to mislead the market.
n.3: UK MAR applies across instruments within scope of trading venues (including MTFs and OTFs) and related instruments, not just regulated markets.

q: Which statement best captures the scope of the Article 15 prohibition?
o: It applies only once a profit has been made from the conduct
It applies only to on-venue trades and never to OTC dealing
It applies only to shares admitted to a UK regulated market
It applies only to authorised firms and their approved persons
It binds any person within UK MAR's scope and also captures attempts
w: Article 15 binds “any person”, covering both natural and legal persons, and captures attempts as well as completed behaviour. The scope of UK MAR then determines which instruments and venues are in play; within that scope, the prohibition is broad and does not depend on the status of the actor or on whether a profit was achieved.

n.2: UK MAR covers more instruments and venues than shares on a regulated market.
n.3: Article 15 binds any person, not just authorised firms.
n.0: No realised profit is required for the prohibition to bite.
n.1: Within scope it can reach OTC as well as on-venue conduct.

q: A trainee is trying to understand how Articles 12 and 15 of UK MAR fit together. Which pairing correctly distinguishes the two?
o: Article 12 covers PDMRs; Article 15 covers investment analysts
Article 12 sets disclosure rules; Article 15 sets stabilisation rules
Article 12 defines manipulation; Article 15 prohibits it and attempts
Article 12 imposes fines; Article 15 sets out criminal penalties
Article 12 prohibits manipulation; Article 15 defines the offences
w: Article 12 contains the taxonomy and examples of behaviours that amount to market manipulation, while Article 15 is the operative ban that outlaws both engaging in and attempting such behaviour. This structure separates the definitional guidance from the prohibition itself.

n.4: The roles are reversed: Article 12 defines, Article 15 prohibits.
n.1: Neither article is about disclosure or stabilisation rules.
n.3: Neither article fixes fines or criminal penalties in this way.
n.0: PDMRs and analysts are dealt with under Articles 19 and 20.

q: Which of the following is captured by the Article 15 prohibition?
o: Considering a strategy without placing or changing any orders
Publishing balanced research with all conflicts disclosed
Running a stabilisation trade under an applicable safe harbour
Attempting to create a false impression of supply or demand
Holding inside information without carrying out any trade
w: Article 15 extends to attempts to manipulate the market, which includes endeavouring to mislead the market about supply, demand or price. Contemplation alone is not captured, and separate regimes apply to research, stabilisation safe harbours and inside information duties.

n.0: Mere contemplation without any order or trade is not caught.
n.1: Balanced, conflict-disclosed research is legitimate, not manipulation.
n.2: Stabilisation within a safe harbour is permitted behaviour.
n.4: Passive holding of inside information falls under the insider-dealing regime.

q: A trader argues that his benchmark submissions cannot breach Article 15 of MAR because prosecutors could not prove he meant to mislead anyone. Which statement about intent in relation to Article 15 is most accurate?
o: Subjective intent to mislead must always be proven to establish a breach
Only deliberate benchmark submissions fall within its scope
Recklessness is the minimum standard and negligence never suffices
Intent is irrelevant since only realised outcomes are assessed
Conduct likely to mislead can breach the ban even without proven intent
w: The definitional test for manipulation (Article 12) captures behaviour that is false or misleading or likely to mislead. Article 15 then prohibits that behaviour. The regime is effects-focused, and the absence of proven subjective intent does not automatically take behaviour outside the prohibition where it is of a kind that misleads or is likely to mislead.

n.0: Proven subjective intent is not always required; the test is effects-focused.
n.2: There is no fixed recklessness-minimum rule under the definition.
n.1: The prohibition is far wider than deliberate benchmark submissions.
n.3: The regime looks at likely-to-mislead conduct, not only realised outcomes.

q: Who is within personal scope of the Article 15 prohibition?
o: Only registered market makers and appointed primary dealers
Only directors and PDMRs of UK-listed corporate issuers
Any person, natural or legal, within UK MAR's scope
Only UK-resident persons dealing on recognised UK venues
Only individuals directly employed by FCA-authorised firms
w: Article 15 applies to "any person" and is not limited by employment status, role or domicile. The perimeter question is determined by UK MAR’s instrument and venue scope; within that perimeter, the prohibition is actor-neutral.

n.4: Article 15 is not limited to employees of authorised firms.
n.0: It is not confined to market makers or primary dealers.
n.1: It is not limited to directors and PDMRs.
n.3: Domicile does not define scope; the perimeter is the instruments and venues.

q: Which statement about attempts under Article 15 is correct?
o: An attempt is caught only during the primary auction window
Only benchmark manipulation can be attempted under UK MAR
Attempted manipulation is banned even if no trade or price move results
An attempt is prohibited only where it yields a profit
Attempted manipulation is outside UK MAR unless a trade executes
w: Article 15 expressly captures attempts. The rule targets conduct designed to manipulate, regardless of whether an order executes, a price moves, or any profit is made. This ensures enforcement can address preparatory or abortive behaviours that threaten market integrity.

n.4: Attempts are prohibited whether or not a trade executes.
n.1: Attempts are not confined to benchmark manipulation.
n.0: There is no auction-window limitation on attempts.
n.3: An attempt is caught regardless of whether any profit arises.

q: A trader is investigated for conduct suspected of breaching the Article 15 prohibition under UK MAR. Which UK authority is primarily responsible for enforcing that prohibition?
o: Takeover Panel
Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS)
Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA)
HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC)
Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)
w: The FCA is the UK’s competent authority for market abuse. It investigates and can impose civil sanctions and prohibitions for contraventions of UK MAR, including the Article 15 prohibition on market manipulation, using domestic enforcement powers.

n.2: The PRA focuses on prudential supervision; it is not the competent authority for market abuse enforcement.
n.0: The Takeover Panel administers the Takeover Code; it does not enforce UK MAR Article 15.
n.1: FOS handles individual customer complaints, not market-abuse enforcement.
n.3: HMRC is responsible for taxation, not UK MAR enforcement.

q: A trader argues their transactions should be exempt from the Article 15 manipulation ban because they conform to an accepted market practice. Which statement best reflects how Article 15 interacts with AMPs?
o: AMPs excuse any conduct provided that it ultimately turns a profit
No conduct within Article 12(1)(a) can ever escape Article 15
AMPs apply only to benchmark submissions and never to trading
Conduct meeting an accepted market practice may fall outside the ban
AMPs turn criminal manipulation into merely civil manipulation
w: Under Article 13, activity falling under Article 12(1)(a) may be outside the Article 15 prohibition where it conforms to an accepted market practice and the person can establish legitimate reasons for entering the transaction. AMPs are narrow, criteria-based carve-outs overseen by the competent authority.

n.1: Article 13 does allow AMP-conforming Article 12(1)(a) conduct to escape the ban.
n.2: AMPs are not restricted to benchmark submissions.
n.0: Profitability does not trigger an AMP; strict criteria must be met.
n.4: AMPs are carve-outs, not a device converting criminal to civil manipulation.

q: A compliance officer is defining which instruments fall within the market manipulation prohibition in Article 15 of UK MAR. Which statement correctly states the venue and instrument perimeter?
o: Only instruments where a request for admission to trading has been formally granted are within scope
Instruments admitted only to an EU regulated market fall within Article 15 scope in the UK
Instruments are within scope only once actual trading in them has commenced on a UK venue
Only financial instruments admitted to a UK regulated market, and not those on an MTF or OTF, are within scope
Instruments admitted, or requested to be admitted, to trading on UK venues, plus related instruments
w: The Article 15 prohibition applies across the UK MAR perimeter, which covers financial instruments admitted to trading or for which admission has been requested on UK venues (regulated markets, MTFs, OTFs) and certain related instruments, with additional reach to benchmarks and emission-allowance products under the regulation.

n.1: UK MAR applies to UK venues and instruments, not by reference to EU regulated markets post-onshoring.
n.3: Scope extends to instruments traded on MTFs and OTFs, not just regulated markets.
n.0: A request for admission to trading is sufficient; formal admission is not required.
n.2: Scope is triggered by admission or a request for admission, not by trading actually starting.

q: Which UK instrument provides for FCA prohibitions and sanctions where Article 15 is contravened?
o: The Criminal Justice Act 1993, Part V
The Money Laundering Regulations 2017, as amended
The MiFID Organisational Regulation 2017/565
The Financial Services Act 2012 enforcement provisions
The FSMA 2000 (Market Abuse) Regulations 2016
w: Domestic enforcement mechanics sit in UK legislation. The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Market Abuse) Regulations 2016 implement and supplement UK MAR, empowering the FCA, for example, to impose prohibition orders and other sanctions for contraventions including Article 15.

n.3: The FS Act 2012 restructured the regulators; it is not the MAR enforcement instrument.
n.1: The MLR 2017 govern anti-money-laundering, not market abuse sanctions.
n.2: The MiFID Org Regulation covers firm organisation, not MAR sanctions.
n.0: CJA 1993 Part V is criminal insider dealing, not FCA MAR enforcement.

q: A compliance officer is training staff on the behaviours caught by UK MAR. What is the effect of Article 12 of UK MAR?
o: It prohibits all insider dealing
It establishes disclosure rules for issuers
It sets penalties for criminal offences
It regulates client money protection
It defines forms of market manipulation
w: Article 12 defines and illustrates the forms of behaviour that constitute market manipulation.

n.0: Insider dealing is addressed separately in UK MAR and the Criminal Justice Act, not in Article 12.
n.2: Penalties are provided through national law, not defined by Article 12 itself.
n.1: Disclosure requirements are set out in Article 17 and related provisions, not Article 12.
n.3: Client money rules are in the FCA's CASS sourcebook, not UK MAR Article 12.

q: Which activity best illustrates 'manipulating transactions' under Article 12?
o: Entering trades to give a false impression of demand
Issuing an unbalanced investment recommendation
Submitting false data to a financial benchmark
Publishing a research report with misleading conclusions
Failing to notify the market of a PDMR's dealing
w: Manipulating transactions involve placing orders or trades that create a false or misleading impression of supply, demand or price.

n.3: Misleading research is dissemination, not manipulating transactions.
n.2: False benchmark data is benchmark manipulation, a separate limb.
n.4: A missed PDMR notification is an Article 19 breach, not a manipulating transaction.
n.1: Unbalanced recommendations engage Article 20, not manipulating transactions.

q: Which behaviour would qualify as a 'manipulating device' under Article 12?
o: Submitting false rate inputs to a benchmark like LIBOR
Selectively releasing inside information to some investors
Publishing generic research without a disclaimer
Using a fictitious device or contrivance to move a price
Failing to disclose a director's share transaction
w: Manipulating devices are artificial schemes or contrivances designed to mislead the market or distort pricing.

n.1: Selective disclosure is unlawful disclosure, not a manipulating device.
n.0: False benchmark inputs are benchmark manipulation, a distinct limb.
n.4: Non-disclosure of a director's trade is an Article 19 breach.
n.2: Missing a research disclaimer is an Article 20 matter, not a device.

q: What form of manipulation does spreading misleading rumours fall under?
o: Manipulating transactions
Manipulating devices
Dissemination
Benchmark manipulation
Legitimate stabilisation measures
w: Dissemination covers spreading false or misleading information likely to influence prices.

n.1: Manipulating devices involve artificial schemes, not the spreading of rumours.
n.3: Benchmark manipulation involves submissions to a benchmark, not market rumours.
n.0: Manipulating transactions require actual trading activity, not information dissemination.
n.4: Legitimate stabilisation is a recognised safe harbour, not unlawful dissemination.

q: Which action best illustrates benchmark manipulation?
o: Publishing an unbalanced analyst report
Withholding disclosure of director trades
Spreading rumours about a takeover
Cross-trading between accounts
Providing false submissions to LIBOR
w: Benchmark manipulation arises when false or misleading inputs are submitted to a benchmark-setting process.

n.2: Rumours about a takeover fall under dissemination, not benchmark manipulation.
n.3: Cross-trading to mislead demand is manipulating transactions, not benchmarks.
n.1: Director trade disclosures are Article 19 duties, not benchmark manipulation.
n.0: Unbalanced analyst reports breach Article 20, not benchmark manipulation rules.

q: A listed company repurchases its own shares within a recognised safe harbour and asks whether this risks a manipulation finding. Under Article 9, which behaviour is treated as legitimate?
o: Placing wash trades to move a share price
Withholding notice of a PDMR's transactions
Releasing false takeover announcements to the market
Carrying out share buy-backs under a safe harbour
Submitting incorrect data to a pricing benchmark
w: Article 9 allows recognised legitimate behaviour such as buy-backs conducted under safe harbour conditions.

n.2: False takeover announcements are manipulation, not legitimate behaviour.
n.4: Incorrect benchmark data is manipulation, not permitted conduct.
n.1: Withholding PDMR notice breaches Article 19.
n.0: Wash trades are a classic manipulating transaction.

q: What is the purpose of accepted market practices under Article 13?
o: To fix the penalties imposed for insider dealing
To require conflict disclosures in investment research
To set out where conduct is not treated as manipulation
To set the reporting deadlines for PDMR dealings
To exempt firms from prudential capital requirements
w: Article 13 defines accepted market practices that allow certain conduct to fall outside the prohibition when conditions are met.

n.0: Article 13 does not set insider-dealing penalties.
n.3: PDMR deadlines are set by Article 19, not Article 13.
n.1: Research conflict disclosure is governed by Article 20.
n.4: Article 13 has nothing to do with capital requirements.

q: Which obligation does Article 19 impose on PDMRs?
o: Disclose client orders transparently
Publish investment research annually
Avoid benchmark submissions
Report their transactions promptly
Approve corporate buy-back programmes
w: Article 19 requires PDMRs to notify the issuer and competent authority of their own transactions promptly.

n.2: Benchmark submissions are not covered by Article 19, which focuses on PDMR disclosures.
n.1: Investment research is governed by Article 20, not Article 19.
n.4: Buy-back programmes are addressed by stabilisation provisions, not PDMR obligations.
n.0: Client order disclosures are covered under COBS, not Article 19.

q: Who must PDMRs notify of their transactions under Article 19?
o: Only the firm's auditors
Only their immediate line manager
Only the company's legal department
Both the PRA and HM Treasury
Both the issuer and the FCA
w: PDMRs must notify both the issuer and the FCA of transactions in the issuer's shares or related instruments.

n.0: Auditors are not the recipients of PDMR notifications under Article 19.
n.1: Line managers are not designated recipients under Article 19.
n.2: The legal department is not the competent authority specified under Article 19.
n.3: The PRA and Treasury are not the required authorities for Article 19 notifications.

q: An analyst is publishing an investment recommendation subject to Article 20 of MAR. What does that article require?
o: Register safe harbours with FCA
Disclose conflicts of interest
Report stabilisation trades weekly
Publish PDMR dealings
Submit benchmark contributions
w: Article 20 requires those providing investment recommendations to disclose any conflicts of interest clearly.

n.4: Benchmark contributions are covered by Article 12 and 15, not Article 20.
n.3: PDMR dealings are Article 19 duties, not Article 20.
n.0: Safe harbours apply under Article 5, not Article 20 recommendations.
n.2: Reporting stabilisation trades is separate and not an Article 20 obligation.

q: A trading desk is reviewing several activities against the market manipulation prohibition. Which conduct is least likely to breach Article 15 when carried out strictly within a published safe harbour?
o: Feeding false inputs into a market benchmark
Layering large visible orders and then cancelling
Price stabilisation meeting all the Article 5 conditions
Spreading takeover rumours across social media
Cross trades arranged to fix the closing price
w: Stabilisation within the Article 5 safe harbour is legitimate behaviour and therefore outside the Article 15 prohibition.

n.4: Fixing closing prices via cross trades is manipulation.
n.1: Layering and cancelling is a manipulating transaction.
n.3: Spreading rumours is dissemination-based manipulation.
n.0: False benchmark inputs are benchmark manipulation.

q: The FCA is deciding whether a particular trading behaviour should be recognised as an Accepted Market Practice. Under Article 13, how are such practices established?
o: By industry trade bodies through voluntary codes
By the competent authority applying the Article 13 criteria
By issuers through their market disclosures
By trading venues within their membership rules
By investment banks under syndicate agreements
w: Accepted Market Practices must be established by the competent authority against the specific criteria in Article 13.

n.0: AMPs are set by the competent authority, not voluntary trade codes.
n.2: Issuer disclosures do not establish AMPs.
n.3: Venue membership rules do not establish AMPs.
n.4: Syndicate agreements cannot create an AMP.

q: Surveillance flags a trader who repeatedly posts large visible buy orders and then pulls them just before execution. Which Article 12 behaviour does this best describe?
o: Publishing an over-optimistic research note
Failing to report a director's share dealing
Feeding incorrect inputs into a benchmark
Placing visible orders to mislead, then cancelling them
Crossing orders internally to cut trading fees
w: Layering involves placing orders to create a false impression of depth or demand and then cancelling to move price.

n.0: An optimistic research note is not layering.
n.2: Incorrect benchmark inputs are benchmark manipulation, not layering.
n.4: Internal crossing to cut fees is not layering.
n.1: A missed director-dealing report is an Article 19 breach.

q: A director's spouse buys shares in the company where the director serves as a PDMR. Under Article 19 of MAR, which statement about the notification obligations is correct?
o: Notifications are needed only where a profit arises
Notifications are due only after the financial year-end
Persons closely associated with PDMRs must also notify dealings
The issuer automatically reports on the PDMR's behalf
Only shares held directly by a PDMR are reportable
w: Article 19 extends notification duties to persons closely associated with PDMRs as well as the PDMRs themselves.

n.4: Reporting is not limited to directly held shares.
n.1: Notifications are due promptly, not only after year-end.
n.3: PDMRs must notify themselves; the issuer does not do it automatically.
n.0: Notification duty does not depend on a profit arising.

q: How does Article 12 treat dissemination of misleading information?
o: As market manipulation where it is likely to affect prices
As legitimate where it comes from anonymous posts
As acceptable if it is retracted within 24 hours
As acceptable if it carries a written disclaimer
As acceptable if no trade follows the statement
w: Dissemination of false or misleading information that is likely to influence prices constitutes market manipulation.

n.2: A later retraction does not cure the dissemination offence.
n.3: A disclaimer does not make misleading dissemination lawful.
n.1: An anonymous source does not legitimise misleading information.
n.4: Manipulation does not require a following trade.

q: A market surveillance analyst is classifying suspected abuse and must separate 'manipulating devices' from 'manipulating transactions'. Which statement best distinguishes the two?
o: Devices use artifices; transactions rely on orders or trades
Devices are lawful while transactions are always unlawful
Devices need benchmarks; transactions need spread rumours
Devices require a profit; transactions require a loss
Devices need issuer consent; transactions need venue consent
w: Manipulating devices involve artifices or contrivances, whereas manipulating transactions involve orders or trades that mislead supply, demand, or price.

n.2: Neither limb is defined by benchmarks or rumours in that way.
n.1: Manipulating devices are not lawful; both limbs are prohibited.
n.4: Neither limb turns on issuer or venue consent.
n.3: Neither limb requires a specific profit or loss.

q: An issuer enters a liquidity contract with a broker to support trading in its own shares. In which situation might this fall outside the Article 15 market manipulation prohibition?
o: When any profits are donated to charity
When executed off-venue outside market hours
When carried out under an accepted market practice
When performed by a broker outside the UK
When disclosed only to professional clients
w: Execution under a competent authority-recognised accepted market practice can place a liquidity contract outside the Article 15 prohibition.

n.3: A foreign broker does not place a contract outside Article 15.
n.0: Donating profits does not legitimise the conduct.
n.4: Limiting disclosure to professionals is irrelevant.
n.1: Off-venue after-hours execution does not create an exemption.

q: A research analyst is preparing an investment recommendation for publication. Under Article 20 of MAR, what obligation applies to the producer?
o: Submit each draft to the issuer for review
Keep records that support the basis of the recommendation
Guarantee they are free of any conflict of interest
Disclose the names of all clients consulted
Publish only recommendations with a positive rating
w: Producers must keep adequate records supporting the recommendation and comply with fair presentation and conflict disclosure duties.

n.3: There is no duty to name all clients consulted.
n.0: Drafts need not be submitted to the issuer for review.
n.2: Conflicts must be disclosed, not guaranteed absent.
n.4: Recommendations need not be limited to positive ratings.

q: Which off-venue behaviour can still breach Article 15?
o: Holding issuer shares for the long term
Private investment club discussions about macroeconomics
OTC trades designed to mislead prices on a venue
Silent observation of order-book movements
Internal model back-testing with historical data
w: OTC conduct intended to mislead venue pricing may constitute manipulation because UK MAR focuses on effects on in-scope instruments.

n.1: General macro discussions are not manipulative, whereas misleading OTC trades can be.
n.4: Back-testing is internal analysis, while misleading trading behaviour targets market perception.
n.3: Observation alone is not manipulative, whereas deceptive OTC trading is.
n.0: Passive holding is not manipulative, whereas deceptive trading is.

q: Which activity is recognised as legitimate behaviour under Article 9 of UK MAR?
o: Submitting inaccurate interest-rate benchmark data
Publishing biased research without disclosing conflicts
Failing to notify a director's share dealing
Spreading misleading takeover rumours to lift trading
Running a stabilisation programme within the set conditions
w: Article 9 recognises stabilisation conducted within specified conditions as legitimate behaviour outside the scope of manipulation.

n.3: Spreading misleading rumours is manipulation.
n.0: Inaccurate benchmark data is benchmark manipulation.
n.2: A missed director-dealing notification breaches Article 19.
n.1: Biased, non-disclosed research breaches Article 20.

q: Why does Article 9 allow stabilisation activities when conditions are met?
o: They exempt issuers from the insider dealing rules
They remove the issuer's disclosure obligations
They lower the firm's regulatory capital requirements
They support orderly markets without misleading investors
They guarantee a trading profit for market makers
w: Stabilisation is permitted because it supports orderly markets without misleading investors when carried out under Article 9 conditions.

n.4: Stabilisation guarantees no profit to market makers.
n.1: It does not remove disclosure obligations.
n.0: It gives no relief from insider-dealing rules.
n.2: It has no bearing on capital requirements.

q: Which factor must the competent authority consider when approving an Accepted Market Practice under Article 13?
o: The political views of the issuer
The impact on market integrity
The nationality of shareholders
The firm’s marketing strategies
The firm’s profitability targets
w: Article 13 requires the authority to consider whether the practice upholds market integrity before recognition as accepted.

n.4: Profitability targets are irrelevant, while market integrity is central.
n.0: Political views are not relevant criteria for AMPs.
n.2: Shareholder nationality is not considered in approving AMPs.
n.3: Marketing strategies are not a recognised criterion for AMPs.

q: Which of the following is an example of conduct permitted under an Accepted Market Practice?
o: Publishing recommendations without stating conflicts
Disseminating false information about an issuer
Submitting fabricated commodity benchmark data
Liquidity-provision arrangements accepted by the FCA as an AMP
Directors concealing their share purchases
w: Liquidity provision arrangements recognised as AMPs can be lawful even if they influence price, as long as conditions are met.

n.1: Disseminating false information is manipulation, not an AMP.
n.2: Fabricated benchmark data is manipulation.
n.4: Concealing share purchases breaches Article 19.
n.0: Undisclosed-conflict recommendations breach Article 20.

q: A trader relies on an Accepted Market Practice to justify a pattern of trading questioned by the regulator. How must the participant demonstrate compliance when relying on an AMP?
o: By recording the nationality of all its clients
By securing the issuer's consent before every trade
By filing daily trade reports to HM Treasury
By ensuring every trade produces a profit
By evidencing the trades were entered for legitimate reasons
w: To rely on an AMP, the participant must show transactions were for legitimate purposes consistent with the approved practice.

n.1: Issuer consent is not the test for relying on an AMP.
n.2: No daily HM Treasury reporting is required.
n.3: Producing a profit is not a condition of the AMP.
n.0: Recording client nationality is not the AMP requirement.

q: A trading venue is assessing whether a practice can be recognised as an Accepted Market Practice under Article 13. Which of the following is NOT a recognition criterion?
o: Consistency with trading venue rules
Potential to damage market confidence
Degree of impact on market liquidity
Profitability of market participants
Degree of transparency provided to the market
w: Profitability is not a recognition criterion, whereas transparency, liquidity, and confidence are factors under Article 13.

n.1: Potential damage to market confidence is explicitly assessed under Article 13.
n.4: Transparency is a required factor in recognising AMPs.
n.0: Consistency with venue rules is considered when approving AMPs.
n.2: Impact on liquidity is considered when assessing AMPs.

q: Why does Article 13 require Accepted Market Practices to be published?
o: So auditors can verify benchmark submissions
So participants know the conditions for permitted conduct
So employees can bypass the insider dealing rules
So firms can lower their capital requirements
So issuers may avoid disclosing PDMR transactions
w: Publication ensures transparency, allowing market participants to understand which behaviours are permitted under Article 13.

n.4: Publication does not let issuers avoid PDMR disclosure.
n.0: It is not about auditors verifying benchmarks.
n.3: It has no effect on capital requirements.
n.2: It does not allow bypassing insider-dealing rules.

q: Which of the following is a legitimate reason for transactions under Article 9?
o: Concealing director dealings from the regulator
Executing buy-backs in line with the safe harbour rules
Issuing investment advice without disclosing conflicts
Spreading false rumours about a planned merger
Submitting fictitious commodity data to move prices
w: Buy-backs executed within the Article 5 safe harbour are recognised by Article 9 as legitimate behaviour.

n.3: Spreading false merger rumours is manipulation.
n.4: Fictitious commodity data is benchmark/price manipulation.
n.0: Concealing director dealings breaches Article 19.
n.2: Undisclosed-conflict advice breaches Article 20.

q: What is the main distinction between Article 9 legitimate behaviour and Article 13 accepted market practices?
o: Article 9 sets specific safe harbours; Article 13 needs authority recognition
Article 9 applies only to benchmarks; Article 13 only to PDMRs
Article 9 exempts all trades; Article 13 exempts only dividends
Article 9 needs FCA approval; Article 13 needs issuer approval
Article 9 sets the penalties; Article 13 defines insider dealing
w: Article 9 defines specific safe harbours, while Article 13 requires the competent authority to recognise practices as accepted.

n.4: Article 9 does not set penalties, nor does Article 13 define insider dealing.
n.3: Article 9 safe harbours need no FCA case-by-case approval; issuer approval is irrelevant.
n.1: Neither article is limited to benchmarks or PDMRs.
n.2: Neither article gives a blanket exemption for all trades or dividends.

q: Which is a key reason authorities restrict Accepted Market Practices to narrow circumstances?
o: To remove the need to disclose PDMR dealings
To encourage more frequent insider trading
To avoid undermining the prohibition on manipulation
To replace national prudential capital rules
To maximise the profitability of regulated firms
w: AMPs are narrowly defined to ensure they do not undermine the broad prohibition against market manipulation.

n.4: AMPs are not designed to boost firm profitability.
n.0: They do not remove PDMR disclosure duties.
n.1: They are not intended to facilitate insider trading.
n.3: They do not replace prudential capital rules.

q: Who must Persons Discharging Managerial Responsibilities notify under Article 19?
o: Both the issuer and the FCA
Only the Prudential Regulation Authority
Only the company's auditors
Only their immediate manager
Only the company’s legal counsel
w: Article 19 requires PDMRs to notify both the issuer and the FCA of their transactions in issuer securities.

n.2: Auditors are not the designated recipients under Article 19; the issuer and FCA are.
n.3: Immediate managers are not notified under Article 19, unlike the issuer and FCA.
n.4: Company legal counsel is not specified in Article 19, unlike the issuer and FCA.
n.1: The PRA is not the competent authority for MAR disclosures; the FCA is.

q: A director of a listed company buys shares in her own firm and must report it under Article 19 of UK MAR. Within what timeframe must this PDMR notify the transaction?
o: By the end of the quarter
Within three business days
Within one month
Only after profits are realised
By the next annual report
w: Article 19 requires notifications to be made within three business days of the transaction.

n.2: One month exceeds the three-day requirement under Article 19.
n.0: Quarterly reporting would be too late; Article 19 requires three days.
n.4: Annual report timing is far beyond the prescribed three-day deadline.
n.3: Profit realisation is irrelevant; notification is based on transaction timing.

q: A director's dealings in her employer's listed shares are being tracked for notification purposes. Which threshold triggers the requirement for PDMRs to notify their transactions?
o: Exceeding €5,000 in a calendar year
Exceeding €1 million in total holdings
Exceeding 5% shareholding in the issuer
Exceeding €500 per transaction
Exceeding €50,000 in a single trade
w: Article 19 sets a de minimis threshold of €5,000 per calendar year before PDMRs must notify transactions.

n.4: The threshold is not €50,000 per trade; Article 19 specifies €5,000 per year.
n.3: €500 is too low; Article 19 sets the threshold at €5,000 annually.
n.1: Total holdings are not the basis; it is annual transaction value.
n.2: Shareholding percentage is unrelated; the rule is based on transaction value.

q: A listed issuer's company secretary is briefing directors on who else must notify their dealings in the company's shares. Under Article 19, which category of persons must also notify?
o: Persons closely associated with PDMRs
Only external auditors of the issuer
Only FCA-approved senior managers
Only investment analysts covering the issuer
Only major shareholders above 3%
w: Article 19 extends the notification requirement to persons closely associated with PDMRs.

n.1: Auditors are not covered; Article 19 refers to PDMRs and their closely associated persons.
n.3: Analysts are not obligated under Article 19, unlike PCAs.
n.4: Shareholding thresholds do not trigger Article 19 duties; transaction value does.
n.2: Senior managers are covered only if they are PDMRs or PCAs.

q: A director at a listed issuer buys shares in the company and asks compliance which of their dealings must be reported under Article 19 of UK MAR. Which transactions are reportable?
o: Dealings in any securities anywhere in the world
Dealings in the shares of competitor companies
Dealings only in the issuer's debt securities
Dealings in the issuer's shares, debt and related derivatives
Dealings in commodities unrelated to the issuer
w: Article 19 requires reporting of transactions in issuer shares, debt, and related derivatives.

n.0: Reporting is confined to the issuer's own instruments, not all securities.
n.2: It covers shares and derivatives too, not debt alone.
n.1: Competitor shares are not within the issuer's PDMR reporting.
n.4: Unrelated commodities are outside Article 19.

q: Why are PDMR disclosures under Article 19 important?
o: They boost transparency and deter abuse by senior insiders
They reduce the firm's FCA capital requirements
They exempt issuers from other disclosure duties
They replace duties under the Prospectus Regulation
They guarantee the issuer meets its profit targets
w: PDMR disclosures enhance transparency and help deter insider abuse by showing transactions of senior insiders.

n.2: PDMR disclosure does not relieve other disclosure duties.
n.1: It has no effect on capital requirements.
n.4: It cannot guarantee profit targets.
n.3: It does not replace Prospectus Regulation duties.

q: What must issuers do upon receiving PDMR transaction notifications?
o: Report it once a year in the issuer's accounts
Publicly disclose the information within the set deadline
Record it only in the internal board minutes
Send it solely to the company's registrar
Forward it to the PRA for a prudential review
w: Issuers must publish PDMR transaction information promptly within the deadline to maintain market transparency.

n.4: The issuer must publish it, not send it to the PRA for review.
n.2: Internal minutes do not satisfy the public-disclosure duty.
n.3: Sending it only to the registrar is not public disclosure.
n.0: It must be published promptly, not annually in the accounts.

q: How does Article 19 define Persons Discharging Managerial Responsibilities?
o: The external auditors appointed to sign off the annual accounts
Any employee of the issuer, irrespective of their seniority or role
All registered shareholders holding stock in the company
External consultants engaged to provide advice to the board
Those with regular access to inside information and power to take management decisions
w: Article 19 defines PDMRs as those with regular access to inside information and decision-making power.

n.1: A PDMR is defined by managerial responsibility, not by being any employee.
n.2: Ordinary shareholders are not PDMRs by virtue of their holding.
n.3: Advisory consultants are not PDMRs unless they meet the managerial test.
n.0: Auditors are not PDMRs of the issuer.

q: A director of a listed issuer enters a derivative transaction and the firm must assess PDMR reporting obligations. Which type of derivative transaction must be reported?
o: Options or swaps linked to the issuer's shares
Derivatives written on a competitor's shares
Interest-rate swaps not referencing the issuer
Commodity futures with no link to the issuer
Currency derivatives unrelated to the issuer
w: Derivatives linked to issuer securities fall within Article 19 and must be reported.

n.4: Unrelated currency derivatives are outside Article 19.
n.3: Commodity futures with no issuer link are not reportable.
n.1: Derivatives on a competitor's shares are outside scope.
n.2: Swaps not referencing the issuer are not reportable.

q: What consequence may follow if a PDMR fails to comply with Article 19?
o: Automatic removal of the PDMR from the board
Automatic exemption from insider dealing liability
Automatic cancellation of all their shareholdings
Loss of the firm's capital requirement reliefs
Regulatory sanctions for breaching disclosure obligations
w: Non-compliance with Article 19 may result in regulatory sanctions for breaching disclosure obligations.

n.2: Non-compliance does not cancel shareholdings automatically.
n.1: It does not grant any insider-dealing exemption.
n.3: It does not trigger loss of capital reliefs.
n.0: There is no automatic board removal for a breach.

q: What is a primary obligation under Article 20 when publishing investment recommendations?
o: Disclose any material interests or conflicts
Ensure only positive recommendations are released
Submit drafts to the issuer for approval
Report recommendations directly to HM Treasury
Guarantee accuracy of future price movements
w: Article 20 requires disclosure of material interests or conflicts when investment recommendations are issued.

n.4: Future accuracy cannot be guaranteed; Article 20 requires disclosure of conflicts instead.
n.2: Issuer approval is not required; independence and disclosure are essential.
n.1: Recommendations must be fair and balanced, not only positive.
n.3: Article 20 does not require reporting recommendations to HM Treasury.

q: Which requirement ensures investment recommendations are fairly presented under Article 20?
o: Distinguishing clearly between fact and opinion
Guaranteeing profit for all investors
Excluding any negative analysis
Providing issuer pre-clearance before publication
Reporting directly to the FCA before release
w: Article 20 requires recommendations to clearly separate fact from opinion to ensure fairness.

n.1: Guaranteeing profit is impossible and not required; clarity is required instead.
n.2: Excluding negatives would bias the analysis; fairness requires balance.
n.3: Issuer pre-clearance is not mandated; independence is required.
n.4: Pre-release submission to the FCA is not required; fair presentation is.

q: A firm publishes investment recommendations to clients and must comply with the disclosure rules. Why must it disclose the methodologies it used?
o: To meet the firm's capital adequacy requirements
To reduce the need for a statutory audit
To let readers assess the basis of the recommendation
To satisfy shareholders' profitability targets
To exempt the firm from its Article 19 duties
w: Article 20 requires methodology disclosure so readers can assess how the recommendation was formed.

n.0: Methodology disclosure is unrelated to capital adequacy.
n.3: It is not about shareholder profitability targets.
n.4: It gives no relief from Article 19 duties.
n.1: It does not reduce statutory audit requirements.

q: Which example breaches Article 20 obligations?
o: Using transparent, disclosed methods to reach the conclusion
Publishing research without disclosing the analyst's holding in the issuer
Openly disclosing every conflict of interest in the report
Clearly separating statements of fact from opinion in a note
Keeping records that substantiate the recommendation made
w: Failure to disclose analyst shareholdings is a breach of Article 20 disclosure obligations.

n.3: Separating fact from opinion is required good practice, not a breach.
n.2: Openly disclosing conflicts complies with Article 20.
n.4: Keeping substantiating records complies with Article 20.
n.0: Using transparent, disclosed methods complies, it is not a breach.

q: Which duty applies to producers of investment recommendations regarding record keeping?
o: Rely solely on issuer data without any notes
Keep only oral explanations given to clients
Keep sufficient records to substantiate the recommendation
Send all records quarterly to HM Treasury
Destroy the supporting documents once published
w: Article 20 requires keeping adequate records to substantiate the recommendation and demonstrate fair presentation.

n.1: Oral explanations alone do not meet the record-keeping duty.
n.0: Relying on issuer data without notes fails the duty.
n.4: Records must be retained, not destroyed after publication.
n.3: There is no quarterly HM Treasury filing requirement.

q: How does Article 20 ensure transparency in investment recommendations?
o: By requiring disclosure of conflicts, interests and methodology
By restricting recommendations to authorised firms only
By requiring disclosure of every shareholder's identity
By requiring FCA pre-approval of every research note
By guaranteeing the issuer's future performance
w: Transparency is achieved by requiring disclosure of conflicts, interests, and methodologies behind recommendations.

n.3: No FCA pre-approval of each research note is required.
n.1: Article 20 is not limited to authorised firms.
n.4: It cannot guarantee future issuer performance.
n.2: It does not require disclosing every shareholder's identity.

q: A firm's in-house analyst is about to have an investment recommendation published through a national newspaper. Which obligation applies when investment recommendations are disseminated via the media in this way?
o: They must carry the same disclosures as formal reports
They need disclosures only where they are positive
They fall outside the Article 20 requirements entirely
They require the issuer's clearance before broadcast
They must guarantee a profit if widely shared
w: Media-distributed recommendations must meet the same disclosure and fair presentation requirements as formal reports.

n.2: Media recommendations are not outside Article 20.
n.1: Disclosure is required regardless of a positive rating.
n.4: No profit can or need be guaranteed.
n.3: Issuer clearance before broadcast is not required.

q: Why are conflict disclosures essential in investment recommendations under Article 20?
o: They guarantee the accuracy of the predictions
They shield analysts from insider dealing liability
They meet the firm's capital adequacy standards
They help investors judge potential bias in the analysis
They remove the need for market disclosures
w: Conflict disclosures allow investors to understand potential bias and make informed decisions.

n.1: Conflict disclosure gives no shield from insider-dealing liability.
n.0: It cannot guarantee the accuracy of predictions.
n.2: It is unrelated to capital adequacy standards.
n.4: It does not remove other market disclosure duties.

q: An analyst is writing an investment recommendation for publication to clients. Under Article 20, what must be avoided when issuing it?
o: Clear disclosure of methodologies used
Separation of fact and opinion in reports
Balanced analysis covering risks and benefits
Selective presentation designed to mislead
Open declaration of analyst shareholdings
w: Selective or misleading presentation violates Article 20, which requires fair and balanced analysis.

n.0: Disclosure of methodologies supports transparency and is required.
n.4: Declaration of shareholdings is mandatory for conflict transparency.
n.2: Balanced analysis is the goal of Article 20, not a breach.
n.1: Separation of fact and opinion ensures clarity, not a violation.

q: A freelance market commentator, not employed by any authorised firm, regularly posts buy and sell recommendations online and asks whether Article 20 of MAR applies to him. Which statement best reflects the scope of Article 20 obligations?
o: They apply only where the recommendation carries a positive rating
They apply only to firms authorised and regulated by the FCA
They apply to anyone producing or disseminating recommendations
They apply only to sell-side analysts at investment banks
They apply only to formally published equity research notes
w: Article 20 applies to any person producing or disseminating investment recommendations, not just authorised firms or analysts.

n.1: Article 20 is not confined to authorised firms.
n.3: It is not limited to sell-side analysts.
n.0: It applies regardless of a positive rating.
n.4: It is not restricted to equity research.

q: What does the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 define as criminal property?
o: Assets disclosed to the National Crime Agency
Property transferred between family members
Any property used in financial markets
Any benefit derived from criminal conduct
Property owned by a convicted individual
w: Criminal property is defined as any benefit derived from criminal conduct, regardless of who holds it.

n.2: Property used in financial markets is not automatically criminal without connection to crime, unlike benefits from criminal conduct.
n.4: Property owned by a convicted individual is not necessarily criminal unless it results from crime.
n.1: Transfers between family members are not criminal unless sourced from criminal conduct.
