n.3: Tipping off is a s333A offence, not s327.
n.0: Arrangements are covered by s328, not s327.
n.2: Prejudicing an investigation is s342, not s327.

q: Section 328 POCA makes it an offence to:
o: Prejudice an investigation into money laundering
Acquire or possess criminal property for personal use
Enter an arrangement facilitating use of criminal property
Fail to disclose a suspicious transaction to the MLRO
Conceal or convert criminal property to disguise it
w: Section 328 criminalises entering into arrangements to facilitate the retention or control of criminal property.

n.1: Acquisition, use or possession is a s329 offence.
n.4: Concealing or converting property is a s327 offence.
n.3: Failure to disclose is a s330 offence.
n.0: Prejudicing an investigation is a s342 offence.

q: A staff member is charged in connection with using funds that came from a client's criminal activity. Which conduct does Section 329 of POCA cover?
o: Overlooking accounting errors
Alerting a suspect of an SAR
Possessing criminal property
Ignoring client suitability checks
Failing to train employees
w: Section 329 makes it an offence to acquire, use, or possess criminal property.

n.1: Alerting suspects is tipping off under Section 333A.
n.4: Training duties are under MLR 2017, not POCA.
n.0: Accounting errors are not criminal property issues.
n.3: Suitability checks are under COBS, not POCA offences.

q: Under Section 330 POCA, what must a person in the regulated sector do?
o: Disclose suspicions of money laundering
File tax returns for clients
Seek legal advice before every transaction
Close accounts automatically
Refuse business with all cash clients
w: Section 330 requires persons in the regulated sector to disclose suspicions of money laundering.

n.1: Tax returns are not part of Section 330 duties.
n.4: Cash clients must be assessed individually, not refused outright.
n.3: Accounts are not closed automatically; suspicions are reported.
n.2: Legal advice is not a prerequisite for disclosure obligations.

q: A relationship manager has just submitted a Suspicious Activity Report on a client's account. Which of the following would amount to a tipping off offence under Section 333A?
o: Concealing funds offshore
Failing to report suspicions
Entering an arrangement with illicit funds
Telling a client an SAR is filed
Holding criminal property
w: Section 333A criminalises tipping off by disclosing that a Suspicious Activity Report has been made.

n.1: Failure to disclose falls under Section 330.
n.4: Holding criminal property is Section 329.
n.2: Arrangements with illicit funds are Section 328 offences.
n.0: Concealing property offshore is Section 327.

q: Section 342 POCA makes it an offence to:
o: Acquire, use or possess property known to be criminal
Conceal or disguise criminal property to hide its origin
Tip off a suspect that a disclosure has been made
Fail to disclose a suspicion to the nominated officer
Prejudice a money laundering investigation by destroying evidence
w: Section 342 criminalises prejudicing an investigation into money laundering, such as destroying evidence.

n.1: Concealing or disguising property is a s327 offence.
n.0: Acquisition, use or possession is a s329 offence.
n.3: Failure to disclose is a s330 offence.
n.2: Tipping off is a s333A offence.

q: What standard applies under the objective test in POCA for reporting suspicions?
o: Whether the client agrees to disclosure
Whether the employee is absolutely certain
Whether the FCA confirms suspicion
Whether a reasonable person would suspect
Whether the NCA issues a notice
w: The objective test requires reporting where a reasonable person with the same information would suspect money laundering.

n.2: FCA confirmation is not required for suspicion.
n.1: Absolute certainty is not needed; suspicion is enough.
n.4: An NCA notice is not needed before reporting.
n.0: Client agreement is irrelevant and disclosure is mandatory.

q: What is the correct internal reporting route for staff who suspect money laundering?
o: Directly to the FCA's financial crime department
Internally to the firm's MLRO or nominated officer
Directly to the local police fraud investigation unit
In writing to the Serious Fraud Office headquarters
To the National Crime Agency's public tip line
w: Staff must report suspicions internally to the Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO) or nominated officer.

n.0: Staff report internally first, not directly to the FCA.
n.2: The police are not the internal AML reporting route.
n.3: The SFO does not receive staff AML suspicion reports.
n.4: Staff report to the MLRO, who alone files SARs to the NCA.

q: Why is disclosure to the NCA considered a defence under POCA?
o: It transfers criminal liability onto the firm's auditors
It suspends the NCA investigation for a set period
Authorised disclosure to the NCA gives a statutory defence
It cancels the firm's ongoing AML compliance duties
It ends the firm's FCA supervision requirements
w: Making an authorised disclosure to the NCA demonstrates cooperation and provides a statutory defence against laundering offences.

n.0: Disclosure does not shift liability to auditors.
n.1: Disclosure does not suspend or delay the investigation.
n.4: Disclosure does not affect FCA supervision.
n.3: Disclosure does not remove any compliance obligations.

q: Which of the following is most likely to breach Section 333A tipping off provisions?
o: Conducting enhanced due diligence on the client
Escalating the suspicion internally to the firm's MLRO
Declining the transaction without giving any reason
Notifying a client their account is under AML review
Submitting a suspicious activity report to the NCA
w: Telling a client their account is under AML review constitutes tipping off under Section 333A.

n.1: Internal escalation to the MLRO is required, not tipping off.
n.4: Filing a SAR to the NCA is a legal duty, not tipping off.
n.2: Silently declining a transaction does not tip off.
n.0: Enhanced due diligence is a compliance measure, not tipping off.

q: A relationship manager at a regulated bank fails to act on clear grounds for suspicion about a customer. Which of these is a Section 330 offence in the regulated sector?
o: Alerting a suspect that a SAR has been submitted
Destroying documents during a laundering investigation
Arranging the transfer of criminal property abroad
Concealing criminal cash by depositing it in a bank
Failing to report a suspicion of money laundering
w: Section 330 makes it an offence in the regulated sector to fail to disclose a suspicion of money laundering.

n.3: Concealing property is a s327 offence, not s330.
n.2: Transferring criminal property is s327/328, not s330.
n.0: Tipping off is a s333A offence, not s330.
n.1: Prejudicing an investigation is s342, not s330.

q: An employee learns that a colleague has filed a Suspicious Activity Report on a client and is tempted to mention it. Under Section 333A, which behaviour is prohibited?
o: Structuring deposits to avoid reporting
Failing to implement due diligence
Acquiring criminal property for personal gain
Not reporting suspicions to the MLRO
Disclosing that a SAR has been filed
w: Section 333A criminalises tipping off, including disclosing that a Suspicious Activity Report has been filed.

n.3: Not reporting suspicions is covered by Section 330, not 333A.
n.2: Acquisition of property is Section 329, not 333A.
n.1: Due diligence failures are MLR issues, not Section 333A.
n.0: Structuring deposits is placement activity, not a 333A offence.

q: During a money laundering investigation, an employee shreds relevant client files. Which of the following is a Section 342 offence under POCA?
o: Failing to escalate a suspicion to the firm's MLRO
Concealing illicit funds by depositing them in accounts
Destroying documents to obstruct a laundering investigation
Arranging loans backed by known criminal property
Alerting a client that a SAR has been filed on them
w: Section 342 criminalises acts like destroying documents to prejudice an investigation into laundering.

n.1: Concealing funds is a s327 offence, not s342.
n.3: Arrangements involving criminal property is s328, not s342.
n.4: Tipping off is a s333A offence, not s342.
n.0: Failure to disclose is a s330 offence, not s342.

q: What is the main implication of the objective test in POCA Part 7?
o: Suspicion must be reported even if uncertain
Only transactions above £5,000 must be disclosed
Employees must seek client consent first
Only senior managers may file SARs
Court approval is needed before reporting
w: The objective test means suspicions must be reported even if evidence is not conclusive.

n.3: All relevant employees must report, not just senior managers.
n.1: There is no monetary threshold for reporting.
n.4: Court approval is not required for SARs.
n.2: Client consent must not be sought, as it risks tipping off.

q: A back-office clerk becomes suspicious that a transaction may involve laundered funds. What is the correct internal reporting obligation for staff in this situation?
o: Report the concern directly to the affected client
Report the suspicion in writing to the High Court
Report the suspicion directly to the FCA supervisor
Report the matter directly to the Serious Fraud Office
Report the suspicion to the nominated officer or MLRO
w: Staff must report suspicions internally to the nominated officer or MLRO.

n.2: Staff report internally to the MLRO, not directly to the FCA.
n.3: The SFO is not the internal AML reporting channel.
n.1: The courts do not receive staff AML suspicion reports.
n.0: Telling the client would risk tipping off.

q: What role does the National Crime Agency play under POCA?
o: It maintains and updates the Corporate Governance Code
It issues the FCA's enforcement and penalty notices
It sets the UK's accounting and auditing standards
It receives and processes suspicious activity reports
It prosecutes all insider dealing cases in the UK
w: The NCA is the authority that receives and analyses suspicious activity reports under POCA.

n.4: Insider dealing is prosecuted by the FCA, not the NCA.
n.1: Enforcement notices are issued by the FCA.
n.0: The Corporate Governance Code is maintained by the FRC.
n.2: Accounting standards are set by the FRC, not the NCA.

q: An employee who becomes suspicious of a client makes an internal report to the MLRO. Why does such disclosure act as a defence against certain POCA offences?
o: It ends the firm's FCA regulatory obligations
It shifts the suspicion onto another named employee
It removes the need for future regulatory audits
It delays the money laundering investigation process
It demonstrates compliance with internal reporting duties
w: Internal disclosure to the MLRO shows compliance and provides a defence against liability for handling criminal property.

n.1: Disclosure does not transfer suspicion to a colleague.
n.3: Disclosure does not delay the investigation.
n.0: Disclosure does not affect FCA regulation.
n.2: Disclosure does not remove audit obligations.

q: A compliance officer is drafting AML training and lists the offences under POCA Part 7. Which of the following should NOT appear on that list?
o: Failing to disclose suspicions
Arranging deals with illicit funds
Providing poor investment advice
Concealing criminal property
Possessing stolen assets
w: Poor investment advice is not a money laundering offence; the others are covered under POCA Part 7.

n.3: Concealment of criminal property is an offence under Section 327.
n.1: Arrangements with illicit funds are criminalised under Section 328.
n.4: Possession of criminal property is criminalised under Section 329.
n.0: Failure to disclose suspicions is a Section 330 offence.

q: Which section of POCA deals with possession of criminal property?
o: Section 328
Section 333A
Section 330
Section 327
Section 329
w: Section 329 makes it an offence to acquire, use, or possess criminal property.

n.3: Section 327 concerns concealing, not possession.
n.0: Section 328 is about arrangements with criminal property.
n.2: Section 330 concerns failure to disclose suspicions.
n.1: Section 333A covers tipping off, not possession.

q: An employee learns that authorities have begun an inquiry into a client and takes an action that could hamper it. Which of the following would amount to prejudicing an investigation under Section 342?
o: Informing a client that a SAR has been made on them
Destroying client records after learning of an inquiry
Depositing criminal funds into a personal bank account
Using laundered money to purchase residential property
Failing to disclose the suspicion to the firm's MLRO
w: Section 342 makes it an offence to prejudice an investigation, such as destroying evidence after learning of an inquiry.

n.2: Depositing criminal funds is concealment under s327.
n.3: Using laundered money is a s327/329 offence, not s342.
n.4: Failure to disclose is a s330 offence, not s342.
n.0: Tipping off is s333A, not prejudicing an investigation.

q: Which section of POCA criminalises concealing, disguising, converting, or transferring criminal property?
o: Section 328
Section 329
Section 327
Section 342
Section 330
w: Section 327 criminalises concealing, disguising, converting, transferring, or removing criminal property.

n.0: s328 covers arrangements facilitating criminal property.
n.1: s329 covers acquisition, use or possession.
n.4: s330 covers failure to disclose in the regulated sector.
n.3: s342 covers prejudicing an investigation.

q: Which section of POCA criminalises acquisition, use, or possession of criminal property?
o: Section 329
Section 328
Section 330
Section 333A
Section 327
w: Section 329 makes it an offence to acquire, use, or possess criminal property.

n.4: Section 327 criminalises concealing or disguising property, not possession.
n.1: Section 328 covers arrangements, not possession.
n.2: Section 330 covers failure to disclose, not possession.
n.3: Section 333A covers tipping off.

q: An adviser in the regulated sector forms a suspicion of money laundering but does not report it. Which section of POCA deals with failure to disclose in the regulated sector?
o: Section 330
Section 327
Section 329
Section 342
Section 328
w: Section 330 criminalises failing to disclose a suspicion of money laundering in the regulated sector.

n.1: s327 covers concealing or converting criminal property.
n.4: s328 covers arrangements involving criminal property.
n.2: s329 covers acquisition, use or possession.
n.3: s342 covers prejudicing an investigation.

q: What does Section 333A of POCA prohibit?
o: Concealing cash deposits
Tipping off by alerting suspects
Failing to disclose a suspicion
Arranging financial transfers abroad
Destroying documents during an investigation
w: Section 333A prohibits tipping off by alerting suspects to investigations or SARs.

n.2: Failure to disclose is a Section 330 offence, not 333A.
n.4: Destroying documents prejudices investigations under Section 342.
n.0: Concealing deposits is a Section 327 offence.
n.3: Arranging transfers abroad may fall under Section 328.

q: Which section of POCA criminalises prejudicing a money laundering investigation?
o: Section 333A
Section 329
Section 342
Section 328
Section 327
w: Section 342 makes it an offence to prejudice an investigation, for example by destroying or falsifying evidence.

n.4: Section 327 concerns concealing criminal property.
n.3: Section 328 relates to arrangements with illicit funds.
n.1: Section 329 is about possession or use, not investigations.
n.0: Section 333A relates to tipping off, not prejudicing investigations.

q: An MLRO is deciding whether a nervous adviser's report about a client should be treated as suspicion under POCA Part 7. What does the objective test in Part 7 mean for how that suspicion is judged?
o: Suspicion is judged by the reasonable person standard
It permits firms to disregard minor suspicions raised
It requires court approval before any SAR is filed
It requires absolute proof that property is criminal
It requires client consent before any disclosure is made
w: The objective test ensures that suspicion is judged by what a reasonable person would suspect given the same information.

n.3: The test needs reasonable grounds to suspect, not absolute proof.
n.1: Suspicions cannot be disregarded because they seem minor.
n.2: No court approval is needed to file a SAR.
n.4: Client consent is not required and would risk tipping off.

q: What is a valid defence against a Section 327 offence?
o: Claiming ignorance of the client’s background
Obtaining approval from the FCA
Making an authorised disclosure to the NCA
Maintaining client confidentiality
Completing due diligence late
w: Making an authorised disclosure to the NCA is a statutory defence against Section 327 offences.

n.0: Ignorance of background is not a defence under POCA.
n.4: Late due diligence does not prevent liability.
n.1: FCA approval does not replace disclosure obligations.
n.3: Client confidentiality cannot override statutory disclosure duties.

q: A junior analyst becomes suspicious that a client's funds may derive from crime. Under POCA, what is the correct internal disclosure obligation?
o: Staff must notify the MLRO promptly
Staff must escalate to auditors first
Staff must notify clients of concerns
Staff must contact the FCA directly
Staff must file SARs personally with the NCA
w: Staff must report suspicions internally to the MLRO or nominated officer before any external filing.

n.3: The FCA is not the internal reporting channel.
n.2: Informing clients risks tipping off and is prohibited.
n.4: SARs are submitted by the MLRO, not every employee directly.
n.1: Auditors are not the correct disclosure channel under POCA.

q: An MLRO is explaining to staff why the tipping-off offence under Section 333A is treated so seriously. What is the main reason for its severity?
o: It raises the firm's operational compliance costs
It risks prejudicing law enforcement investigations
It lowers customer satisfaction and retention scores
It reduces the firm's mandatory AML training duties
It amounts to a direct breach of the Companies Act 2006
w: Tipping off is serious because it risks prejudicing law enforcement investigations into money laundering.

n.0: Tipping off's gravity is legal, not about costs.
n.4: Tipping off is a POCA offence, not a Companies Act breach.
n.2: Its seriousness is obstructing justice, not customer metrics.
n.3: It does not affect training obligations.

q: Which is a key implication of POCA Part 7 for firms?
o: Only senior managers need to receive AML training
Reporting duties apply only to cash transactions
Court approval is required before any disclosure
All suspicions must be proven before being reported
Suspicious activity reports must be filed promptly
w: POCA Part 7 requires firms to file Suspicious Activity Reports promptly when suspicions arise.

n.0: Relevant staff, not only senior managers, need AML training.
n.3: Reasonable suspicion, not proof, triggers reporting.
n.1: Reporting duties cover all activity, not just cash.
n.2: No court approval is needed to disclose.

q: A new compliance analyst is asked where the FCA's rules on systems and controls to combat financial crime are found. Which handbook sourcebook sets out those requirements?
o: SYSC
COBS
ICOBS
MAR
CASS
w: The SYSC sourcebook contains rules on systems and controls for financial crime prevention, including money laundering obligations.

n.1: COBS governs conduct of business, not AML systems.
n.4: CASS sets client asset rules, not AML controls.
n.3: MAR covers market abuse, not financial crime systems.
n.2: ICOBS applies to insurance conduct, not AML controls.

q: Under SYSC, who is primarily responsible for oversight of AML systems within a firm?
o: The FCA supervisory team directly oversees it
Independent external compliance consultants
The client's own appointed external auditor
The PRA's prudential supervision team directly
The firm's senior management under SYSC rules
w: SYSC places responsibility on senior management to ensure effective AML systems and controls are in place.

n.0: SYSC places the duty on the firm, not the FCA directly.
n.3: The PRA does not run a firm's AML systems.
n.1: Responsibility cannot be outsourced to consultants.
n.2: The client's auditor has no such oversight role.

q: A junior member of staff who spots a suspicious transaction is told to escalate it internally. Under SYSC, what is the role of the Money Laundering Reporting Officer in what happens next?
o: To manage firm-wide IT policies
To draft client contracts
To approve all customer transactions
To submit SARs to the NCA
To conduct investment suitability reviews
w: The MLRO’s role includes receiving internal reports and submitting Suspicious Activity Reports to the NCA.

n.2: MLROs do not approve every transaction; they review suspicious activity.
n.4: Suitability reviews are a conduct requirement, not an MLRO duty.
n.0: IT policies are not within the MLRO’s AML role.
n.1: Client contracts are not an MLRO function.

q: A compliance manager is citing the specific SYSC provision that obliges the firm to maintain systems and controls against financial crime. Which provision is it?
o: SYSC 7.1.2
SYSC 4.3.4
SYSC 2.2.9
SYSC 3.2.6
SYSC 1.1.1
w: SYSC 3.2.6 requires firms to establish systems and controls to counter financial crime, including money laundering.

n.4: SYSC 1.1.1 is an application provision, not financial crime systems.
n.1: SYSC 4.3.4 does not set the financial crime systems requirement.
n.0: SYSC 7.1.2 concerns risk control, not the AML systems rule.
n.2: SYSC 2.2.9 is not the financial crime provision.

q: Which officer typically acts as the nominated officer for AML purposes in a firm?
o: The firm's appointed Chief Risk Officer
The firm's external statutory auditor
The firm's in-house legal counsel team
The firm's Chief Financial Officer
The Money Laundering Reporting Officer
w: The MLRO is usually designated as the nominated officer responsible for AML reporting within the firm.

n.3: The CFO handles finance, not AML reporting.
n.0: The CRO manages risk generally, not the nominated officer role.
n.1: An external auditor cannot be the nominated officer.
n.2: Legal counsel does not act as the nominated officer.

q: Which regulator applies SYSC rules to ensure firms maintain adequate AML systems?
o: The Insolvency Service
The Bank of England alone
FCA and PRA
HMRC only
Companies House
w: Both the FCA and PRA apply SYSC to ensure firms maintain adequate AML systems and controls.

n.3: HMRC supervises certain businesses but not FCA/PRA regulated firms.
n.0: The Insolvency Service has no role in AML controls.
n.4: Companies House registers companies but does not apply SYSC rules.
n.1: The Bank of England oversees monetary policy, not SYSC rules directly.

q: Which of the following is a key system required under SYSC 3.2.6 (A)-(J)?
o: Publishing regulatory market announcements
Daily reconciliation of client share prices
Recording clients' marketing consent preferences
A risk assessment of money laundering exposure
Calculating interest rate swap valuations
w: SYSC 3.2.6 requires risk-based systems, including assessment of exposure to money laundering risk.

n.1: Share-price reconciliation is not an AML systems requirement.
n.0: Market announcements are unrelated to AML controls.
n.2: Marketing preferences are not part of financial crime systems.
n.4: Swap valuation is a market task, not an AML control.

q: During an FCA visit, an MLRO is asked to demonstrate how the firm meets its anti-money-laundering obligations. Which SYSC requirement applies specifically to record-keeping of AML controls?
o: Firms must publish all employee emails
Firms must report only annual profits
Firms must submit client complaints monthly
Firms must maintain evidence of compliance
Firms must archive marketing materials
w: SYSC requires firms to maintain clear records to demonstrate compliance with AML systems and controls.

n.1: Profit reporting is unrelated to SYSC AML obligations.
n.0: Publishing emails is not an AML requirement.
n.4: Marketing materials are not the focus of SYSC AML rules.
n.2: Client complaint reporting is a DISP requirement, not SYSC AML.

q: A newly authorised firm is putting its financial crime governance in place under SYSC 6.3. Who must it appoint for AML oversight?
o: A dedicated Money Laundering Reporting Officer
An external financial crime consultancy firm
A junior compliance trainee to hold the role
An independent non-executive board director
A dedicated FCA on-site supervisory officer
w: SYSC 6.3 requires firms to appoint a dedicated MLRO with responsibility for AML oversight.

n.1: The MLRO must be internal, not an outside consultancy.
n.2: The role requires seniority, not a trainee.
n.3: A NED is not the required AML appointment.
n.4: The FCA does not supply a firm's MLRO.

q: A compliance officer is reviewing the firm's AML framework against the FCA's expectations in SYSC 6.3. What is one of those expectations?
o: That firms eliminate every client complaint received
That firms maintain effective internal reporting procedures
That firms apply identical controls ignoring risk
That firms outsource the entire AML function abroad
That firms guarantee complete prevention of all fraud
w: SYSC 6.3 requires firms to maintain effective procedures for reporting and monitoring AML issues internally.

n.4: No firm can guarantee total fraud prevention.
n.0: AML systems are not about eliminating complaints.
n.3: The AML function cannot be wholly outsourced.
n.2: Controls must be risk-based, not identical for all.

q: What is the key aim of SYSC rules on systems and controls?
o: To remove all competition between regulated firms
To ensure firms manage financial crime risks effectively
To regulate international trade tariffs and duties
To control foreign exchange rates in the market
To dictate the investment strategy for every client
w: SYSC rules aim to ensure firms establish systems and controls to manage financial crime risks effectively.

n.4: SYSC does not set client investment strategies.
n.0: SYSC does not aim to remove competition.
n.2: Trade tariffs are outside SYSC's scope.
n.3: Exchange rates are not controlled by SYSC.

q: A firm is reviewing its governance to reduce financial crime risk. What must the firm ensure under SYSC 3.2.6(A)?
o: Effective allocation of responsibilities within the firm
Quarterly reporting of firm profits to the FCA
Automatic approval of every client transaction
Annual publication of staff training statistics
External review of all client contracts yearly
w: SYSC 3.2.6 (A) requires effective allocation of responsibilities within firms to reduce financial crime risk.

n.1: Profit reporting is not a SYSC 3.2.6(A) requirement.
n.3: Publishing training statistics is not required.
n.2: Transactions must be monitored, not auto-approved.
n.4: External contract review is not the (A) requirement.

q: What is the MLRO required to do when receiving internal disclosures?
o: Submit a SAR to the NCA where suspicion is justified
File the annual tax returns for the firm's clients
Approve the firm's outgoing marketing campaigns
Set the interest rates charged on client loans
Audit and approve the board meeting minutes
w: The MLRO must consider internal disclosures and submit SARs to the NCA if suspicion is justified.

n.2: Marketing approval is not an MLRO duty.
n.3: Setting loan rates is unrelated to the MLRO role.
n.1: The MLRO does not file client tax returns.
n.4: Auditing board minutes is not an MLRO function.

q: Why does SYSC require firms to have effective internal reporting procedures?
o: To standardise the investment returns paid to clients
To increase the firm's shareholder dividend payouts
To streamline the firm's HR recruitment process
To let suspicions be escalated internally and addressed
To cut the firm's annual compliance training budget
w: Internal reporting procedures allow suspicions of money laundering to be escalated and addressed through the MLRO.

n.1: Internal reporting is unrelated to dividends.
n.2: It serves AML, not recruitment.
n.4: Its purpose is escalation, not cutting training.
n.0: It does not standardise investment returns.

q: A compliance officer is reviewing the firm's AML arrangements against SYSC 6.3. Which of the following is NOT an FCA expectation under that section?
o: Documenting AML policies and procedures
Guaranteeing zero suspicious activity
Maintaining proportionate AML systems
Appointing an MLRO
Ensuring effective reporting lines
w: The FCA expects robust systems, not a guarantee of zero suspicious activity, which is unrealistic.

n.3: Appointing an MLRO is explicitly required by SYSC 6.3.
n.2: Proportionate AML systems are required by FCA rules.
n.4: Effective reporting lines are required under SYSC.
n.0: AML policies and procedures must be documented under FCA rules.

q: What is one function of SYSC 3.2.6 (B)?
o: Maintaining adequate resources for AML compliance
Conducting external client satisfaction surveys
Managing the firm's corporate branding strategy
Filing shareholder resolutions with the registry
Publishing the firm's regulated investment advice
w: SYSC 3.2.6 (B) requires firms to maintain adequate resources to ensure AML compliance.

n.4: Publishing advice is unrelated to AML resourcing.
n.1: Client surveys are not a SYSC 3.2.6(B) function.
n.2: Branding is not an AML systems requirement.
n.3: Filing resolutions is not part of AML compliance.

q: Which officer must be a point of contact with regulators on AML matters?
o: The firm's appointed external auditor
The firm's Chief Investment Officer
The firm's Chief Executive Officer
The Money Laundering Reporting Officer
The firm's head of marketing function
w: The MLRO serves as the point of contact with regulators on AML matters.

n.2: The CEO is not the AML regulatory contact.
n.1: The CIO handles investments, not AML liaison.
n.0: An external auditor is not the AML contact point.
n.4: The head of marketing has no AML liaison role.

q: A compliance officer at a wealth manager is reviewing whether the firm's systems and controls meet the FCA's expectations under SYSC. Which of the following is one of those expectations?
o: Defining the firm's corporate tax planning policy
Setting the country's national interest rate
Publishing the firm's analyst recommendations
Guaranteeing profits on every client account
Regular AML training for all relevant staff
w: SYSC and FCA guidance expect firms to provide regular AML training to staff whose roles are relevant to financial crime prevention.

n.3: Firms cannot guarantee client profits.
n.2: Publishing analyst notes is unrelated to SYSC AML duties.
n.1: Interest rates are set by the Bank of England, not firms.
n.0: Tax policy is not a SYSC AML expectation.

q: A firm's staff handbook describes the MLRO's role under POCA and SYSC. Which of the following is a core responsibility of the nominated officer?
o: Receiving internal disclosures of suspicion from staff
Designing the firm's corporate logos and branding
Setting employee compensation levels across the firm
Providing tax planning services to the firm's clients
Approving the firm's external advertising campaigns
w: The nominated officer (often the MLRO) is responsible for receiving internal disclosures of suspicion.

n.3: Tax planning is not a nominated officer duty.
n.2: Pay is not set by the nominated officer.
n.1: Branding design is unrelated to the AML role.
n.4: Advertising approval is not a nominated officer function.

q: Which principle underpins SYSC’s requirements for AML systems?
o: A marketing-led approach
A risk-based approach
A cost-minimisation approach
A client-consent approach
A fixed uniform approach
w: SYSC requires firms to apply a risk-based approach to AML systems and controls.

n.4: Controls should vary by risk, not be uniform.
n.2: Cost minimisation cannot override AML obligations.
n.0: Marketing priorities do not determine AML systems.
n.3: Client consent is irrelevant to AML reporting obligations.

q: A compliance officer at an investment firm is documenting the AML governance framework required by SYSC 3.2.6 (C). Which of the following is one of the responsibilities it sets out?
o: Setting the firm's client loan interest rate policy
Publishing the firm's annual dividend forecasts
Defining the firm's corporate branding guidelines
Establishing clear reporting lines for AML compliance
Approving all of the firm's IT procurement spend
w: SYSC 3.2.6 (C) requires firms to establish clear reporting lines to ensure AML compliance and accountability.

n.0: Interest rate policy is not a SYSC 3.2.6(C) matter.
n.2: Branding is unrelated to AML reporting lines.
n.1: Dividend forecasts are not part of this rule.
n.4: IT procurement approval is not required here.

q: A firm's internal audit team wants to know which SYSC rule requires it to assess the effectiveness of its anti-money laundering systems regularly. Which rule applies?
o: SYSC 1.1.1
SYSC 4.4.1
SYSC 7.1.2
SYSC 3.2.6 (E)
SYSC 2.2.9
w: SYSC 3.2.6 (E) requires regular assessment of AML system effectiveness.

n.0: SYSC 1.1.1 is an application provision, not the AML review rule.
n.2: SYSC 7.1.2 concerns risk control, not AML system review.
n.4: SYSC 2.2.9 does not require AML effectiveness review.
n.1: SYSC 4.4.1 is not the AML monitoring provision.

q: A firm is reviewing its internal controls to reduce the risk of AML failings. Which system is expected under SYSC 3.2.6 (D)?
o: Quarterly dividend analysis
Client entertainment approvals
Adequate segregation of duties
Annual product marketing campaigns

n.0: Relocation frequency is not the reason.
n.2: PEPs are not barred from offshore accounts.
n.3: PEPs can undergo due diligence; that is not the reason.

q: When assessing the risk posed by a PEP, what additional measure is typically required by firms?
o: Automatic refusal of account opening
Imposition of higher banking charges
Verification of source of wealth and funds
Review of personal social media accounts
Requirement to hold assets in sterling only
w: Enhanced due diligence requires firms to establish the legitimacy of the PEP’s source of wealth and funds. This helps identify if money is derived from corrupt practices and ensures the integrity of the financial system.

n.3: Social media activity is not part of mandated checks, although adverse media screening is common.
n.0: PEPs are not automatically refused service; they require additional checks and monitoring.
n.1: Enhanced due diligence does not involve imposing higher fees.
n.4: There is no requirement for PEPs to hold assets only in sterling.

q: Which relationship is most likely to make someone a PEP under JMLSG guidance?
o: Being the spouse of a senior government minister
Being a frequently published university academic
Being a director of a small private UK company
Being a high-earning corporate finance lawyer
Being a widely known professional sports athlete
w: Close family members of individuals in prominent public functions are also classified as politically exposed persons. This extension recognises the risk of corruption being facilitated through relatives.

n.3: High income alone does not create PEP status.
n.4: Fame as an athlete does not make a PEP.
n.2: A private company directorship is not a public function.
n.1: An academic does not hold a prominent public function.

q: During onboarding, a firm's checks reveal that a prospective client is a politically exposed person. What must the firm do before establishing the relationship?
o: Cap the client's access to international payments
Obtain senior management approval before onboarding
Notify the client's current employer immediately
Require the client to file quarterly income reports
Reject the client's application without any review
w: JMLSG requires firms to obtain senior management approval before establishing a business relationship with a politically exposed person. This ensures that risks are considered at the highest level of decision-making.

n.4: PEPs are not automatically rejected.
n.3: Quarterly income reports are not required.
n.0: Enhanced due diligence does not mean capping payments.
n.2: Informing the employer is not required and risks tipping off.

q: Which category of persons is NOT typically considered a PEP under JMLSG?
o: Heads of major state-owned enterprises
Senior military officers of a state
Sitting members of a national parliament
Accredited ambassadors and senior diplomats
Local government primary school teachers
w: Local government school teachers are not classified as politically exposed persons. The definition is limited to those holding high-level public functions or their associates.

n.1: Senior military officials are PEPs.
n.0: Heads of state-owned enterprises are PEPs.
n.2: MPs hold a prominent public function and are PEPs.
n.3: Ambassadors are PEPs.

q: Why is ongoing monitoring particularly important for relationships with PEPs?
o: Because their accounts must be frozen after a year
Because they are barred from using any credit cards
Because they are exempt from standard due diligence
Because their risk can change during time in public office
Because they must report their investments publicly
w: Ongoing monitoring is crucial because the level of risk associated with a PEP can change over time, particularly during or after their time in office. Continuous monitoring helps identify suspicious activities as circumstances evolve.

n.2: PEPs are not exempt from due diligence.
n.0: Their accounts are not frozen after a year.
n.1: They are not barred from credit cards.
n.4: They need not report investments publicly.

q: When does a person typically stop being treated as a PEP under UK regulations?
o: Once the person closes every overseas account held
Once the person reaches the state retirement age
As soon as the person relocates outside the UK
After leaving the prominent role for at least 12 months
Immediately upon leaving the public role held
w: UK regulations generally apply PEP treatment for at least 12 months after the individual ceases to hold a prominent public function. This cooling-off period accounts for the residual risk of influence and misuse of power.

n.4: Risk persists, so status does not end immediately.
n.1: Retirement age does not end PEP status.
n.2: Relocation does not remove PEP status.
n.0: Closing overseas accounts does not end it.

q: Which of the following best describes an 'associated PEP'?
o: A live-in domestic household employee or servant
The head teacher of a fee-paying private school
A close business associate of a senior politician
A generally wealthy self-made entrepreneur
A mid-ranking civil servant within a ministry
w: Associated PEPs include close business partners of individuals holding prominent public functions. This reflects the risk that influence and corruption can be channelled indirectly.

n.3: Personal wealth alone does not create associated-PEP status.
n.4: A mid-level civil servant is not an associated PEP.
n.1: A private head teacher is not a PEP associate.
n.0: A household employee is not an associated PEP.

q: What type of risk assessment must firms carry out when dealing with PEPs?
o: A fixed checklist of the client's personal preferences
A personality test gauging the client's trustworthiness
A geography-only assessment of the client's country
A risk-based review of role, country and connections
A purely financial creditworthiness check alone
w: Enhanced due diligence for PEPs requires a holistic, risk-based assessment considering the individual’s role, jurisdiction, business connections, and potential exposure to corruption.

n.0: A preferences checklist is not an AML risk review.
n.1: Trustworthiness personality tests are not used.
n.4: Creditworthiness alone is not a PEP risk assessment.
n.2: Geography alone is insufficient for PEP risk.

q: A firm's senior management is drafting its high-level AML policy statement in line with JMLSG guidance. What must they explicitly address to satisfy regulatory expectations?
o: A full list of competitor firms in the same market
The firm's annual marketing budget and growth targets
Commitment to a compliance culture and sufficient resources
A breakdown of client profitability by market segment
A promise that low-risk clients are never reviewed
w: Regulators expect high-level AML policy statements to set the tone from the top, showing commitment to compliance and ensuring adequate resources are dedicated to AML/CFT systems. This requirement is critical to embedding a culture of compliance and accountability throughout the firm.

n.1: Marketing budgets are not part of an AML policy statement.
n.3: Customer profitability is not an AML policy element.
n.0: Competitor lists are irrelevant to AML policy.
n.4: All clients must be subject to review; none are never reviewed.

q: An MLRO is designing the firm's AML framework in line with JMLSG guidance. Which element most accurately reflects the purpose of a risk-based approach?
o: Refusing to engage any client in a higher-risk sector
Proportionate controls based on client, product and country risk
Building a simpler framework only to cut staff workload
Relying on external auditors to spot all AML risks
Applying identical due diligence to all clients alike
w: The risk-based approach is central to JMLSG guidance. It requires firms to assess inherent risks from clients, products, services, and geographies, and to calibrate controls accordingly. This ensures resources are directed effectively without creating a one-size-fits-all system.

n.4: Due diligence must vary with risk, not be identical.
n.2: The aim is effective control, not reduced workload.
n.3: Firms cannot rely on auditors to find all risks.
n.0: Higher-risk sectors are managed, not blanket-refused.

q: The FCA asks a firm to prove that its high-level AML policy is actually being applied, consistent with JMLSG recommendations. How should the firm evidence this?
o: Keeping only verbal assurances from senior management
Giving regulators copies of competitors' AML policies
Documenting procedures, staff training and monitoring outcomes
Showing high profitability across all client accounts
Restricting all business to low-risk clients only
w: Evidence of compliance must be demonstrable and auditable. This includes documented procedures, training programmes, and monitoring records. Regulators require proof that the firm’s policy has been implemented and is effective in practice, not just on paper.

n.0: Verbal assurances alone do not evidence compliance.
n.3: Profitability does not demonstrate AML compliance.
n.1: Competitors' policies do not evidence a firm's own compliance.
n.4: Restricting to low-risk clients is not evidence of the policy.

q: Which risk factor is most critical under JMLSG when determining the intensity of customer due diligence?
o: The client’s preference for in-person versus digital banking
The frequency of client interactions with staff
The geographic location and associated jurisdictional risks
The length of time the client has been with the firm
The client’s chosen investment portfolio performance
w: Jurisdictional risk is a key factor in assessing AML risk. Clients from countries with weak AML controls or high corruption levels pose heightened risks, requiring enhanced due diligence. This aligns with FATF recommendations and JMLSG guidance.

n.1: Interaction frequency has little impact on inherent AML risk.
n.0: Client channel preference is operational, not risk-based.
n.4: Investment performance is irrelevant to AML risk.
n.3: Length of relationship may influence familiarity but does not determine inherent risk level.

q: A firm's compliance head presents the updated AML policy to the board for sign-off. Under JMLSG, why is senior management approval of the policy required?
o: To reassure clients about the firm's financial results
To shift responsibility away from compliance staff
To show accountability and direct resources appropriately
Only to protect the firm against reputational loss
To avoid the need for further regulatory inspections
w: Senior management approval ensures accountability at the highest level. Regulators expect leadership to own AML policies and confirm that adequate resources, systems, and staff are in place to manage risks effectively.

n.3: The purpose is broader than reputation alone.
n.4: Approval does not remove regulatory inspections.
n.1: It does not shift responsibility off compliance.
n.0: It is not about reassuring clients on profits.

q: How do firms apply proportionality under JMLSG’s risk-based approach?
o: Reducing due diligence where operating costs are high
Scaling due diligence to match the assessed risk profile
Focusing solely on financial sanctions screening
Exempting politically exposed persons from extra checks
Applying the same measures to all clients for consistency
w: Proportionality is central to a risk-based approach. It allows firms to apply simplified due diligence for low-risk customers and enhanced due diligence for higher-risk ones, ensuring resources are targeted effectively.

n.4: Identical measures are the opposite of proportionality.
n.0: Due diligence is set by risk, not cost.
n.3: PEPs require enhanced, not reduced, checks.
n.2: Proportionality covers more than sanctions screening.

q: Which of the following best describes the function of ongoing monitoring under JMLSG’s risk-based procedures?
o: To automate all due diligence with no staff input
To evaluate the profitability of each business unit
To give regulators a forecast of future client growth
To reassure shareholders about long-term firm returns
To flag transactions that do not fit the client's profile
w: Ongoing monitoring is designed to ensure that client activity remains consistent with expected patterns and risk assessments. It is a key mechanism for detecting money laundering or terrorist financing in real time.

n.1: Monitoring targets suspicious activity, not profitability.
n.2: It is not a client growth forecast.
n.3: It is unrelated to shareholder reassurance.
n.0: Monitoring supports, not replaces, staff judgement.

q: A small firm considers simply copying an off-the-shelf AML template. Following JMLSG guidance, why must its AML procedures instead be tailored?
o: Because regulators reject all published industry guidance
Because templates are banned under UK AML regulations
Because staff cannot understand any standardised template
Because each firm's clients and channels pose unique risks
Because tailored procedures raise the firm's profits
w: JMLSG stresses that AML procedures must reflect the specific risks of the firm. A generic template cannot adequately address differences in client types, jurisdictions, and services offered, which regulators expect firms to consider.

n.0: Regulators accept industry guidance like JMLSG.
n.2: Staff can understand templates; that is not the reason.
n.1: Templates are not unlawful.
n.4: Tailoring is about risk, not profit.

q: Under JMLSG, how should a firm demonstrate that its AML policy is effectively implemented?
o: Through internal audits, testing and corrective action records
By issuing annual press releases about its commitment
By taking out insurance against any AML breaches
By publishing a yearly client satisfaction survey result
By benchmarking against industry profitability levels
w: Implementation must be evidenced through ongoing compliance testing, independent internal audits, and documentation of corrective actions. Regulators require proof that the policy is operational, not just theoretical.

n.1: Press releases do not evidence implementation.
n.4: Profitability benchmarking is not evidence of AML.
n.3: Satisfaction surveys do not show AML implementation.
n.2: Insurance does not demonstrate compliance.

q: An FCA supervisor is reviewing a firm's documented risk-based AML procedures during a visit. What does the regulator expect those procedures to demonstrate?
o: That they link identified risks to proportionate controls
That they detail relationship managers' remuneration
That they treat every client as low-risk to save cost
That they describe the firm's full competitive strategy
That they include forecasts of next year's turnover
w: Regulators expect documented procedures to show how risks are identified and managed through proportionate controls. They assess whether monitoring aligns with the risk-based framework set out in JMLSG guidance.

n.4: Turnover forecasts are not part of AML procedures.
n.3: Competitive strategy is irrelevant to AML review.
n.1: Staff pay detail is not expected here.
n.2: Treating all clients as low-risk defeats the risk-based approach.

q: Under JMLSG guidance, what is the principal obligation of firms in relation to the UK financial sanctions regime?
o: Give sanctioned persons limited retail banking access
To verify the profitability of every client each year
Not make funds available to any sanctioned person or entity
To disclose internal profit margins to HM Treasury
Exempt politically exposed persons from sanctions checks
w: Firms must ensure that they do not make funds or economic resources available, directly or indirectly, to designated persons or entities. Compliance with sanctions lists, maintained by OFSI and other authorities, is mandatory and forms a cornerstone of the financial crime framework.

n.1: Sanctions duty is not about client profitability.
n.0: Sanctioned persons must get no access, not limited access.
n.3: Profit margins need not be disclosed to HM Treasury.
n.4: PEPs are still subject to sanctions checks.

q: During screening, a firm identifies a potential match between a client and a name on the sanctions list. Under JMLSG guidance, what is the immediate step required?
o: Seek the client's consent before acting further
Halt all transactions and report the match to OFSI
Escalate the matter to the firm's marketing team
Continue transactions until the regulator confirms
Immediately notify the matched client's own employer
w: When a sanctions match is suspected, firms must freeze the account, halt transactions, and report immediately to OFSI. Transactions cannot proceed until confirmation and specific instructions are given by the competent authority.

n.4: The employer is not notified on a sanctions match.
n.3: Transactions must stop, not continue, pending confirmation.
n.2: Marketing has no role in sanctions handling.
n.0: Client consent is not sought and risks tipping off.

q: A compliance officer discovers a client appears on a sanctions list and needs to know which UK body enforces financial sanctions and should be notified. Which body is responsible for enforcing financial sanctions within the UK?
o: The Financial Ombudsman Service for the UK
The FCA's Prudential Regulation Authority
The London Stock Exchange market operator
The European Central Bank based in Frankfurt
The Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI)
w: The Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI), part of HM Treasury, administers and enforces financial sanctions in the UK. Firms must report breaches or frozen assets to OFSI without delay.

n.0: The FOS resolves complaints, it does not enforce sanctions.
n.1: The PRA is a prudential regulator, not the sanctions body.
n.3: The ECB has no UK sanctions role.
n.2: The LSE is a market, not a sanctions enforcer.

q: An MLRO is briefing new staff on how the firm treats a client who appears on a sanctions list versus a client rated higher AML risk. Under JMLSG guidance, what is a key difference between the two regimes?
o: Sanctions rules apply only to retail banks, AML applies to all financial firms
AML requires identical checks for all clients, sanctions does not
Sanctions compliance is strict liability, whereas AML is risk-based
AML obligations derive from HMRC, sanctions from the FCA
Sanctions compliance can be waived if client due diligence is complete
w: AML requirements are risk-based and allow proportionality in controls. By contrast, sanctions compliance is absolute (strict liability). Firms cannot make funds available to designated persons under any circumstances, regardless of perceived risk.

n.1: AML differentiates by risk level; not all clients are treated identically.
n.0: Sanctions rules apply to all UK financial firms, not just retail banks.
n.3: AML is supervised by multiple regulators; sanctions are enforced by OFSI, not the FCA alone.
n.4: Sanctions compliance cannot be waived; it is absolute.

q: A firm processes a payment for a client that turns out to breach financial sanctions. What penalty can OFSI impose on the firm?
o: A requirement to publish its financial accounts early
Civil monetary penalties and possible criminal prosecution
An outright ban on onboarding any new clients
Only a temporary loss of the firm's FCA authorisation
Suspension of the firm's directors with no appeal
w: OFSI can impose civil monetary penalties for breaches of financial sanctions, and serious cases may also lead to criminal prosecution. This reflects the gravity of sanctions breaches, which are considered strict liability offences.

n.3: Penalties go beyond FCA authorisation loss.
n.0: Early publication of accounts is not a sanctions penalty.
n.4: OFSI does not summarily suspend directors.
n.2: OFSI does not impose a client onboarding ban.

q: How often must firms screen their client base against updated sanctions lists?
o: Only once at client onboarding
Whenever there is an update to the sanctions list
Annually, regardless of list updates
Only if the client requests a financial transfer abroad
Every five years as part of periodic review
w: Firms must re-screen their client base whenever sanctions lists are updated. OFSI frequently updates designations, and firms are required to ensure their client databases reflect these changes immediately.

n.0: One-time onboarding screening is insufficient; sanctions lists are dynamic.
n.2: Annual checks may miss critical updates; re-screening is required at every update.
n.4: Five-year reviews are too infrequent to meet sanctions compliance obligations.
n.3: Re-screening is not triggered solely by transfers abroad; it applies universally.

q: Why are sanctions considered a 'zero-tolerance' compliance area compared with AML?
o: Because sanctions apply only to domestic transactions
Because sanctions apply only to high-net-worth clients
Because a risk assessment cannot justify a sanctions breach
Because sanctions breaches carry only criminal penalties
Because AML work can be outsourced but sanctions cannot
w: Sanctions rules are absolute. Firms cannot justify breaches by reference to internal risk assessments. Even inadvertent dealings with a designated person constitute a breach, hence the zero-tolerance approach.

n.1: Sanctions apply to all clients, not only wealthy ones.
n.4: Outsourcing is not the distinguishing point.
n.3: Sanctions breaches can carry civil penalties too.
n.0: Sanctions apply to international dealings as well.

q: What is the regulatory expectation if a firm discovers it has made funds available to a sanctioned entity inadvertently?
o: Tell the client and let them move the funds elsewhere
Wait for the next regulatory visit to disclose it
Log it internally but take no further external action
Freeze the assets and report the breach at once to OFSI
Reverse the transaction without telling any regulator
w: If a breach occurs, even inadvertently, the firm must freeze assets and report to OFSI without delay. This transparency is required under strict liability rules and protects the firm from more severe enforcement action.

n.0: Warning the client could facilitate evasion.
n.2: A breach must be reported externally to OFSI.
n.4: Reversing quietly still requires reporting.
n.1: Reporting cannot wait for the next visit.

q: A firm processes a payment for a company later found to be acting for a sanctioned individual. Which situation does this illustrate that firms must guard against?
o: Processing a payment for a sanctioned person's front company
Applying simplified due diligence to small deposit accounts
Opening a PEP account with enhanced due diligence applied
Letting clients from low-risk countries bank online
Onboarding a client after verifying official ID documents
w: Sanctions apply to indirect as well as direct dealings. A front company acting on behalf of a sanctioned person constitutes a breach, as funds are still made available to the designated individual.

n.4: Verified onboarding is compliant, not a breach.
n.2: Opening a PEP account with EDD is proper practice.
n.3: Low-risk online banking is not a sanctions breach.
n.1: Simplified due diligence on small deposits is permitted.

q: Which is a common control firms must implement to comply with UK sanctions obligations?
o: Regular audits of rival firms' overall market share
Restricting business to domestic customers only
Automated screening against updated sanctions lists
Quarterly reports on customer satisfaction levels
Annual benchmarking of every employee's salary
w: Automated screening systems are critical to ensuring clients and transactions are checked against updated sanctions lists. Given the frequency of updates, automation ensures compliance is efficient and accurate.

n.4: Salary benchmarking is unrelated to sanctions.
n.3: Satisfaction reports do not screen for sanctions.
n.0: Competitor audits are not a sanctions control.
n.1: Limiting to domestic clients is not a sanctions control.

q: According to JMLSG 5.1.1–5.1.15, what is the primary objective of 'Know Your Customer' (KYC) in the context of money laundering prevention?
o: To confirm the client can pay the firm's advisory fees
To produce a credit score for the client's loan eligibility
To understand a client's identity, business and expected activity
To reduce the operational cost of onboarding new clients
To give clients tailored investment performance reports
w: KYC is designed to ensure firms understand who their clients are, the nature of their business or occupation, and the expected level and type of transactions. This baseline enables detection of anomalies that may indicate money laundering or terrorist financing.

n.1: KYC is for AML, not credit scoring.
n.3: KYC is not aimed at cutting onboarding costs.
n.0: Fee affordability is not the purpose of KYC.
n.4: KYC is not about producing performance reports.

q: A private bank's relationship manager is opening an account for a new client and, following JMLSG guidance, considers which KYC step is most critical to the relationship. Which is it?
o: Determining the client’s preferred method of communication
Verifying the client’s identity using reliable, independent sources
Checking the client’s social media presence
Assessing the client’s level of satisfaction with other financial firms
Confirming the client’s annual holiday destination
w: Identity verification through independent and reliable documentation is the cornerstone of KYC. Without accurate verification, firms cannot establish the legitimacy of the client or assess potential AML risks effectively.

n.4: Travel habits are irrelevant to AML obligations.
n.2: Social media is not considered a reliable verification source under JMLSG.
n.3: Client satisfaction surveys are unrelated to KYC requirements.
n.0: Communication preferences are operational, not compliance-focused.

q: What is the regulatory expectation if a firm cannot complete customer due diligence under JMLSG 5.1?
o: It must not open, or must end, the business relationship
It may pass full responsibility to a credit reference agency
It may proceed if the client gives a personal guarantee
It may complete the checks after the first transaction
It may onboard but block transactions over 10,000 pounds
w: If a firm cannot complete CDD, it must not enter into the business relationship, or must terminate it if already in place. Proceeding without adequate checks exposes the firm to regulatory breach and potential facilitation of money laundering.

n.4: Incomplete CDD bars the relationship; a cap is not permitted.
n.2: A personal guarantee does not replace CDD.
n.3: CDD must precede, not follow, transactions.
n.1: Responsibility cannot be delegated to a credit agency.

q: During onboarding, a relationship manager records an 'expected account activity profile' for a new client as JMLSG suggests. Why is establishing this profile important?
o: It creates a baseline so deviations can be flagged as suspicious activity
It helps the firm forecast quarterly revenue from client accounts
It benchmarks client transactions against industry profitability data
It allows clients to agree their own AML monitoring thresholds
It lets relationship managers target clients with tailored marketing
w: An expected activity profile provides a baseline against which unusual or inconsistent activity can be flagged. This helps firms spot patterns that may indicate money laundering or terrorist financing, fulfilling ongoing monitoring obligations.

n.4: Marketing is not the purpose of an activity profile; it exists for AML monitoring.
n.3: Clients cannot set their own compliance thresholds; the firm sets monitoring standards.
n.1: Profiles are for detecting anomalies, not revenue forecasting.
n.2: Profitability benchmarking is unrelated to AML activity profiling.

q: An onboarding analyst uses a credit reference agency to help verify a new retail client's identity. How do credit reference agencies assist firms in the KYC process?
o: They supply independent data corroborating identity and financial history
They set the firm's internal money laundering risk appetite
They approve client onboarding decisions on the regulator's behalf
They remove the need for any further customer due diligence
They guarantee a client has no involvement in money laundering
w: Credit reference agencies provide reliable data that can corroborate client identity and offer insight into financial history. This data supports but does not replace the firm’s wider due diligence responsibilities under AML rules.

n.4: No CRA can guarantee a client is free of money laundering involvement.
n.3: CRA data supports but never replaces the firm's wider due diligence.
n.1: Firms set their own risk appetite; CRAs do not.
n.2: Onboarding decisions rest with the firm, not the CRA or regulator.

q: Which of the following situations would trigger enhanced KYC checks under JMLSG guidance?
o: Client opting to bank through a mobile application
Client requesting a modest overdraft facility on account
Client funds originating from a high-risk jurisdiction
Client choosing to communicate mainly by secure email
Client moving to a new address within the same city
w: Transactions or funds linked to high-risk jurisdictions elevate money laundering risk. This requires firms to apply enhanced due diligence, including deeper verification of source of wealth and closer transaction monitoring.

n.3: Communication preference alone is not a high-risk trigger.
n.1: A routine overdraft request does not elevate money laundering risk.
n.4: A local address change is normal and does not trigger enhanced checks.
n.0: Using a mobile app is common and not a risk factor.

q: How does JMLSG recommend firms deal with information gaps identified during KYC?
o: Record the gaps and continue the relationship as normal
Delegate responsibility for closing the gaps to the client
Apply further due diligence until enough information is obtained
Replace KYC entirely with ongoing transaction monitoring
Defer all KYC until twelve months of account activity pass
w: Information gaps compromise a firm’s ability to detect suspicious activity. JMLSG guidance requires firms to resolve these gaps through additional due diligence before allowing the relationship to progress fully.

n.0: Recording gaps and proceeding leaves the firm unable to detect suspicious activity.
n.1: KYC responsibility rests with the firm and cannot be delegated to the client.
n.4: KYC must be resolved before the relationship progresses, not deferred a year.
n.3: Monitoring supplements but never replaces customer due diligence.

q: Which risk does reliance on credit reference agencies NOT mitigate in the KYC process?
o: Confirming a customer's previous credit and repayment history
Establishing the purpose and intended nature of the relationship
Flagging adverse financial records such as defaults
Verifying a customer's current residential address details
Providing corroboration of a customer's claimed identity
w: While credit reference agencies assist with identity and financial history checks, they cannot establish the purpose or intended nature of the relationship. This requires direct dialogue between the firm and the client as part of CDD.

n.3: CRAs do help verify address data, so this risk is mitigated.
n.0: CRAs do confirm credit history, so this is not the exception.
n.4: CRAs do corroborate identity, so this risk is covered.
n.2: CRAs do flag adverse records, so this is mitigated, not the exception.

q: An onboarding officer wants to verify a young client who is new to the UK using credit reference agency data. In relation to KYC, what is a critical limitation of relying on this data?
o: It removes the need for firms to identify beneficial ownership
It replaces the legal requirement to file suspicious activity reports
It may not cover individuals without significant credit history
It automatically exempts low-income clients from due diligence
It is always inaccurate and unreliable
w: Credit reference data may be incomplete for clients with limited or no credit history, such as young people or those new to the UK. Firms must therefore supplement this with other due diligence measures.

n.4: Credit reference data is not always inaccurate; it is reliable but not universal.
n.0: Beneficial ownership identification remains a legal requirement.
n.3: Low income does not exempt clients from due diligence.
n.1: Suspicious activity reporting obligations remain regardless of credit agency data.

q: A private bank's MLRO is explaining to new staff why customer due diligence cannot be a one-off exercise at onboarding. Under JMLSG, why is ongoing KYC integral to AML compliance?
o: Because regulators require firms to refresh marketing preferences regularly
Because customer circumstances and risk profiles can change over time
Because it allows firms to avoid transaction monitoring altogether
Because it eliminates the need for senior management oversight
Because it reduces the cost of compliance audits
w: Ongoing KYC ensures that changes in a customer’s circumstances, activities, or risk factors are identified promptly. This dynamic process enables firms to adjust monitoring and apply enhanced due diligence where necessary.

n.0: Marketing preferences are unrelated to AML compliance.
n.2: Ongoing KYC supplements transaction monitoring; it does not replace it.
n.4: The objective is risk management, not cost reduction.
n.3: Senior management oversight remains a core requirement of AML frameworks.

q: When relying on a credit reference agency (CRA) for customer verification, what must a firm still demonstrate to remain compliant with JMLSG guidance?
o: That all compliance duties are outsourced to the CRA permanently
That the CRA data matches other institutions' customer lists
That the customer gave explicit written consent for AML checks
That the CRA is more profitable than its main competitors
That the CRA's data is reliable, current and from an independent source
w: JMLSG requires firms to ensure that data used for customer due diligence is from a reliable and independent source. When CRAs are used, firms must assess the quality of the data and cannot delegate full responsibility for compliance to the third party.

n.2: Written client consent is not a JMLSG requirement for using CRA data.
n.1: Peer customer lists are not the benchmark for CRA data quality.
n.3: A CRA's profitability is irrelevant to data reliability.
n.0: Firms cannot permanently outsource compliance responsibility to a CRA.

q: What is a significant limitation of using CRA data as the sole basis for KYC, particularly in relation to AML obligations?
o: It ends the need to monitor politically exposed persons
It may exclude people with no credit history, such as new UK arrivals
It removes the need to identify beneficial ownership entirely
It guarantees compliance across all jurisdictions without more
It is inherently unreliable for every category of customer
w: Reliance solely on CRA data creates blind spots for individuals with little or no credit history, such as migrants, young adults, or those outside traditional financial systems. Firms must therefore adopt supplementary measures to achieve full compliance with AML obligations.

n.4: CRA data is useful for many customers, not inherently unreliable for all.
n.2: Beneficial ownership must still be identified; CRA use does not remove this.
n.3: CRA data gives no cross-jurisdiction compliance guarantee.
n.0: PEP monitoring remains required regardless of CRA use.

q: How does JMLSG expect firms to mitigate the residual risk when using CRA data in customer onboarding?
o: Exempt clients the CRA rates positively from ongoing monitoring
Raise risk scores upward until CRA data becomes complete
Apply CRA checks only to clients already judged low risk
Supplement CRA data with further independent verification where gaps exist
Rely solely on the CRA's annual audit statements as sufficient evidence of identity
w: Residual risk must be mitigated by layering CRA data with other verification sources, especially where data gaps are identified. This ensures compliance with the regulatory requirement for robust and risk-sensitive customer due diligence.

n.4: An audit statement does not mitigate residual data gaps in onboarding.
n.2: CRA checks are not limited to low-risk clients; risk-sensitive layering is needed.
n.1: Inflating risk scores does not fill data gaps or reduce residual risk.
n.0: No client is exempt from ongoing monitoring on the basis of a CRA rating.

q: What role can CRA data play in identifying potential money laundering risks beyond simple identity verification?
o: It can conclusively certify a customer's source of wealth
It can permanently exempt customers from all sanctions screening requirements
It can determine a customer's political affiliations directly
It can establish a customer's tax residency status automatically
It can reveal adverse financial history suggesting vulnerability to misuse
w: CRA reports may show defaults, bankruptcies, or adverse financial history. While not proof of money laundering, such information may increase the risk profile of a client, prompting firms to conduct enhanced due diligence where appropriate.

n.2: CRA data does not reveal political affiliations.
n.0: CRA data cannot conclusively certify source of wealth.
n.1: CRA data never exempts a client from sanctions screening.
n.3: CRA data does not automatically establish tax residency.

q: A firm onboards a corporate client and relies mainly on credit reference agency data for its AML checks. What is the key regulatory risk of over-relying on CRA data in this way?
o: Failure to meet the firm's minimum quarterly profit margins
Failure to advertise competitively against rival firms
Failure to gather customer satisfaction feedback data
Failure to lighten the compliance team's daily workload
Failure to identify the beneficial owners of corporate structures
w: CRA data typically covers individuals but does not extend to beneficial ownership of corporate entities. Over-reliance could result in gaps in compliance and exposure to regulatory penalties if beneficial ownership is not properly identified.

n.0: Profit margins are a commercial matter, not an AML regulatory risk.
n.2: Customer satisfaction data is not an AML compliance concern.
n.1: Advertising competitiveness is unrelated to AML compliance.
n.3: Workload reduction is not the regulatory risk of over-reliance.

q: Why does JMLSG caution against sole reliance on electronic verification methods, including CRAs?
o: CRA data can never be used as evidence in a court
Customers routinely object to electronic checks as intrusive
Regulators prohibit every form of digital identity verification
Electronic systems cannot support a risk-based approach
Data sources may hold inaccuracies or omissions needing cross-checking
w: Electronic verification, including CRA use, can be effective but must be combined with other checks to mitigate inaccuracies or omissions. JMLSG warns that over-reliance without layering creates compliance gaps.

n.2: Regulators permit digital verification; they do not prohibit it.
n.0: CRA data is not barred from use as evidence.
n.1: Client objection is not the reason JMLSG cautions against sole reliance.
n.3: Electronic systems can and do support a risk-based approach.

q: A firm relies on credit reference agency data for verification but is onboarding a complex corporate client. In which situation is CRA data most likely to be insufficient under JMLSG's risk-based approach?
o: When the client is a salaried employee with a long credit history
When the client is based in a low-risk jurisdiction with robust AML laws
When the client has maintained consistent address records
When the client is a complex corporate structure with opaque ownership
When the client’s financial activity aligns with declared occupation
w: CRA data is often limited to individuals and simple entities. For complex corporate structures, especially those with opaque ownership, CRA information is inadequate. Firms must apply additional enhanced due diligence measures to identify beneficial owners.

n.0: Straightforward individual clients are well covered by CRA data.
n.2: Stable address history typically enhances the reliability of CRA checks.
n.4: Alignment of activity with occupation reduces suspicion rather than raises it.
n.1: Low-risk jurisdictions generally support CRA use without major issues.

q: A firm's onboarding system flags a new client as a possible sanctions match, but the compliance officer suspects it is a common-name coincidence. How should the firm address the risk of 'false positives' when using CRA data for sanctions or AML screening?
o: Outsource all follow-up work to the CRA on its own
Delay verification until after the account starts trading
Ignore every positive match until the regulator makes contact
Automatically reject any client showing a positive match
Carry out a secondary manual review to confirm or dismiss matches
w: False positives are common when screening against sanctions or politically exposed persons. Firms must conduct secondary reviews to confirm genuine matches, ensuring both compliance and fair treatment of clients.

n.2: Ignoring matches until a regulator calls breaches AML obligations.
n.0: Follow-up on matches cannot be outsourced wholesale to the CRA.
n.3: Auto-rejecting every match is unfair and mishandles false positives.
n.1: Verification must occur before, not after, account activity.

q: A firm relies heavily on credit reference agency outputs when onboarding clients. Which of the following is an example of over-reliance on CRA data that could lead to enforcement action?
o: Confirming address via CRA while also making in-person checks
Applying CRA checks together with full documentary verification of identity
Verifying identity via CRA but not assessing source of wealth or funds
Employing CRA data alongside full sanctions list screening
Using CRA data as one layer of a wider risk-based framework
w: CRA data cannot verify the source of wealth or funds. Firms that fail to conduct these additional checks while relying solely on CRA outputs are at risk of regulatory breach for insufficient customer due diligence.

n.1: Combining CRA with documentary checks is good practice, not over-reliance.
n.4: Using CRA as one layer of a wider framework is proper, not over-reliance.
n.0: CRA plus in-person checks is layered diligence, not a breach.
n.3: CRA plus sanctions screening is sound practice, not over-reliance.

q: What key principle must firms remember when integrating CRA data into their AML frameworks?
o: CRA data is sufficient for high-value clients without further checks
CRA data guarantees full compliance with FATF requirements
CRA data eliminates the need for a risk-based approach
CRA data exempts firms from filing suspicious activity reports
CRA data supports but never substitutes full customer due diligence
w: JMLSG guidance is clear that CRA data can play an important role, but it must be integrated into a broader, risk-based framework. Firms remain responsible for conducting comprehensive CDD, including beneficial ownership and ongoing monitoring.

n.1: FATF compliance requires broader measures than CRA data alone.
n.3: Suspicious activity reporting is a statutory duty unaffected by CRA reliance.
n.2: The risk-based approach remains mandatory in AML compliance.
n.0: High-value clients require enhanced scrutiny, not reduced checks.

q: A firm's monitoring team keeps reviewing an established client's transactions over time. Under JMLSG guidance, what is the principal purpose of this ongoing monitoring?
o: To confirm the client keeps paying advisory fees on time
To avoid having to screen customers against relevant sanctions and watchlists
To keep transactions consistent with the customer's profile and risk rating
To reduce how often periodic customer due diligence is needed
To check whether the client is meeting the firm's sales targets
w: Ongoing monitoring is designed to identify whether client activity is consistent with the firm’s understanding of the customer’s risk profile. Unusual or inconsistent activity can trigger suspicion and the need to report internally to the MLRO.

n.4: Sales targets are a commercial matter, not the aim of AML monitoring.
n.0: Fee payment is irrelevant to the purpose of ongoing monitoring.
n.3: Monitoring supplements periodic CDD; it does not reduce the need for it.
n.1: Sanctions screening remains required and is not avoided by monitoring.

q: Which of the following transactions would most likely trigger a suspicious activity report (SAR)?
o: A client paying their monthly mortgage instalment on time
A client making a routine annual ISA contribution
A client switching from paper to electronic bank statements for convenience
A client asking for an updated account balance statement
A client suddenly wiring large sums to an unrelated high-risk country
w: Large transfers to high-risk jurisdictions that lack an apparent commercial purpose are red flags under AML rules. Such activity should be escalated to the MLRO for consideration of filing a SAR with the NCA.

n.0: Routine mortgage payment is normal and not a SAR trigger.
n.2: A statement-format change is not suspicious.
n.1: A routine ISA contribution is normal activity.
n.3: Requesting a balance statement is an ordinary service request.

q: A relationship manager questions why the firm keeps monitoring a client it has served without incident for fifteen years. Why is ongoing monitoring essential even for long-standing clients?
o: Because clients demand constant updates from their banks
Because regulators require firms to reissue marketing material periodically
Because a client’s circumstances and risk profile may change over time
Because it replaces the need for independent audits
Because it improves customer loyalty and satisfaction
w: Risk is dynamic. A client who was low risk at onboarding may become higher risk due to changes in jurisdiction, occupation, or transaction behaviour. Ongoing monitoring allows firms to adapt controls accordingly.

n.1: Marketing requirements are not the purpose of monitoring.
n.4: Customer loyalty is not the regulatory driver.
n.3: Audits remain mandatory regardless of monitoring.
