n.4: It is not confined to unregulated firms.
n.3: It uses many methods, not only cash smuggling.
n.1: Terrorist financing is squarely within the FCA's financial-crime remit.

q: Under JMLSG Preface 9, what aspect of terrorist financing makes it particularly challenging for firms?
o: It always involves foreign exchange manipulation
It depends on insider trading within capital markets
It often uses funds from legitimate sources, not criminal activity
It requires firms to track personal tax returns abroad
It is carried out solely by large and well-organised criminal syndicates
w: The fact that terrorist financing may originate from lawful income makes it harder to identify compared to money laundering, which by definition deals with proceeds of crime. Preventative controls are essential to detect misuse.

n.0: Terrorist financing does not always involve forex manipulation.
n.3: Tracking foreign tax returns is not the challenge described.
n.1: It does not depend on insider trading.
n.4: It is not carried out only by organised syndicates.

q: A firm is updating its CTF controls using the FCA Financial Crime Guide. Which preventative measure does that guide highlight to combat terrorist financing?
o: Ongoing risk-based monitoring of customer activity
Automatic rejection of clients with low credit scores
Eliminating cross-border business relationships
Outsourcing monitoring responsibilities entirely to CRAs
Annual profit disclosures to shareholders
w: The FCA stresses a risk-based approach with ongoing monitoring of customer activity. This allows firms to detect transactions inconsistent with a customer’s profile, a vital element of counter-terrorist financing controls.

n.1: Credit scores are not a proxy for terrorism risk.
n.4: Profit disclosures are unrelated to terrorism prevention.
n.2: Cross-border relationships are not inherently suspicious.
n.3: Responsibility cannot be outsourced; firms remain accountable.

q: How does the PRA’s oversight intersect with terrorist financing rules?
o: By setting client due diligence requirements independently of the FCA regime
By making regulated firms keep robust governance and systems against misuse
By prosecuting individuals for terrorism offences
By compiling the UK Consolidated Sanctions List
By funding government counter-terrorism operations
w: The PRA focuses on firm governance, systems, and resilience, ensuring regulated firms cannot be exploited for terrorist financing. This complements statutory obligations under terrorism laws and FCA rules.

n.3: OFSI, not the PRA, compiles the sanctions list.
n.2: The PRA does not prosecute terrorism offences.
n.4: The PRA does not fund counter-terrorism operations.
n.0: CDD rules are set with the FCA, not by the PRA alone.

q: An MLRO cites JMLSG Preface 27 when explaining why the firm cannot treat FCA rules and the Terrorism Act as alternatives. Why does the guidance stress consistency between them?
o: JMLSG guidance substitutes for statutory reporting duties
Firms need follow only one regime if they operate abroad
Firms must satisfy both regulatory rules and criminal law duties at once
FCA rules automatically override the criminal offences in the Terrorism Act
The PRA alone is responsible for enforcing terrorist financing
w: Preface 27 highlights that firms must comply with both regulatory frameworks (FCA rules) and legal obligations (Terrorism Act). JMLSG guidance explains how to operationalise this dual compliance.

n.3: FCA rules do not override Terrorism Act criminal offences.
n.0: JMLSG guidance does not substitute for statutory reporting.
n.1: Firms must follow both regimes, not just one, when abroad.
n.4: The PRA is not the sole enforcer of terrorist financing rules.

q: An MLRO is briefing new staff on why counter-terrorist financing controls differ from anti-money-laundering ones. Which statement captures an essential difference between terrorist financing and laundering criminal proceeds?
o: Terrorist financing does not require customer due diligence
Terrorist financing may use funds not linked to any prior crime
Terrorist financing can never involve cross-border activity
Money laundering carries no reporting obligations under POCA
Laundering always involves transactions under 10,000 pounds
w: Unlike money laundering, which necessarily deals with criminal proceeds, terrorist financing can involve entirely legitimate income diverted for terrorism purposes. This makes detection more complex.

n.4: Laundering is not limited to sums under 10,000 pounds.
n.2: Terrorist financing can involve cross-border activity.
n.3: Money laundering carries clear POCA reporting obligations.
n.0: Terrorist financing does require customer due diligence.

q: Which preventative control is common to both money laundering and terrorist financing regimes?
o: Exemption from due diligence for long-standing clients
Ongoing monitoring and suspicious activity reporting
Quarterly publication of client profitability ratios
Mandatory disclosure of client marketing preferences
Provision of customer satisfaction surveys
w: Both money laundering and terrorist financing regimes require ongoing monitoring and suspicious activity reporting. These obligations are central to identifying unusual transactions and preventing misuse of financial systems.

n.3: Marketing preferences are irrelevant to AML/CFT controls.
n.2: Profitability ratios are not a compliance requirement.
n.4: Surveys are customer service tools, not AML measures.
n.0: Long-standing clients are not exempt from CDD obligations.

q: A new MLRO is briefing the board on JMLSG Preface 28. Why must the firm align its internal controls with the terrorism legislation as well as the FCA rules?
o: Terrorist financing is a criminal offence, so firms must satisfy both the law and regulatory rules
Because meeting the FCA's financial crime rules automatically discharges the Terrorism Act obligations
Because JMLSG guidance carries the force of statute and so must be followed to the letter
Because firms may substitute their PRA prudential controls for Terrorism Act compliance
Because terrorism offences fall outside the FATF standards and so require a wholly separate framework
w: Preface 28 reinforces that terrorism-related obligations are legal as well as regulatory. Firms must demonstrate compliance with statutory terrorism offences as part of their systems and controls.

n.2: JMLSG guidance is not statute; it is evidential good practice, not binding law.
n.1: The FCA rules and the Terrorism Act are separate obligations; one does not discharge the other.
n.4: Terrorist financing is squarely within the FATF standards, not exempt from them.
n.3: Prudential controls cannot substitute for compliance with the criminal financing offences.

q: A firm is designing its financial crime framework and asks how the FCA expects terrorist financing risks to be handled. What is the FCA's stance?
o: They must be fully integrated with money laundering and other crime risks
They are optional if firms concentrate on fraud prevention
They may be considered only in rare and exceptional business circumstances
They can be delegated entirely to outside agencies
They are not relevant for firms based only in the UK
w: The FCA expects terrorist financing risks to be assessed alongside money laundering and wider financial crime risks in firm-wide frameworks. This ensures a holistic and proportionate response to financial crime threats.

n.2: TF risks must always be considered, not only exceptionally.
n.1: TF assessment is not optional even with a fraud focus.
n.4: TF risk is relevant to UK-based firms too.
n.3: TF assessment cannot be delegated entirely to outside agencies.

q: A trainee asks why JMLSG Preface 29 stresses aligning its terrorism guidance with FCA and PRA expectations. What is the reason for that emphasis?
o: Consistency across guidance and regulation strengthens compliance and reduces ambiguity
Because the Terrorism Act applies only where the FCA has granted its prior approval
Because the FCA's rules apply only to firms that are established outside the UK
Because the PRA's rules exempt insurers from all terrorism-related obligations
Because the JMLSG guidance is itself legally binding on every regulated firm
w: Preface 29 stresses that consistency across JMLSG, FCA, and PRA expectations ensures firms understand their obligations clearly. This integrated framework supports effective prevention of terrorist financing.

n.4: JMLSG guidance is not binding law.
n.2: FCA rules apply to UK-authorised firms, not only overseas ones.
n.3: Insurers are not exempt from CTF obligations.
n.1: The Terrorism Act applies irrespective of FCA approval.

q: A bank's financial crime team is concerned that terrorist financing could be routed through legitimate-looking charitable donations. Which preventative measure directly addresses this risk?
o: Enhanced due diligence on charities and non-profit organisations
Monitoring client satisfaction surveys each year
Providing free compliance training to all donors
Automatically rejecting all donations from overseas clients
Requiring charities to hold only sterling accounts
w: Charities and NPOs can be abused to funnel funds to terrorist groups. Enhanced due diligence and governance checks ensure legitimate activities are distinguished from potential terrorist financing.

n.3: Blanket rejection of overseas donations is not a targeted control.
n.4: Requiring sterling-only accounts does not address TF risk.
n.1: Satisfaction surveys are not an AML control.
n.2: Donor training is not the measure that addresses charity misuse.

q: How does terrorist financing differ from money laundering in terms of fund flow direction?
o: Terrorist financing requires physical cash transfers, whereas money laundering does not
Laundering disguises illicit funds as legitimate; financing channels funds to illegitimate ends
Money laundering always relies on shell companies, whereas terrorist financing never does
Money laundering applies only to transactions carried out through retail banking channels
Terrorist financing can involve only funds that flow across international borders
w: Money laundering cleanses criminal proceeds to re-enter the legitimate economy. Terrorist financing channels legitimate or illicit funds into supporting terrorism, regardless of their origin.

n.2: Money laundering does not always use shell companies.
n.0: Terrorist financing does not require physical cash.
n.3: Money laundering is not limited to retail banking.
n.4: Terrorist financing can be entirely domestic.

q: A compliance officer wants an example of a preventative control from the FCA Financial Crime Guide. Which of the following best demonstrates one?
o: Offering clients incentives for online-only services
Publishing all client names on a public register
Screening customers against sanctions and watchlists before onboarding
Making clients waive their confidentiality agreements
Requiring clients to disclose their personal political affiliations in full
w: Sanctions and watchlist screening is a preventative control explicitly endorsed by FCA and JMLSG guidance to identify terrorism-related risks before clients are onboarded.

n.4: Recording political affiliations is not an endorsed control.
n.3: Waiving confidentiality is not a financial crime control.
n.0: Online-only incentives are marketing, not a control.
n.1: Publishing client names publicly is not a control and breaches privacy.

q: A bank's financial crime team notes that the PRA, FCA and JMLSG all publish AML expectations. Why does it matter that these expectations remain consistent with one another?
o: Because JMLSG guidance replaces suspicious activity reporting
Because the PRA's rules on their own directly create new criminal offences
Because FCA guidance overrides statutory terrorism law
Consistency prevents regulatory arbitrage and keeps compliance coherent
Because it lets firms exempt high-value clients from CDD
w: When PRA, FCA, and JMLSG guidance align, firms face clear obligations and cannot exploit differences between frameworks. This strengthens prevention and detection of terrorist financing.

n.1: PRA rules alone do not create criminal offences.
n.2: FCA guidance does not override statutory terrorism law.
n.0: JMLSG guidance does not replace SAR reporting.
n.4: No client is exempt from CDD due to their value.

q: A payments firm worries that terrorist financing may hide within many small transfers. What preventative approach is recommended for detecting it?
o: Annual customer surveys
Automatic exemption of all transfers below £1,000
Monitoring only transfers over £100,000
Pattern and behavioural transaction monitoring
Requiring clients to confirm intent for each transfer
w: Small-value transfers can still fund terrorism. Behavioural and pattern-based monitoring allows firms to detect unusual activity inconsistent with customer profiles, even at low values.

n.1: Exemptions below thresholds create vulnerabilities.
n.0: Surveys are irrelevant to monitoring obligations.
n.4: Client intent confirmation is not feasible or compliant.
n.2: High thresholds miss smaller terrorist financing flows.

q: Which of the following illustrates the interaction of FCA, PRA, JMLSG, and Terrorism Act obligations?
o: Terrorism Act offences are enforced by the PRA, so firms discharge them by holding adequate regulatory capital
Meeting the PRA's prudential requirements is treated as evidence of full compliance with FCA conduct and Terrorism Act duties
Comply with FCA rules and JMLSG guidance, meet PRA prudential duties, and avoid Terrorism Act offences
Firms may follow JMLSG guidance alone, as it consolidates the FCA, PRA and Terrorism Act requirements into one binding code
FCA and JMLSG requirements govern conduct, while the Terrorism Act applies only to firms that handle physical cash
w: Each framework plays a role: JMLSG offers practical steps; FCA sets regulatory rules; PRA ensures prudential soundness; and the Terrorism Act sets criminal offences. Firms must integrate all obligations.

n.3: JMLSG guidance is not binding law and does not replace the distinct FCA, PRA and Terrorism Act obligations.
n.1: Prudential compliance is separate and is not a substitute for conduct rules or the criminal financing offences.
n.0: Terrorism Act offences are criminal matters for the courts, not discharged by holding regulatory capital.
n.4: The Terrorism Act financing offences apply regardless of whether physical cash is involved.

q: A financial crime lead explains why the firm's CDD process guards against both money laundering and terrorist financing. Why is customer due diligence equally important for preventing both?
o: Because completing CDD exempts the firm from having to make suspicious activity reports
Because it allows the firm to maximise the profitability of every client relationship it takes on
It establishes identity and risk profile, underpinning detection of both crime types
Because CDD discharges the firm's wider FCA financial-crime systems-and-controls duties
Because it prevents clients from later referring a dispute to the Financial Ombudsman Service
w: CDD creates the baseline understanding of clients, essential for detecting both illicit proceeds and potential terrorist misuse of funds. It supports monitoring and SAR obligations under both regimes.

n.1: CDD is a financial-crime control, not a profitability tool.
n.0: CDD does not remove the obligation to report suspicious activity.
n.3: CDD is one part of a wider systems-and-controls framework, not a substitute for it.
n.4: CDD is unrelated to a client's access to the Ombudsman.

q: What type of preventative control is particularly important given the overlap between terrorist financing and sanctions compliance?
o: Delegating sanctions screening entirely to the clients
Collecting all customer passwords for regulatory review
Publishing quarterly profit results to the shareholders
Regular screening of customers and transactions against OFSI lists
Sending annual customer newsletters explaining terrorism law
w: Sanctions screening is vital as it helps identify and block dealings with designated individuals and organisations. It is a core preventative measure emphasised by JMLSG and FCA rules.

n.4: Newsletters are not a sanctions or AML control.
n.2: Publishing profit results is unrelated to sanctions compliance.
n.1: Collecting customer passwords is not a control and is improper.
n.0: Sanctions screening cannot be delegated to clients.

q: A compliance head is designing terrorism-risk controls and wants to know how FCA and PRA expectations sit alongside JMLSG guidance. How do these interact?
o: They force firms to adopt identical controls regardless of their business model
They drop the need for sanctions checks when risk is low
They remove the need for firms to file any SARs
They set oversight and prudential rules firms apply through JMLSG guidance
They let firms address laundering but not terrorist financing
w: FCA and PRA rules set supervisory expectations; JMLSG explains how firms can meet them in practice. Firms must implement controls proportionate to their business model and risk exposure.

n.2: They do not remove the duty to file SARs.
n.4: Firms must address terrorist financing too, not only laundering.
n.0: Controls should be proportionate, not identical for all models.
n.1: Sanctions checks are required even when risk is assessed low.

q: A trainer is explaining to compliance staff why the terrorist financing regime leans on prevention. Why are preventative measures stressed more heavily here than in traditional money laundering?
o: Stopping funds reaching terrorists beats tracing them after use
Because terrorist financing never involves regulated firms
Because laundering is prosecuted only after another conviction
Because regulators cannot impose penalties for terrorist financing
Because preventative measures are optional under JMLSG guidance
w: Terrorist financing often uses small, legitimate transactions, making recovery impossible once funds are deployed. Preventative measures are the only effective way to block terrorism-related funds.

n.3: Regulators can and do impose penalties for terrorist financing.
n.2: Laundering does not require a prior conviction to prosecute.
n.1: Terrorist financing can involve regulated firms.
n.4: Preventative measures are expected, not optional, under JMLSG.

q: Why does JMLSG guidance emphasise preventative controls rather than relying on detection after the fact?
o: Because prevention replaces statutory reporting obligations
Once funds reach terrorism they are hard to trace or recover
Because the FCA prohibits the use of detection measures
Because prevention removes the need for sanctions screening
Because terrorist financing is not a criminal offence in the UK
w: Preventative measures such as sanctions screening and customer due diligence are vital because funds used for terrorism are often small, legitimate, and almost impossible to recover once transferred.

n.4: Terrorist financing is a criminal offence in the UK.
n.2: The FCA does not prohibit detection measures.
n.3: Prevention does not remove the need for sanctions screening.
n.0: Prevention does not replace statutory reporting obligations.

q: A compliance officer is updating the firm's financial crime framework to address counter-terrorist financing. Which FCA expectation is most directly relevant to this work?
o: Firms must have regulators approve all staff pay rises
Firms must hold effective systems and controls to prevent financial crime
Firms must publish their annual dividend yields
Firms must report their client satisfaction statistics
Firms must share their proprietary trading algorithms with direct competitors
w: The FCA requires firms to maintain proportionate systems and controls to prevent financial crime, including terrorist financing. This aligns with JMLSG guidance and statutory duties.

n.2: Publishing dividend yields is not a financial crime control.
n.3: Client satisfaction statistics are not an AML requirement.
n.4: Sharing algorithms with competitors is not required.
n.0: Regulators do not approve staff pay rises.

q: How does the Terrorism Act 2000 complement FCA and PRA frameworks?
o: It exempts certain firms from due diligence obligations
It requires firms to submit marketing material for approval
It sets prudential capital requirements for the banks
It lets firms approve their own sanctions lists
It creates criminal offences firms must prevent through compliance
w: The Terrorism Act criminalises financing of terrorism. FCA and PRA frameworks require firms to have systems that prevent these offences from being facilitated through financial institutions.

n.2: Capital requirements come from prudential rules, not the Terrorism Act.
n.1: The Act does not require marketing material approval.
n.0: The Act does not exempt firms from due diligence.
n.3: Firms cannot approve their own sanctions lists.

q: During a CFT training session, a compliance officer explains why terrorist financing risk is uniquely hard to spot. Which factor makes it distinct from laundering the proceeds of crime?
o: It is prosecuted under civil law and not criminal law
It requires a minimum threshold of 10,000 pounds
It needs no prior criminal conduct to generate the funds
It can occur only through physical smuggling of cash
It applies only to firms with international operations
w: Terrorist financing may involve legitimate funds raised through salaries, donations, or small contributions. Unlike money laundering, it does not always require proceeds of crime.

n.3: Terrorist financing is not limited to cash smuggling.
n.0: It is prosecuted under criminal, not civil, law.
n.4: It applies to domestic firms too, not only international ones.
n.1: There is no 10,000-pound minimum threshold.

q: Which preventative control demonstrates the integration of PRA requirements with terrorism legislation?
o: Permitting firms to outsource SAR duties to their clients
Requiring firms to disclose their dividend payouts quarterly
Exempting firms from OFSI sanctions duties whenever capital buffers are high
Ensuring governance and risk systems address terrorist financing risks
Letting firms stop CDD checks for UK national customers
w: PRA requires firms to maintain governance and risk frameworks that incorporate financial crime threats. This integrates with terrorism legislation to ensure firms cannot be exploited for terrorist financing.

n.1: Disclosing dividends is not a terrorist financing control.
n.4: CDD checks are not waived for UK nationals.
n.0: SAR duties cannot be outsourced to clients.
n.2: High capital buffers do not exempt firms from OFSI duties.

q: A firm is building a single financial crime framework covering both money laundering and terrorism. Why do JMLSG Preface 27-29 stress treating terrorism obligations as integral to compliance?
o: Because the FCA's rules may be set aside wherever a firm follows the JMLSG guidance instead
Terrorism offences are criminal, so guidance, rules and the law must be integrated cohesively
Because meeting the PRA's prudential supervision by itself provides full compliance with the framework
Because the Terrorism Act's offences apply only to banks that operate across national borders
Because sanctions obligations become optional once robust customer due diligence is in place
w: JMLSG highlights that compliance cannot be fragmented. Firms must consider terrorism law, FCA/PRA expectations, and JMLSG guidance together to ensure robust prevention of terrorist financing.

n.2: Prudential supervision alone does not deliver full financial-crime compliance.
n.0: JMLSG guidance does not displace the FCA rules.
n.3: The Terrorism Act offences are not limited to cross-border banks.
n.4: Sanctions obligations are never optional.

q: Which preventative practice is endorsed by FCA, PRA, and JMLSG for terrorist financing controls?
o: Adopting a risk-based approach tailored to the client base and business
Exempting long-term clients from any periodic reviews
Ending all cross-border business as a standard practice
Applying identical monitoring thresholds to all firms regardless of size
Relying only on CRA checks for all client verification
w: All three frameworks endorse a risk-based approach, meaning preventative measures must be proportionate to the risk profile of clients and the firm’s operations.

n.3: Thresholds should be proportionate, not identical across all firms.
n.2: Ending all cross-border business is not an endorsed control.
n.4: Sole reliance on CRA checks is discouraged, not endorsed.
n.1: Long-term clients are not exempt from periodic reviews.

q: A compliance trainer is explaining why counter-terrorist financing focuses on prevention rather than reacting after the event. What is one reason preventative measures are more effective?
o: Regulators have no power to punish firms after any breach
Sanctions lists are only optional for UK-based firms
Courts cannot enforce the Terrorism Act after an attack
FCA rules exempt firms from TF controls once detected
Disrupting funding before it reaches terrorists can stop attacks
w: Preventing funds from reaching terrorist groups is critical as disruption is most effective at the financing stage. Once funds are in terrorist hands, detection has limited deterrent effect.

n.0: Regulators retain power to punish firms after a breach.
n.2: Courts can enforce the Terrorism Act after an attack.
n.1: Sanctions lists are mandatory, not optional, for UK firms.
n.3: FCA rules do not exempt firms from TF controls after detection.

q: An MLRO is explaining to new staff why terrorist financing is hard to detect. Which example best illustrates that difficulty of telling it apart from legitimate activity?
o: A client switching to a new bank purely for a better savings rate
A household utility bill paid by monthly direct debit
An employee expense claim for genuine business travel
A routine ISA contribution made once every year
A small regular donation to a charity that is a terrorist front
w: Terrorist financing can appear indistinguishable from legitimate charitable or personal transactions, making preventative measures like sanctions screening essential.

n.0: Switching banks for a better rate is plainly legitimate.
n.2: A genuine business travel claim is ordinary activity.
n.1: A utility bill by direct debit is clearly legitimate.
n.3: A routine ISA contribution is plainly legitimate.

q: An MLRO is explaining to trainees how the FCA, PRA, JMLSG and the Terrorism Act fit together on financial crime. How do these sources collectively shape a firm's obligations?
o: By waiving the framework for firms that meet their annual profitability targets
By addressing money laundering exclusively and leaving terrorist financing out of scope
By requiring only a one-off compliance check to be completed at client onboarding
By letting each firm select whichever single regime it finds most convenient to follow
A combined framework of regulatory expectations, guidance, prudential oversight and criminal offences
w: FCA rules, PRA oversight, JMLSG guidance, and Terrorism Act offences together create a layered compliance framework. Firms must satisfy all elements to ensure effective prevention of terrorist financing.

n.3: Firms cannot pick one regime; the obligations operate together.
n.2: Financial-crime controls must be ongoing, not a one-off onboarding check.
n.1: The framework covers terrorist financing as well as money laundering.
n.0: Profitability does not exempt a firm from these obligations.

q: What is the primary purpose of the Bribery Act 2010 within UK criminal law?
o: It replaces the Proceeds of Crime Act for corruption cases
It consolidates prior bribery offences into a single modern statute
It transfers bribery prosecutions from the SFO to the FCA
It applies solely to bribery committed by public officials
It creates only civil penalties for corporate hospitality
w: The Act modernises and consolidates prior common law and statutory bribery offences into a single, comprehensive framework.

n.2: The SFO and CPS still prosecute bribery; the FCA is not the prosecutor.
n.4: Bribery Act offences are criminal, not merely civil hospitality penalties.
n.3: The Act covers private and commercial bribery, not just public officials.
n.0: POCA deals with proceeds of crime; it is not replaced by the Bribery Act.

q: Which conduct falls within Section 1 of the Bribery Act 2010?
o: Requesting an advantage as a reward for improper performance
Offering or giving an advantage to induce improper performance
Failing to keep an adequate written hospitality register
Bribing a foreign public official to secure a contract
Negligently disclosing inside information to a rival
w: Section 1 criminalises promising, offering or giving an advantage intending to induce improper performance of a relevant function or activity.

n.0: Requesting or accepting an advantage is Section 2, not Section 1.
n.2: Poor record-keeping is not itself the active bribery offence in Section 1.
n.3: Bribing a foreign public official is dealt with under Section 6.
n.4: Disclosing inside information concerns market abuse, not Section 1 bribery.

q: Who commits an offence under Section 2 of the Bribery Act 2010?
o: An official influenced to award business to a bidder
A person who offers a bribe to induce improper performance
A person who requests or accepts an advantage for improper performance
A company whose associated person bribes another party
A firm that fails to keep a written hospitality register
w: Section 2 criminalises requesting, agreeing to receive, or accepting an advantage in return for improper performance of a relevant function.

n.1: Offering or giving an advantage is the Section 1 offence, not Section 2.
n.4: A missing hospitality register is not the Section 2 receiving offence.
n.3: Corporate failure to prevent bribery is the Section 7 offence.
n.0: Bribery of a foreign public official falls under Section 6.

q: A firm's agent is negotiating an overseas contract and offers a payment to a foreign government official. Under Section 6 of the Bribery Act, when does the bribery offence occur?
o: When a UK firm lawfully pays taxes in an overseas country
When a company donates openly to a registered foreign charity
When a foreign official accepts routine hospitality in the UK
When intending to influence a foreign official to obtain or retain business
When an agent declines to make a facilitation payment
w: Section 6 covers intending to influence a foreign public official to obtain or retain business or an advantage in business.

n.2: Routine, legitimate hospitality is not, by itself, a Section 6 bribe.
n.0: Paying lawful overseas taxes is not bribery of an official.
n.4: Refusing to pay a facilitation payment is not an offence at all.
n.1: An open, legitimate charitable donation is not influencing an official for business.

q: A compliance officer is mapping the Bribery Act offences and notes that most require proof that a function was performed improperly. Which section does NOT rely on the improper performance test?
o: Section 1, offering an advantage to another
Section 2, accepting an advantage from another
Section 3, defining a relevant function or activity
Section 4, defining improper performance itself
Section 6, bribery of a foreign public official
w: Section 6 does not rely on the improper performance test; it focuses on intent to influence an official for business advantage.

n.0: Section 1 relies on the improper performance test.
n.1: Section 2 also relies on the improper performance test.
n.3: Section 4 is the very section that defines improper performance.
n.2: Section 3 defines the functions the improper performance test judges.

q: A sales agent acting for a company pays a bribe to win a contract, though the board knew nothing of it. Why is the Bribery Act Section 7 offence described as strict liability for organisations?
o: It requires proof that the directors personally profited
Prosecutors must prove the board knew of every payment made
It applies only to companies that have a UK stock listing
Liability arises if an associated person bribes, absent adequate procedures
Liability attaches only to bribes actually paid inside the UK
w: If a person associated with the organisation bribes, the organisation is liable unless it proves adequate procedures to prevent bribery.

n.1: Strict liability means board knowledge need not be proved.
n.2: Section 7 is not limited to UK-listed companies.
n.0: No proof of personal director gain is required.
n.4: Section 7 has extraterritorial reach, not just UK-paid bribes.

q: A UK company faces a Section 7 Bribery Act charge after an overseas agent paid a bribe to win a contract. How can the company defend itself against this failure-to-prevent charge?
o: By proving it had adequate procedures to prevent bribery
By relying on legal advice from local overseas counsel
By proving the payment was fully tax-deductible
By showing the agent acted as an independent contractor
By showing the payment reflected normal market practice
w: The sole statutory defence is demonstrating that adequate procedures to prevent bribery were in place and proportionate to the risk.

n.4: Market practice is no defence to a Section 7 charge.
n.2: Tax treatment of a payment is irrelevant to the defence.
n.1: Reliance on local counsel is not the statutory defence.
n.3: An associated person can include an independent agent; this is no defence.

q: Where does Section 3’s concept of a relevant function or activity primarily bite?
o: Only statutory decisions taken by government ministers
Functions expected to be performed in good faith, impartially, or in trust
Only activities that are physically performed within the UK
Only private commercial sales negotiations between firms
Only functions that are governed by a formal written mandate
w: Section 3 covers functions of a public nature or connected with business where good faith, impartiality, or a position of trust is expected.

n.3: Section 3 is far broader than private sales negotiations.
n.0: It is not confined to ministerial statutory decisions.
n.2: Relevant functions can be performed outside the UK.
n.4: A written mandate is not required for a function to be relevant.

q: Which statement best reflects Section 4’s test for improper performance?
o: It depends on the payer's own subjective intentions
It focuses solely on decisions made in the public sector
It applies the expectation of a reasonable person in the UK
It applies only where the advantage is paid in cash
It requires proof of a contractual breach in every case
w: Improper performance is judged against what a reasonable person in the UK would expect of that function or activity.

n.4: No contractual breach need be shown for improper performance.
n.1: The test covers private functions, not only the public sector.
n.0: The test is objective, not based on the payer's subjective view.
n.3: The form of the advantage, cash or otherwise, is irrelevant.

q: A compliance officer is assessing whether a non-cash benefit offered to a client could amount to bribery. What does Section 5 indicate about a 'financial or other advantage'?
o: It applies only to payments in sterling
It excludes intangible benefits like internships
It is broadly defined and not limited to money
It requires board approval to qualify
It must exceed a statutory minimum value
w: The concept is deliberately broad, encompassing money and non-monetary benefits capable of influencing performance or decisions.

n.4: There is no minimum statutory threshold, because any advantage can qualify.
n.1: Intangible benefits can count, since the definition is broad and inclusive.
n.0: Currency is irrelevant, as any valuable advantage, monetary or otherwise, may qualify.
n.3: Corporate approvals do not define advantage, because the statute looks at influence, not governance processes.

q: A client relationship at an investment firm has just ended and the MLRO is deciding how long to keep the file. Under UK AML rules, how long must customer due diligence records generally be retained after the relationship ends?
o: Seven years
One year
Three years
Ten years
Five years
w: Firms must retain AML-related customer due diligence records and supporting documents for five years after the relationship ends or an occasional transaction is completed, enabling regulators to review them if necessary.

n.1: One year is insufficient under AML law; the statutory requirement is longer to ensure proper oversight.
n.2: Three years would not satisfy UK AML regulations, as firms are required to keep such records for five years.
n.0: Seven years may be relevant for general company law records, but AML requires five years specifically.
n.3: Ten years retention is not mandated by UK AML, which specifies five years after the end of the business relationship.

q: A firm is deciding what to keep on file to satisfy its AML record-keeping duties. Which type of documentation is typically required to be retained?
o: Customer identification documents and records of transactions
Copies of press releases the firm has issued
Minutes of the company's annual general meetings
Only staff attendance sheets from internal AML training
Supplier invoices for office equipment purchases
w: AML regulations require firms to retain customer identification documents, evidence of verification, and supporting records of transactions to allow for reconstruction if needed.

n.3: Training attendance sheets alone do not satisfy AML retention.
n.2: AGM minutes are not the core AML records required.
n.4: Office equipment invoices are not AML-required records.
n.1: Press releases are not customer or transaction records.

q: A firm is designing its AML record-keeping systems. Why must those records be maintained in a manner that is readily accessible?
o: So shareholders can review the firm's transparency data on demand
So marketing teams can analyse customer spending patterns
So regulators and law enforcement can trace transactions promptly
So auditors can obtain non-financial reporting statistics
So press enquiries about the firm can be answered quickly
w: AML rules require records to be kept in a way that allows quick access for authorities investigating money laundering or related offences.

n.0: Accessibility is for authorities, not shareholder convenience.
n.4: AML accessibility is not about answering press enquiries.
n.1: The purpose is investigation, not marketing analysis.
n.3: It is not about supplying non-financial reporting data.

q: Which regulation underpins AML record-keeping requirements in the UK?
o: The Market Abuse Regulation and its transparency requirements
The Companies Act 2006 and its associated record-keeping provisions
The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds Regulations 2017
The Criminal Justice Act 1993 governing insider dealing offences
The UK Corporate Governance Code applying to listed companies
w: The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 establish the UK framework for AML record keeping, customer due diligence, and reporting obligations.

n.1: The Companies Act governs company records, not AML record-keeping.
n.3: The CJA 1993 covers insider dealing, not AML record retention.
n.0: MAR addresses market abuse, not AML records.
n.4: The Governance Code is a comply-or-explain code, not AML law.

q: In relation to AML, what is the key purpose of transaction record retention?
o: To provide supporting evidence for tax deductions
To respond to customer service feedback requests
To allow individual transactions to be reconstructed later
To support the firm's internal marketing analytics
To assist the preparation of the annual shareholder report
w: Transaction records must be sufficient to enable the reconstruction of transactions, assisting investigators in establishing potential money laundering trails.

n.4: Retention is for investigators, not shareholder reporting.
n.3: It is not maintained for marketing analytics.
n.1: It is not aimed at customer feedback handling.
n.0: Transaction records are not kept for tax deductions.

q: During an FCA visit, a firm must produce its records of past suspicious activity reports. Under CFT obligations, why must those SAR records be retained?
o: To demonstrate compliance with reporting duties if audited
To support the calculation of dividend distributions
To answer GDPR subject access requests from clients
To help the firm plan its future marketing campaigns
To provide an evidence trail for the firm's advertising spend
w: Firms must keep records of SARs to demonstrate compliance with obligations to report suspicious transactions and to assist regulators if investigations arise.

n.4: SAR records are not kept to justify advertising spend.
n.3: They are not retained for marketing planning.
n.2: SAR retention is not about GDPR subject access.
n.1: SARs have nothing to do with dividend calculation.

q: For combating the financing of terrorism (CFT), what type of customer information must be retained?
o: Customer lifestyle and product preference surveys
Notes taken during internal boardroom meetings
Internal HR disciplinary and grievance records
Customer identity and beneficial ownership details
Supplier quality assurance certificates and audits
w: CFT record-keeping requires retaining key information including identity, beneficial ownership, and verification data to ensure that customers and transactions are not linked to terrorist financing.

n.0: Lifestyle surveys are not the CFT information required.
n.1: Boardroom notes are not CFT customer records.
n.2: HR disciplinary files are not CFT records.
n.4: Supplier QA certificates are unrelated to CFT retention.

q: A firm is setting the retention period for its counter-terrorist-financing records. Why must these be kept for the same period as its AML records?
o: To keep the firm's compliance manuals and branding consistent across departments
To support the preparation of the annual financial statements for shareholders
To let customers review the historic marketing offers they have received
To match the retention schedule applied to the firm's payroll records
To align with investigations that often span both money laundering and terrorist financing
w: AML and CFT obligations overlap, so aligning retention ensures regulators can examine both sets of risks over the same timeframe.

n.0: Retention is set for investigatory needs, not manual branding.
n.2: It is not driven by customer access to marketing history.
n.3: Payroll schedules are unrelated to CFT record retention.
n.1: Financial statements do not set the CFT retention period.

q: What is a key difference in focus between AML and CFT record-keeping requirements?
o: AML is global in reach; CFT is confined to the UK
AML requires records; CFT imposes no retention duty at all
AML addresses fraud; CFT covers only insider dealing
AML applies only to banks; CFT only applies to charities
AML targets criminal proceeds; CFT prevents terrorist funding
w: While AML aims to detect and prevent laundering of criminal proceeds, CFT specifically addresses preventing the movement of funds intended to support terrorism.

n.1: CFT also imposes record-keeping duties.
n.3: AML and CFT are not limited to banks and charities respectively.
n.0: CFT is not confined to UK territory.
n.2: Neither is limited to fraud or insider dealing alone.

q: A UK firm's MLRO is justifying to the board why detailed anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing records must be kept for years. Why are both AML and CFT record-keeping obligations critical for UK firms?
o: They ensure that staff bonus schemes are correctly funded
They lower the firm's spending on customer profiling
They support detecting, investigating and prosecuting financial crime
They are required only for annual reports to shareholders
They remove the need for GDPR-compliant data storage
w: AML and CFT record-keeping ensures regulators and law enforcement can detect, investigate, and prosecute offences involving illicit finance and terrorism support.

n.0: They are not about funding bonus schemes.
n.3: They serve enforcement, not just shareholder reporting.
n.4: They do not remove GDPR storage obligations.
n.1: They are not designed to cut marketing costs.

q: A paraplanner reviewing the firm's retention schedule asks what the core UK data protection principle on how long personal data may be kept actually requires. What is that principle?
o: Personal data must be destroyed after exactly five years
Personal data must be kept until the client requests deletion
Personal data must not be kept longer than necessary
Personal data must be archived for at least ten years
Personal data must be retained indefinitely if encrypted
w: The UK GDPR principle requires that personal data be retained only for as long as necessary for the purposes for which it was collected.

n.0: Five years is not a universal limit, since necessity depends on the purpose of the processing.
n.4: Encryption does not justify indefinite retention, as data must still be deleted when no longer necessary.
n.1: Client requests matter, but firms must apply necessity tests regardless of whether deletion is requested.
n.3: Ten years is not a blanket requirement, because data must be retained only as long as necessary.

q: Which legislation underpins current UK data protection obligations?
o: The Companies Act 2006
The Criminal Justice Act 1993
The Proceeds of Crime Act 2002
The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000
The UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018
w: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 provide the legal framework for processing, retention, and protection of personal data in the UK.

n.3: FSMA 2000 governs financial services, not data protection.
n.2: POCA 2002 addresses money laundering, not data protection.
n.1: The Criminal Justice Act 1993 deals with insider dealing.
n.0: The Companies Act 2006 governs company law, not data protection.

q: Why must firms document retention schedules for client personal data?
o: To demonstrate accountability to the Information Commissioner's Office
To support shareholders' annual reporting duties
To increase client engagement with the firm's services
To resolve customer complaints more efficiently only
To meet the marketing department's internal targets
w: Retention schedules demonstrate accountability by showing regulators that data is held only as long as necessary and lawfully disposed of thereafter.

n.2: Retention schedules are not a client engagement tool.
n.4: They are not set to meet marketing targets.
n.1: They are not for shareholder reporting.
n.3: Complaints handling is not their main purpose.

q: Which of the following best describes the 'storage limitation' principle?
o: Data must be backed up every month
Data must be retained in paper form for seven years
Data must be anonymised immediately upon collection
Data must be encrypted before storage
Data must be kept only for as long as necessary
w: The storage limitation principle requires that personal data not be kept longer than necessary for the purposes for which it was collected.

n.0: Backup frequency is an IT control, not a legal storage principle.
n.3: Encryption supports security but does not define retention duration.
n.2: Immediate anonymisation is not required; retention must be proportionate.
n.1: Paper retention for seven years is not mandated by data protection law.

q: What must firms ensure when deleting client personal data?
o: That deletion is secure and irreversible
That deletion occurs only if the client pays a fee
That deletion is delayed until shareholder approval
That records are retained on marketing systems only
That the data can still be restored if needed
w: Data deletion must be secure and irreversible to comply with data protection principles and prevent unauthorised recovery of sensitive information.

n.4: Restorability contradicts secure deletion requirements under data protection law.
n.3: Marketing systems must also delete data when retention ends.
n.2: Shareholder approval is irrelevant; data deletion must follow legal requirements.
n.1: Clients cannot be charged a fee to exercise their deletion rights.

q: A firm's data protection officer is drafting a policy governing how long customer records are kept. Under data protection rules, what is the role of a retention policy?
o: To set marketing strategies for using customer data
To supply auditors with the firm's profit forecasts
To require tax records to be destroyed within a year
To permit indefinite storage of encrypted records
To set maximum retention periods for personal data
w: A retention policy sets maximum retention periods to ensure data is not held longer than necessary for the purposes collected.

n.3: Encryption does not justify indefinite retention.
n.0: A retention policy is not a marketing strategy.
n.1: It does not provide auditors with profit forecasts.
n.2: It does not mandate early destruction of tax records.

q: Which authority enforces UK data protection requirements?
o: The Financial Conduct Authority
The Competition and Markets Authority
The Information Commissioner's Office
The Prudential Regulation Authority
The Serious Fraud Office
w: The Information Commissioner’s Office is the regulator responsible for enforcing UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 requirements.

n.0: The FCA regulates financial conduct, not data protection.
n.3: The PRA supervises prudential soundness, not data protection.
n.1: The CMA enforces competition law, not data protection.
n.4: The SFO prosecutes serious fraud, not data protection.

q: When processing client data, what must firms do to comply with data minimisation?
o: Collect only the data necessary for the specified purpose
Retain all client data permanently within secure archives
Gather all possible client data for potential future use
Collect data freely unless the client objects to it
Share all collected data across group companies by default
w: Data minimisation requires collecting only what is strictly necessary for the specified lawful purpose, avoiding excessive or irrelevant information.

n.2: Collecting data for undefined future use breaches minimisation.
n.1: Permanent retention of all data breaches minimisation.
n.3: Minimisation is not an opt-out based on objection.
n.4: Default group-wide sharing is not data minimisation.

q: A firm must keep certain client records for statutory periods even after a relationship ends. Under data protection law, which lawful basis most commonly justifies retaining this client data for regulatory purposes?
o: Consent
Contract performance
Legitimate interest
Public task
Legal obligation
w: Legal obligation is the lawful basis for retaining data where regulators require specific records to be kept for statutory periods.

n.0: Consent can be withdrawn and is not reliable for statutory retention duties.
n.2: Legitimate interests are valid in some cases but not for mandatory regulatory retention.
n.1: Contract performance may justify processing but not long-term statutory retention.
n.3: Public task applies to authorities, not private firms retaining records for regulation.

q: Why is regular review of retained client data important?
o: To minimise IT system upgrade costs
To comply with client requests for product brochures
To ensure data is deleted when no longer necessary
To align with quarterly shareholder updates
To maximise the value of marketing databases
w: Regular reviews ensure personal data is removed when it no longer serves a lawful purpose, meeting the storage limitation principle.

n.4: Marketing benefits are not the purpose; reviews exist to enforce lawful retention.
n.3: Shareholder updates do not determine personal data retention.
n.0: IT costs are separate; review addresses lawful necessity of data retention.
n.1: Product brochures are unrelated; reviews are for compliance with necessity.

q: What is the central purpose of the Disclosure and Transparency Rules (DTR)?
o: To set prudential capital requirements for UK banks
To ensure inside information is disclosed to the market promptly
To regulate the political donations that firms may make
To impose corporate social responsibility obligations
To govern how firms advertise to retail investors
w: The DTR aim to ensure that issuers disclose inside information promptly, supporting market integrity and investor confidence.

n.2: The DTR do not regulate political donations.
n.0: Capital requirements are set by the PRA, not the DTR.
n.3: CSR duties are not the purpose of the DTR.
n.4: Advertising to retail investors is governed by other FCA rules.

q: A listed company's board learns of a material development that could move its share price. Why must this inside information be disclosed without delay under DTR 2.1.3?
o: To reduce the marketing costs incurred by issuers
To prevent selective disclosure that could distort market prices
To help investment banks set their bonus pools
To give firms time to complete their quarterly audits
To provide regulators with annual fee calculations
w: Immediate disclosure prevents unfair advantages and ensures that all investors have equal access to material information affecting prices.

n.3: Delay for audits is not the reason for prompt disclosure.
n.4: It has nothing to do with regulator fee calculations.
n.2: Bonus pools are unrelated to disclosure timing.
n.0: Reducing marketing costs is not the aim.

q: Which of the following qualifies as inside information under DTR 2.1.3?
o: Public statements already made by government ministers
General knowledge of sector-wide market conditions
Published analyst forecasts printed in the financial press
Non-public facts likely to significantly affect the share price
Annual reports that were filed more than two years ago
w: Inside information is precise, non-public information that would likely have a significant effect on prices if made public.

n.2: Published analyst forecasts are already public information.
n.1: General sector conditions are public, not inside information.
n.4: Old, filed annual reports are public and historic.
n.0: Ministers' public statements are not non-public information.

q: A listed issuer is negotiating a sensitive acquisition and wants to hold back an announcement of inside information. Under DTR 2.5, what is the issuer's obligation regarding delaying disclosure?
o: Disclosure can always be delayed until the next annual report
Disclosure can be avoided if the data is stored securely
Disclosure may be delayed if shareholders vote to approve it
Delay is allowed if it protects legitimate interests and does not mislead
Disclosure is unnecessary if the board votes against it
w: Disclosure may be delayed only if legitimate interests justify it, the public is not misled, and confidentiality is preserved.

n.0: Delay to the annual report is not permitted under DTR 2.5.
n.2: Delay does not depend on a shareholder vote.

Approved Reporting Mechanisms
The Competition and Markets Authority platform

q: A firm needs to make the details of an executed equity trade public under MiFIR. Which system ensures post-trade transparency for equity trades?

A central securities depository handling settlement

An Approved Reporting Mechanism, known as an ARM
An Approved Publication Arrangement, known as an APA

q: An operations analyst is completing an electronic transaction report and checks which identifier for the reporting firm is mandatory. Which is it?

q: What does the storage limitation principle require firms to do with personal data?

Hold the data for a fixed statutory minimum of at least ten years

n.1: Erasure deletes data; it does not transfer it in a reusable format.

q: What is a key obligation of FCA-regulated firms regarding records of processing activities?
o: Destroy all processing records after one year
Keep records of processing purposes and data categories
Submit processing logs to the FCA each quarter
Publish all client data processing activity on the public website
Store all such records only in paper format
w: Firms must maintain records detailing processing purposes, categories of data and recipients as evidence of compliance with accountability requirements.

n.2: Records are kept internally, not filed quarterly with the FCA.
n.3: Processing records are not published publicly.
n.4: Records may be electronic; paper-only is not required.
n.0: Records are not automatically destroyed after a year.

q: Which lawful basis would a firm most appropriately rely on to comply with anti-money laundering legislation?
o: Legitimate interests
Vital interests
Contractual necessity
Consent
Legal obligation
w: When processing is required to comply with statutory duties such as AML checks, the lawful basis is legal obligation.

n.3: Consent is not valid where processing is mandatory by law.
n.0: Legitimate interests are secondary where a specific legal obligation applies.
n.1: Vital interests apply only to life-or-death situations.
n.2: Contractual necessity is relevant to contracts, not legal compliance duties.

q: Which individual right specifically allows people to demand correction of incorrect personal information?
o: The right to data portability between services
The right to rectification of inaccurate data
The right to be informed about processing
The right to restriction of processing
The right to object to direct marketing
w: The right to rectification gives individuals the ability to have inaccurate or incomplete personal data corrected without undue delay.

n.3: Restriction pauses processing; it does not correct data.
n.4: The right to object stops processing; it does not correct data.
n.0: Portability transfers data; it does not correct it.
n.2: Being informed concerns transparency, not correcting data.

q: What is the maximum timeframe for responding to a subject access request under the Act?
o: One month
Six weeks
Ten business days
Two weeks
Three months
w: Firms must respond to subject access requests without undue delay and within one month, extendable by two months in complex cases.

n.4: Three months is only possible as an extension, not the default period.
n.1: Six weeks is not a statutory timeframe.
n.3: Two weeks is shorter than the legally permitted period.
n.2: Ten business days was a former standard under US rules, not UK law.

q: Which principle ensures that firms collect only the personal data necessary for their stated purposes?
o: Accuracy
Data minimisation
Storage limitation
Fairness
Purpose limitation
w: Data minimisation requires that firms do not collect excessive or irrelevant personal data, limiting collection strictly to what is necessary.

n.4: Purpose limitation restricts processing to stated purposes, not the amount of data collected.
n.0: Accuracy requires correctness of data, not minimisation.
n.2: Storage limitation governs retention, not collection volume.
n.3: Fairness concerns transparency and rights, not minimisation.

q: A firm's data protection officer is assessing potential exposure after a lower-tier breach of data protection obligations. What is the maximum fine that can apply?
o: £10 million or 3% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher
£17.5 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher
£5 million or 1% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher
£8.7 million or 5% of global annual profit, whichever is higher
£8.7 million or 2% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher
w: For less serious breaches, fines can reach £8.7 million or 2% of global turnover, whichever is higher.

n.1: £17.5m/4% is the higher tier for the most serious breaches, not lesser ones.
n.0: £10m/3% is not a DPA penalty figure.
n.2: £5m/1% is not a DPA penalty figure.
n.3: The measure is 2% of turnover, not 5% of profit.

q: A former customer of a wealth manager emails to say the firm no longer needs to hold his personal data now that his account is closed, and asks for it to be deleted. Which right is he exercising?
o: Right to restriction
Right to object
Right to portability
Right to rectification
Right to erasure
w: The right to erasure, sometimes called the ‘right to be forgotten’, allows individuals to request deletion of personal data when it is no longer necessary for the original purpose or where consent has been withdrawn.

n.2: Portability enables individuals to receive and reuse their data, not erase it.
n.3: Rectification is concerned with correcting inaccurate information, not deleting it.
n.1: Objecting allows individuals to stop processing for certain purposes, but not necessarily delete data.
n.0: Restriction temporarily limits processing but does not require deletion.

q: Under the accountability principle, what must firms be able to demonstrate?
o: All data is stored in encrypted cloud services
Compliance with all data protection principles
ICO approval for every processing activity
That consent is the lawful basis in all cases
Retention schedules are identical across the industry
w: The accountability principle requires firms to show they have policies, records and controls in place to demonstrate compliance with the data protection principles.

n.2: The ICO does not pre-approve each processing activity.
n.3: Consent is not always the lawful basis; other bases apply depending on context.
n.0: Encryption is a safeguard but accountability goes far beyond technical controls.
n.4: Retention schedules vary by purpose and sector, not uniform across the industry.

q: Which lawful basis allows processing if it is necessary to protect someone’s life?
o: Vital interests
Legitimate interests
Contractual necessity
Consent
Legal obligation
w: Vital interests apply in emergencies where processing is necessary to protect someone’s life, for example in medical contexts.

n.3: Consent is not feasible in emergencies where the individual may be incapacitated.
n.4: Legal obligation applies where law mandates processing, not to protect life directly.
n.1: Legitimate interests require balancing against rights and do not apply in life-or-death cases.
n.2: Contractual necessity relates to contracts, not emergencies.

q: What does the purpose limitation principle prevent firms from doing?
o: Collecting more personal data than is necessary
Failing to encrypt personal data during its storage and transfer
Storing personal data for longer than is needed
Giving regulators inaccurate personal data
Using data for purposes incompatible with those first collected
w: Purpose limitation requires data to be used only for the purposes specified at collection and prohibits incompatible re-use without a lawful basis.

n.2: That is storage limitation, not purpose limitation.
n.0: That is data minimisation, not purpose limitation.
n.1: That is the security principle, not purpose limitation.
n.3: That relates to accuracy, not purpose limitation.

q: Which regulator is empowered to enforce the Data Protection Act 2018 in the UK?
o: The Competition and Markets Authority, the CMA
The Prudential Regulation Authority, the PRA
The Financial Conduct Authority, the FCA
The Information Commissioner's Office, the ICO
The Bank of England's financial policy committee
w: The ICO is the UK’s independent regulator for data protection, with powers to investigate, audit and issue fines for breaches.

n.2: The FCA regulates conduct in financial services, not data protection.
n.1: The PRA supervises prudential soundness, not the DPA.
n.0: The CMA oversees competition, not data protection.
n.4: The Bank of England does not enforce the DPA.

q: What is the purpose of privacy notices under the Data Protection Act 2018?
o: To replace the individual's statutory right of access entirely
To explain how a person's data is collected and used
To get regulator sign-off before any new processing
To justify the firm's profit from using the data
To request indefinite retention of client data
w: Privacy notices are the primary tool for communicating to individuals how their personal data will be collected, used, stored and shared, supporting transparency.

n.2: Privacy notices inform individuals; they do not seek regulator sign-off.
n.3: They are not a means of justifying profit.
n.4: They do not authorise indefinite retention.
n.0: They complement, not replace, the right of access.

q: A firm receives an unusually complicated subject access request and asks whether it can take longer than one month to respond. In what circumstance may the deadline be extended?
o: Whenever the firm simply chooses to take longer
When the client has debts outstanding to the firm
When the ICO has not yet responded to the firm
When key staff are away from the office on annual leave
When the request is especially complex or numerous
w: The Act allows an extension of up to two months if a request is complex or numerous, but firms must notify the individual within the initial one-month period.

n.3: Staff leave is not a valid reason to extend the deadline.
n.1: Outstanding debts do not justify an extension.
n.2: The extension does not depend on the ICO responding.
n.0: A firm cannot extend the deadline at will.

q: What is the lawful basis for processing employee payroll information?
o: Legitimate interests pursued by the employer
Public task carried out in the public interest
Contractual necessity under the employment contract
Consent that is given freely by the individual employee
Vital interests protecting the employee's life
w: Payroll processing is necessary for the performance of an employment contract, making contractual necessity the correct basis.

n.3: Payroll is required by the contract, so consent is not the basis.
n.0: Legitimate interests is not needed where a contract requires the processing.
n.4: Vital interests concerns life-or-death situations, not payroll.
n.1: Public task applies to public authorities, not routine payroll.

q: What must firms do if they rely on consent as their lawful basis?
o: Make the service conditional on giving consent
Report every recorded consent to the FCA at the end of each month
Treat the consent as permanent once it is given
Bundle the consent within all customer contracts
Let individuals withdraw consent as easily as they gave it
w: Consent must be freely given and withdrawable at any time, and firms must ensure withdrawal is as easy as giving consent.

n.3: Bundled consent is invalid, not a requirement.
n.0: Making a service conditional on consent invalidates it.
n.2: Consent can be withdrawn; it is not permanent.
n.1: Consents are not reported monthly to the FCA.

q: Which principle obliges firms to ensure data remains accurate and up to date?
o: Storage limitation
Accuracy
Purpose limitation
Integrity and confidentiality
Data minimisation
w: The accuracy principle requires firms to take reasonable steps to ensure data is correct and updated where necessary, reducing risks of harm from outdated information.

n.3: Integrity and confidentiality concern data security, not correctness.
n.2: Purpose limitation deals with restricting data use to stated purposes.
n.0: Storage limitation relates to how long data is kept, not accuracy.
n.4: Data minimisation restricts the volume of data collected, not its accuracy.

q: Which regulator has the power to enforce the Data Protection Act 2018 in the UK?
o: The Competition and Markets Authority, the CMA
The Serious Fraud Office, the SFO
The Financial Conduct Authority, the FCA
The Information Commissioner's Office, the ICO
The Prudential Regulation Authority, the PRA
w: The ICO is the UK’s independent data protection regulator. It enforces the Data Protection Act 2018 by issuing fines, undertaking audits, and compelling compliance through enforcement notices.

n.2: The FCA regulates financial conduct, not data protection.
n.4: The PRA handles prudential regulation, not the DPA.
n.0: The CMA oversees competition, not data protection.
n.1: The SFO investigates serious fraud, not data protection.

q: What is the maximum financial penalty the ICO can impose for the most serious breaches of data protection law?
o: £17.5 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher
£5 million, imposed as one single fixed penalty for every firm alike
£10 million or 1% of the firm's UK turnover, whichever is higher
£1 million, regardless of the firm's size or turnover
£8.7 million or 2% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher
w: For the most serious breaches, the ICO can impose fines of up to £17.5 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher. This mirrors the GDPR penalty structure.

n.2: The measure is global turnover at 4%, not 1% of UK turnover.
n.4: £8.7m/2% is the standard tier, not the maximum for serious breaches.
n.1: There is no £5 million fixed penalty; it is turnover-based.
n.3: There is no flat £1 million cap under the DPA.

q: A firm suffers a data breach and the compliance team considers what action the ICO may take against it for non-compliance. Which enforcement action is available to the ICO?
o: Appoint administrators to take over the firm
Directly imprison the firm's appointed data protection officer
Freeze the personal assets of the firm's directors
Directly revoke a firm's FCA regulatory permissions
Issue enforcement notices requiring corrective action
w: The ICO can issue enforcement notices requiring firms to take specific corrective actions, such as ceasing unlawful processing or improving data security measures.

n.3: The ICO cannot revoke FCA permissions; that is the FCA's power.
n.0: The ICO does not appoint administrators to run firms.
n.2: The ICO cannot freeze directors' personal assets.
n.1: The ICO cannot imprison staff; it issues notices and fines.

q: What type of notice can the ICO issue to investigate a firm’s data processing practices?
o: A conduct requirements notice issued by the FCA in its place
An improvement notice setting a compliance deadline
An information notice requiring information to be provided
A suspension notice halting the firm's trading
A prohibition notice banning the firm's activity
w: An information notice allows the ICO to require organisations to provide information relevant to assessing their compliance with data protection obligations.

n.1: The ICO uses assessment/enforcement notices, not an 'improvement notice', to investigate.
n.3: A suspension notice halting trading is not an ICO investigative tool.
n.4: A prohibition notice is not how the ICO gathers information.
n.0: A conduct notice is not the ICO's investigative instrument.

q: What is a key difference between assessment notices and enforcement notices issued by the ICO?
o: Assessment notices are criminal sanctions, enforcement notices are civil sanctions
Assessment notices suspend data transfers, enforcement notices suspend staff
Assessment notices are optional, enforcement notices are voluntary
Assessment notices allow inspections, enforcement notices require action
Assessment notices impose financial penalties, enforcement notices do not
w: Assessment notices permit the ICO to enter premises and inspect processing, while enforcement notices require a firm to take or stop certain actions to ensure compliance.

n.4: Financial penalties are separate sanctions, not the function of assessment notices.
n.2: Neither notice is optional or voluntary; both are binding.
n.1: These notices do not suspend transfers or staff; they regulate compliance practices.
n.0: Both notices are civil regulatory tools, not criminal sanctions.

q: A wealth firm receives an information notice from the ICO but decides not to respond. What action can the ICO take in response to the firm's refusal to comply?
o: Impose imprisonment directly
Automatically revoke the firm’s banking licence
Instruct the FCA to close the firm
Seize directors’ personal property
Apply to the courts for enforcement
w: If a firm fails to comply with an information notice, the ICO can apply to the courts to enforce compliance, making refusal a contempt of court issue.

n.1: The ICO cannot revoke banking licences; that is outside its remit.
n.2: The ICO cannot instruct the FCA to close firms.
n.0: Imprisonment is only available via criminal prosecution, not direct ICO action.
n.3: The ICO cannot seize personal property of directors.

q: What is the maximum penalty for less serious breaches under the ICO’s fining powers?
o: £17.5 million or 4% of global annual turnover, if higher
£5 million regardless of the firm's size or turnover
£8.7 million or 2% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher
£10 million or just 1% of the firm's UK-only annual turnover figure
£1 million applied as a flat cap for all firms
w: For less serious breaches, the ICO may impose fines up to £8.7 million or 2% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.

n.4: There is no £1 million flat cap; penalties are turnover-based.
n.1: There is no £5 million fixed penalty for lesser breaches.
n.0: £17.5m/4% is the higher tier for the most serious breaches.
n.3: The standard tier is 2% of global turnover, not 1% of UK turnover.

q: Which of the following can trigger an ICO investigation?
o: A data breach notification from a firm
Failure to publish quarterly profit statements
Failure to renew Companies House filings
Requests from the FCA for a market abuse case
Complaints about financial product mis-selling
w: The ICO may launch an investigation following a data breach notification or a complaint about unlawful data processing.

n.1: Profit statements are unrelated to data protection obligations.
n.4: Mis-selling complaints are within the FCA’s jurisdiction, not the ICO’s.
n.3: Market abuse is regulated by the FCA, not the ICO.
n.2: Companies House filings are outside the ICO’s remit.

q: What is the purpose of an enforcement notice from the ICO?
o: To suspend all of the firm's directors from office
To compel a firm to comply with data protection law
To confiscate the firm's premises, property and equipment
To remove the firm's listing on the stock exchange
To force changes to the firm's board membership
w: An enforcement notice requires a firm to take specific steps to comply with the law, such as stopping unlawful processing or implementing stronger safeguards.

n.0: Enforcement notices require compliance; they do not suspend directors.
n.2: The ICO cannot confiscate a firm's property via such a notice.
n.3: An enforcement notice does not delist a firm.
n.4: It does not dictate board membership.

q: The ICO is escalating its oversight of a firm's data handling beyond the threat of fines. In addition to fines, which power strengthens the ICO's ability to check compliance?
o: Forcing the automatic dismissal of firm employees
Issuing assessment notices to inspect data processing
Approving or blocking the firm's proposed mergers
Rewriting and reissuing the firm's corporate governance code
Setting the interest rates the firm may charge
w: Assessment notices give the ICO authority to enter premises and inspect data processing systems to ensure compliance with the law.

n.0: The ICO cannot force dismissal of employees.
n.4: The ICO does not set firms' interest rates.
n.2: Merger approval is the CMA's role, not the ICO's.
n.3: The ICO does not rewrite governance codes.

q: The finance director of an investment firm is explaining to the board why the firm must hold a Capital Adequacy Requirement. What is its main purpose?
o: To guarantee shareholders a profit every financial year
To fund the firm's marketing and distribution costs
To ensure firms hold enough capital to absorb unexpected losses
To bring an end to the firm's ongoing supervision by the FCA entirely
To remove the firm's need to borrow externally
w: Capital Adequacy Requirements are designed to ensure that investment firms maintain enough financial resources to absorb losses, protect clients, and safeguard market stability.

n.0: Capital rules absorb losses; they do not guarantee profits.
n.4: They do not remove the need for external borrowing.
n.3: They do not end a firm's supervision.
n.1: They are not intended to fund marketing costs.

q: A newly authorised investment firm asks why it must hold a minimum level of regulatory capital. Why does the FCA impose capital adequacy requirements on such firms?
o: To raise extra tax revenue for the government
To deliberately limit competition between authorised firms
To align dividend levels across the whole industry
To protect clients and counterparties from firm default
To guarantee directors a minimum annual salary
w: Capital adequacy protects clients, counterparties, and markets by reducing the likelihood of insolvency and ensuring firms can meet obligations even in stress scenarios.

n.4: Capital rules protect clients, not directors' salaries.
n.0: They are not a means of raising tax.
n.2: They do not align industry dividends.
n.1: They are not designed to limit competition.

q: A prudential analyst is explaining why the firm holds a capital buffer to absorb trading and operational losses. Which risk does the Capital Adequacy Requirement primarily address?
o: Staff turnover risk
Currency translation risk
Liquidity preference risk
Reputational risk only
Insolvency risk
w: The key aim is to reduce insolvency risk by ensuring firms hold capital buffers to absorb trading or operational losses.

n.2: Liquidity is important but is addressed separately from capital adequacy.
n.1: Currency risk is managed through hedging, not prudential capital standards.
n.0: Staff turnover is an HR issue, not prudential capital requirement.
n.3: Reputation matters, but capital adequacy specifically targets solvency risk.

q: Which of the following best explains why minimum capital levels are set for investment firms?
o: To confine all authorised firms to domestic operations only
To stop firms from paying any executive bonuses
To deter small firms from entering the market
To provide a buffer against operational and market risks
To keep banks and investment firms exactly equal
w: Minimum capital ensures that firms have a buffer to cover operational, market, and credit risks, reducing the likelihood of failure in stressed conditions.

n.1: Minimum capital is a loss buffer, not a bonus ban.
n.4: It is not about equalising banks and investment firms.
n.2: It is not intended to deter market entry.
n.0: It does not restrict firms to domestic activity.

q: A retail client asks an adviser how capital adequacy rules actually help protect them. What effect do those prudential rules have on client protection?
o: They guarantee investment returns for every client
They stop firms from charging any client fees
They ensure clients receive a dividend each year
They completely remove market volatility for all investors
They reduce the risk of client loss if a firm defaults
w: By ensuring firms have enough capital to withstand losses, capital adequacy rules reduce the risk of client funds being compromised by firm default.

n.0: Capital rules reduce default risk; they do not guarantee returns.
n.1: They do not prevent firms charging fees.
n.2: They do not ensure annual dividends.
n.3: They cannot remove market volatility.

q: Which type of capital is typically emphasised under capital adequacy requirements?
o: Deferred tax assets held on the balance sheet
High-quality capital such as Tier 1 common equity
Unrealised goodwill from past acquisitions
Reserves specifically set aside for future marketing spend
Projected future profits not yet earned
w: Tier 1 capital, such as common equity, provides the strongest buffer against losses and is the focus of capital adequacy requirements.

n.0: Deferred tax assets are low-quality and often deducted from capital.
n.2: Goodwill is intangible and excluded from core capital.
n.4: Future profits are not counted as regulatory capital.
n.3: Marketing reserves are not regulatory capital.
