q: How do capital adequacy requirements support market confidence?
o: By removing the need for firms to be audited
By setting mandatory annual profit targets for every regulated firm
By making all firms offer identical investment products
By requiring firms to publish their trading strategies
By assuring participants that firms can withstand financial shocks
w: Capital adequacy assures clients and counterparties that regulated firms can survive losses without collapsing, which underpins market confidence.

n.2: Capital rules do not standardise product offerings.
n.1: They do not set profit targets.
n.0: They do not remove audit requirements.
n.3: They do not require publishing trading strategies.

q: A prudential risk officer is briefing the board on why capital adequacy rules matter and considers what would most likely happen if firms operated without them. What is the most likely outcome?
o: Higher systemic risk and a greater chance of firm failure
Enhanced liquidity right across every single financial market
Greater stability right across the whole sector
Guaranteed investor protection from all losses
Improved transparency of the fees clients pay
w: Without capital adequacy, firms may not withstand losses, increasing the chance of failure and systemic instability.

n.2: Removing capital rules would reduce stability, not increase it.
n.3: It would not guarantee investor protection; the opposite is true.
n.4: It would not improve fee transparency.
n.1: It would not enhance market liquidity.

q: A prudential specialist explains how the capital adequacy rules a firm must hold relate to the FCA's aims. How do those rules align with the FCA's statutory objectives?
o: They provide subsidies to firms that are expanding overseas
They support market integrity and protect consumers
They decide which products may be marketed
They dictate each firm's remuneration policy
They set the tax policy for investment firms
w: Capital adequacy aligns with the FCA’s objectives by protecting consumers and maintaining market integrity through firm resilience.

n.4: Capital rules are not tax policy.
n.3: They do not dictate remuneration policies.
n.2: They do not decide which products may be marketed.
n.0: They do not subsidise overseas expansion.

q: What does capital adequacy regulation ultimately seek to protect?
o: Shareholders' guaranteed dividend return on their invested equity
The tax revenue government collects from financial services firms
The firm's ability to maximise short-term proprietary trading gains
Clients, counterparties and the stability of the financial system
Senior managers' remuneration and annual bonus arrangements
w: The ultimate aim is to protect clients, counterparties, and the financial system by ensuring firms have sufficient resources to withstand shocks.

n.0: Capital rules protect stability, not shareholder returns, which are never guaranteed.
n.2: The aim is resilience to shocks, not maximising trading profits.
n.1: Protecting tax revenue is not the purpose of prudential capital rules.
n.4: Executive pay is unrelated to the objective of capital adequacy.

q: Which firms are directly subject to the FCA Conduct of Business Sourcebook (COBS)?
o: General insurers underwriting private motor insurance policies
Consumer credit firms advancing unsecured personal loans
Payment providers executing cross-border currency transfers
Firms doing designated investment business from a UK establishment
Mortgage lenders arranging regulated first-charge home loans
w: COBS applies to designated investment business carried out from a UK establishment, such as investment advisers and portfolio managers.

n.4: Regulated mortgage business is governed by MCOB, not COBS.
n.0: General insurance conduct falls under ICOBS, not COBS.
n.2: Payment services are governed by the PSRs, not COBS.
n.1: Consumer credit lending is governed by CONC, not COBS.

q: A UK-authorised firm manages client portfolios from its London office. Which conduct regime applies?
o: BCOBS
COBS
ICOBS
CONC
MCOB
w: Portfolio management is designated investment business, so COBS applies to the firm when it operates from the UK.

n.4: MCOB covers mortgage business, not portfolio management.
n.2: ICOBS governs general insurance activities, not investment management.
n.0: BCOBS applies to banking conduct, not discretionary investment services.
n.3: CONC applies to consumer credit, not investment management.

q: COBS applies to a client outside the UK when:
o: The financial instrument is listed on a UK-recognised exchange
The firm's adviser physically travels overseas to meet them
The client formally elects to be covered by UK conduct rules
The activity is carried on from a UK establishment
The client holds citizenship of an EU member state
w: COBS application depends on the location of the establishment providing the service, not the client’s nationality or product venue.

n.2: Client election does not determine COBS territorial scope.
n.4: Nationality is irrelevant to the establishment test.
n.0: The listing venue of the product does not fix COBS scope.
n.1: Where the adviser travels does not change the establishment test.

q: How are appointed representatives brought within COBS?
o: Through the product manufacturer accepting distributor duties
Through registration of the AR on the PRA's own register
Through the responsibility of their principal firm
Through individual approval under the Senior Managers Regime
Through direct authorisation granted to them by the FCA
w: Appointed representatives act under a principal, and the principal carries responsibility for ensuring COBS compliance.

n.4: ARs are exempt persons, not directly authorised by the FCA.
n.1: ARs are not brought in via any PRA register.
n.0: A manufacturer's product duties do not bring an AR into COBS.
n.3: SM&CR approval is not how ARs come within COBS.

q: A firm operates an authorised unit trust and needs to identify the FCA Handbook module that primarily governs the fund's operation. Which module is it?
o: COBS
ICOBS
BCOBS
MCOB
COLL
w: Authorised fund operation is under COLL, not COBS. COBS applies where firms provide investment services to clients.

n.0: COBS covers investment services to clients, not scheme operation.
n.2: BCOBS applies to banking, not collective investment schemes.
n.1: ICOBS applies to insurance, not funds.
n.3: MCOB applies to mortgages, not funds.

q: A firm reclassifies a large institutional client as an eligible counterparty. What is the impact of that classification under COBS?
o: Only retail disclosure requirements remain in force
Only the best execution obligation continues to apply
All COBS conduct rules cease to apply to the relationship
Certain conduct protections no longer apply to the business
The client receives enhanced retail-style protections
w: ECPs benefit from a lighter regime; many conduct protections are disapplied compared with professional or retail clients.

n.2: ECP status disapplies certain rules, not all of them.
n.1: Best execution is among the protections disapplied for ECPs.
n.0: Retail disclosure rules are not the only surviving rules.
n.4: ECPs get lighter, not enhanced, protection.

q: A high-street bank offers personal current accounts to retail customers and needs to identify the applicable conduct rules. Which FCA sourcebook applies to firms offering personal current accounts?
o: BCOBS, the Banking Conduct of Business Sourcebook
COBS, the Conduct of Business Sourcebook for investments
MCOB, the Mortgages and Home Finance Conduct sourcebook
ICOBS, the Insurance Conduct of Business Sourcebook
CONC, the Consumer Credit sourcebook for lending
w: BCOBS applies to retail banking business. COBS applies instead to investment business.

n.1: COBS covers investment business, not personal current accounts.
n.2: MCOB covers mortgages, not current accounts.
n.3: ICOBS covers insurance, not banking accounts.
n.4: CONC covers consumer credit, not current accounts.

q: Which activity would be regulated under MCOB rather than COBS?
o: Managing a portfolio of listed equities
Providing investment research to retail clients
Advising on pension transfers
Arranging a regulated mortgage contract
Operating a collective investment scheme
w: Mortgage contracts fall under MCOB, not COBS. COBS applies to designated investment business.

n.0: Portfolio management is designated investment business under COBS.
n.1: Investment research is within the COBS framework.
n.2: Pension transfer advice falls under COBS.
n.4: Fund operation is governed by COLL, not MCOB.

q: Which FCA rulebook section clarifies which firms COBS applies to?
o: ICOBS 3.2
SYSC 1.2
COBS 1.1
BCOBS 5.1
MCOB 2.1
w: COBS 1.1 sets out the general application provisions and clarifies the scope of firms subject to COBS.

n.4: MCOB 2.1 deals with mortgages, not COBS application.
n.3: BCOBS covers banking conduct, not investment conduct scope.
n.0: ICOBS 3.2 addresses insurance conduct, not COBS scope.
n.1: SYSC covers systems and controls, not the application of COBS.

q: An adviser at a general insurance broker is checking which sourcebook governs their sales activity. Which of the following would fall under ICOBS rather than COBS?
o: Executing client orders in shares
Advising on equity derivatives
Selling motor insurance policies
Discretionary portfolio management
Providing custody of securities
w: ICOBS governs insurance distribution such as selling motor policies. COBS applies to investment business.

n.3: Portfolio management is designated investment business under COBS.
n.1: Equity derivative advice is COBS territory, not ICOBS.
n.0: Executing share trades is subject to COBS.
n.4: Custody of securities falls under CASS and COBS, not ICOBS.

q: A firm advising on and arranging investments from its London office is checking whether COBS applies. Which type of business is expressly covered when carried on from a UK establishment?
o: Consumer credit lending carried on from a UK establishment
Payment remittance services from a UK establishment
Mortgage mediation carried on from a UK establishment
Designated investment business carried on from a UK establishment
General insurance underwriting from a UK establishment
w: COBS applies primarily to designated investment business carried on from a UK establishment, such as advising on and arranging investments.

n.2: Mortgage mediation is covered by MCOB, not COBS.
n.0: Consumer credit lending is covered by CONC, not COBS.
n.4: General insurance is covered by ICOBS, not COBS.
n.1: Payment remittance falls under the PSRs, not COBS.

q: Which client classification allows certain COBS rules to be disapplied?
o: Eligible counterparty
Professional client
Retail client
High net worth individual
Local authority
w: COBS contains exemptions where a client is classified as an eligible counterparty, allowing disapplication of certain conduct rules.

n.2: Retail clients receive the highest level of protection under COBS.
n.1: Professional clients retain key COBS protections; exemptions are narrower than for eligible counterparties.
n.3: High net worth does not itself change COBS application unless classified formally.
n.4: Local authorities may be retail or professional, not automatically ECPs.

q: Which transaction is explicitly included in COBS Annex 1 Part 1(1)?
o: Arranging regulated first-charge residential mortgages
Providing money remittance and payment transfer services
Reception and transmission of orders in financial instruments
Issuing and underwriting private motor insurance contracts
Provision of consumer credit loans to individual borrowers
w: Reception and transmission of orders in financial instruments is one of the core designated investment activities covered by COBS Annex 1 Part 1(1).

n.4: Consumer lending is not a designated investment activity.
n.3: Insurance underwriting is an ICOBS activity, not Annex 1.
n.0: Arranging mortgages is an MCOB activity, not Annex 1.
n.1: Money remittance is a payment service, not Annex 1.

q: Which of the following best describes transactions between regulated market participants under COBS?
o: They are completely exempt from all financial regulation
They may qualify as eligible counterparty business
They are governed only by the mortgage sourcebook MCOB
They fall solely under the FSCS compensation rules
They are covered exclusively by the banking sourcebook
w: COBS Annex 1 Part 1(4) covers business conducted between regulated market participants and classifies them as eligible counterparty transactions.

n.0: Such transactions remain regulated, just under a lighter regime.
n.2: They are investment dealings, not mortgage business.
n.3: FSCS rules do not govern the conduct of these dealings.
n.4: BCOBS covers banking, not investment counterparty dealing.

q: A firm is checking whether the activity it performs is a regulated investment service under COBS Annex 1 Part 1(1). Which of the following is listed there?
o: Issuing unsecured personal loans to consumers
Providing residential estate agency services
Arranging general insurance contracts for retail buyers
Execution of client orders in financial instruments
Providing general legal advice to corporate clients
w: Execution of client orders in financial instruments is a core investment service under Annex 1 Part 1(1).

n.4: Legal advice is not a designated investment service.
n.0: Consumer lending falls under CONC, not COBS Annex 1.
n.2: Insurance arranging falls under ICOBS, not Annex 1.
n.1: Estate agency is not a designated investment service.

q: Which business is considered eligible counterparty business under COBS?
o: Advising private individuals on residential mortgages
Offering business current accounts to small enterprises
Providing consumer hire agreements to retail customers
Dealing on own account between authorised investment firms
Selling travel insurance policies to retail customers
w: Transactions between investment firms, such as dealing on own account, fall within eligible counterparty business provisions under COBS.

n.2: Consumer hire is a CONC activity, not ECP business.
n.4: Selling travel insurance is ICOBS business, not ECP.
n.0: Mortgage advice is MCOB business, not ECP dealing.
n.1: Current accounts are BCOBS banking, not ECP business.

q: Which of the following activities is captured under COBS Annex 1 Part 1(1)?
o: Insurance claims handling
Estate agency services
Investment advice
Mortgage broking
Debt collection
w: Providing investment advice on financial instruments is one of the designated activities listed under COBS Annex 1 Part 1(1).

n.0: Insurance activities are governed by ICOBS, not COBS.
n.4: Debt collection is not part of designated investment business.
n.1: Estate agency is not an FCA-regulated investment service.
n.3: Mortgage broking falls under MCOB, not COBS.

q: Which activity falls under Annex 1 Part 1(1) investment services requiring COBS compliance?
o: Motor insurance broking
Consumer loan broking
Debt counselling
Portfolio management
Payment initiation services
w: Portfolio management is a designated investment activity listed under COBS Annex 1 Part 1(1).

n.0: Insurance broking is under ICOBS, not COBS.
n.1: Consumer loan broking falls under CONC, not COBS.
n.4: Payment initiation is covered by PSRs, not COBS.
n.2: Debt counselling is regulated under CONC, not COBS.

q: Two FCA-authorised investment firms execute trades directly with one another in the wholesale market. Under COBS, how is this business classified?
o: Eligible counterparty business between two authorised firms
Regulated mortgage activity falling under the MCOB rules
Retail client business requiring full suitability checks
Insurance mediation governed by the ICOBS sourcebook
Consumer credit activity regulated under the CONC rules
w: Transactions between regulated market participants are classed as eligible counterparty business under COBS Annex 1 Part 1(4).

n.2: Two authorised firms dealing directly is ECP, not retail, business.
n.4: This is investment dealing, not consumer credit under CONC.
n.1: This is investment dealing, not mortgage business under MCOB.
n.3: This is investment dealing, not insurance mediation under ICOBS.

q: Which activity is recognised under COBS as designated investment business?
o: Underwriting of financial instruments in a securities issue
Granting unsecured personal loans to retail consumers
Arranging regulated second-charge mortgage contracts
Selling buildings and contents household insurance
Providing conveyancing and general legal services
w: Underwriting of financial instruments is a designated investment activity within Annex 1 Part 1(1).

n.1: Personal lending is a CONC activity, not designated investment business.
n.3: Household insurance is ICOBS business, not Annex 1.
n.2: Second-charge mortgages fall under MCOB, not Annex 1.
n.4: Legal and conveyancing work is not designated investment business.

q: Which activity listed in Annex 1 Part 1(1) falls directly under COBS when carried on from a UK establishment?
o: Issuing consumer credit agreements
Arranging second-charge mortgages
Providing foreign exchange for travel
Selling home contents insurance
Dealing on own account
w: Dealing on own account is a designated investment activity in Annex 1 Part 1(1) and falls within COBS when carried on in the UK.

n.0: Consumer credit agreements are regulated under CONC, not COBS.
n.3: Insurance distribution is governed by ICOBS, not COBS.
n.1: Mortgage business is regulated under MCOB, not COBS.
n.2: Foreign exchange for travel is generally unregulated and outside COBS scope.

q: A broker deals with a large bank on a wholesale basis and wants to apply the lightest client protections permitted by COBS. Which category of clients can it treat as eligible counterparties?
o: Private individuals with £100,000 to invest
Retail consumers
Small businesses with fewer than 10 employees
Investment firms and credit institutions
Charitable organisations
w: Investment firms and credit institutions are eligible counterparties under COBS for designated investment business.

n.1: Retail clients always receive the highest protection and cannot be treated as ECPs.
n.4: Charities are not automatically ECPs under COBS.
n.2: Small enterprises may be professional clients but not automatically ECPs.
n.0: Private wealth does not itself confer ECP status under COBS.

q: Which of the following services is specifically recognised under COBS Annex 1 Part 1(1)?
o: Operating residential estate agency businesses
Safekeeping and administration of financial instruments
Providing everyday retail banking and deposit services
Arranging buildings and contents household insurance
Granting personal loans and overdrafts to consumers
w: Custody services, including safekeeping of financial instruments, are included within Annex 1 Part 1(1) activities covered by COBS.

n.4: Consumer lending falls under CONC, not COBS Annex 1.
n.3: Household insurance falls under ICOBS, not Annex 1.
n.2: Retail banking is BCOBS business, not Annex 1.
n.0: Estate agency is not a designated investment activity.

q: Under COBS Annex 1 Part 1(4), transactions between which parties may be classified as eligible counterparty business?
o: Two FCA-authorised investment firms
A mortgage broker and a homebuyer
A bank and a retail consumer
An insurer and a motorist
A payday lender and an individual borrower
w: Transactions between regulated firms, such as two authorised investment firms, fall into eligible counterparty business under COBS Annex 1 Part 1(4).

n.2: Retail client transactions are never classified as ECP business.
n.1: Mortgage activities are under MCOB, not COBS ECP rules.
n.3: Insurance transactions are under ICOBS, not COBS Annex 1(4).
n.4: Consumer credit activity is under CONC, not COBS.

q: A firm reviews its activities to work out which of them bring it within the scope of COBS. Which of the following investment services triggers COBS application?
o: Selling annual travel insurance to holidaymakers
Providing personal tax and accountancy advice
Issuing unsecured personal loans to consumers
Producing investment research and financial analysis
Arranging assured shorthold tenancy agreements
w: Investment research provided to clients is an investment service captured under COBS Annex 1 Part 1(1).

n.1: Tax advice is not a designated investment service.
n.2: Personal lending is a CONC activity, not COBS.
n.0: Travel insurance is ICOBS business, not COBS.
n.4: Tenancy arranging is not a designated investment service.

q: A firm trades solely with other regulated entities as eligible counterparties. Which statement best describes how COBS applies to that business?
o: Every FCA conduct rule ceases to apply to the business
Certain core protections are disapplied for wholesale dealings
Only financial promotion obligations remain in force
COBS does not apply at all to UK-authorised firms
COBS applies as though all clients were retail clients
w: ECP business has a lighter regulatory regime; COBS disapplies certain protections to facilitate wholesale trading between regulated entities.

n.0: Only certain protections are disapplied, not every rule.
n.2: Financial promotion rules are not the only surviving rules.
n.4: ECP business gets lighter, not full retail, treatment.
n.3: COBS still applies to UK-authorised firms doing ECP business.

q: Which activity in Annex 1 Part 1(1) involves managing portfolios on a discretionary client mandate?
o: Provision of investment research
Safekeeping of assets
Portfolio management
Execution of orders
Reception and transmission of orders
w: Portfolio management, under Annex 1 Part 1(1), refers to discretionary management of investments on behalf of a client, and is subject to COBS.

n.3: Execution of orders is a separate designated service but not discretionary management.
n.4: Reception and transmission involves passing orders, not managing them.
n.1: Safekeeping relates to custody, not portfolio management.
n.0: Investment research provides information but is not portfolio management.

q: Which services are explicitly investment services under COBS Annex 1 Part 1(1)?
o: Issuing general insurance contracts
Offering current accounts to individuals
Advising on investments
Arranging residential mortgages
Providing consumer hire agreements
w: Advising on investments in financial instruments is a designated activity within Annex 1 Part 1(1) and therefore subject to COBS.

n.3: Mortgage intermediation is covered by MCOB.
n.4: Consumer hire is regulated under consumer credit rules, not COBS.
n.0: Insurance contracts are under ICOBS, not COBS.
n.1: Bank accounts are regulated under BCOBS, not COBS.

q: What type of transaction between regulated market participants would be classified under COBS Annex 1 Part 1(4)?
o: Advance of an unsecured personal loan to a consumer
Providing money remittance services to an individual
Sale of private motor insurance to a retail customer
A bond trade executed between two authorised investment banks
Arranging a regulated mortgage for a first-time buyer
w: Wholesale trades such as bond transactions between regulated investment firms are treated as eligible counterparty business under Annex 1 Part 1(4).

n.2: Selling insurance to a retail client is ICOBS, not ECP business.
n.0: A personal loan is CONC business, not ECP dealing.
n.4: Arranging a mortgage is MCOB business, not ECP dealing.
n.1: Money remittance is a payment service, not ECP business.

q: A firm is checking whether one of its activities falls within COBS Annex 1 Part 1(1) as an investment service. Which of the following is included?
o: Providing buildings and contents insurance to consumers
Acting as a letting agent for residential property
Granting hire-purchase agreements to retail customers
Operating business current accounts for small firms
Placing financial instruments without a firm commitment basis
w: Placing financial instruments is an investment service covered under Annex 1 Part 1(1) and subject to COBS when carried out by UK-authorised firms.

n.0: Household insurance is ICOBS business, not Annex 1.
n.2: Hire-purchase is a CONC activity, not Annex 1.
n.3: Current accounts are BCOBS banking, not Annex 1.
n.1: Letting agency is not a designated investment service.

q: A UK-authorised firm advises a client resident in Germany via video calls, with all advisers operating from its London office. Which regime applies to this activity?
o: Only German MiFID rules, because the client is resident in Germany
ICOBS, because the client is a consumer
COBS, because the service is carried on from a UK establishment
No FCA rules, because the client is outside the UK
MCOB, because advice is given remotely
w: COBS application is determined by the location of the establishment, not the residence of the client. If the activity is carried out from a UK base, COBS applies.

n.3: Client location does not exempt the firm from COBS if the activity originates from the UK.
n.4: MCOB relates to mortgages, not investment advice.
n.0: MiFID rules may also apply cross-border, but FCA expects UK firms to follow COBS when services are provided from UK establishments.
n.1: ICOBS applies to insurance distribution, not investment advice.

q: A French bank operates an investment business through a branch in London. Which statement best describes how COBS applies to that branch's activities?
o: PRA rules replace COBS in all of these circumstances
COBS applies to investment business carried on from the UK branch
Only the French home-state conduct rules will apply
Only BCOBS applies, whatever the activity involves
COBS does not apply because the head office is overseas
w: COBS applies to designated investment business carried on from a UK establishment, even if the firm’s head office is in another jurisdiction.

n.4: The establishment test catches UK-branch activity despite the overseas head office.
n.2: UK-branch investment business is subject to COBS, not only home-state rules.
n.3: BCOBS covers banking, not investment business done from the branch.
n.0: PRA prudential rules do not replace COBS conduct rules.

q: A UK investment manager runs discretionary portfolios for clients based in Asia. Where does COBS apply?
o: Only partly, depending on relevant double tax treaties
Only to advice given, never to portfolio management
Not at all, because the clients are all based overseas
Only where the client specifically requests UK protection
In full, since the portfolios are managed from the UK
w: COBS attaches to the location of the service provider’s establishment, not the client’s domicile. Running portfolios from the UK brings the activity within scope.

n.2: Client location does not remove COBS where management is UK-based.
n.0: Tax treaties do not determine COBS conduct scope.
n.3: COBS scope does not depend on a client request.
n.1: COBS covers portfolio management, not just advice.

q: How does COBS apply to an EEA investment firm operating in London through a branch?
o: Only home-state rules apply, wherever business occurs
The branch is exempt because of its passporting rights
COBS does not apply to any part of its UK business
COBS applies to UK clients only, not to EEA clients
COBS applies to investment business carried on from the London branch
w: Any firm, UK or overseas, that carries on designated investment business from a UK establishment must comply with COBS.

n.2: A UK branch's designated investment business is caught by COBS.
n.0: UK-branch business is not governed solely by home-state rules.
n.3: COBS applies by establishment, not by client location.
n.1: Passporting does not exempt a UK branch from COBS.

q: A firm operating from a UK establishment provides services to clients based overseas and asks how COBS applies. Which statement best describes the role of COBS territoriality?
o: It applies to UK-authorised firms but never to foreign branches
It applies only when the client is personally resident in the UK
It applies to business from UK establishments, whatever the client location
It does not apply where the services are delivered digitally online
It applies to investment advice but not to order execution work
w: The territorial scope test looks at the location of the establishment providing the service, not the client or delivery channel.

n.1: Client residence does not govern the establishment test.
n.0: UK branches of foreign firms are also caught by COBS.
n.4: COBS covers execution as well as advice.
n.3: Digital delivery does not remove COBS application.

q: A US investment firm with no UK branch executes trades for clients who happen to live in the UK. How does COBS apply to that firm?
o: It applies because the clients are resident in the UK
It applies, but only to the firm's UK retail clients
It applies because the trades involve UK-listed securities
It does not apply, since the firm has no UK establishment
It applies because the firm is regulated in the United States
w: COBS applies to activities carried on from a UK establishment. A firm with no UK presence is outside direct scope, though it may face perimeter obligations.

n.0: Client residence alone does not bring a non-UK firm into COBS.
n.2: The listing venue does not trigger COBS for an overseas firm.
n.4: US regulation does not make COBS apply.
n.1: With no UK establishment, COBS does not apply to any client type.

q: How is an appointed representative carrying on business from a UK office brought into COBS?
o: Through supervision by the AR's own home-state regulator
Through direct authorisation granted to it by the FCA
Through the principal's responsibility for COBS compliance
Through the client formally electing to be under UK rules
Through an individual waiver specially granted by the FCA
w: An appointed representative acts under its principal’s authorisation. The principal is responsible for ensuring COBS compliance in the UK establishment.

n.1: ARs are exempt persons, not directly authorised by the FCA.
n.0: There is no separate home-state regulator route for a UK AR.
n.3: Client election does not bring an AR within COBS.
n.4: An FCA waiver is not the mechanism that catches an AR.

q: Which activity conducted from a UK office is caught by COBS even if the client is in the US?
o: Providing an unsecured personal loan to the client
Selling private motor insurance to the customer
Execution of equity trades on behalf of the client
Arranging a consumer hire agreement for the customer
Offering a personal current account to the customer
w: Execution of client orders is a designated investment service, and being carried on from a UK office makes it subject to COBS, regardless of client location.

n.3: Consumer hire is a CONC activity, not caught by COBS.
n.1: Motor insurance is ICOBS business, not COBS.
n.0: A personal loan is CONC business, not COBS.
n.4: A current account is BCOBS banking, not COBS.

q: Which principle explains why COBS applies to UK establishments of overseas firms?
o: The instrument's listing venue determines the scope
The client's nationality is the determining factor
Scope depends on the place of business, not on incorporation
Passporting rights override the FCA's conduct rules
Branches are always exempt from FCA requirements
w: COBS focuses on where the business is carried out (establishment test). A UK branch of an overseas firm is caught by the rules.

n.1: Nationality does not decide COBS territorial scope.
n.0: The listing venue does not determine COBS scope.
n.3: Passporting does not override FCA conduct rules for UK branches.
n.4: UK branches are not exempt; they are caught by COBS.

q: Which of these would fall outside COBS application?
o: A UK bank providing investment advice from London
An EEA firm operating a branch in Manchester
A principal supervising an appointed representative in London
An investment firm with no permanent UK place of business
A UK fund manager managing US clients’ assets from London
w: Without a UK establishment, a firm’s activities fall outside COBS territorial application, though other UK rules may apply at the perimeter.

n.0: A UK bank advising from London is squarely in scope.
n.1: A branch in Manchester is a UK establishment, so COBS applies.
n.2: Appointed representatives are caught through their principal’s authorisation.
n.4: UK fund management for overseas clients is covered by COBS.

q: A UK-authorised firm executes derivatives trades for a Canadian pension fund entirely from its London office. How does COBS apply to this business?
o: COBS applies only if the trades are on a UK exchange
COBS applies, as the trades are executed from a UK establishment
COBS applies only to retail clients, not institutions
COBS does not apply where the business is wholesale
COBS does not apply because the client is not based in the UK
w: The key determinant is the location of the establishment. Activities carried out from the UK are within COBS scope, regardless of client domicile or market venue.

n.4: Client domicile does not remove COBS where trading is UK-based.
n.0: The market venue does not determine COBS application.
n.2: COBS is not limited to retail clients only.
n.3: Wholesale business is still within COBS, under a lighter regime.

q: A Swiss firm opens a representative office in London but conducts all of its investment business from Zurich. How does COBS apply to it?
o: COBS applies because the firm holds FCA recognition
COBS applies to Zurich business where UK clients feature
COBS applies to all of the firm's Zurich activities
COBS applies whenever the firm issues research reports
COBS does not apply, as no investment business is done from the UK
w: COBS is based on the establishment test. If no designated investment business is carried out from the UK office, COBS does not apply.

n.2: COBS does not reach Zurich activity via the London office.
n.1: UK clients alone do not bring Zurich business into COBS.
n.0: A representative office without investment activity is not caught.
n.3: Issuing research from Zurich does not trigger UK COBS.

q: How would COBS apply to an investment adviser in Dublin marketing services into the UK without a UK office?
o: COBS applies because UK clients are being targeted
COBS applies if the service is marketed in sterling
COBS applies only where the client signs in the UK
COBS applies because the FCA oversees all EU-based firms
COBS does not apply directly, as there is no UK establishment
w: Without a UK place of business, COBS does not apply directly. Other rules, such as perimeter guidance and MiFID passporting, may be relevant.

n.0: Targeting UK clients does not, alone, bring a Dublin firm into COBS.
n.3: The FCA does not directly regulate all EU firms.
n.1: Pricing in sterling does not trigger COBS.
n.2: Where the client signs does not determine the establishment test.

q: A UK branch of a US broker-dealer provides custody of securities. Which rules apply?
o: No FCA rules apply, because the head office is US-based
Only BCOBS applies, because custody is a banking service
Only US SEC rules apply, because the firm is American
Only MCOB applies, because custody is linked to mortgages
COBS and CASS apply, as custody is investment business from a UK branch
w: Safekeeping and administration of financial instruments is a designated activity. Carried out from a UK branch, COBS applies, and custody obligations fall under CASS.

n.0: A US head office does not exempt UK-branch custody from FCA rules.
n.2: UK-branch custody is subject to FCA rules, not only the SEC.
n.1: Custody is a designated investment activity, not banking under BCOBS.
n.3: Custody is unrelated to mortgages and MCOB.

q: An FCA-authorised firm has offices in Edinburgh and Frankfurt. Which activities trigger COBS?
o: Edinburgh activities, since the UK office is a permanent establishment
Only dealings with the firm's UK-based retail clients
Only dealings with the firm's UK institutional clients
All of the firm's client dealings anywhere in the world
Frankfurt activities, regardless of any UK connection at all
w: COBS applies to designated investment business carried on from the UK establishment. Frankfurt activity is subject to local EU rules instead.

n.4: Frankfurt activity is subject to local EU rules, not COBS.
n.3: COBS does not reach the firm's activities worldwide.
n.1: COBS applies by establishment, not only to UK retail clients.
n.2: COBS is not limited to UK institutional clients.

q: How does the application of COBS differ between UK and overseas branches of the same firm?
o: COBS applies only where the clients are UK nationals
Both branches must comply with COBS everywhere in the world
UK branches follow COBS; overseas branches follow local conduct rules
COBS applies only to digital transactions, not others
Overseas branches are exempt from any conduct rules at all
w: The establishment test is key. UK branches apply COBS, while overseas establishments are governed by their home jurisdictions.

n.1: COBS does not apply globally to overseas branches.
n.4: Overseas branches follow their own home rules, not no rules.
n.0: COBS applies by establishment, not by client nationality.
n.3: COBS is not limited to digital transactions.

q: A firm assesses which of its activities bring it within the scope of COBS. Which type of client transaction is NOT sufficient on its own to bring COBS into scope?
o: Giving investment advice to clients from a Manchester office
Dealing with UK clients from the firm's New York branch
Running discretionary portfolios from an Edinburgh office
Providing custody of clients' shares from a Birmingham office
Executing client equity trades from the firm's London desk
w: Dealing with UK clients from an overseas office does not automatically bring the activity under COBS, as the firm has no UK establishment in that scenario.

n.0: Advice from Manchester is UK-establishment business, so COBS applies.
n.4: Execution from London is UK-establishment business, so COBS applies.
n.2: Managing portfolios from Edinburgh brings COBS into scope.
n.3: Custody from Birmingham is UK-establishment business under COBS.

q: A UK-authorised firm gives investment advice to clients based in Spain, but the advice is provided from its London office. Which statement is correct about COBS?
o: COBS applies only where Spanish law expressly requires it
COBS does not apply when the advice is given remotely
COBS does not apply because the clients are based in Spain
COBS applies, since the advice is given from a UK establishment
COBS applies only to the firm's wholesale clients
w: Cross-border services are still subject to COBS if carried on from a UK base. Client location does not negate FCA jurisdiction.

n.2: Client location in Spain does not remove UK-based COBS.
n.0: Spanish law does not decide whether COBS applies.
n.4: COBS is not limited to wholesale clients.
n.1: Remote delivery does not remove COBS.

q: A UK branch conducts designated investment business with a counterparty classified as an eligible counterparty and questions whether COBS still applies. Why does COBS apply in this case?
o: Because eligible counterparties receive full retail protections
Because client classification overrides the territorial test
Because place of business fixes scope before client classification
Because the FCA holds jurisdiction over firms worldwide
Because only retail clients ever fall within COBS scope
w: The establishment test applies first. Eligible counterparty classification determines the level of protection but does not remove the application of COBS to the UK branch.

n.0: ECPs get the lightest, not full retail, protections.
n.3: The FCA does not hold worldwide jurisdiction over all firms.
n.1: The establishment test applies before classification, not after.
n.4: COBS is not limited to retail clients.

q: A firm with clients in several countries is working out whether COBS applies to a piece of investment business. Which factor is decisive for COBS application?
o: Nationality of the client
Currency of the transaction
Time zone in which the trade is executed
Market on which the product is listed
Permanent place of business in the UK
w: The central criterion is whether the designated investment business is carried on from a UK establishment. Other factors are not determinative.

n.0: Client nationality is irrelevant under COBS scope rules.
n.1: Transaction currency does not change jurisdiction.
n.3: Listing venue does not decide COBS applicability.
n.2: Execution time zone is irrelevant; establishment location is key.

q: Who holds responsibility for ensuring that an appointed representative complies with COBS?
o: The representative’s clients
The FCA directly
The principal firm
The appointed representative itself
The product manufacturer
w: Under COBS 1.1.1, an appointed representative acts under the responsibility of its principal, which must ensure compliance with FCA rules including COBS.

n.3: Appointed representatives are not directly authorised and do not bear primary regulatory responsibility.
n.1: The FCA supervises the principal, not the AR directly.
n.0: Clients cannot enforce FCA compliance on behalf of the AR.
n.4: Product manufacturers are not accountable for AR conduct under COBS.

q: How are financial promotions issued by an appointed representative treated under COBS?
o: They are approved automatically if issued digitally
They are exempt from FCA oversight
They only need approval if targeting retail clients
They are treated as client communications, not financial promotions
They must be approved by the principal firm before communication
w: COBS 4.1 requires financial promotions issued by ARs to be approved by their principal before being made, ensuring compliance with fair, clear and not misleading standards.

n.1: AR promotions are not exempt from FCA standards.
n.2: Approval is needed for all promotions, not just retail-facing ones.
n.3: Promotions remain subject to financial promotion rules, not downgraded to ordinary communications.
n.0: Digital format does not change approval obligations.

q: What is the primary obligation of a principal firm regarding its appointed representatives under COBS?
o: Allowing them complete autonomy over their own conduct
Supervising their conduct and ensuring COBS compliance
Ensuring they each hold direct authorisation from the FCA
Treating them as the equivalent of professional clients
Reporting them to the FCA as fully independent entities
w: The principal must supervise its ARs, ensuring they comply with COBS requirements for fair treatment of clients and proper conduct of business.

n.0: The principal must supervise ARs, not grant full autonomy.
n.4: ARs act under the principal, not as independent entities.
n.3: ARs are not clients; they are exempt persons under supervision.
n.2: ARs do not hold direct FCA authorisation.

q: Which rule in COBS applies to financial promotions from appointed representatives?
o: COBS 6.1
COBS 4.1
COBS 2.1
MCOB 3.1
ICOBS 2.2
w: COBS 4.1 sets out the rules for financial promotions, requiring them to be fair, clear and not misleading, and approved by a regulated firm if issued by an AR.

n.2: COBS 2.1 contains general client principles, not promotion rules.
n.0: COBS 6.1 concerns client disclosures, not promotions.
n.3: MCOB covers mortgage promotions, not COBS.
n.4: ICOBS 2.2 covers insurance conduct, not investment promotions.

q: A principal firm has been lax in overseeing one of its appointed representatives. Under COBS, what is the key risk the principal faces?
o: The AR must apply for direct authorisation immediately
Clients lose FSCS protection
The AR becomes directly liable to the FCA
The principal is liable for breaches of COBS by the AR
The AR can transfer responsibility to another principal without FCA oversight
w: Under COBS 1.1.1 and FCA principles, the principal bears liability for COBS breaches by its appointed representatives.

n.2: ARs are not directly liable to the FCA; accountability rests with the principal.
n.1: FSCS protection is not withdrawn due to oversight failures.
n.0: An AR does not become directly authorised unless applying formally.
n.4: Transfers of principals must be FCA-approved; ARs cannot reassign freely.

q: How must a financial promotion by an appointed representative be characterised under COBS?
o: Fair, clear and not misleading
Compliant only if aimed at retail clients
Detailed but selective
Optimistic and persuasive
Exempt if communicated verbally
w: COBS 4.1 states that all promotions, including those by ARs, must be fair, clear and not misleading.

n.3: Promotions must not be overly persuasive at the expense of accuracy.
n.2: Selective disclosure is prohibited; balance is required.
n.1: The rule applies regardless of target audience.
n.4: Verbal communications remain within scope if they are promotions.

q: An appointed representative wants to send out a promotional leaflet to prospects. What must its principal firm do before allowing the AR to distribute it?
o: Confirm the AR holds separate MiFID authorisation
Approve the promotion to ensure it complies with the rules
Submit the promotion to the PRA for prior approval
Register the financial promotion with the FCA first
Obtain the client's written consent to the promotion
w: The principal must approve financial promotions issued by ARs to ensure they comply with COBS standards before being communicated.

n.3: Promotions are not registered with the FCA in advance.
n.4: Client consent is not required to approve a promotion.
n.2: The PRA does not approve financial promotions.
n.0: An AR does not hold its own MiFID authorisation.

q: A mortgage-and-investment network takes on an appointed representative to expand its distribution. Which activity is the AR prohibited from carrying out without the principal's oversight?
o: Issuing financial promotions without the principal's approval
Communicating with institutional and wholesale clients
Keeping its own internal compliance procedures manual
Meeting prospective clients on a face-to-face basis
Providing investment advice under the principal's oversight
w: ARs cannot issue financial promotions independently; they must be approved and monitored by their principal under COBS 4.1.

n.4: ARs may advise clients under the principal's oversight.
n.3: ARs may meet clients face-to-face in the normal course of business.
n.1: ARs may communicate with institutional clients.
n.2: An AR keeping internal procedures is not prohibited conduct.

q: What is the main regulatory justification for requiring principal approval of AR financial promotions?
o: To centralise all marketing directly under FCA control
To restrict ARs to dealing with professional clients
To permit ARs to use only digital advertising channels
To make each AR individually accountable to the FCA
To ensure promotions are fair, clear and not misleading
w: Principal approval ensures that AR promotions meet FCA standards, preventing misleading or unfair communications in the market.

n.0: Approval is not about centralising marketing under the FCA.
n.3: The principal, not the AR, is accountable for the promotion.
n.1: Approval does not restrict ARs to professional clients.
n.2: Approval is unrelated to limiting ARs to digital channels.

q: A mortgage network signs up a small brokerage to sell under its name and oversight. Under COBS 1.1.1, what is the regulatory status of that brokerage as an appointed representative?
o: Firms regulated independently of any principal firm
Clients automatically classified as professional clients
Market participants treated as eligible counterparties
Exempt persons acting under the responsibility of their principal
Persons directly authorised and regulated by the FCA
w: Appointed representatives are exempt persons under FSMA, acting under the responsibility and oversight of their principal firm.

n.4: ARs are exempt persons, not directly authorised.
n.0: ARs act under a principal, not independently.
n.1: ARs are not clients of a firm by status.
n.2: ARs are not classified as eligible counterparties by status.

q: An appointed representative circulates a brochure about a new investment product to prospects without obtaining its principal's approval. What breach has occurred under COBS?
o: Unauthorised financial promotion
Breach of best execution obligations
Breach of CASS custody standards
Breach of client categorisation rules
Breach of suitability requirements
w: Financial promotions by ARs must be approved by their principal before issue. Circulating without approval is an unauthorised promotion.

n.3: Client categorisation was not the issue in this case.
n.1: Best execution relates to order handling, not brochures.
n.2: CASS governs custody, not promotions.
n.4: Suitability applies to advice, not promotional approval.

q: How does the FCA ensure oversight of appointed representatives under COBS?
o: By holding the principal accountable for the AR's activity
By exempting ARs from the financial promotion rules
By restricting ARs to wholesale business activity only
By requiring ARs to obtain temporary FCA registration
By directly supervising each individual AR itself
w: FCA supervision operates through the principal firm, which is legally responsible for the AR’s compliance with COBS.

n.4: The FCA supervises through the principal, not each AR directly.
n.3: ARs do not obtain temporary FCA registration.
n.2: ARs are not restricted to wholesale business.
n.1: AR promotions are subject to the rules, not exempt.

q: What must a principal firm do if an appointed representative issues misleading financial promotions?
o: Reclassify the clients as professional to cut duties
Take remedial action and accept responsibility for the breach
Refer the AR directly to the PRA for enforcement
Temporarily suspend the FCA's rules covering the AR
Wait until the FCA opens its own investigation first
w: The principal must remedy breaches and accept responsibility, as ARs act under their oversight for COBS compliance.

n.3: A firm cannot suspend FCA rules.
n.2: The PRA does not enforce AR promotion breaches.
n.0: Reclassifying clients does not cure a promotion breach.
n.4: The principal must act, not wait for the FCA.

q: Why does COBS 4.1 require principals to pre-approve AR promotions?
o: To let ARs operate fully independently of principals
To speed up the distribution of new investment products
To remove the need for any client categorisation
To prevent unfair or misleading client communications
To simplify the firm's annual tax and VAT reporting
w: Pre-approval ensures that all communications meet FCA standards for being fair, clear and not misleading before reaching clients.

n.4: Approval is unrelated to tax reporting.
n.1: The aim is consumer protection, not faster distribution.
n.0: Approval keeps ARs under oversight, not independent.
n.2: Approval does not remove client categorisation duties.

q: Which of the following is within the FCA’s expectations for principals under COBS?
o: Leaving approval entirely to AR discretion
Permitting ARs to classify themselves as eligible counterparties
Allowing ARs to market unapproved overseas products
Regular monitoring of AR financial promotions
Requiring ARs to seek direct FCA approval
w: Principals are expected to monitor their ARs to ensure that financial promotions comply with COBS 4.1 standards.

n.0: Approval cannot be left to AR discretion.
n.4: ARs cannot directly seek FCA approval of promotions.
n.2: Promotions of unapproved overseas products are prohibited.
n.1: ECP status applies to clients, not ARs.

q: An appointed representative creates a social media advert for a new bond issue. Under COBS, what must occur first?
o: The principal must approve the advert before posting
The advert is exempt if fewer than 50 people see it
The AR can self-certify compliance
The AR can circulate freely as long as disclaimers are used
The AR can post immediately if it targets professionals only
w: All financial promotions by ARs, including digital or social media, require principal approval under COBS 4.1.

n.4: Professional targeting does not exempt approval obligations.
n.2: Self-certification is not permitted.
n.1: Audience size does not exempt promotions from COBS rules.
n.3: Disclaimers do not replace principal approval requirements.

q: What happens if a principal allows an AR to issue unapproved promotions repeatedly?
o: The promotions become valid through market custom
The PRA revokes the AR's own direct authorisation
The AR is automatically removed from the FCA register
The FCA imposes sanctions on the clients involved
The FCA may take enforcement action against the principal
w: Failure to supervise ARs appropriately may trigger FCA enforcement against the principal, including fines and restrictions.

n.2: There is no automatic register removal for the AR.
n.0: Non-compliant promotions do not become valid by custom.
n.3: Clients are not sanctioned for the firm's failings.
n.1: An AR has no direct authorisation for the PRA to revoke.

q: A principal firm is reviewing a promotional email sent by one of its appointed representatives. Under COBS, how should the AR's communications with clients be regarded?
o: As marketing material only if to retail clients
As unregulated third-party statements
As communications of the principal firm
As personal views outside FCA rules
As exempt from FCA oversight
w: All communications from ARs are legally treated as communications of the principal, and must therefore meet COBS standards.

n.4: AR communications are not exempt; they fall under principal responsibility.
n.1: They are regulated as firm communications, not independent.
n.3: Personal disclaimers do not override the rules.
n.0: The rule applies regardless of client type.

q: Why is principal oversight of ARs particularly strict under COBS financial promotion rules?
o: Because ARs operate as wholly unsupervised entities
Because ARs are always treated as eligible counterparties
Because ARs are entirely barred from the FSCS scheme
Because promotions to professionals are always exempt
Because promotions directly affect retail market integrity
w: Financial promotions are critical to retail protection. Principal oversight ensures compliance with fairness and prevents consumer detriment.

n.1: ARs are not classified as eligible counterparties.
n.2: FSCS access is not the reason for strict oversight.
n.0: ARs are supervised by their principal, not unsupervised.
n.3: Promotions to professionals are not always exempt.

q: If an AR’s promotion breaches COBS, who is accountable to the FCA?
o: The principal firm
The client receiving the promotion
The AR individually
The marketing agency producing the material
The FCA’s promotions unit
w: Responsibility rests with the principal, which is accountable for ensuring AR compliance with financial promotion rules.

n.2: ARs are not directly accountable under FSMA.
n.1: Clients are not liable for firm breaches.
n.3: Third-party agencies are not responsible to the FCA; the principal remains liable.
n.4: The promotions unit enforces standards but does not assume liability.

q: A firm needs to send a client disclosure in a form that meets the Glossary definition of a durable medium for COBS purposes. Which of the following qualifies?
o: A web banner that disappears after viewing
An advert broadcast on television
A PDF document emailed to the client
A verbal explanation recorded in a meeting
A poster displayed in the firm’s reception
w: A durable medium must allow the client to store the information in a way accessible for future reference. A PDF meets this requirement.

n.3: Verbal explanations do not meet the definition, as the client cannot store and reproduce them reliably.
n.4: Posters are not personal or durable for the client’s use.
n.1: Broadcasts are transient and cannot be stored by the client without action.
n.0: Disappearing banners do not qualify as durable mediums.

q: Which key condition must be met for a website to serve as a durable medium under COBS?
o: The website must be accessible without any password
The client is notified of the website's address and its content
The website must be reachable only in business hours
The website must include promotional marketing videos
The website must hold at least three years of archived data
w: For a website to be considered a durable medium, clients must be personally notified of the address and information made available in a retrievable format.

n.4: There is no fixed three-year archive requirement.
n.0: Password protection does not disqualify a durable medium.
n.2: Restricting access to business hours is not a condition.
n.3: Promotional videos are not a durable-medium condition.

q: Which of the following would NOT normally be considered a durable medium?
o: Transient pop-up alerts shown on a trading platform
PDF files downloaded and saved on the client's device
Printed contract letters posted to the client
Emails retained in the client's own inbox
CD-ROMs supplied to the client with agreements
w: Transient pop-up messages cannot be stored and reproduced, so they fail the durable medium test.

n.2: A posted printed letter is a classic durable medium.
n.1: A saved PDF can be stored and reproduced, so it qualifies.
n.3: A stored email meets the durable medium test.
n.4: A CD-ROM can store and reproduce information unchanged.

q: A firm plans to send its clients key contractual information by email rather than post. Why does it matter that this electronic communication qualifies as a durable medium under COBS?
o: So that clients receive more colourful and engaging documents
So that firms can avoid keeping any transaction records at all
So that the FCA can audit each client message in real time
So that firms can reduce their document printing costs each year
So clients can store and reproduce it unchanged for as long as needed
w: Durable mediums ensure clients can retain key information unchanged, meeting the regulatory objectives of transparency and client protection.

n.3: Cost saving is not the regulatory purpose.
n.2: Real-time FCA auditing is not the purpose of durable media.
n.0: Presentation quality is not the objective.
n.1: Durable media do not remove record-keeping duties.

q: A firm wants to satisfy its disclosure obligations by making information available on its website rather than sending documents. Which condition must be met for the website to be treated as equivalent to a durable medium?
o: The firm must guarantee round-the-clock live chat support
The website must be open to every internet user freely
The information stays accessible for as long as the client needs it
The site must contain the firm's financial promotions
The site must be hosted only on servers based in the UK
w: COBS requires that the information remains accessible in an unchanged form for as long as reasonably needed by the client.

n.1: Public access to all users is not required.
n.4: UK-only hosting is not a durable-medium condition.
n.0: Live chat support is not required for durability.
n.3: Containing promotions is not a durable-medium condition.

q: A wealth manager wants to send its terms of business by posting them on its website instead of on paper. Under the Glossary, which condition must be met for a website to substitute for a durable medium?
o: The website must include interactive financial calculators
The FCA must pre-approve the website before its use
The firm must update the website's content every day
The website must be accessible without a password
The client consents to using the website instead of paper
w: Client consent is a key requirement when substituting website communication for traditional durable mediums.

n.2: Daily updating is not a Glossary condition.
n.3: Password-free access is not required.
n.0: Interactive calculators are not a condition.
n.1: The FCA does not pre-approve firms' websites.

q: Which of the following communications best meets the COBS test of a durable medium?
o: Flash message on a trading app that disappears instantly
Oral advice during a phone call without a record
Interactive chatbot message without storage option
Email with attached contract in PDF format
Advertisement on social media feed
w: Emails with attached PDFs meet the durability criteria: accessible, storable, and unalterable for reference.

n.0: Ephemeral pop-ups are not durable mediums.
n.1: Oral advice without a recording does not meet the test.
n.4: Social media adverts are transient and not personal.
n.2: Chatbot messages without storage cannot be considered durable.

q: A compliance officer is asked why COBS bothers to define the term 'durable medium' at all. What is the regulatory purpose of the definition?
o: To encourage new banking technology and innovation
To reduce a firm's legal liability for its disclosures
To exempt firms' own websites from FCA supervision entirely
To assist firms with their digital marketing campaigns
To ensure clients can store key information unchanged
w: The definition ensures clients can retain key disclosures and agreements in a secure, unalterable format for future reference.

n.3: The purpose is client protection, not marketing.
n.1: It is not to reduce firms' disclosure liability.
n.0: Promoting technology is not the aim.
n.2: Websites are not exempted from FCA supervision.

q: A firm wants to rely on its website to deliver terms of business as a durable medium. Which scenario would fail to meet the website conditions under COBS?
o: A firm hosts terms online and also emails a notification
A firm posts terms online with consent and notification
A firm posts terms online without telling clients the web address
A firm sends the written terms in a posted letter
A firm emails a PDF copy of the terms to each client
w: For a website to count as a durable medium, clients must be notified of the website and its content. Failure to notify means the condition is not met.

n.4: Emailing a PDF meets the durable medium requirement.
n.3: A posted letter is a valid durable medium.
n.0: Online hosting plus a notification email satisfies the conditions.
n.1: With consent and notification, the website conditions are met.

q: How do the FCA Glossary website conditions interact with client consent requirements?
o: Consent is assumed where the website is written in English
Consent is irrelevant if the firm provides retail services
Clients must consent to website use and be notified of availability
Consent is needed only for clients based in the EEA
Consent is optional whenever the website is publicly open
w: Both client consent and notification of website location/content are required for website delivery to meet durable medium conditions.

n.4: Consent is required even for a public website.
n.1: Consent is not irrelevant for retail services; it is required.
n.3: Consent is not limited to EEA clients.
n.0: Consent is not assumed from the site's language.

q: Which of the following best explains why a firm cannot rely solely on a website to provide disclosures unless website conditions are met?
o: Because clients need guaranteed access to unchanged information
Because website use is limited to wholesale clients only
Because the FCA requires hard copies for all retail clients
Because websites are never reliable for regulatory disclosure
Because the FCA bans the use of electronic media entirely
w: The website conditions ensure clients can access information reliably and store it unchanged, matching the protection offered by a durable medium.

n.4: The FCA does not ban electronic media.
n.3: Websites can be reliable when the conditions are met.
n.2: Hard copies are not mandatory for all retail clients.
n.1: Website use is not limited to wholesale clients.

q: A firm plans to send key disclosures to clients electronically and asks what makes something a durable medium rather than an ordinary email or webpage. Which feature is essential?
o: The medium must be purely promotional in its nature
The medium must allow two-way interactive messaging
The information must be communicated to the client orally
The firm can edit the stored information at any time
The client can store and reproduce the information unchanged
w: A durable medium guarantees that the client can store, reproduce, and rely on the information in its original form over time.

n.3: A durable medium must not be alterable by the firm at will.
n.2: Oral communication is not a durable medium.
n.0: A durable medium need not be promotional.
n.1: Interactivity is not a feature of a durable medium.

q: Which of the following would meet FCA website conditions for replacing paper-based disclosure?
o: The firm provides documents only to those who ask for them
The firm notifies clients, gains consent and ensures lasting access
The firm posts the terms online without notifying clients
The firm allows access that expires after only 24 hours
The firm makes clients find the terms via search engines
w: Client notification, consent, and ongoing access are the core requirements for websites to qualify as durable mediums under COBS.

n.2: Posting without notification fails the website conditions.
n.3: Access expiring in 24 hours is not access for as long as needed.
n.0: Providing only on request does not meet notification duties.
n.4: Making clients search does not satisfy notification or access.

q: Why is email generally considered a durable medium under COBS?
o: Because emails are regulated separately from promotions
Because every email sent is automatically encrypted
Because email use is restricted to retail clients only
Because all electronic communications automatically qualify
Because the content can be stored and reproduced unchanged
w: Emails meet the durable medium definition as they can be stored and retrieved without alteration, offering a permanent record.

n.3: Not all electronic communications automatically qualify.
n.0: Separate regulation of emails is not why they are durable.
n.1: Emails are not automatically encrypted.
n.2: Email use is not restricted to retail clients.

q: Which of the following is an example of information that must be provided to clients using a durable medium?
o: Details of the firm's office decoration and layout
The firm's advertising slogans and marketing taglines
The firm's terms of business agreement with the client
General press releases issued to the news media
Internal staff job descriptions and their duties
w: Key contractual and disclosure documents, such as terms of business, must be given in a durable medium to ensure clients can access them reliably.

n.0: Office decoration details need not be given in a durable medium.
n.4: Internal job descriptions are not client disclosures.
n.3: Press releases are not durable-medium client disclosures.
n.1: Advertising slogans are not required in a durable medium.

q: A firm wants to provide its terms and periodic reports through its website rather than by post. Which condition must be met for such website disclosures to satisfy durable medium requirements?
o: The site must offer an interactive live chat feature
The site must display promotional marketing banners
The firm must have the FCA moderate the site daily
Clients are notified in advance and can store the information
The content must appear in several different languages
w: Durable medium conditions require notification and the ability for clients to access and retain the information in an unaltered form.

n.0: Live chat is not a durable-medium condition.
n.4: Multiple languages are not required.
n.1: Promotional banners are not a condition.
n.2: The FCA does not moderate firms' sites.

q: Why might a firm’s mobile app storing disclosures permanently qualify as a durable medium?
o: Because apps are exempt from the website conditions
Because all mobile apps are automatically FCA-approved
Because the information can be retained and reproduced unaltered
Because clients are unable to delete stored information
Because apps always store all information fully offline
w: If the app allows clients to store and retrieve disclosures unchanged, it meets the durable medium standard under COBS.

n.1: Apps are not automatically FCA-approved.
n.4: Apps do not always store everything offline.
n.3: Durability does not depend on clients being unable to delete.
n.0: Apps are not exempt from durable-medium conditions.

q: Which factor makes a PDF attachment more reliable than a website notice for COBS disclosures?
o: It carries more colourful branding and company logos
It can always be opened without any internet connection
It has an unlimited potential for wider distribution
It can be shared easily across social media platforms
It is held by the client and cannot later be altered by the firm
w: Durability requires that the client can keep the information unchanged. A PDF file provided to the client achieves this, unlike a live website subject to edits.

n.0: Branding is irrelevant to durable-medium reliability.
n.1: Offline access is not what makes it more reliable for COBS.
n.2: Distribution potential is not the relevant durability factor.
n.3: Social-media sharing is unrelated to durable-medium status.

q: A firm plans to satisfy a disclosure requirement by posting the information on its own website. What is the main limitation of using a website as a durable medium?
o: Website disclosures are never legally binding at all
The firm controls the content and can alter it without notice
Websites always require a paid subscription to view
Websites are prohibited outright under the COBS rules
Websites cannot be accessed by clients outside the UK
w: Websites can be altered unilaterally, which is why conditions exist requiring notification and client access to information in a durable form.

n.4: Websites are accessible outside the UK.
n.2: Websites do not always require a paid subscription.
n.0: Website disclosures can be legally effective when conditions are met.
n.3: Websites are not prohibited under COBS.

q: Which is the clearest example of non-compliance with website conditions?
o: Providing hard-copy disclosure documents to clients by post
Posting disclosures online without notifying clients or gaining consent
Archiving the documents online with email alerts sent to clients
Offering disclosures through a secure PDF portal with access codes
Sending clients an email with their signed contract attached
w: Without notifying clients and securing consent, simply posting information online fails to meet FCA Glossary website conditions.

n.4: An emailed attached contract meets the durable medium test.
n.0: Posted hard-copy disclosures are compliant.
n.3: A secure PDF portal with codes can satisfy the conditions.
n.2: Online archiving with email alerts meets notification duties.

q: Under COBS 3.2, which best describes a 'client' for the purpose of the rules?
o: A person to whom a firm provides designated investment services
Any person who merely reads a firm's financial promotion
Any person insured under a general insurance contract
Any counterparty to a regulated mortgage agreement
Any ordinary member of the general investing public
w: COBS 3.2 defines a client as a person to whom a firm provides, intends to provide, or has provided designated investment business or ancillary services.

n.1: Simply reading a promotion does not make someone a client.
n.4: A general member of the public is not a client by that alone.
n.2: An insurance policyholder is an ICOBS matter, not a COBS client.
n.3: A mortgage counterparty is an MCOB matter, not a COBS client.

q: Which of the following persons would be considered a client under COBS 3.2?
o: A prospective investor receiving advice from the firm
An employee under an HR benefits scheme
An unrelated individual reading the firm’s annual report
A retail shopper purchasing consumer goods
A borrower taking out a regulated mortgage
w: A prospective investor being advised is captured as a client under COBS definitions, as services are being provided or intended.

n.2: Annual report readers are not necessarily clients.
n.3: Consumer goods buyers are outside financial regulation scope.
n.4: Mortgage borrowers are clients under MCOB, not COBS.
n.1: Employees are not clients unless provided regulated investment services.

q: Which party does COBS 3.2 exclude from the client definition?
o: A professional investor acting under a discretionary mandate
A retail investor receiving personal investment advice
An eligible counterparty acting purely as a market counterparty
A high-net-worth individual signing an advisory agreement
A pension fund receiving portfolio management services
w: When a firm treats a person as an eligible counterparty, that party is not considered a client for the purposes of the conduct rules in COBS.

n.1: A retail investor receiving advice is a client under COBS.
n.0: A professional investor under mandate is still a client.
n.4: A pension fund receiving management is a client.
n.3: An individual signing an advisory agreement is a client.

q: What is the significance of being classified as a 'client' under COBS?
o: The person becomes entitled to specific conduct protections
The person must always act as an eligible counterparty
The person is entirely exempt from FCA regulation
The person is restricted to wholesale business only
The person must be registered directly with the FCA
w: Being a client under COBS brings entitlement to protections and conduct standards appropriate to the categorisation (retail, professional, or ECP).

n.2: Client status brings protection, it does not confer exemption.
n.4: Clients are not required to register with the FCA.
n.1: Being a client does not force eligible counterparty status.
n.3: Client status does not restrict a person to wholesale business.

q: Which firm relationship would create client status under COBS?
o: Selling a private motor insurance policy to a driver
Distributing a general press release to journalists
Displaying an investment advertisement on a billboard
Providing investment research tailored to an individual investor
Arranging a regulated residential mortgage loan
w: A firm providing personalised investment research or advice to an investor creates a client relationship under COBS.

n.1: A press release to journalists creates no client relationship.
n.2: A billboard advert does not, alone, create client status.
n.0: Selling motor insurance is ICOBS business, not a COBS client.
n.4: Arranging a mortgage is MCOB business, not a COBS client.

q: Which of the following is an example of a 'client' under COBS 3.2?
o: A pension scheme receiving investment management services
A consumer simply opening an instant-access savings account
A borrower entering into a regulated mortgage contract
A newspaper reader glancing at an investment advert
A company issuing its own shares directly to the public
w: The pension scheme is a client because it receives regulated investment services from the firm.

n.3: A reader glancing at an advert is not a COBS client.
n.1: Opening a savings account is BCOBS banking, not a COBS client.
n.2: A mortgage borrower is an MCOB matter, not a COBS client.
n.4: A company issuing its own shares is not a COBS client here.

q: A firm is deciding whether a person qualifies as a client under COBS 3.2. Which of the following is NOT required for someone to be treated as a client?
o: Having executed trades through the firm
Entering into an advisory agreement
Reading promotional material without engaging the firm
Receiving portfolio management services
Having received or intended to receive investment services
w: Mere exposure to promotional material does not create a client relationship under COBS unless services are being provided.

n.4: Service provision or intention to provide creates client status.
n.0: Execution of trades establishes client status.
n.1: Advisory agreements create a client relationship.
n.3: Portfolio management clearly establishes client status.

q: Why is the definition of 'client' under COBS important for firms?
o: It exempts the firm from all FSCS levy liability
It lets the firm avoid its MiFID obligations entirely
It permits the firm to skip all suitability checks
It determines which conduct rules apply to each relationship
It ensures only UK nationals may receive services
w: The definition sets the scope of the rules, ensuring firms apply the right protections depending on whether a person is a client and what type of client they are.

n.0: The definition does not remove FSCS levy liability.
n.1: It does not let firms avoid MiFID obligations.
n.4: It has nothing to do with restricting services to UK nationals.
n.2: It does not let firms bypass suitability checks.

q: A paraplanner is checking the COBS definition of a 'client' before onboarding a prospect who has not yet traded. Which statement correctly summarises COBS 3.2?
o: A client is only a person who has actually executed one or more trades with the firm
A client is only a person who is domiciled or resident within the United Kingdom
A client is only a person who falls within the retail client category
A client is any person who happens to read one of the firm's financial promotions
Anyone the firm provides, intends to provide, or has provided investment services to
w: The COBS definition includes current, prospective, and past service recipients of designated investment business.

n.0: Intending clients are included; execution is not required.
n.2: Clients include professionals and eligible counterparties, not only retail.
n.3: Merely reading a promotion does not make someone a client.
n.1: Client status does not depend on UK domicile.

q: A compliance officer is reviewing who qualifies as a client under COBS. Which of the following would most clearly fall outside the definition of a client?
o: A pension fund under discretionary management
A journalist reporting on an investment firm
A professional investor party to a mandate
A retail investor receiving portfolio advice
A corporate treasury department using execution services
w: A journalist writing about a firm without receiving investment services is not a client. Clients are those to whom services are or will be provided.

n.3: Retail investors advised are clients.
n.4: Corporate treasuries using services are clients.
n.0: Pension funds under management are clients.
n.2: Professional investors receiving services are clients.

q: A new adviser at a wealth manager asks why the firm sorts every incoming client into a category before dealing. What is the core purpose of COBS 3.1 on client categorisation?
o: To ensure firms apply the right conduct rules to each client type
To let firms opt out of all suitability requirements
To align the UK banking rules directly with ICOBS
To guarantee that every client receives identical protections
To exempt firms from FCA oversight when facing professionals
w: COBS 3.1 sets the framework for categorising clients as retail, professional, or eligible counterparties, which determines the protections and rules that apply.

n.4: Categorisation does not exempt firms from oversight.
n.3: Protections differ by category; they are not identical.
n.2: Categorisation is unrelated to aligning banking with ICOBS.
n.1: It does not let firms opt out of suitability duties.

q: How does client categorisation affect the application of COBS rules?
o: The level of conduct protection varies with the client's classification
Every client receives an identical level of conduct protection
Client classification only matters for the client's tax treatment
Retail clients may waive their classification without any effect
Client classification only affects the FSCS coverage level
w: The FCA sets varying levels of protection: retail clients receive the highest, professionals less, and ECPs the lightest conduct protections.

n.1: Protection varies by category, so it is not identical.
n.4: Classification affects far more than FSCS coverage.
n.2: Classification is not merely about tax treatment.
