n.3: Changing classification has real consequences, not none.

q: A firm is onboarding a new client and setting their regulatory classification. Under COBS 3.1, which document must the firm provide before categorisation takes effect?
o: A personalised suitability report for the client
An FSCS compensation scheme coverage factsheet
A full prospectus for each individual investment held
A PRIIPs key information document for every product
A written notice of their categorisation and its implications
w: Firms must inform clients of their categorisation, explain the protections it affords, and outline the right to request re-categorisation.

n.2: A prospectus is not required for categorisation to take effect.
n.0: A suitability report is not the categorisation notice.
n.3: A PRIIPs KID is a product document, not a categorisation notice.
n.1: An FSCS factsheet is not the categorisation requirement.

q: A firm is categorising its clients under COBS 3 and lists the categories it recognises. Which of the following is NOT a formal FCA client category?
o: Eligible counterparty
Retail client
High-net-worth client
Professional client
Per se professional client
w: ‘High-net-worth client’ is not a formal COBS category. The FCA recognises retail, professional, and eligible counterparty classifications.

n.1: Retail client is a formal category.
n.3: Professional client is a formal category.
n.0: Eligible counterparty is a formal category.
n.4: Per se professional clients are defined within professional classification.

q: A new brokerage is setting up its onboarding process and must classify each incoming client. Why must firms categorise clients under COBS 3.1?
o: To apply proportionate rules and appropriate client protections
To allocate clients to product distribution mailing lists
To let firms charge professionals substantially higher fees
To determine a client's eligibility for FCA registration
To decide which currency the client must transact in
w: Categorisation ensures proportionate regulation by tailoring rules and protections to retail, professional, and eligible counterparty categories.

n.1: Categorisation is not about marketing distribution lists.
n.3: Clients do not need FCA registration; this is not the purpose.
n.2: Categorisation is not a mechanism for charging higher fees.
n.4: It does not dictate the transaction currency.

q: A professional client asks the firm to be treated as a retail client for greater protection. Which COBS rule permits a client to request re-categorisation?
o: COBS 4.1
MCOB 2.1
COBS 3.1
COBS 6.1
ICOBS 3.2
w: COBS 3.1 explicitly allows clients to request re-categorisation, subject to conditions and firm assessment of appropriateness.

n.0: COBS 4.1 covers promotions, not categorisation.
n.3: COBS 6.1 relates to disclosure of costs and charges.
n.1: MCOB applies to mortgages, not investment categorisation.
n.4: ICOBS 3.2 relates to insurance conduct rules.

q: A firm categorises a new customer under COBS 3.1 and considers the effect on its duties. How does that categorisation affect the firm's obligations?
o: It decides whether the firm must be authorised by the PRA
It determines whether the firm must maintain a website
It sets which disclosure, suitability and reporting rules apply
It sets the firm's own regulatory capital adequacy levels
It exempts the firm from its anti-money-laundering duties
w: Categorisation drives the conduct obligations under COBS, such as suitability for retail clients or limited requirements for eligible counterparties.

n.0: Categorisation does not determine PRA authorisation.
n.4: It does not exempt firms from AML duties.
n.3: It does not set the firm's capital requirements.
n.1: It does not decide whether a firm must have a website.

q: A client categorised as retail wants to understand their options over how the firm treats them. Which right does COBS 3.1 give the client in respect of categorisation?
o: To avoid every suitability assessment in all circumstances
To require the FCA itself to approve their categorisation
To request re-categorisation and learn the protections lost or gained
To choose their categorisation on personal preference alone
To opt out of the COBS conduct regime altogether entirely
w: Clients may request to be treated differently, but firms must assess appropriateness and explain the implications of changing category.

n.1: The FCA does not approve individual client categorisations.
n.3: Re-categorisation depends on tests, not preference alone.
n.4: Clients cannot opt out of the COBS regime entirely.
n.0: Clients cannot avoid all suitability assessments.

q: What is a firm required to do when categorising a client for the first time?
o: Seek FCA approval before classifying the new client
Classify the client on their account balance size alone
Automatically treat the client as a professional client
Inform the client of their category and explain its impact
Obtain a suitability report from the client's other firm
w: Firms must notify clients of their classification and the protections it entails under COBS 3.1, ensuring informed consent.

n.2: The default is retail, not automatic professional treatment.
n.1: Classification is not based on account balance alone.
n.0: FCA approval is not needed to classify a client.
n.4: A report from another firm is not required to classify.

q: How does COBS 3.1 ensure client protection is proportionate?
o: By exempting firms that categorise clients from their record-keeping requirements
By focusing its protections only on wholesale, and not retail, business
By varying obligations for retail, professional and eligible-counterparty clients
By allowing firms to categorise all of their clients as professionals for convenience
By mandating identical treatment and protections for every client regardless of type
w: COBS 3.1 ensures that the level of protection is calibrated to the sophistication of the client, with retail given the most protections.

n.4: Protection is proportionate, not identical for all clients.
n.3: Firms cannot simply categorise everyone as professional.
n.1: COBS protections extend to retail, not only wholesale, business.
n.0: Categorisation does not remove record-keeping duties.

q: Which best describes a retail client under COBS 3.4?
o: A client who executes trades only on a regulated market venue
A credit institution authorised under the CRD framework
A large institutional occupational pension fund scheme
A client who is neither a professional client nor an eligible counterparty
A corporate treasury holding well over EUR 20 million in assets
w: Retail clients are defined as those not meeting the criteria for professional clients or eligible counterparties, receiving the highest regulatory protection.

n.0: Trading only on a regulated market does not make one retail.
n.4: A large corporate treasury is typically professional, not retail.
n.2: An institutional pension fund is a per se professional client.
n.1: A credit institution is a per se professional client.

q: Why do retail clients receive the highest level of conduct protection?
o: Because they always deal through professional clients
Because they invest only in packaged retail products
Because they are wholly exempt from the FCA's rules
Because they are presumed less experienced and knowledgeable
Because they are subject to much lower transaction volumes
w: Retail clients are presumed to lack the expertise of professional or ECPs, so COBS provides them with maximum protections including disclosures and suitability.

n.4: Transaction volume is not the reason for the protection.
n.1: Retail clients are not limited to packaged products.
n.2: Retail clients are protected by, not exempt from, FCA rules.
n.0: Retail clients do not always deal through professionals.

q: A firm is categorising a new customer who is investing their own personal savings. Under COBS, which categorisation would this person normally receive?
o: A large listed corporate meeting the professional size tests
An FCA-authorised investment management business
An individual investing their own personal savings
A supranational organisation such as the World Bank
A credit institution dealing in the wholesale market
w: Individuals investing their savings fall under retail client categorisation unless they opt up and meet professional criteria.

n.4: A credit institution is a per se professional client.
n.1: An authorised investment firm is a per se professional client.
n.3: A supranational body is a per se professional client.
n.0: A large corporate meeting the size tests is professional, not retail.

q: What obligation applies specifically when advising retail clients under COBS?
o: Disclosure of the full costs and charges is optional
The firm may simply assume the client's product knowledge
The best execution obligation does not apply to them
A suitability assessment must always be carried out
A simplified prospectus may be omitted entirely
w: Suitability assessments are mandatory for retail advice, ensuring the recommended product meets the client’s objectives and risk tolerance.

n.1: Firms cannot assume retail clients' product knowledge.
n.2: Best execution does apply to retail client orders.
n.0: Cost and charges disclosure is required, not optional.
n.4: Required disclosures cannot simply be omitted for retail clients.

q: A private individual opens an account with an investment firm for the first time and no reclassification has taken place. What is this person's default client classification under COBS?
o: Professional client
Retail client
Eligible counterparty
Institutional client
High-net-worth professional
w: The FCA requires that individuals are treated as retail clients by default to ensure they receive maximum protections unless reclassified properly.

n.0: Professional status must be evidenced and agreed.
n.2: ECP is reserved for firms and certain institutions, not individuals by default.
n.4: ‘High-net-worth professional’ is not a formal FCA category.
n.3: Institutional is not a defined COBS category.

q: A firm is drawing up different service standards for retail and professional clients. How does the FCA's treatment of retail clients compare with that of professionals?
o: Retail clients must self-certify their own knowledge
Retail clients are exempt from the best execution rules
Retail clients get fuller disclosure and suitability requirements
Retail clients face higher minimum investment thresholds
Retail clients have lighter disclosure rules than professionals
w: Retail clients receive detailed disclosure, cost transparency, and suitability tests, reflecting their presumed lower knowledge base.

n.4: Retail clients get more, not lighter, disclosure.
n.0: Retail clients are not required to self-certify knowledge.
n.1: Best execution applies to retail clients.
n.3: There is no higher minimum investment threshold for retail clients.

q: A firm is comparing the protections owed to its retail clients with those owed to eligible counterparties. Which retail client protection is not typically extended to eligible counterparties?
o: The rules on disclosing and limiting third-party inducements
The requirement to identify and manage conflicts of interest
The duty to act honestly, fairly and professionally
A detailed suitability assessment and full risk disclosure
The clear, fair and not misleading communication rule
w: Retail clients benefit from suitability and disclosure obligations that are not required for eligible counterparties.

n.2: Acting honestly, fairly and professionally still applies to ECPs.
n.4: The clear, fair and not misleading rule still applies broadly.
n.1: Conflicts of interest rules still apply to ECP business.
n.0: Inducement rules continue to apply to ECP business.

q: A compliance officer reviews five prospective clients to set default categories. Which of these clients would always be treated as retail unless reclassified?
o: A MiFID investment firm
A bank executing trades on behalf of clients
An individual investing in ISAs
A government treasury department
A large insurer managing its own funds
w: Individual retail investors are classified as retail by default, unless formally opted up to professional under set criteria.

n.1: Banks are per se professional or eligible counterparties.
n.3: Government bodies are per se professionals.
n.0: MiFID firms are per se professional clients.
n.4: Insurers are per se professional clients.

q: Why is treating clients as retail the FCA’s default position?
o: It allows firms to limit their liability to clients
It reduces the compliance costs that firms must bear
It exempts retail clients from all AML identity checks
It promotes greater efficiency in the wholesale markets
It gives the greatest protection to those who most need it
w: Defaulting to retail ensures that inexperienced investors get the maximum safeguards unless proven otherwise.

n.1: The default is about protection, not cutting firms' costs.
n.0: It does not exist to limit firms' liability.
n.3: It is not aimed at wholesale market efficiency.
n.2: Retail clients are not exempt from AML checks.

q: A firm is checking which of its account types can never fall within the retail client definition. Which of these client types is always outside it?
o: Small charities investing reserves
Employees using workplace ISAs
Authorised investment firms
Individual retail investors
Pension savers in personal SIPPs
w: Authorised investment firms are per se professional or eligible counterparties, not retail clients.

n.3: Individuals investing their savings are retail by default.
n.0: Charities are typically retail unless reclassified.
n.1: Employees using ISAs are retail.
n.4: Pension savers are treated as retail clients.

q: A discretionary manager is approached by someone acting as an agent on behalf of an underlying investor. Under COBS 2.4.1, whom should the firm treat as its client?
o: The firm may choose freely whether to treat the agent or principal as the client
Neither the agent nor the principal is considered a client
Both the agent and principal are treated as clients simultaneously
The underlying person represented by the agent is regarded as the client
The agent is always regarded as the client
w: COBS 2.4.1 clarifies that where a person acts as agent, the person represented by the agent is treated as the firm’s client for categorisation and protections.

n.4: The agent is not the client unless also receiving services for itself.
n.2: Dual treatment is not the default under COBS 2.4.
n.1: One party must be the client; it cannot be neither.
n.0: The firm does not have discretion to switch arbitrarily; rules specify the principal as the client.

q: A corporate treasurer places trades with a broker, acting as agent for the company that employs her. Under COBS, who is the broker's client?
o: The treasurer personally
Both the treasurer and the company equally
The FCA
No client exists in this scenario
The company employing the treasurer
w: The principal, in this case the company, is the client. The treasurer is acting as agent.

n.0: The treasurer personally is not the client.
n.1: Dual treatment is not recognised in this context.
n.2: The FCA is not a party to this client relationship.
n.3: A client always exists where services are provided.

q: A firm is instructed by an agent who is acting on behalf of an underlying principal. Which statement best reflects how COBS 2.4.2 treats this arrangement?
o: Agents are entirely exempt from the protections that COBS provides
An agent is in every case to be categorised as a professional client
A firm may by default classify any agent as an eligible counterparty
An agent must be registered with the FCA before it is able to act
Where an agent acts for a principal, the firm owes COBS duties to the principal
w: The rules ensure that the principal, not the agent, is recognised as the client in such cases.

n.1: Agent status does not automatically make the person professional.
n.3: Registration with the FCA is not a precondition to acting as agent.
n.0: COBS protections are not disapplied simply because an agent is involved.
n.2: There is no default eligible-counterparty classification for agents.

q: If an investment adviser is instructed by a solicitor on behalf of a trust, who is treated as the client?
o: The trustee bank
Both solicitor and trust
The FCA
The solicitor personally
The trust
w: The trust, represented by the solicitor, is the client under COBS categorisation rules.

n.3: The solicitor is acting as an agent, not the client.
n.1: Dual treatment is not applied here.
n.2: The FCA is not a client in any transaction.
n.0: The trustee bank is not necessarily the client unless it is the principal.

q: Why does COBS require firms to identify the principal when an agent is used?
o: So that the firm can avoid its best execution duties
So the right level of protection and categorisation applies
So the firm can treat the agent as retail by default
So that the firm can bypass all suitability requirements
So the agent bears responsibility for all client losses
w: Correct identification ensures the appropriate protections, disclosures, and obligations are applied to the ultimate client.

n.0: Identifying the principal is not to avoid best execution.
n.2: The firm looks through to the client, not treats the agent as retail.
n.4: It does not shift responsibility for losses onto the agent.
n.3: It is not a means to bypass suitability requirements.

q: A firm mistakenly treats an agent acting for an underlying principal as the client itself. What is the consequence of this categorisation error?
o: The FCA automatically voids the whole client agreement
The true client may not receive the appropriate protections
The whole transaction becomes legally unenforceable
The agent gains its own right to FSCS compensation
The firm becomes fully exempt from its COBS duties
w: If the agent is treated as the client, the actual principal could miss required protections under COBS, leaving the firm in breach.

n.0: The FCA does not automatically void the agreement.
n.4: The firm is not exempted from COBS; it may be in breach.
n.3: The agent does not thereby gain FSCS rights.
n.2: The transaction is not automatically unenforceable.

q: When an AR (appointed representative) acts as agent, who must the firm categorise under COBS?
o: The appointed representative itself as the client
The FCA itself, acting as the relevant client
The AR's own principal firm as the client
Both the AR and its client jointly together
The AR's own client, rather than the AR itself
w: The AR is acting as agent; the actual client of the AR is the party that must be categorised and protected under COBS.

n.0: The AR is the agent, not the client to be categorised.
n.3: Only the underlying client, not both parties, is categorised.
n.1: The FCA is a regulator, not the client.
n.2: The principal is not the client here; the AR's client is.

q: Which of the following scenarios illustrates COBS 2.4.3?
o: Where a firm looks through the agent to find the ultimate client
Where a firm applies CASS in place of the COBS rules
Where a firm may disregard the categorisation rules
Where a firm classifies the agent as retail by default
Where a firm treats all parties as eligible counterparties
w: COBS 2.4.3 reinforces that the ultimate person for whom the agent acts is the client, ensuring correct categorisation.

n.3: The firm identifies the ultimate client, not the agent as retail.
n.2: Categorisation rules cannot be disregarded.
n.4: Parties are not all treated as eligible counterparties.
n.1: CASS does not replace COBS categorisation rules.

q: A wealth manager takes instructions from a solicitor who is acting on behalf of a private individual. Who is categorised as the client under COBS?
o: The FCA
The private client
The lawyer
Neither party
Both lawyer and client
w: The lawyer is acting as agent; the private individual receiving advice is the client under COBS.

n.2: The lawyer is only an agent, not the client.
n.4: Dual classification does not apply here.
n.3: One party must be the client; it cannot be neither.
n.0: The FCA is regulator, not client.

q: An adviser deals with a person acting on behalf of another and must decide who the client is under the COBS agency rules. Why do these agent rules matter in practice?
o: Because they ensure the agent will always receive a fee for the introduction
Misidentifying the client can apply the wrong protections and cause regulatory breaches
Because identifying an agent exempts the firm from the MiFID conduct rules
Because the agent rules let firms avoid retail protections altogether
Because they mean that no suitability requirements apply to the transaction
w: Correct identification ensures appropriate application of disclosures, suitability, and protections. Misidentification could expose firms to breaches and sanctions.

n.3: The rules do not let firms avoid retail protections.
n.2: They do not exempt firms from MiFID conduct rules.
n.0: They do not guarantee the agent a fee.
n.4: Suitability rules still apply.

q: A retail client asks to be reclassified as professional to access more products. Under COBS 3.5.3, what must the client provide to be treated as an elective professional client?
o: A written request to opt up plus confirmation of understanding
A verbal agreement reached during a client meeting
An FCA-issued registration certificate for the client
Documentary proof of the client's UK tax residency
Evidence of an investment portfolio above GBP 1 million
w: Clients must provide a written request to be re-categorised as professional and confirm they understand the protections they may lose.

n.1: A verbal agreement is insufficient; the request must be written.
n.4: A GBP 1 million portfolio is not the elective professional test.
n.3: UK residency is not a condition for elective professional status.
n.2: No FCA registration certificate is issued to clients.

q: A firm is assessing whether a wealthy individual can be treated as an elective professional client under COBS 3.5.3B. Which of the following is one of the key tests it must apply?
o: Employment in any profession for at least five years
Holding a personal current account with a UK bank
Ownership of residential property within the UK
A frequency of significant-size transactions over the past year
Being a member of an occupational pension scheme
w: COBS 3.5.3B lists transaction frequency as one of the criteria firms must consider when assessing elective professional status.

n.0: General employment length is not the qualitative-test criterion.
n.1: Holding a UK bank account is irrelevant to the test.
n.2: Owning UK property is not part of the test.
n.4: Pension scheme membership is not a criterion.

q: Which of the following must a firm assess before agreeing elective professional status?
o: The client's nationality and their country of birth
The client's personal credit score and credit rating
The client's expertise, experience and knowledge of investments
The client's marital status and family situation
The client's marketing and contact preferences
w: Firms must be reasonably assured the client has expertise, experience, and knowledge to make investment decisions and understand risks.

n.0: Nationality is not part of the qualitative assessment.
n.4: Marketing preferences are irrelevant to the test.
n.3: Marital status is not assessed for professional status.
n.1: Credit score is not part of the qualitative test.

q: Which financial instrument threshold is cited in COBS 3.5.3C as a criterion for elective professional clients?
o: Portfolio value exceeding €500,000
Mortgage borrowing exceeding £250,000
FSCS coverage above £85,000
Minimum ISA holdings of £20,000
Annual salary exceeding £50,000
w: A client with a portfolio exceeding €500,000 may satisfy one of the quantitative tests for elective professional status.

n.4: Salary thresholds are not used as categorisation criteria.
n.1: Mortgage borrowing is not relevant to professional categorisation.
n.2: FSCS coverage limits are unrelated to categorisation.
n.3: ISA holdings alone do not determine client status.

q: What additional safeguard does COBS 3.5.3E require before re-categorising a client?
o: A signed statutory declaration made by the client
A written warning from the firm about the protections lost
Proof of at least three years' trading experience
A minimum annual income of at least GBP 100,000
Prior approval obtained from the FCA for the change
w: Firms must provide a clear written warning of the protections the client will lose and obtain confirmation of understanding before re-categorisation.

n.4: FCA approval is not required to re-categorise a client.
n.2: A fixed three-year trading requirement is not the safeguard here.
n.0: A statutory declaration is not the required safeguard.
n.3: There is no GBP 100,000 income threshold safeguard.

q: Which of the following is a per se professional client, not requiring elective categorisation?
o: A pensioner investing £50,000 in ISAs
An individual investor with a £600,000 portfolio
An SME with fewer than 10 employees
A high-net-worth individual
An authorised investment firm
w: Firms and other authorised entities are classified automatically as per se professional clients under COBS 3.5.

n.1: This may qualify for elective professional, not per se professional.
n.3: High-net-worth status alone is not an FCA category.
n.0: Retail investors remain retail by default.
n.2: Small businesses do not automatically qualify as professional clients.

q: During a file review, a compliance officer checks the records kept for clients treated as elective professionals. Why must the firm retain those records?
o: To evidence compliance with the COBS 3.5 tests and consent
To prove the client holds valid life insurance cover
To monitor the firm's annual FSCS levy payments
To record the client's contact and marketing preferences
To provide evidence of the client's tax compliance
w: Firms must evidence that the criteria, warnings, and client confirmations required for elective professional categorisation have been met.

n.4: Records are not kept to evidence the client's tax compliance.
n.3: They are not kept to record marketing preferences.
n.2: They are unrelated to monitoring FSCS levy payments.
n.1: They are not kept to prove the client's insurance cover.

q: A retail investor asks to opt up to elective professional status, and the firm applies the COBS 3.5.3B tests. Which of the following is NOT one of those tests?
o: Experience in trading financial instruments
Carrying out an average of 10 significant transactions per quarter in the last year
Owning a UK property valued above £1 million
Having worked in financial services for at least one year in a professional role
Holding at least €500,000 in a portfolio
w: Property ownership is irrelevant to elective professional classification. The tests focus on financial expertise and experience.

n.4: Portfolio thresholds are part of the criteria.
n.3: Relevant industry employment is a valid test.
n.1: Transaction frequency is a recognised measure.
n.0: Trading experience is central to professional categorisation.

q: An experienced corporate treasurer, currently a retail client, asks to be treated as a professional. Why does COBS permit elective professional categorisation?
o: Some retail clients have enough knowledge and experience to be treated as professionals
To ensure that all high-net-worth individuals are automatically professional clients
To ensure that all clients are able to access complex derivative products
To enable firms to place clients outside the scope of regulatory oversight
To allow firms to reduce their disclosure obligations for every client
w: Elective professional categorisation acknowledges that some individuals or entities meet knowledge and experience standards comparable to per se professionals.

n.3: Elective categorisation does not remove regulatory oversight.
n.1: Wealth alone does not make a client automatically professional.
n.4: It does not reduce disclosure duties across the board.
n.2: It is not a mechanism to give everyone access to complex products.

q: What must firms always explain when agreeing to treat a client as an elective professional?
o: That the client must trade only through a UK exchange
That the client will obtain useful tax advantages
That the client will gain new FSCS compensation cover
The protections the client will lose against retail status
That the client will now pay noticeably lower fees
w: Firms must warn clients explicitly of the protections they will forgo when opting up to professional status, including suitability and disclosure rights.

n.4: Opting up does not guarantee lower fees.
n.2: Opting up does not add FSCS cover; it reduces protections.
n.1: There are no tax advantages from re-categorisation.
n.0: Opting up does not restrict trading to a UK exchange.

q: A large corporate wants to be treated as an elective eligible counterparty by a broker. Under COBS 3.6.4, what must it do to obtain that status?
o: Trade exclusively in derivative financial instruments
Automatically qualify by holding EUR 500,000 in assets
Request the categorisation in writing and get the firm's agreement
Be nominated for the status by another eligible counterparty
Register the elective categorisation directly with the FCA
w: A client must request elective ECP status and the firm must agree, ensuring the client understands the implications.

n.1: There is no automatic asset-threshold qualification for ECP status.
n.4: Clients do not register elective status with the FCA.
n.3: Nomination by another counterparty is not the route.
n.0: Trading only derivatives does not confer ECP status.

q: Which type of client may be opted up to elective ECP status under COBS?
o: A consumer purchasing general insurance
A mortgage borrower
Any member of the public
A professional client
A retail client by default
w: Only professional clients can be opted up to elective eligible counterparty status. Retail clients cannot be treated directly as ECPs.

n.4: Retail clients cannot be directly re-categorised as ECPs.
n.2: The general public are not automatically eligible.
n.1: Mortgage clients are categorised under MCOB, not COBS ECP rules.
n.0: Insurance consumers are governed by ICOBS, not ECP rules.

q: A firm wants to reclassify an existing client as an elective eligible counterparty. Which test must it satisfy before granting that status?
o: Confirming that the client earns over £100,000 annually
Confirming the client has UK residency
Confirming that the client is already a professional client
Confirming the client has FSCS eligibility
Confirming the client has traded at least 100 times in a year
w: A firm may only grant elective ECP status to a client already categorised as professional, ensuring a baseline of sophistication.

n.0: Income thresholds are not part of the ECP test.
n.1: Residency does not determine ECP eligibility.
n.4: Trading frequency is part of elective professional criteria, not ECPs.
n.3: FSCS eligibility is unrelated to categorisation as ECP.

q: A firm is classifying two sophisticated customers, one as an elective professional client and the other as an elective eligible counterparty. Why do COBS rules distinguish between these two categories?
o: Because ECPs must always be established within the UK
Because ECPs are automatically retail clients in some cases
Because ECPs are exempt from anti-money-laundering duties
Because ECPs are required to pay much higher FCA levies
Because ECPs get even fewer protections than professional clients
w: Eligible counterparties receive the lightest conduct protections, fewer than professional clients, so the classification requires stricter controls.

n.3: The distinction is not about FCA levies.
n.0: ECPs need not be UK-established.
n.2: ECPs are not exempt from AML duties.
n.1: ECPs are not automatically retail clients.

q: Which activities can be carried out with elective eligible counterparties under COBS?
o: Offering retail general insurance products to consumers
Providing regulated mortgage advice to individual borrowers
Arranging regulated consumer credit loans
Dealing on own account, executing orders, and receiving and transmitting orders
Providing cash ISAs to personal savers
w: ECP rules apply to core investment services such as execution and dealing. Consumer credit, mortgages, and insurance are outside COBS.

n.1: Mortgage advice is not an eligible-counterparty activity.
n.0: Retail insurance is outside eligible-counterparty business.
n.4: Cash ISAs are retail products, not eligible-counterparty activity.
n.2: Consumer credit lending is not within these activities.

q: What safeguard must a firm provide when re-categorising a professional client as an elective ECP?
o: A test confirming the client's nationality and residence
A written warning explaining the loss of conduct protections
A check of the client's minimum invested balance size
A mandatory cooling-off period lasting fourteen days
An FCA certificate confirming the client's eligibility
w: Clients must be warned in writing about the protections they will lose when moving to elective ECP status, similar to elective professional re-categorisation.

n.4: The FCA does not issue eligibility certificates for this.
n.2: There is no minimum-balance check safeguard here.
n.3: No mandatory 14-day cooling-off period applies.
n.0: Nationality is not the relevant safeguard.

q: Which of the following is NOT a category that can be treated as elective eligible counterparty?
o: Corporate entity meeting professional criteria
Per se professional client
Retail client
Elective professional client
Professional client
w: Retail clients cannot be classified directly as elective ECPs; only professional clients (per se or elective) may be opted up.

n.4: Professional clients can be treated as elective ECPs.
n.1: Per se professionals may elect to be ECPs.
n.3: Elective professionals may also be opted up to ECP.
n.0: Corporates qualifying as professionals may be treated as ECPs.

q: A corporate client asks to be reclassified as an elective eligible counterparty, and the firm considers why COBS restricts this so tightly. Why is elective ECP classification tightly controlled under COBS?
o: Because ECPs lose key protections like suitability and best execution
Because ECPs need FCA approval for every single transaction
Because ECPs are automatically covered by the FSCS scheme
Because ECPs are entirely exempt from all FCA regulation
Because ECPs may trade only on UK-based trading venues
w: ECPs receive the least protection; suitability and some disclosure requirements are disapplied, so firms must ensure clients are genuinely sophisticated.

n.3: ECPs are not exempt from all FCA regulation.
n.4: ECPs are not restricted to UK trading venues.
n.2: ECPs are not automatically covered by the FSCS.
n.1: ECPs do not need FCA approval for each transaction.

q: A firm agrees to treat a client as an elective eligible counterparty. What must the firm record when granting elective ECP status?
o: The client's salary, home address, and five-year investment returns
The client's tax residency and VAT registration number details
Written PRA approval confirming the counterparty reclassification decision
The client's signed waiver of all FSCS and ombudsman access rights
The client's request, the firm's consent, and warnings about lost protections
w: Firms must keep records of the client’s request, the firm’s consent, and the required warnings about reduced protections.

n.0: Personal financial data like salary is not the required categorisation record.
n.2: The PRA does not approve client categorisation; it is the firm's decision.
n.3: ECP status reduces protections but is recorded via request, consent and warnings, not a rights waiver.
n.1: Tax and VAT details are irrelevant to recording elective ECP status.

q: A firm proposes to treat a professional client as a retail client so they receive additional safeguards. Under COBS 3.7, what is meant by providing a client with a higher level of protection?
o: Removing FCA oversight for clients who request wholesale treatment
Assigning a client to a lower category to simplify the firm's compliance
Exempting professional clients from all disclosure and reporting duties
Treating a client in a category that gives greater safeguards than their default
Treating every new client as an eligible counterparty by default
w: COBS 3.7 permits firms to categorise clients at a higher protection level (e.g., treating a professional as retail), but never at a lower level without consent and tests.

n.1: Higher protection means moving up, not down to a lower-protection category.
n.0: Categorisation never removes FCA oversight.
n.2: Professional clients still receive disclosures; status does not exempt them.
n.4: ECP is the lowest protection level, the opposite of higher protection.

q: An experienced professional client asks to be treated as retail by the firm under COBS 3.7. Why might the firm agree to this re-categorisation?
o: To give stronger protections, such as suitability and fuller disclosures
To relieve the firm of its anti-money-laundering obligations for that client
To reduce the firm's own administrative burden in servicing the client
To obtain a discount on the fees the firm pays to the FCA
To exempt the client from the appropriateness test for complex products
w: A professional may be treated as retail to ensure they receive the fullest set of protections, particularly around advice and disclosure.

n.1: Re-categorising to retail does not affect AML obligations.
n.3: It does not reduce the firm's FCA fees.
n.4: It increases, not removes, protections such as appropriateness.
n.2: The purpose is stronger client protection, not less firm admin.

q: Which of the following is an example of providing a higher level of protection?
o: Letting a client waive suitability and appropriateness requirements
Downgrading a professional to ECP to lower the firm's costs
Treating a retail client as an eligible counterparty for execution
Treating a small professional client as retail for suitability checks
Reclassifying a retail client as professional to reduce disclosures
w: Upgrading a professional to retail increases safeguards such as detailed disclosures and suitability tests.

n.2: Retail to ECP lowers protection, not raises it.
n.4: Retail to professional reduces safeguards, the opposite of higher protection.
n.0: Clients cannot waive suitability; this is not raising protection.
n.1: Professional to ECP reduces protection.

q: Who decides if a client is to be given a higher level of protection?
o: The courts, through enforcement orders made against the firm
The FCA, by issuing a special permission for each client
The firm, which may treat any client as belonging to a more protected category
The relevant trade association overseeing the firm's sector
The client alone, by opting out of professional status at will
w: Firms have discretion to treat clients as more protected than their default categorisation. This is one-way only, from less to more protected.

n.1: The FCA does not issue per-client permissions for categorisation.
n.4: Higher protection is the firm's discretion, not a unilateral client opt-out.
n.0: Courts do not set client categorisation.
n.3: Trade associations have no role in client categorisation.

q: What is a regulatory benefit of giving clients higher protection under COBS?
o: It exempts the firm from FCA transaction reporting obligations
It removes the need for a complaint-handling procedure
It guarantees the firm higher profitability on each account
It allows the firm to disapply MiFID conduct standards entirely
It reduces the risk of client detriment by applying more stringent standards
w: Applying stronger protections reduces regulatory and conduct risks, protecting the client and the firm’s compliance position.

n.0: Higher protection does not exempt firms from reporting.
n.3: MiFID standards cannot be disapplied by upgrading protection.
n.2: Protection level does not guarantee profitability.
n.1: Complaint handling is always required.

q: Which principle underpins COBS 3.7 on higher client protection?
o: A firm may always offer more protection, but not less without a formal process
A firm may exempt wholesale clients from all COBS conduct rules
A firm must charge higher fees whenever it offers higher protection
A firm must reduce protection whenever a client requests it
A client can be upgraded automatically without the firm's knowledge
w: COBS permits firms to treat clients more protectively than required, but not the reverse without proper re-categorisation procedures.

n.3: Reducing protection requires tests and consent, not an automatic right on request.
n.4: Categorisation is a firm decision, not automatic without its knowledge.
n.2: There is no rule linking protection level to fees.
n.1: Wholesale clients are not exempt from all COBS rules.

q: A firm agrees to treat a professional client as retail at that client's request. What obligations then apply to the firm in dealing with them?
o: Reduced reporting duties compared with genuine retail clients
Exemption from the firm's best execution obligations
No suitability testing, but enhanced FSCS compensation limits
Full retail conduct obligations, including suitability and disclosure
Automatic reclassification of the client as an eligible counterparty
w: Once a professional is treated as retail, all obligations applicable to retail clients, such as detailed disclosure and suitability, apply in full.

n.2: Treating as retail adds suitability, it does not remove it.
n.0: Retail treatment means full, not reduced, reporting duties.
n.4: Retail treatment is the opposite of ECP status.
n.1: Best execution still applies to retail clients.

q: A firm decides to categorise a professional client as retail even though the client qualifies for professional status. Why might a firm choose to upgrade professional clients to retail in this way?
o: To escape the MiFID II product governance requirements
To avoid keeping any records of the client's categorisation
To reduce the firm's operational and administrative costs
To manage compliance risk by applying the highest protection standards
To exempt the firm from the FCA's Principles for Businesses
w: Providing higher protection reduces regulatory risk, since applying retail standards ensures compliance with the strictest requirements.

n.1: Upgrading increases record-keeping, it does not remove it.
n.4: The FCA Principles always apply.
n.2: Higher protection raises costs, it does not reduce them.
n.0: Product governance rules still apply.

q: Which of these scenarios demonstrates COBS 3.7 in practice?
o: A bank is classified as ECP but treated as retail
A pension fund is classified as professional but treated as retail by the firm
A firm removes suitability checks for retail clients
An individual investor is classified as retail but treated as an eligible counterparty
A corporate client is downgraded without consent
w: Applying retail standards to a professional client increases protections, illustrating the use of COBS 3.7.

n.3: Treating retail as ECP reduces protections, not increases.
n.0: Banks as ECPs can be given more protection, but not less by default.
n.2: Removing suitability reduces protections, contrary to COBS 3.7.
n.4: Unconsented downgrades breach FCA rules.

q: A wealth manager decides to treat a professional client as a retail client to give them greater protection. What documentation and approach does the firm need to follow?
o: Register the client with the PRA as a retail customer
Seek prior approval from a relevant industry trade body
Obtain an FCA certificate confirming the client's new category
Record the decision and apply retail standards consistently to the client
Have the client sign a statutory declaration before a solicitor
w: Firms must document the decision to treat a client as more protected and then consistently apply the higher standard of conduct.

n.2: No FCA certificate is issued for categorisation.
n.0: The PRA does not register clients in this way.
n.1: Trade bodies do not approve categorisation.
n.4: No statutory declaration is required.

q: According to COBS 3.3.1A, what must a firm do when first categorising a client?
o: Register the client with the FCA as a retail investor
Notify the client in writing of their category and explain its implications
Disclose the firm's FSCS levy contributions to the client
Apply professional status automatically to every new client
Provide the client with a PRIIPs key information document
w: Firms must inform clients of their categorisation and set out the protections it provides, in line with COBS 3.3.1A requirements.

n.3: The default is retail applied after notification, not automatic professional status.
n.0: Firms do not register clients with the FCA on categorisation.
n.4: A PRIIPs KID is product disclosure, not a categorisation notice.
n.2: FSCS levy details are not part of categorisation notification.

q: Why must firms provide clients with categorisation notifications under COBS?
o: To exempt the firm from its best-execution obligations to the client
To enable the FCA to collect its periodic fees from the client
So clients understand their protections and right to request re-categorisation
To remove the need to carry out suitability tests for every client
To allow the firm to reduce the disclosures it must otherwise give
w: The purpose of notification is transparency: clients must understand their categorisation and the right to request a different status if appropriate.

n.4: Notification does not reduce required disclosures.
n.0: It does not switch off best execution.
n.1: It is unrelated to FCA fee collection.
n.3: Suitability still applies where relevant.

q: Which details must be included in a client categorisation notification?
o: A copy of the FCA's most recent annual report
Confirmation of the client's eligibility to claim under the FSCS
The category applied, its implications, and the right to request re-categorisation
The firm's own regulatory capital adequacy ratio
The client's tax residency status and national insurance number
w: Notifications must set out the client’s category, what it means in terms of protections, and the right to request re-categorisation.

n.4: Tax residency and NI number are not part of the categorisation notice.
n.1: FSCS eligibility is separate from the categorisation notification.
n.3: The firm's capital ratio is not disclosed in the notice.
n.0: The FCA's annual report is irrelevant to categorisation.

q: A professional client asks a firm to re-categorise him as a retail client. Under COBS 3.3.1B, what must the firm do when acting on this request?
o: Obtain the FCA's prior approval before the change takes effect
Notify the client in writing of the new category and its effects
File the change with the PRA within thirty business days
Reclassify the client as an eligible counterparty by default
Provide a statutory auditor's confirmation of the client's status
w: Where re-categorisation occurs, firms must notify clients of the change and its consequences, fulfilling transparency requirements.

n.0: Re-categorisation does not require FCA approval.
n.2: No PRA filing is required.
n.3: Re-categorisation is not an automatic move to ECP.
n.4: No auditor confirmation is required.

q: A firm is about to notify a new individual client of the category it is being placed in. Which is the default category unless the client is properly re-categorised?
o: Institutional client
High-net-worth professional
Eligible counterparty
Retail client
Professional client
w: Retail is the default category, and firms must notify individuals accordingly unless proper re-categorisation is requested and approved.

n.4: Professional status must be formally opted into, not the default.
n.2: ECP is reserved for firms and certain institutions, not individuals by default.
n.0: Institutional client is not a formal FCA category.
n.1: High-net-worth professional is not a recognised category in COBS.

q: What right must firms notify clients of under COBS 3.3?
o: The right to request re-categorisation to a different client status
The right to unlimited FSCS compensation on any claim
The right to be exempt from anti-money-laundering checks
The right to waive every protection that COBS provides
The right to trade entirely outside UK regulatory oversight

n.3: Clients cannot waive all COBS protections.
n.1: FSCS compensation is capped, not unlimited.
n.4: Authorised firms' clients remain within UK regulation.

q: Why is written notification of categorisation essential under COBS?
o: It replaces the need for any product disclosure documents
It makes the client an eligible counterparty automatically
It exempts the firm from wider record-keeping requirements
It provides evidence the client was informed of their category and protections
It allows the firm to market a wider range of products

n.0: Product disclosures are still required separately.
n.1: Notification does not change the client to ECP.

That the client may only ever trade in pounds sterling
The consequences for the client's conduct protections and regulatory obligations
That the client must appoint an appointed representative

n.0: Clients are not restricted to packaged products.
n.1: Clients are never exempt from FCA oversight.
n.4: Clients need not appoint an appointed representative.

q: A firm has categorised its clients and notified them accordingly under COBS 3.3.1A/B. How should the firm document its compliance with these notification requirements?

Keep records of the notifications sent and client acknowledgements received
Rely solely on verbal explanations given during meetings
Reconfirm each client's categorisation with the FCA annually
Outsource all categorisation responsibility to a third party

n.2: Verbal-only evidence does not meet record-keeping duties.
n.4: Responsibility cannot be outsourced away.
n.3: No annual FCA confirmation of categorisation is required.

q: What is the key regulatory objective of requiring firms to notify clients of categorisation?
o: Boosting the marketing of the firm's investment products
Collecting regulatory fees on behalf of the FCA
Simplifying the firm's product governance procedures
Streamlining the firm's anti-money-laundering compliance
Transparency and informed consent in the client relationship
w: Notifying clients ensures transparency and enables them to make informed decisions about whether to remain in or change category.

n.0: The objective is transparency, not marketing.
n.1: Firms do not collect FCA fees via categorisation.
n.3: Categorisation is unrelated to AML streamlining.
n.2: Product governance is a separate matter.

q: What must a MiFID firm do regarding a client agreement before providing investment services?
o: Provide the agreement in a durable medium before services start
Email only a summary, with full terms following within six months
Post a paper agreement within thirty days after the first trade
Obtain a handwritten signature before making any initial contact
Record verbal consent by phone without sending anything in writing

n.1: Full terms cannot be deferred for six months.

q: When may a MiFID firm provide the client agreement immediately after starting the service?

When the client requests immediate execution via distance communication
Whenever the firm is too busy to send the terms beforehand
Whenever the service is discretionary portfolio management
Whenever the client is classified as an eligible counterparty

n.4: ECP status does not trigger the distance exception.
n.0: Documentation cannot be wholly waived.
n.3: Discretionary management is not itself the exception.

q: A firm is finalising a MiFID client agreement in a durable medium and the paraplanner queries whether the retail client must physically sign it. Which statement best describes signature requirements for MiFID client agreements?

A wet-ink signature is compulsory for every retail client
A digital signature is compulsory for all professional clients
A signature is not mandatory if the agreement is duly provided
No agreement is needed at all if recorded calls are kept

n.1: No wet signature is mandated for retail clients.
n.2: No digital signature is mandated for professionals.
n.0: Signature rules do not turn on instrument complexity.
n.4: An agreement is still required regardless of call recordings.

q: How should a non-MiFID firm handle client agreements for designated investment business to a retail client?
o: Rely on website terms without notifying the client at all
Enter into a written agreement before the business is conducted
Issue a fee schedule now, with full terms following later
Send a brochure only after the first transaction settles
Give a verbal summary only if the relationship is short
w: For non-MiFID designated investment business to a retail client, a written client agreement must be in place before carrying on the business.

n.3: The written agreement must precede the business.
n.0: Unnotified post-trade material does not satisfy the rule.
n.2: Unnotified website terms do not satisfy the rule.
n.4: A verbal summary does not meet the written requirement.

q: Why must client agreements be provided in a durable medium?
o: To ensure terms can be stored unchanged and later reproduced
To remove the need for any suitability assessment
To reduce the firm's printing and postage costs
To let the firm amend terms unilaterally without notice
To eliminate the firm's periodic reporting obligations

n.2: Durable medium is about record integrity, not cost.
n.1: It does not remove suitability duties.
n.3: It does not permit silent unilateral changes.
n.4: Reporting obligations remain.

q: Which content must a MiFID client agreement typically include at a minimum?
o: Only the firm’s complaints email address
A waiver of all client rights
Detailed personal tax computations
Scope of services and costs/charges
Forecasts of guaranteed investment returns
w: The agreement should set out the service scope and costs/charges so clients understand what is provided and what they will pay.

n.4: Guaranteed returns are inappropriate, because agreements must present accurate terms and charges, not certainties.
n.2: Personal tax computations are beyond the minimum, because core terms and costs suffice.
n.1: Waiving all rights is incompatible with protections, because agreements must fairly set terms and costs.
n.0: A complaints email alone is insufficient, because scope and costs must be included.

q: A non-MiFID firm is onboarding a professional client and is deciding whether it must supply a written client agreement. When is it required to provide one?
o: Always, before any contact is made with the client
Only after the first discretionary trade is executed
When required by the firm's policy or the terms of the mandate
Only where complex instruments are being recommended
Never, because professional clients receive no documents

n.0: There is no rule requiring it before all contact.
n.1: It is not tied to the first trade.
n.4: Professionals do receive documents where relevant.
n.3: It is not limited to complex instruments.

q: Where may a MiFID client agreement be stored to meet durable-medium requirements?
o: Only as a single paper original held at the branch
On a public website with no notification to the client
Only as an audio recording of the onboarding phone call
In a dashboard that can edit the content silently later
On a system where the client can store and reproduce it unchanged

n.0: Durable media are not limited to a branch paper original.
n.1: Unnotified website posting is not durable provision.
n.3: Silently editable content is not a durable medium.
n.2: An audio-only recording does not meet the standard here.

q: A firm is reviewing which counterparties need a written client agreement for its non-MiFID business. Which client type is generally outside that requirement?
o: Eligible counterparties
Retail clients
Retail clients using execution-only services
New-to-firm retail clients
High-net-worth retail clients
w: Eligible counterparties are generally outside the non-MiFID written client-agreement requirement that is aimed at retail designated investment business.

n.1: Retail clients are the focus of the written requirement, because non-MiFID rules target them.
n.4: Wealth does not change retail status, because retail designated business still needs a written agreement.
n.3: Being new does not exempt documentation, because written agreements are required for retail designated business.
n.2: Execution-only does not remove the written requirement, because it still involves designated investment business to retail clients.

q: How should a firm evidence acceptance of MiFID terms if no signature is taken?
o: Send the terms to a generic shared company inbox
Retain durable-medium evidence of provision and the client's consent to proceed
Assume the client has consented once they log in online
Record a voicemail to the client stating the headline fees
Rely on internal meeting notes recorded by the adviser only
w: Firms should keep durable-medium evidence that terms were provided and that the client agreed to proceed under those terms.

n.4: Internal notes alone do not evidence client acceptance.
n.2: A login does not evidence acceptance of terms.
n.3: A fee voicemail does not evidence provision and consent.
n.0: Sending to a generic inbox is not provision to the client.

q: When can a MiFID firm rely on post-trade provision of terms during a telephone order?
o: When the telephone call happens to take place outside business hours
When prior provision is impossible on the call and the client requests execution
When the client is one who trades frequently with the firm
When the instrument being dealt in is a non-complex product
When a third-party introducer, rather than the client, placed the order
w: If prior provision is not possible with the distance medium and the client requests immediate execution, terms may follow immediately after.

n.2: Frequent trading does not trigger the post-trade allowance.
n.0: The time of the call is not the test.
n.3: Non-complex status is not the relevant condition.
n.4: An introducer's involvement is not the test.

q: A MiFID client refuses to sign the terms of business but still wants trading to begin. What is the firm's duty in this situation?
o: Take a deposit now and send the terms at year-end
Open the account but delay documentation indefinitely
Refuse the service until a wet-ink signature is obtained
Proceed relying only on the client's verbal request
Proceed if terms were provided in a durable medium and acceptance is evidenced

n.3: A verbal request alone is not enough; durable evidence is needed.
n.1: Documentation cannot be delayed indefinitely.
n.0: Terms cannot be deferred to year-end.

q: Which statement aligns with non-MiFID COBS rules for retail execution-only business?
o: A banner on the firm's website counts as the agreement
A written client agreement must still be in place before the business
Only complex products require a written client agreement
A factsheet sent after the trade replaces the agreement
No documentation is necessary for execution-only transactions
w: For non-MiFID designated investment business to retail clients, a written client agreement is required before conducting the business, even execution-only.

n.4: A written agreement is still required for retail designated business.
n.0: A website banner is not the agreement.
n.3: A post-trade factsheet does not replace it.
n.2: The requirement is not limited to complex products.

q: Which element should appear in a discretionary management agreement under MiFID?
o: The client's full lifetime personal tax plan
The mandate scope, the fee basis, and the reporting frequency
A guaranteed minimum performance target for the portfolio
An annual permission letting the firm skip suitability
A clause excluding the firm's regulatory duties
w: Discretionary agreements document the mandate, fees, and reporting frequency to clarify authority and how the service will be delivered.
