n.0: A lifetime tax plan is not a mandate element.
n.4: Regulatory duties cannot be excluded by clause.
n.3: Suitability cannot be waived by permission.

q: How must a firm notify a client that terms are on a website to satisfy durable-medium rules?
o: Do nothing, since clients can find the terms themselves
Allow the marketing team to edit the terms freely
Upload screenshots of the terms without any text access
Give targeted notice and ensure the client can store unchanged copies
Rely only on a single link on the firm's homepage
w: Clients must be notified how to access and store terms in a form that can be reproduced unchanged, meeting durability expectations.

n.0: The client must be specifically notified.
n.4: A homepage link alone is insufficient.
n.1: Editable terms are not durable.
n.2: Non-reproducible screenshots do not meet the standard.

q: Which timing rule applies when onboarding a MiFID professional client remotely?
o: Provide the client agreement within thirty working days of the service beginning
Provide the agreement after execution whenever the relevant market is volatile
Provide the agreement first, unless distance constraints justify immediate post-commencement provision
Provide terms only if the professional client specifically requests them
Provide the agreement only after the first periodic report has been sent to the client
w: MiFID requires prior provision, with a narrow distance-communication exception permitting immediate post-commencement provision when prior delivery is impossible.

n.0: There is no thirty-working-day allowance; terms come before service save for the distance exception.
n.4: Terms are not deferred to after the first report.
n.3: Professional clients are still owed the agreement; it is not request-only.
n.1: Market volatility does not justify deferring terms.

q: Which statement about client categorisation and agreements is accurate?
o: Eligible counterparty status requires a signed paper contract
Elective professional status ends the MiFID provision duty
Professional status removes all of the firm's documentation duties
Retail status strengthens the written agreement requirement under non-MiFID
Retail status requires handwritten signatures for MiFID business
w: Under non-MiFID, written client agreements particularly apply to retail designated investment business, reflecting higher protection needs.

n.2: Professional status does not remove documentation duties.
n.1: MiFID provision duties still apply to elective professionals.
n.0: ECP status does not mandate a signed paper contract.
n.4: MiFID does not require handwritten signatures for retail.

q: What must a firm do if using an introducer for MiFID onboarding?
o: Rely on the introducer's own brochure as the agreement
Ensure the client still receives the firm's agreement in a durable medium
Provide terms only once suitability has been assessed
Replace the agreement with a terms webpage without notice
Skip provision entirely if the introducer is authorised
w: Introducers do not displace duties; the firm must provide its client agreement in a durable medium to the client.

n.0: An introducer's brochure is not the firm's agreement.
n.4: An authorised introducer does not remove the firm's duty.
n.2: Terms come before service, not after suitability.
n.3: An unnotified webpage does not satisfy the duty.

q: A firm is deciding whether a proposed update warrants reissuing a client's MiFID terms of business. Which change would require it to issue updated terms?
o: A minor branding refresh applied to the terms PDF
A change to the firm's receptionist contact details
A generic market outlook note added as an insert
An update to the firm's website colour scheme
Material changes to the services or costs affecting the agreement
w: When material aspects of services or charges change, firms should provide updated terms so clients remain informed on the agreed basis.

n.0: Minor branding is not a material change.
n.1: Receptionist details are not material terms.
n.3: A colour scheme change is immaterial.
n.2: A market outlook insert is not a term change.

q: Where a non-MiFID firm upgrades a retail client to elective professional, what should it confirm regarding agreements?
o: That no documentation is needed from that point onward
That the prior retail terms become void automatically
That the documentation remains appropriate for the new categorisation
That the terms can be removed from the client portal
That a handwritten signature is now mandatory for the client
w: Following re-categorisation, the firm should ensure the agreement remains appropriate to status and services, updating as necessary.

n.0: Documentation is still required after re-categorisation.
n.4: No handwritten signature becomes mandatory.
n.3: Terms should not simply be removed.
n.1: Prior terms do not automatically void.

q: Which item best evidences durable-medium provision of MiFID terms pre-service?
o: A website link added without notifying the client
PDF terms emailed to the client with explicit acceptance captured
A voicemail left stating only the headline fees
A brochure handed to a member of the client's family
An internal memo confirming the intention to send terms
w: Emailed PDF terms, coupled with explicit acceptance, demonstrate provision in a durable medium before services commence.

n.2: A fee voicemail is not durable provision.
n.0: An unnotified link is insufficient.
n.4: An intention memo is not provision.
n.3: Handing terms to a relative is not provision to the client.

q: What must a non-MiFID retail client agreement cover as a baseline?
o: The services to be provided and the basis of the firm's remuneration
A disclaimer removing the client's right to complain
A commitment that returns will be entirely tax-free
An irrevocable power of attorney over the client's affairs
Predicted outperformance of the portfolio versus benchmarks
w: Non-MiFID retail agreements must set out service scope and remuneration so clients understand the nature and cost of the service.

n.4: Firms cannot predict outperformance.
n.1: Complaint rights cannot be removed.
n.3: An irrevocable power of attorney is not a baseline term.
n.2: No tax-free return commitment can be given.

q: A wealth manager is moving a portfolio client from a commission basis to an ongoing percentage fee. When must the firm re-issue the client agreement to reflect this fee model change?
o: Only at the client's next scheduled annual review
Before applying the new charging basis to the client
After the first invoice using the new fees is sent
Never, provided the website displays the change
Only if the client raises a complaint about the fees
w: Material changes like fee model updates must be communicated in durable form before they take effect for the client.

n.0: Notice must precede the change, not wait for annual review.
n.2: It must be before, not after, the first new invoice.
n.3: A website display is not enough.
n.4: A complaint is not the trigger.

q: Which approach satisfies MiFID when onboarding via live chat (distance medium)?
o: Provide a downloadable agreement in-chat and capture consent before trading
Paste the fees into the chat without the full agreement
Send a marketing flyer in the chat and then proceed
Execute the first trade and email the terms the following week
Link to the homepage with no storage instructions given
w: Providing a downloadable agreement in the chat and capturing explicit consent ensures durable provision and documented acceptance before trading.

n.3: Terms must come before trading, not a week later.
n.2: A flyer is not the agreement.
n.1: Fees alone are not the agreement.
n.4: A bare homepage link is not durable provision.

q: Which statement about client agreement signatures under non-MiFID is correct?
o: Only complex products require any client signature
A signature can replace providing the written terms
Professional clients must always sign the terms electronically
A signature is not universally required; the focus is a written agreement
A wet-ink signature is compulsory for every retail client
w: Non-MiFID rules require a written agreement for retail designated business; they do not universally mandate a specific signature form.

n.4: No wet signature is universally required.
n.2: Electronic signature is not mandatory for professionals.
n.1: A signature does not replace providing terms.
n.0: Signature rules do not turn on product complexity.

q: Which factor determines whether post-commencement provision is allowed under MiFID?
o: The length of the settlement cycle applicable to the instrument
Being unable to provide terms first because of the distance medium and the client's urgent request
The workload of the dealing desk during a busy trading period
The level of liquidity in the relevant market on that particular day
The length of time the client has already been with the firm
w: Post-commencement provision is only allowed when prior delivery is impossible due to the distance medium and the client requests immediate execution.

n.4: Client tenure does not trigger the post-commencement allowance.
n.3: Market liquidity is not the relevant test.
n.2: Desk workload does not justify post-commencement provision.
n.0: The settlement cycle is not the determining factor.

q: What should a firm do if a MiFID client refuses electronic delivery of terms?
o: Place a trade now and post the terms later that month
Provide a paper durable copy before service, or use the distance exception
Send a link to the firm's homepage legal footer
Ask the introducer to send their own brochure instead
Proceed to service without providing any documentation
w: The firm must still provide terms in a durable medium—paper if requested—before service or immediately after under the narrow distance exception.

n.4: Documentation is still required.
n.0: Terms cannot be deferred to later in the month.
n.2: A legal-footer link is not durable provision.
n.3: An introducer brochure does not satisfy the duty.

q: Which statement best fits MiFID language requirements in client agreements?
o: State that arranging translation is entirely the client's responsibility
Provide documents only in English whatever the client's preference
State the languages in which the client may communicate and receive documents
Rely on machine-translated terms without telling the client
Offer only oral staff translations instead of documents
w: Agreements should specify available communication languages so clients understand in which language services and documents will be provided.

n.1: Firms must state available languages, not force English only.
n.3: Undisclosed machine translation is not compliant.
n.4: Oral translation does not replace documents.
n.0: Translation is not simply the client's burden.

q: A MiFID firm offers a bundled service combining advice and custody and is drafting the client agreement. Which practice aligns with COBS for documenting the bundle?
o: Provide only the annual name of the bundle
Provide the costs only on the firm's website ticker
List the components without stating the service scope
Break down the components and disclose the aggregate cost in the agreement
Describe the bundle but withhold the costs until invoicing
w: Client agreements should describe service components and associated costs clearly so clients understand the bundled service and charges.

n.4: Costs cannot be withheld until invoicing.
n.1: A website ticker is not adequate cost disclosure.
n.2: Scope must be stated.
n.0: A bundle name alone is not disclosure.

q: A MiFID firm plans to deliver its terms of business to clients through a secure online portal rather than by post. How should the firm properly document a client's consent to receive these terms this way?
o: Record the client's explicit opt-in and provide downloadable, unalterable copies
Rely on the introducer's confirmation of consent alone
Assume consent as soon as the client registers online
Use a pop-up that disappears without being logged
Provide view-only pages that cannot be downloaded
w: Firms should capture explicit opt-in and ensure the client can download and store unchanged copies, meeting durable-medium standards.

n.2: Registration is not explicit consent.
n.3: An unlogged pop-up does not evidence consent.
n.4: View-only pages are not durable.
n.1: An introducer's word is not the client's consent.

q: Under MiFID (COBS 2.2A), when must a firm provide information on the nature and risks of the service and designated investments?
o: Only upon the client’s written request
When the client upgrades to professional status
At the end of the first reporting period
Within 30 days after the first transaction
In good time before providing the service
w: MiFID requires firms to give clients appropriate information about the nature and risks of the service and of the designated investments in good time before providing the service, so the client can make informed decisions.

n.3: Post-transaction delivery is too late, because the client must be informed before services are provided.
n.0: Provision is mandatory; it does not depend on a client request, because pre-service disclosure is a firm obligation.
n.2: Periodic reports come later; they do not replace pre-service disclosures, because clients need information upfront.
n.1: Client categorisation does not remove the timing requirement, because MiFID still expects pre-service disclosure for professionals (proportionately).

q: A MiFID firm is preparing the pre-service information pack for a retail client about to invest in a designated investment. Which item must be included in the pre-service disclosures?
o: Only the instrument's legal ISIN code
A guaranteed illustration of the investment's future performance
A waiver of the client's statutory rights
The material risks of the investment and the relevant risk warnings
A forecast of expected future market returns
w: MiFID pre-service information must describe the nature of the product and its material risks using fair, clear and not misleading language so clients understand potential losses and volatility.

n.1: Guaranteed illustrations are prohibited.
n.4: Return forecasts are not the required risk disclosure.
n.2: Statutory rights cannot be waived.
n.0: An ISIN alone is not adequate disclosure.

q: A firm is about to provide MiFID investment services to a new client. What is required regarding costs and charges before the service is provided?
o: Only the firm's headline management fee percentage
A generic range of fees provided after the first report
An ex-ante disclosure of all costs and charges, including third-party payments
A verbal fee summary with no durable record kept
Deferred disclosure where the product is non-complex
w: MiFID requires ex-ante disclosure of all costs and charges in good time before the service, covering the firm’s fees and any third-party payments, to enable comparability and informed consent.

n.0: All costs must be shown, not just the headline fee.
n.1: Disclosure must be ex-ante, not after the first report.
n.4: Non-complex products do not defer cost disclosure.
n.3: A durable record is required, not a verbal summary.

q: A non-MiFID investment firm is onboarding a new advisory client under COBS 2.2 and 6.1.1-4. Which statement about its information duties is correct?
o: Providing a link to the firm's homepage is sufficient to meet the duty
No pre-service information is needed where the client is dealt with on an execution-only basis
Give appropriate pre-service information about the firm, its services and the risks
The required information may be provided after the client's first trade has settled
Only clients categorised as professional require written pre-service information
w: For Non-MiFID designated investment business, COBS 2.2 and 6.1.1-4 require firms to give clients appropriate information in good time before business, covering who the firm is, what it will do, and the risks involved.

n.1: Execution-only clients still require appropriate information.
n.3: Information is provided before service, not after the first trade.
n.0: A homepage link is not adequate pre-service information.
n.4: The duty is not limited to professional clients.

q: How should risk disclosures be calibrated under MiFID for different client categories?
o: Professional clients require no risk disclosures at all
They should be appropriate and proportionate to the client type and service
Eligible counterparties must receive the most granular detail
Retail clients should get less detail to avoid confusing them
All clients must receive identical risk text for every service
w: MiFID expects firms to provide information that is appropriate for the client’s category and the service offered, ensuring clarity without omitting material risks.

n.3: Retail clients generally need more, not less, detail.
n.0: Professionals still receive appropriate risk disclosure.
n.2: ECPs receive the least, not the most, detail.
n.4: Disclosure is tailored, not identical for all.

q: A paraplanner is drafting pre-service information and must meet the 'fair, clear and not misleading' standard. Which of the following best describes that standard?
o: Balanced, accurate disclosure that avoids exaggeration and concealment
Marketing-led wording that emphasises the product's benefits
Complex technical jargon used to demonstrate expertise
Selective use of risk factors chosen to support the sale
Reliance on past performance as a predictor of future returns
w: Both MiFID and Non-MiFID regimes require pre-service information to be fair, clear and not misleading, meaning balanced presentation of features, costs and risks without omissions or undue prominence.

n.1: Benefit-led marketing bias breaches the standard.
n.2: Jargon that obscures meaning is not clear.
n.3: Selective risk disclosure is misleading.
n.4: Past performance is not a reliable predictor.

q: A firm is onboarding a client for a discretionary portfolio management service under MiFID and prepares the pre-service disclosures. Prior to providing the service, which information is required?
o: The client's full personal tax projections for the year
The nature and risks of the mandate, the costs and charges, and reporting
A guarantee that the portfolio will outperform its benchmark
Only the name of the appointed custodian for the portfolio
A statement that risks are minimal due to diversification
w: Before starting discretionary management, firms must explain the nature and risks of the service, give ex-ante costs and charges, and set expectations for reporting so clients understand how the service operates.

n.3: The custodian name alone is insufficient.
n.2: Outperformance cannot be guaranteed.
n.0: Tax projections are not the required disclosure.
n.4: Diversification does not make risks minimal.

q: A wealth firm's compliance officer is drafting the product literature a non-MiFID client will see before an investment service begins. Under COBS 2.2, what must that information achieve?
o: Enable the client to reasonably understand the product's nature and risks
Be provided only after suitability has been assessed
Be restricted to legal terms and definitions only
Maximise sales conversions through persuasive messaging
Exclude any cost implications to keep it concise
w: COBS 2.2 expects firms to give sufficient, balanced information so clients can reasonably understand a product’s nature, risks and implications before proceeding.

n.3: The aim is understanding, not conversions.
n.2: Information is not limited to legal terms.
n.1: Information comes before, not only after, suitability.
n.4: Costs must be included, not excluded.

q: Before providing a MiFID investment service, a firm gives a client its costs and charges disclosure. How should those costs and charges be presented?
o: Aggregate all costs and charges and show their cumulative effect on returns
Refer to a generic pricing webpage without figures
Provide only separate line items with no overall total
Promise to include the totals in the first periodic report
Disclose only the entry and exit fees to the client
w: MiFID ex-ante disclosures should aggregate costs and charges and illustrate their cumulative effect on returns so clients can compare and assess value.

n.2: A cumulative total is required, not line items alone.
n.4: Entry and exit fees alone are incomplete.
n.1: A figure-free webpage is inadequate.
n.3: Totals come before service, not in the first report.

q: A Non-MiFID discretionary firm is preparing pre-service information for a new client under COBS 14.3.1-10. What pre-service expectation is connected to the firm's later reporting?
o: Requiring the client to prepare and draft their own valuation statements
Promising that the client's risk profile will be reassessed only once a year
Guaranteeing that the portfolio will deliver positive performance every month
Advising the client at the outset that no reports of any kind will be sent
Setting clear expectations about the service and how and when information will be reported
w: Pre-service information should help clients understand the service and the expected form and frequency of information they will receive, aligning with subsequent client reporting obligations.

n.2: Firms cannot guarantee monthly positive performance.
n.3: Clients must receive reporting; not none.
n.1: A once-a-year-only reassessment promise is not the pre-service expectation.
n.0: The firm, not the client, prepares statements.

q: Under MiFID, when must a firm provide information about inducements and third-party payments?
o: Ex-ante, before providing the service
Within 12 months after the service
After the first suitability report is sent
Only for retail clients, never for professionals
Only if the client asks in writing
w: MiFID requires disclosure of inducements and third-party payments in good time before providing the service, so the client can assess conflicts and true costs.

n.1: Twelve months later is far too late, because clients must know inducements before agreeing to services.
n.4: Disclosure is mandatory regardless of client request, because transparency is a firm obligation.
n.3: Professionals also require disclosure, although level of detail may be proportionate.
n.2: Suitability reports do not substitute for ex-ante inducement disclosures.

q: Which is required in pre-service disclosures about complex financial instruments under MiFID?
o: A forecast of the high expected returns on the instrument
A clear explanation of risks such as leverage, illiquidity, and total loss
An exemption from risk disclosure for professional clients
Only a general statement that investments can fall in value
A promise that risks are minimal if the product is held long-term
w: MiFID requires detailed, comprehensible risk disclosures for complex instruments, covering features like leverage, liquidity constraints and possible total loss.

n.3: A generic statement is not enough for complex products.
n.0: Return forecasts are not risk disclosure.
n.4: Long holding does not minimise risk.
n.2: Professionals are not exempt from risk disclosure.

q: What does COBS 2.2A require regarding conflicts of interest disclosures?
o: Disclosure that may be omitted for experienced clients
No disclosure at all provided the firm keeps a conflicts policy
Disclosure made only to the firm's retail clients
A summary of conflicts, the nature of the risks, and mitigation steps taken
Detailed disclosure given only after a conflict has arisen
w: Firms must provide a clear summary of conflicts, the nature of risks posed, and steps taken to manage them, so clients can decide whether to proceed.

n.1: A policy does not remove the disclosure duty.
n.2: Conflicts disclosure is not limited to retail.
n.4: Disclosure comes before, not only after, a conflict.
n.0: Experience does not remove the duty.

q: How should Non-MiFID firms disclose the risk of loss in designated investments?
o: Provide the risk detail solely for derivative products
Make clear that the client may lose some or all of the money invested
Avoid mentioning loss so as not to deter the client
State only that values can fluctuate from day to day
State that losses are automatically reimbursed by the FSCS
w: Non-MiFID disclosures must clearly set out the risk of loss so clients understand they may lose some or all invested capital.

n.2: Loss must be disclosed, not hidden.
n.3: Daily fluctuation alone understates the risk of loss.
n.0: Risk detail is not limited to derivatives.
n.4: The FSCS does not automatically reimburse investment losses.

q: Which statement best describes ‘good time’ under MiFID pre-service information rules?
o: Sufficiently early for the client to consider it before being bound
Any time before the firm's first regulatory report is due
After executing a transaction but within one week of it
Immediately after a marketing brochure has been sent
Only when the client is about to make a formal complaint
w: Good time means providing information early enough that clients can read and understand it before being bound to the service or investment.

n.1: Good time is before commitment, not before a report.
n.2: It must be before, not after, execution.
n.3: It is not tied to sending a brochure.
n.4: It is unrelated to complaints.

q: How should firms present Non-MiFID cost disclosures under COBS 6.1?
o: Orally only, during the firm's initial client meetings
Deferred until the end of the firm's financial year
In small-print footnotes appended after the signed contract
Clearly and in a durable medium, detailing the nature and amount of remuneration
By quoting industry averages rather than the actual charges
w: Non-MiFID firms must disclose the nature and amount of remuneration clearly and in durable form before providing services.

n.0: Oral-only disclosure is not durable.
n.2: Post-contract small print is not adequate.
n.4: Actual charges, not averages, must be disclosed.
n.1: Disclosure cannot be deferred to year-end.

q: Which MiFID disclosure duty applies to packaged products with leverage?
o: Give only marketing language emphasising the growth potential
Explain how leverage works and its potential for amplified losses
Defer the explanation until after the first loss occurs
Promise that leverage boosts returns with no downside
Simply provide the packaged product's ISIN code
w: MiFID requires firms to explain clearly how leverage works and that it can magnify both gains and losses, including the risk of losing more than the initial investment.

n.4: An ISIN is not a leverage explanation.
n.3: Leverage has downside; no no-downside promise is valid.
n.0: Marketing language is not risk disclosure.
n.2: Explanation must precede, not follow, losses.

q: What does COBS 14.3 require regarding periodic reporting and pre-service disclosures?
o: Clients must be told in advance the form, content, and frequency of reports
No disclosure of the reporting arrangements is required
Reports may be withheld whenever the client seems satisfied
The frequency may be omitted when the client is professional
Reports may be sent at random intervals without any notice
w: COBS 14.3 links pre-service disclosure to client reporting; clients must know how, when and what information will be reported to them.

n.2: Reports cannot be withheld on satisfaction.
n.3: Frequency is disclosed for professionals too.
n.1: Reporting arrangements must be disclosed.
n.4: Random unnotified reporting is not permitted.

q: Under MiFID, how should firms explain currency risk in cross-border investments?
o: Omit currency risk entirely for professional clients
Assure the client that the currency risk is negligible
Highlight that exchange-rate moves can raise or lower returns and capital
State only that all returns are quoted in pounds sterling
Defer disclosure until the first exchange-rate move occurs
w: Firms must explain that exchange rates can materially affect returns and capital value so clients appreciate the risks of cross-border investments.

n.3: Quoting in sterling does not disclose the risk.
n.1: Currency risk is not negligible.
n.4: Disclosure precedes, not follows, FX movements.
n.0: Professionals are not exempt from this disclosure.

q: A Non-MiFID advisory firm earns commission that could sway its recommendations. Under COBS 6.1.4, what conflicts duty applies?
o: Inform clients of conflicts and remuneration structures that may create bias
Disclose conflicts only to retail clients, not professionals
Conflicts need not be disclosed where they appear minor
Disclose conflicts only if the FCA specifically requests it
Avoid disclosure wherever it might reduce the firm's sales
w: Non-MiFID firms must tell clients about conflicts and remuneration structures that could influence the service, supporting fair decision-making.

n.2: Even minor conflicts must be disclosed, not judged away.
n.1: Conflicts disclosure is not retail-only.
n.3: It is not contingent on an FCA request.
n.4: Sales impact is not a reason to withhold.

q: Which MiFID rule applies to providing information about safeguarding of client assets?
o: Disclose nothing about custody unless the client asks
Provide the details only after the first annual audit
Refer clients to generic FCA webpages instead of disclosing
Explain how assets are held, including custody arrangements and protections
State only that the assets are safe, without any detail
w: MiFID requires firms to give clients clear pre-service information on how their assets will be safeguarded, including custody arrangements and investor protections.

n.0: Custody must be disclosed proactively.
n.1: It cannot wait for the first audit.
n.4: A bare assurance is not adequate.
n.2: Generic webpages do not replace disclosure.

q: A financial planning firm doing Non-MiFID business is preparing a client agreement and asks its compliance officer what COBS 6.1 requires it to tell clients about commissions. What must be disclosed?
o: Only the commission rates that exceed five percent
Commissions disclosed only within the firm's periodic reports
The nature and the amount of commission the firm or associates receive
That commissions exist, but not their actual amount
Nothing at all where the commission is paid by third parties
w: Non-MiFID rules require firms to disclose clearly the nature and amount of commissions received in relation to the client service, in good time before provision.

n.3: The amount, not just existence, must be disclosed.
n.0: There is no five-percent threshold.
n.4: Third-party commissions must still be disclosed.
n.1: Disclosure comes before service, not only in reports.

q: When providing MiFID information electronically, what condition must be met?
o: Clients must consent and the format must allow durable storage and reproduction
Electronic provision always suffices with no conditions attached
The firm may alter the content without notifying the clients
Electronic delivery removes the need for accuracy
Provision is valid only once the client prints the file
w: Electronic delivery is valid if clients consent and the format allows them to store the information unchanged and reproduce it in the future.

n.1: Conditions of consent and durability apply.
n.2: Silent alteration is not permitted.
n.3: Accuracy is always required.
n.4: Validity does not depend on the client printing it.

q: An adviser is preparing an ex-ante cost illustration for a MiFID client. Which element must the disclosure show about the cumulative charges?
o: Only the performance fee, where one actually applies
The overall effect of the costs and charges on the investment return
Nothing at all where the charges are relatively small
A generic estimate that is not tied to the client
Only the firm's initial upfront fee for the service
w: MiFID requires ex-ante cost disclosures to show not just each charge but their overall cumulative effect on returns, so clients see total impact.

n.4: The initial fee alone is incomplete.
n.0: Performance fees alone are incomplete.
n.3: A generic estimate is not client-specific.
n.2: Small charges must still be disclosed.

q: What must Non-MiFID disclosures include about the firm itself under COBS 2.2?
o: Only the firm's registered trading name for the service
No details at all of the firm's authorisation status
A marketing strapline with no factual information
The firm's name, its regulatory status, and its contact details
Just the address of the firm's registered office
w: COBS 2.2 requires firms to provide clients with clear information on the firm’s identity, regulatory status, and contact details before services begin.

n.0: The trading name alone is insufficient.
n.4: The office address alone is insufficient.
n.1: Authorisation status must be given.
n.2: A strapline is not factual disclosure.

q: A client's structured product changes materially in the risks it carries partway through the relationship. Under MiFID, when must the firm update its risk disclosures?
o: When material changes arise in the nature of the service or investment
Only at the client's annual review meeting
Never, once the first disclosure has been provided
Only if the FCA writes to the firm about it
Only when the underlying product ceases trading
w: If the nature or risks of the service or investment change materially, firms must update disclosures so clients remain accurately informed.

n.2: Disclosures must be updated on material change.
n.3: It is not triggered by an FCA letter.
n.1: It is not limited to the annual review.
n.4: It is not limited to product delisting.

q: How should Non-MiFID firms explain product illiquidity pre-service?
o: Give the detail only after the client first has difficulty
State clearly that the client may be unable to sell or may face large costs
Avoid mentioning liquidity to encourage the client to invest
Say that liquidity risk applies only to retail clients
Describe liquidity only where the product is listed
w: Non-MiFID rules require fair disclosure of material risks, including illiquidity, so clients know they may not be able to sell easily or may face high exit costs.

n.2: Illiquidity must be disclosed, not hidden.
n.4: It is not limited to listed products.
n.0: Disclosure precedes, not follows, difficulty.
n.3: Liquidity risk is not retail-only.

q: Which MiFID rule applies to performance information in pre-service documents?
o: Performance information is banned under all circumstances
Past performance may be shown fairly, over five years, with clear warnings
Warnings may be omitted where the client is professional
The firm may guarantee that past performance will continue
Only the product's positive performance history should appear
w: MiFID permits past performance data if presented fairly, with appropriate context and warnings that it is not a reliable indicator of future results.

n.3: Past performance cannot be guaranteed to continue.
n.4: Selective positive-only history is misleading.
n.0: Performance data is permitted, not banned.
n.2: Warnings apply to professionals too.

q: Under Non-MiFID COBS 14.3, how must periodic statement obligations be framed at outset?
o: Provide only the client's cash balance in each report
Defer any explanation until after the first year
Send the reports solely when the client demands them
No disclosure is needed; the reports can simply be ad hoc
Disclose upfront how often statements are issued and what they cover
w: Non-MiFID firms must tell clients before service what form, frequency, and content of reports they will receive, aligning expectations with later delivery.

n.3: Upfront disclosure is required, not ad hoc reporting.
n.0: A cash balance alone is inadequate.
n.2: Reporting is not purely on-demand.
n.1: Explanation cannot be deferred a year.

q: How should firms explain counterparty risk in derivative products pre-service?
o: Say default risk applies only in rare crises and can be ignored
Avoid discussing counterparty failure to reduce the client's concern
Explain default risk only after a counterparty has failed
State only that the relevant market is well regulated
Clarify that the client could suffer loss if the counterparty defaults
w: Pre-service disclosures should explain counterparty risk clearly so clients understand they may lose value if the contracting party fails to meet obligations.

n.1: Counterparty risk must be disclosed, not hidden.
n.3: Market regulation does not remove counterparty risk.
n.0: Default risk cannot be dismissed as ignorable.
n.2: Disclosure precedes, not follows, a default.

q: A MiFID wealth manager is onboarding a client for a discretionary portfolio service. What must the firm disclose to the client before it begins providing that service?
o: A forecast of guaranteed returns on the portfolio
The types of financial instruments involved and the associated risks
That any losses on the portfolio will be covered by the firm
Only a brief marketing statement about the service
Only the address of the appointed custodian for the account
w: COBS 6.1ZA requires firms offering discretionary management to provide detailed information about the types of financial instruments, strategies, and risks before providing the service.

n.4: The custodian address alone is insufficient.
n.0: Guaranteed returns cannot be forecast.
n.2: Firms do not cover client losses.
n.3: A marketing statement is not adequate disclosure.

q: A brokerage offers an execution-only dealing service where clients place their own orders online. Which MiFID disclosure duty still applies to the firm?
o: Disclose everything only after the trade has been confirmed
Disclose only the name of the product being traded

n.1: All costs and charges must be covered, not just a headline rate.

q: What duty applies to MiFID firms when providing information about financial instruments offered on an execution-only basis?

n.1: Disclosure comes before, not after, settlement.
n.0: A product name alone is insufficient.

Solely to protect the firm itself from potential liability to the client

q: A MiFID firm offers both discretionary management and execution-only services and is drafting its onboarding pack. Which statement best describes its pre-service disclosure duty across both service types?

n.4: Professional clients still require relevant pre-service information.
n.0: Durable-medium disclosure is not limited to retail clients.

q: A MiFID portfolio manager plans to outsource part of a client's mandate to a third party. What must it disclose to the client about this delegation?

That appropriateness applies only where the client is retail
That no appropriateness or suitability assessment is carried out

q: Which MiFID disclosure must firms provide regarding investment strategies in portfolio management?

Only the target return percentage for the portfolio
Information on the strategies used, the risks, and the instrument types
That strategies may be changed without informing the client
No disclosure of strategy is needed before service

q: A firm conducting non-MiFID business receives commission from a product provider for placing client business. Under COBS 6.1.6, how must the firm disclose this remuneration to the client?

q: What must firms explain to clients about custody of assets in managed accounts under MiFID?

The custody arrangements only once the client has made a complaint
Only a general assurance to the client that the assets are safe
w: MiFID requires firms to disclose custody arrangements, including who holds the assets, risks of third-party custody, and protections in place before service.

n.1: Disclosure is not limited to overseas custodians.
n.3: Disclosure is proactive, not triggered by a complaint.

Warn the client that appropriateness must be assessed before the trade

That the firm's head office is located in central London
That the firm is authorised and regulated by the FCA or relevant authority

n.1: Longevity is not the required disclosure.
n.3: Location is not the required disclosure.

n.1: Disclosure is not deferred to a quarterly report.

q: What must execution-only clients be told about the firm’s responsibility under MiFID?

That execution-only applies only to derivative products
That execution-only removes all of the client's protections

That the portfolio's performance will always exceed the benchmark

n.4: Custody arrangements do affect client risk.

n.1: Inducements are disclosed regardless of category.
n.0: Disclosure is ex-ante, not year-end.

That disclosing service limitations is entirely optional

n.2: Limitations are not retail-only.
n.3: Disclosure is required, not optional.

Explain the reporting arrangements only to clients categorised as retail

How designated investments are held, including custody and protections

n.1: Safeguarding disclosure is not retail-only.

n.2: Arrangements must be disclosed.

That clients are personally liable for other clients' debts

That the assets are guaranteed by the local overseas regulator

n.0: Protections can differ overseas.

That the disclosure is required only for retail clients

n.4: Clients must be informed.
n.2: Disclosure is not retail-only.

q: A firm holds some client money in an account that is not segregated from its own funds. Why must it explain the risk of non-segregated accounts to clients?

n.2: The risk is loss on insolvency, not any difference in interest paid
n.1: FSCS cover can still apply; the point is loss of assets on firm failure
n.4: There is no daily FCA reporting rule for non-segregated balances

q: What must MiFID firms disclose about investor compensation schemes when safeguarding assets?

That compensation cover exists only for deposits, never investments
Whether clients are covered by a compensation scheme and its scope of protection

n.1: Firms do not personally guarantee shortfalls; a scheme pays out
n.0: There is no seven-day deadline for compensation-scheme claims

q: Under Non-MiFID COBS 6.1.7, what should firms tell clients about holding money in a client bank account?

That all client money is at all times fully guaranteed by the FCA
That client money may be mixed with the firm's own funds without any risk
That client money is held in a designated client bank account, segregated from firm money

n.0: Segregation applies to client money generally, not only retail.
n.1: There is no small-sums disclosure exemption.
n.3: Client money must not be mixed with firm money.

Disclose that affiliated custodians are used and the related conflict risks

n.0: Assets need not be registered in a parent company's name
n.2: Disclosure applies to affiliated custodians whether UK-based or overseas

q: A broker intends to hold some client money with a bank based outside the UK. Why must clients be informed when their money is held with a credit institution overseas?

q: A firm is preparing product information to give clients before they invest, in line with COBS 4.2.1. What must the firm ensure about that information?
o: It complies only with the advertising-industry standards and nothing more
It is detailed enough to obscure the product's key risks
It has been pre-approved by the FCA before distribution
It highlights only the firm's own competitive advantages
It is sufficient for the client to make an informed investment decision
w: COBS 4.2.1 requires that information be adequate, fair, clear and not misleading, enabling clients to make informed investment decisions.

n.1: Information must reveal key risks, not obscure them
n.3: Information must be balanced, not just the firm's advantages
n.0: It must meet COBS standards, not advertising standards only
n.2: The FCA does not pre-approve promotions before distribution

q: A marketing team is drafting a promotion aimed at MiFID retail clients. Under COBS 4.5A.3, which additional requirement applies to that communication?
o: MiFID clients are exempt from financial promotion rules
Risk and reward must be disclosed in equal prominence
Promotions can omit charges for simplicity
Past performance can be cherry-picked
Only rewards must be highlighted
w: COBS 4.5A.3 requires that retail client communications under MiFID show risks and rewards with equal prominence to prevent bias.

n.4: Rewards cannot be highlighted without equal risk disclosure.
n.3: Cherry-picking would mislead; full context is required.
n.0: MiFID clients are covered by stricter rules, not exemptions.
n.2: Charges must be disclosed to ensure transparency.

q: What does 'clear' mean within the FCA’s requirement for client communications?
o: The communication uses simple, comprehensible language
The firm provides only numerical data without explanation
The content is aimed solely at expert audiences
The communication can be lengthy and complex if accurate
The firm removes all references to risk
w: Clarity means information must be understandable to the intended audience, avoiding jargon or complexity that obscures meaning.

n.4: Risks must be disclosed clearly, not omitted.
n.2: Communications must be clear to the actual audience, not just experts.
n.3: Excessive length or complexity undermines clarity.
n.1: Data must be explained to ensure clients understand it.

q: When a financial promotion includes tax advantages, what must also be made clear?
o: That every investor will receive an identical tax benefit in all cases
That tax treatment depends on each client's individual circumstances
That the stated tax advantages are guaranteed by the FCA
That the tax rules are permanent and will never change
That the tax benefits apply only to institutional clients
w: Promotions must state that tax treatment depends on individual circumstances and may change in the future, ensuring clients are not misled.

n.0: Tax outcomes vary by individual; they are not identical for all
n.2: The FCA does not guarantee any tax advantage
n.3: Tax rules can change; they are not permanent
n.4: Tax treatment is not confined to institutional clients

q: A firm carrying on Non-MiFID business is drafting a promotion for a savings product under COBS 4.1. Which overarching principle must the promotion satisfy?
o: They must be communicated in a fair, clear and not misleading way
They must first be approved by HM Treasury before they may be used
They may highlight only the positive aspects of the product
They may exclude retail clients from their scope entirely
They must guarantee the product's future performance
w: COBS 4.1 applies the same overarching principle of fairness, clarity and accuracy to Non-MiFID promotions, ensuring client protection across business types.

n.1: HM Treasury does not approve individual financial promotions
n.2: Promotions must be balanced, not just the positive aspects
n.3: Non-MiFID promotion rules do apply to retail clients
n.4: Promotions must not guarantee future performance

q: A marketing team at a retail investment firm is drafting a promotion aimed at first-time investors. When the compliance officer reviews it, which of the following would she flag as prohibited under FCA rules on communicating with clients?
o: Including relevant benchmarks to allow a comparison
Providing risk disclosures alongside the stated benefits
Translating the material into plain, accessible language
Stating that the tax treatment may change in the future
Using jargon that confuses the promotion's likely audience
w: Jargon or technical terms that confuse or mislead the intended audience are prohibited as they breach the clarity requirement.

n.1: Showing risks alongside benefits is required, not prohibited
n.2: Using plain language is encouraged, not prohibited
n.0: Including relevant benchmarks is permitted, not prohibited
n.3: Noting that tax rules may change is required, not prohibited

q: Which element must be included when disclosing costs and charges in a financial promotion?
o: Only the initial charge applying to the product
All costs and charges, in both aggregated and itemised form
Only a vague reference to the possibility of some future fees
Only any performance-based fees that may apply
Only a disclaimer stating that the costs are uncertain
w: The FCA requires disclosure of all costs and charges, presented clearly and in detail, so clients can understand the full impact on their investment.

n.0: All costs must be shown, not the initial charge alone
n.2: Costs must be specific, not a vague reference to possible fees
n.3: All costs must be disclosed, not only performance fees
n.4: A disclaimer of uncertainty does not satisfy the disclosure duty

q: According to COBS, what is the main purpose of requiring financial promotions to be fair, clear and not misleading?
o: To reduce the length of promotional documents
To protect clients by allowing informed decisions
To increase competition between firms
To comply only with advertising industry codes
To ensure firms maximise sales of financial products
w: The purpose of this rule is to protect clients, particularly retail clients, by ensuring they receive information that enables them to make informed and balanced decisions about financial products or services.

n.4: Maximising sales is not the regulatory objective; client protection is.
n.3: The requirement is FCA-driven, not based only on advertising codes.
n.2: While competition may result, the rule’s aim is consumer protection.
n.0: Length reduction is not relevant; clarity and fairness are.

q: Under COBS, when is it acceptable to omit material information in client communications?
o: When the firm assumes the client already knows the risks
Where the FCA has first given the firm its verbal consent to omit it
When including it might confuse the client
When it is genuinely not relevant to the product or service offered
When leaving it out makes the promotion more appealing
w: Material information can only be omitted if it is genuinely irrelevant to the product or service being described. Otherwise, omission would mislead the client and breach FCA rules.

n.2: Potential confusion does not justify omitting material information
n.0: A firm cannot assume client knowledge to omit material risks
n.4: Omitting information to boost appeal is misleading and prohibited
n.1: The FCA does not give verbal consent to omit material information

q: When firms use comparisons in financial promotions, what must they ensure?
o: That the comparison is fair, meaningful and presented in a balanced way
That no benchmarks are included within the comparison
That only the product's most positive features are put into the comparison
That the comparison rests on future projections alone
That competitor firms are never actually named
w: Any comparisons must be accurate, fair and balanced, enabling the client to make a meaningful evaluation without being misled.

n.2: Comparisons must be balanced, not confined to positive features
n.3: Comparisons must not rest solely on future projections
n.1: Meaningful comparison may require relevant benchmarks
n.4: There is no rule that competitors must never be named

q: Which disclosure is mandatory when including simulated past performance in client communications?
o: That risks are not applicable to hypothetical data
That the FCA has endorsed the figures
That the figures are hypothetical and based on assumptions
That the projections are guaranteed
That simulated performance is equivalent to actual performance
w: Simulated past performance must be clearly identified as hypothetical, with explanation of the assumptions used, so clients do not confuse it with real results.

n.4: Equating simulated and actual performance would mislead clients.
n.3: Guarantees cannot be made on hypothetical data.
n.1: The FCA does not endorse figures within promotions.
n.0: Risks still apply; assumptions may not hold true.

q: Under COBS rules, what must a firm ensure about risk warnings in financial promotions?
o: They appear in small print at the end of the document
They are prominent and in the same language as the promotion
They may be replaced with a single generic standard disclaimer
They may be omitted where the client is sophisticated
They may be provided to the client only by verbal means
w: Risk warnings must be clear, prominent, and in the same language as the promotion to ensure clients properly understand the risks involved.

n.0: Risk warnings must be prominent, not buried in small print
n.3: Risk warnings cannot be dropped for sophisticated clients
n.2: A generic disclaimer does not replace a specific risk warning
n.4: A verbal-only warning does not meet the prominence requirement

q: A firm's promotion displays a fund's gross performance figures. What additional disclosure must accompany those figures?
o: That clients will definitely achieve even higher returns
That charges and commissions will reduce the actual return
That tax is irrelevant to the performance outcome
That the figures shown are guaranteed by the FCA
That gross performance is superior to net performance
w: Where gross performance is shown, firms must disclose that charges, commissions and fees will reduce actual returns, ensuring clients are not misled about outcomes.

n.3: The FCA does not guarantee any performance figures
n.0: Gross figures do not promise higher returns; charges reduce them
n.4: Gross is not superior; net performance is what clients receive
n.2: Tax can affect the outcome and is not irrelevant

q: In relation to COBS 4.5, what applies when firms communicate with retail clients about MiFID products?
o: Charges may be left out where they are hard to calculate
MiFID retail clients fall outside the promotion standards
They must be fair, clear, not misleading, and show risks and benefits equally
Benefits may be given greater prominence than the risks
Firms may play down the product's risks wherever they are also giving advice
w: COBS 4.5 requires that MiFID retail promotions be balanced, presenting risks and benefits with equal prominence to safeguard clients from bias.

n.4: Giving advice does not permit downplaying risks
n.3: Risks and benefits must have equal prominence
n.1: MiFID retail clients are covered by the promotion standards
n.0: Difficulty of calculation does not excuse omitting charges

q: Which of the following statements about financial promotions is TRUE under FCA rules?
o: They must be accurate and not create false impressions
They can imply FCA endorsement if authorised
They can ignore likely audience sophistication
They are only regulated if issued in print form
They must always be drafted in technical legal language
w: Promotions must be accurate, balanced and not misleading in any format, including online, to ensure clients are not given false impressions.

n.4: Technical legal language is not required; clarity is.
n.2: Communications must match the sophistication of the target audience.
n.3: The rules apply across all media, not just print.
n.1: Implying FCA endorsement is prohibited.

q: A marketing team wants to include projected returns in a promotion for a structured product. When using such forecasts in a financial promotion, what is required?
o: They must rest on reasonable assumptions and be disclosed as estimates
They may be shown without any accompanying risk warning
They are prohibited in every set of circumstances
They may be freely exaggerated in order to attract more client interest
They must imply that the future outcomes are guaranteed
w: Forecasts may be used if based on reasonable assumptions and accompanied by prominent disclosure that they are estimates and subject to risks.

n.3: Forecasts must be reasonable and honest, not exaggerated
n.1: Forecasts require prominent risk warnings
n.4: Forecasts must not imply guaranteed outcomes
n.2: Forecasts are permitted if properly based and disclosed

q: A marketing team is drafting a financial promotion for a structured product. Under FCA rules, which of the following must be avoided?
o: Using relevant benchmarks for a meaningful comparison
Giving a balanced presentation of risks and rewards
Stating that the tax rules may change in the future
Disclosing the product's fees and charges clearly
Using misleading titles or names that disguise the risk
w: Misleading titles, names or labels that disguise the true risk or nature of the product must be avoided, as they breach the requirement for fair, clear and not misleading communication.

n.1: Balanced presentation is required, not something to avoid
n.3: Clear disclosure of charges is required, not to be avoided
n.0: Using relevant benchmarks is permitted, not prohibited
n.2: Warning that tax rules may change is required, not prohibited

q: A marketing team wants to include a fund's past performance figures in a promotion. Which requirement must the promotion satisfy when showing that comparison?
o: Past results may be implied to guarantee future outcomes
The figures may be shown without any benchmark reference
Figures must cover at least the previous five years, where available
The figures may be limited to two favourable months
Only the very best-performing individual years need ever be selected
w: Where past performance is shown, it must cover at least five years if available, presented in a balanced manner with clear warnings that it is not a guide to the future.

n.4: Best-year cherry-picking breaches the balanced-presentation rule
n.3: Two favourable months is not acceptable; five years applies
n.0: Past performance must never be implied to guarantee the future
n.1: A relevant benchmark should be shown, not omitted

q: A firm is drafting a communication to retail clients about the costs of its products. Under FCA rules, what is the primary requirement for disclosing charges?
o: Charges may be omitted where they are complex to explain
Only the product's initial charge needs to be disclosed
Charges must be disclosed in a clear, itemised and aggregate form
Charge disclosure is optional where advice is provided
Charges may simply be described as being the usual industry standard
w: Charges must be transparent, shown in both aggregated and itemised form, to ensure retail clients fully understand the costs of products and services.

n.1: All charges must be disclosed, not the initial charge alone
n.4: A vague industry-standard label is not adequate disclosure
n.0: Complexity does not excuse omitting charges
n.3: Charge disclosure is not optional when advice is given

q: A firm is designing a promotion aimed specifically at experienced professional investors. What must the firm ensure about the communication for that audience segment?
o: That the communication suits the likely knowledge of that audience
That it implies the FCA endorses the promotion's content
That it focuses solely on the product's advantages
That it leaves out risk information for the sake of simplicity
That it uses complex terminology to impress the clients
w: Firms must tailor promotions so they are clear, fair and not misleading to the likely audience, taking account of their knowledge and experience.

n.4: Complex terminology that confuses the audience is prohibited
n.3: Risk information must be kept, not dropped for simplicity
n.2: Communications must be balanced, not solely advantages
n.1: Implying FCA endorsement is misleading and prohibited

q: Which requirement applies when quoting gross yield figures in promotions?
o: They may be presented instead of the net yield figure
They may leave out the product's tax implications
They may be shown without any explanation wherever they are positive
They may be presented to clients as guaranteed outcomes
They must carry a disclosure that charges reduce the actual return
w: Gross yield figures must be accompanied by a clear explanation that fees, charges and tax will reduce actual returns, ensuring transparency.

n.2: A positive figure still needs the charges-reduce-return disclosure
n.0: Net yield should also be shown; gross does not replace it
n.1: Tax implications should be noted, not omitted
n.3: Yield figures must not be presented as guaranteed

q: A firm is drafting a non-MiFID financial promotion under COBS 4.2 and must decide how to present the risks. How should risk information be treated?
o: Provide only generic disclaimers
Provide risks with equal prominence to benefits
Disclose risks separately in a different document
Omit risks if the product is simple
Only disclose risks if requested by the client
w: COBS 4.2 requires that risk disclosures be clear, specific and given the same prominence as benefits, preventing biased or misleading impressions.

n.4: Risks must always be disclosed, not just when requested.
n.3: Even simple products require risk disclosures.
n.2: Risks must appear within the same communication, not elsewhere.
n.0: Generic disclaimers are insufficient; specific risks must be stated.

q: A firm is presenting projected investment returns in a client brochure. Which of the following is a requirement under COBS for the presentation of those returns?
o: Returns may be based only on selective favourable periods
Returns may be presented completely in isolation from any risk information
Returns may be quoted without disclosing the related fees
Returns must not be shown as guaranteed unless they are genuinely risk-free
Firms may emphasise only the best-case return scenarios
w: COBS rules prevent returns being described as guaranteed unless they are genuinely risk-free. All claims must be fair, balanced and supported by risk disclosures.

n.4: Emphasising only best-case scenarios is unbalanced and misleading
n.2: Fees must be disclosed alongside quoted returns
n.1: Returns must be shown with the relevant risk information
n.0: Selective favourable periods misrepresent performance

q: Under FCA COBS rules, when is it acceptable to present forecasts in absolute monetary terms?
o: When they rest on reasonable assumptions and include risk disclosures
When no basis for the calculation is given to the client
When the FCA authorises the forecast case by case
When the tax treatment is excluded from the figures
Whenever the firm wishes to emphasise the product's growth potential
w: Forecasts may be shown in monetary terms if they are based on reasonable assumptions, explained clearly, and accompanied by disclosures about risks and uncertainties.

n.4: A desire to emphasise growth is not a proper basis for a forecast
n.1: A stated, reasonable basis is required for any forecast
n.3: Relevant tax treatment should not be excluded
n.2: The FCA does not authorise individual forecasts case by case

q: A marketing team is drafting a promotion aimed at retail clients for both MiFID and non-MiFID products. Which principle underpins all such financial promotions under COBS?
o: They must guarantee the client's tax advantages
They must be fair, clear and not misleading
They must exclude all performance information
They must be designed to maximise the firm's product sales
They must be drafted in formal legal language
w: The overarching principle is that all communications and promotions must be fair, clear and not misleading, regardless of product type or business classification.

n.3: The aim is fair communication, not maximising sales
n.0: Promotions must not guarantee tax advantages
n.2: Performance information is not required to be excluded
n.4: Plain, understandable language is expected, not legal jargon

q: Which of the following is a breach of FCA requirements for retail promotions?
o: Giving balanced prominence to risks and benefits
Disclosing the product's charges in clear terms
Making exaggerated claims about the potential returns
Including a warning that the tax rules may change
Using plain language to explain the product features
w: Exaggerated claims about returns create misleading impressions and are prohibited under the 'fair, clear and not misleading' standard.

n.0: Balanced presentation complies with the rules; it is not a breach
n.1: Clear disclosure of charges is compliant, not a breach
n.3: Warning that tax rules may change is compliant, not a breach
n.4: Using plain language is good practice, not a breach

q: What does ‘fair’ mean in the context of FCA client communications?
o: That the communication gives a balanced view of benefits and risks
That the firm may omit charges where they are small
That the firm shows only the most positive scenarios
That the communication favours the most profitable clients
That the firm prioritises making its sales over being fully accurate
w: Fairness means presenting a balanced view of the product or service, showing both risks and rewards, enabling clients to make properly informed decisions.

n.4: Fairness means accuracy over sales, not the reverse
n.3: Fairness is not about favouring profitable clients
n.1: Charges cannot be omitted simply because they are small
n.2: Showing only positive scenarios is unbalanced, not fair

q: A firm is checking a draft promotion that describes an investment as safe. Which statement about financial promotions under FCA rules is TRUE?
o: They may rely on a disclaimer alone to offset a misleading claim
They may exclude charges that are difficult to calculate
They need be clear only where aimed at professional clients
They must not imply a product is risk-free unless it genuinely is
They may guarantee investment returns to retail clients
w: Promotions must never suggest that products are risk-free unless that is factually correct, and all risks must be disclosed clearly.

n.4: Promotions must not guarantee returns to retail clients
n.1: Difficulty of calculation does not excuse omitting charges
n.0: A disclaimer cannot cure an otherwise misleading promotion
n.2: Clarity is required for all clients, not professionals only

q: A marketing team wants an EIS promotion to highlight the tax reliefs available to investors, and compliance reviews the required wording. What is required when financial promotions include statements about future tax treatment?
o: A warning that tax treatment depends on circumstances and may change
A statement that all clients will benefit equally from the tax reliefs
A statement that tax is irrelevant to investment outcomes
A statement that the tax advantages are FCA-guaranteed
An assurance that the tax position will stay constant
w: Promotions must state that tax treatment depends on the investor’s personal circumstances and is subject to change, ensuring clients are not misled.

n.4: Tax rules can change; no assurance of constancy can be given
n.1: Tax benefits vary by individual, not equal for all clients
n.3: The FCA does not guarantee tax advantages
n.2: Tax can affect outcomes and is not irrelevant

q: What does 'not misleading' mean in the context of FCA communications?
o: That only professional clients receive this protection
That figures may be exaggerated if explained in small print
That communications must not create a false or distorted impression
That firms may stress positives without mentioning the risks
That disclaimers on their own are enough to protect against liability
w: Not misleading means the communication must not give a false or distorted impression, whether by omission, exaggeration or selective presentation.

n.3: Risks must be mentioned, not omitted while stressing positives
n.4: Disclaimers alone do not cure a misleading communication
n.1: Exaggerated figures are not saved by small-print explanation
n.0: The protection applies to all clients, not professionals only

q: Which of the following would breach COBS rules on financial promotions?
o: Warning the client that the tax rules may change
Giving equal prominence to both the risks and the benefits
Including a clear disclosure of the product's charges
Cherry-picking favourable time periods for performance data
Using plain language to explain the product features
w: Selecting only favourable time periods for performance data misleads clients and breaches the fair, clear and not misleading requirement.

n.1: Equal prominence of risks and benefits complies with the rules
n.2: Clear disclosure of charges is compliant, not a breach
n.0: Warning that tax rules may change is compliant, not a breach
n.4: Using plain language is good practice, not a breach

q: A compliance officer is reviewing the fee schedule an adviser plans to give a retail client. In what format must the firm present the costs and charges disclosure?
o: Charges disclosure is optional in Non-MiFID business
Only variable costs
Only initial costs
Both aggregated and itemised, presented clearly
Only aggregated totals
w: Firms must disclose costs in both aggregate and itemised form so clients have a full and transparent understanding of the product’s costs.

n.4: Aggregates alone lack necessary detail.
n.2: Initial costs are not sufficient disclosure.
n.1: All costs, not just variable, must be disclosed.
n.0: Non-MiFID promotions are also subject to clear disclosure requirements.

q: A firm is preparing to send key information to a client ahead of them signing an investment agreement. Under COBS, what must the firm ensure about the timing of this communication?
o: That information is sent only after the client signs the agreement
That the communications are provided only in cases where the client requests them
That information is given in good time before the client is bound by a contract
That the FCA sets the communication timing for each product
That timing does not matter provided the information is accurate
w: Firms must provide information in good time before the client is bound by an agreement, giving them adequate opportunity to consider the details.

n.0: Information must come before the client is bound, not after signing
n.4: Timing does matter; it must be in good time beforehand
n.1: Information must be provided proactively, not only on request
n.3: The firm, not the FCA, must ensure timely disclosure

q: Which of the following is prohibited when producing communications for retail clients?
o: Disclosing that the tax rules may change in future
Including balanced risk disclosures in the material
Warning the client that forecasts are only estimates
Using exaggerated terms such as 'guaranteed riches'
Providing comparisons against relevant benchmarks
w: Exaggerated, misleading claims such as ‘guaranteed riches’ breach the fair, clear and not misleading requirement of COBS rules.

n.1: Balanced risk disclosure is required, not prohibited
n.4: Comparison with relevant benchmarks is permitted
n.2: Warning that forecasts are estimates is required, not prohibited
n.0: Disclosing that tax rules may change is required, not prohibited

q: What must be included when presenting performance information to retail clients?
o: A guarantee that the future returns will match the past performance results
A clear statement that past performance is no reliable guide to the future
Performance figures presented with the charges excluded
Only the top-performing years of the performance data
Performance data limited to a single favourable quarter
w: Any inclusion of past performance must carry the clear warning that it is not a reliable indicator of future results, ensuring clients are not misled.

n.0: Past performance must never be presented as a guarantee of the future
n.3: Selecting only top years breaches the balanced-presentation rule
n.2: Performance must reflect charges, not exclude them
n.4: A single favourable quarter misrepresents performance

q: A compliance officer is briefing advisers on a communication standard that holds regardless of whether the business is MiFID or non-MiFID. Which rule applies equally to both?
o: Only the product's benefits need to be disclosed to clients
Client understanding of the material is entirely optional
All communications must be fair, clear and not misleading
Promotions may rely on a disclaimer on its own
Communications may guarantee the client's future returns
w: The central principle of fairness, clarity and non-misleading communication applies to all FCA-regulated business, whether MiFID or Non-MiFID.

n.0: Risks as well as benefits must be disclosed
n.4: Communications must not guarantee returns
n.1: Communications must be understandable, not optionally so
n.3: Disclaimers alone cannot cure a misleading promotion

q: Which of the following BEST describes the FCA’s aim with communication rules under COBS?
o: To ensure clients receive balanced, comprehensible and accurate information
To let firms omit the risks where it is convenient
To restrict all of the firm's communications to professional clients only
To align with general advertising-industry practice
To maximise the firm's overall level of profitability
w: The FCA’s objective is to protect consumers by ensuring communications give a balanced, clear and accurate picture of financial products and services.

n.4: The aim is client protection, not maximising firm profit
n.1: The rules do not let firms omit risks for convenience
n.3: The aim is consumer protection, beyond advertising practice
n.2: The rules protect all clients, not professionals only

q: A marketing team is drafting a promotional brochure for a new investment product and asks compliance about the rules that apply. What is the primary purpose of the FCA financial promotion rules under COBS 4.1?
o: To guarantee the future performance of the product
To align the firm only with the general advertising-industry standards
To promote the firm's own overall profitability
To remove the need to disclose the product's risks
To ensure clients receive fair, clear and not misleading information
w: The financial promotion rules exist to ensure all communications are fair, clear and not misleading so that clients can make informed decisions about financial products and services.

n.0: The rules do not guarantee product performance
n.2: The purpose is client protection, not firm profit
n.3: Risk disclosure is required, not removed
n.1: The rules go beyond advertising-industry standards

q: Which FCA Principle for Businesses is directly reinforced by the financial promotion rules?
o: Principle 3: Management and control
Principle 1: Integrity
Principle 8: Conflicts of interest
Principle 6: Treating customers fairly
Principle 10: Clients' assets
w: The rules support Principle 6, which requires firms to treat customers fairly, by ensuring they receive balanced and understandable information about products and services.

n.1: Principle 1 concerns integrity, not fair treatment of customers
n.0: Principle 3 covers management and control, not customer fairness
n.2: Principle 8 addresses conflicts of interest, not customer fairness
n.4: Principle 10 concerns client assets, not customer fairness

q: A marketing manager drafting a product promotion is reminded of Principle 7. How does that Principle relate to the financial promotion rules?
o: It lets firms prioritise the benefits over the risks
It exempts digital promotions from any regulation
It applies only to investment products, and never to related services
It requires that all communications are fair, clear and not misleading
It applies only to the firm's professional clients
w: Principle 7 underlines that all client communications must be fair, clear and not misleading, which forms the foundation of the COBS 4.1 financial promotion rules.

n.0: Principle 7 requires balance, not prioritising benefits over risks
n.4: Principle 7 applies to all clients, not professionals only
n.1: Digital promotions are not exempt from the rules
n.2: The principle covers services as well as products

q: Which of the following BEST describes the application of the financial promotion rules under COBS 4.1?
o: They apply only to advice, and not to any promotions
They apply only where the FCA pre-approves the material
They apply only to the firm's printed promotional material and adverts
They apply only where the client requests them
They apply to all forms of client communication, whatever the medium
w: COBS 4.1 applies to all communications with clients, including digital, verbal and printed, ensuring consistent consumer protection across mediums.

n.2: The rules cover all media, not printed material alone
n.0: The rules cover promotions as well as advice
n.1: The FCA does not pre-approve promotions as a condition
n.3: The rules apply generally, not only on client request

q: What do the financial promotion rules primarily seek to prevent?
o: The disclosure of the product's charges and fees
The use of plain language within any advertising
Firms from being able to make any profit at all
Clients from accessing benchmark comparisons
Clients being misled into unsuitable investments
w: The rules aim to stop clients being misled into inappropriate or unsuitable investments through unclear, biased or incomplete communications.

n.2: The rules do not aim to stop firms making a profit
n.1: Plain language is encouraged, not something to prevent
n.3: Benchmark comparisons help clients; they are not prevented
n.0: Charge disclosure is required, not something to prevent

q: Why is the relationship between financial promotion rules and Principle 6 important?
o: It lets firms omit risk information where it is positive
It limits the rules to the firm's professional clients only
It ensures clients are treated fairly through transparent communication
It guarantees that the firm will achieve a higher overall level of sales
It removes the firm's duty to disclose its charges
w: Principle 6 requires firms to treat customers fairly, and financial promotion rules ensure this by mandating balanced, transparent and fair information in communications.

n.3: The link concerns fair treatment, not higher sales
n.4: Charge disclosure duties remain; they are not removed
n.1: The rules protect all clients, not professionals only
n.0: Risk information cannot be omitted; balance is required

q: A reviewer is checking a promotion aimed at retail investors against Principle 7. Which of the following would be considered a breach in financial promotions?
o: Presenting both risks and rewards with equal prominence
Translating material into plain language for retail clients
Disclosing charges in itemised and aggregate form
Using technical jargon that confuses the intended audience
Providing clear warnings about tax treatment
w: Principle 7 requires communications to be clear and comprehensible; using jargon that confuses clients breaches this obligation.

n.4: Tax disclosures are appropriate and required.
n.2: Charges disclosure is compliant, not a breach.
n.0: Balanced risk-reward presentation is required under Principle 7.
n.1: Plain language supports clarity and compliance.

q: How do the financial promotion rules interact with the FCA’s consumer protection objective?
o: They require the FCA to pre-vet every promotion before it is issued
They shift responsibility for product risk entirely onto the client
They set a fixed cap on the returns a firm is allowed to advertise
They ensure clients get the information needed to make informed choices
They apply only to promotions aimed at professional investors
w: The financial promotion rules protect consumers by ensuring communications are fair, clear and not misleading, helping clients make properly informed decisions.

n.0: The FCA does not pre-approve or pre-vet firms' financial promotions.
n.1: Firms must explain risks; the rules do not transfer risk to clients.
n.4: The rules protect retail clients too, not only professionals.
n.2: There is no rule capping advertised returns; balance and fairness apply.

q: A marketing manager at an investment firm is drafting a fund promotion and wants to comply with Principle 6. Which approach best demonstrates that compliance?
o: Presenting only the headline benefits to grab the client's attention
Placing all material risk information within the terms and conditions
Disclosing all costs and charges to clients in a transparent way
Emphasising past gains as a reliable guide to future returns
Quoting gross returns and leaving charges for the client to work out
